<meta>Shelfmark: Barocci-187. Augm 2372. This page begins the primary text of the manuscript, following the introductory title pages. It establishes the biographical context for Plotinus's philosophical works.</meta>

<note>An ornamental horizontal headpiece featuring an interlaced knotwork or guilloche pattern in black ink.</note>

### ※ Porphyry on the life of Plotinus and the order of his books ※

---

Plotinus, the philosopher who lived in our time, seemed like one ashamed that he was in a body. From such a disposition, he could not bear to talk about his ancestry, his parents, or his homeland. Regarding a painter or sculptor, he so thoroughly disdained the idea of sitting for them—as he said to Amelius when he begged him to allow a likeness of him to be made—that he remarked: "Is it not enough to carry this image <note>Greek: "eidolon." In Neoplatonic thought, the physical body is seen as a mere shadow or reflection of the true, spiritual self.</note> which nature has placed around us, but must I also leave behind an image of an image <note>A reference to Plato’s critique of art as being two steps removed from reality.</note>, longer-lasting, as if it were one of those works worth seeing?" For this reason, he refused.

But since Carterius, the most excellent of such artists, was a friend and attended his lectures (for anyone who wished could attend), he gradually memorized Plotinus's features through constant observation. After this, painting the image from memory, and with Amelius helping to ensure the likeness was accurate, the portrait of Plotinus was painted without him ever knowing.

He also seemed to always have a sickly body. The colic pains in his stomach, which often occurred, made him refuse the use of enemas provided by doctors, saying that such treatment was not at all fitting for an elderly man. He also turned away from the use of medicines derived from wild animals <note>Greek: "theriou pharmakou." These were ancient medicinal preparations, often containing animal parts or viper flesh, thought to be potent remedies.</note>, saying he did not know what those derived from irrational animals would do to the human body; nor did he use public baths daily. However, using a daily rubbing with oil <note>Greek: "aleimmati." Massage with oil was a standard hygienic and medical practice in antiquity.</note> at home, he was not careless regarding his health.

It happened that the servants who rubbed him died from the plague <note>Likely a reference to the "Plague of Cyprian," a pandemic that afflicted the Roman Empire in the mid-3rd century AD.</note>, and because he did not neglect his own care even slightly, the disease gradually increased. While he was alive, no outward signs of the disease appeared. But after his servants died, the sores grew severe and the discharge increased, as his companion Eustochius said, who arrived to be with him. Eustochius, caring for him until the very end, remained present; as he said, Plotinus would not allow his other friends to approach him, so they would not be contaminated by his illness.

I, Porphyry, happened at that time to be living in Lilybaeum <note>Modern-day Marsala, Sicily. Porphyry had traveled there on Plotinus's advice to recover from a bout of depression.</note>. So I was not present at his death, nor was I neglecting his suffering. He happened to be living on the estate that belonged to Zethus, an old companion of his who had died, provided by his friends because of his physical weakness and the lack of basic needs in the countryside. When he was dying, as Eustochius said while caring for him, he did not smile <note>unclear: "εἴπατα" - likely a scribal error or variant for a word regarding his speech or expression</note>. Having arrived, Plotinus said to him: "I have been waiting for you," and "strive to bring the divine in us back to the divine in the universe." <note>This famous final statement summarizes Plotinus's philosophy: the return of the individual soul to the "One" or the Universal Divine.</note> And not much...

<note>A circular library stamp at the bottom center of the page, featuring the text "The Bodleian Library" <note>original Latin: "BIBLIOTHECA BODLEIANA"</note> encircling a central coat of arms or emblem.</note>

<summary>This page contains the opening of Porphyry’s biography of his teacher Plotinus, highlighting the philosopher's extreme asceticism, his refusal to have his portrait painted, and the beginning of the account of his final illness and death.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the editorial history of Plotinus’s works. While the previous page touched upon the broader context of manuscript transmission and medical cataloging, this page provides the specific bibliographic structure of the *Enneads* as organized by his student, Porphyry. It marks the transition from biographical anecdotes to the formal arrangement of the philosophical corpus.</meta>

This was done so as to be easily viewed at a glance. Delighting in maintaining the number nine, and because I happened to hit upon both a perfect number and these "groups of nine" <note>original: "ἐννεάσιν" (enneasin) — hence the title *Enneads*</note>, I have divided the fifty-four books into six groups of nine. Indeed, I distributed his entire treatise into six Enneads. In the **First Ennead**, I arranged the more ethical subjects, which are as follows:

1. On what is the Living Being and what is Man.
2. On Virtues.
3. On Happiness <note>original: "εὐδαιμονίας" (eudaimonias) — refers to human flourishing or the highest good.</note>.
4. Whether Happiness increases with the extension of time.
5. On the Beautiful.
7. On the First Good and other virtues. <note>The original text skips number 6 in this sequence.</note>
8. From where do Evils come.
9. On the Rational Exit <note>original: "εὐλόγου ἐξαγωγῆς" — a Stoic and Neoplatonic term for suicide.</note>.

This, then, is the first Ennead, containing ethical themes. We then arranged the **Second Ennead**, which contains physical matters; in it, we cataloged the things concerning the cosmos and what pertains to it. It contains the following:

1. On the World.
2. On Circular Motion.
3. On Fate.
4. On Generation.
5. On how the Stars act.
7. On Matter. <note>The original text skips number 6 in this sequence.</note>
8. On the fact that Acting is not Being.
9. Against the Gnostics.

The **Third Ennead**, also containing physical matters, we arranged to include the contemplations <note>original: "θεωρίας" (theorias) — refers to philosophical vision or study.</note> regarding the cosmos. It contains the following:

1. On the Descent into the Cosmos.
2. On Providence.
3. On Providence (second part).
4. On the Spirit <note>original: "δαίμονος" (daimonos) — a personal guardian or guiding spirit, not a "demon" in the modern sense.</note> that has fallen to our lot.
5. On Love.
7. On the fact that Causes are Incorporeal. <note>The original text skips number 6 in this sequence.</note>
8. On Contemplation and the Ascent to the One.
9. On the Contemplations regarding the Cosmos.

These three Enneads are thus arranged together in one volume. The **Fourth Ennead**, containing the contemplation regarding the **Soul**, holds the fourth place in order. It contains the following:

1. On the Contemplation of the Soul.
2. On the Essence of the Soul.
3. On the Difficulties <note>original: "ἀποριῶν" (aporiōn) — philosophical puzzles or "dead-ends" that require resolution.</note> of the Soul.
4. On the Difficulties of the Soul (second part).
5. On the Difficulties of the Soul (third part).
7. On the Immortality of the Soul. <note>The original text skips number 6 in this sequence.</note>
8. On the Descent of the Soul into Bodies.
9. On Sensation and Memory.

We then arranged the **Fifth Ennead**, containing in it the theorems regarding the **Mind** <note>original: "νοῦ" (nou) — often translated as Intellect or Divine Mind.</note>,

<column-break/>

where they are examined positively and do not come into being. This Ennead contains:

1. On the Three Primary Hypostases <note>original: "ὑποστάσεων" (hypostaseōn) — the fundamental levels of reality: The One, Mind, and Soul.</note>.
2. On the Generation of things after the First, and on the First.
3. On the Intellectual Hypostases, and that which is Beyond.
4. On the fact that the Intelligible objects are not outside the Mind.
5. On the fact that the Intelligible is not outside the Mind, and on the Good.
7. On the Ascent to the Intelligible realm. <note>The original text skips number 6 in this sequence.</note>
8. On the Genera of Being.
9. On how the Second comes from the First, and on the One.

These are the five Enneads. The **Sixth Ennead** contains the theorems regarding the **One**, as well as the genera of being, the Good, and the One. It contains the following:

1. On the Genera of Being (first part).
2. On the Genera of Being (second part).
3. On the Genera of Being (third part).
4. On the fact that Being is everywhere whole and one.
5. On the fact that Being is everywhere whole and one (second part).
7. On the Intellectual Hypostases. <note>The original text skips number 6 in this sequence.</note>
8. On the Good and the One.
9. On the Free Will and Volition of the One.
10. On the Good or the One.

<margin>
Ennead 1: Ethical matters
Ennead 2: Physical matters
Ennead 3: Physical matters
Ennead 4: Matters concerning the Soul
Ennead 5: Matters concerning the Mind
Ennead 6: Matters concerning the One
</margin>

In this manner, I divided the books of Plotinus, which are fifty-four in number, into six Enneads. I, Porphyry, have published the summaries <note>original: "ὑποθέσεις" (hypotheseis)</note> for them, and I have placed the headings <note>original: "κεφάλαια" (kephalaia) — table of contents or chapter titles.</note> of the discourses under them all, except for the one "On the Beautiful," because it was not at hand for us. Thus, in addition to the summaries and headings, one possesses not only the works of Plotinus but also the explanations of Porphyry concerning them.

<summary>This page details Porphyry's systematic organization of Plotinus's 54 treatises into six "Enneads" (groups of nine), categorized by theme: Ethics, Physics, Soul, Mind, and The One. Porphyry also notes his own editorial contributions, including summaries and chapter headings for the collection.</summary>

Of Plotinus, he did not cease. He used to send the children there, having learned of the place from the Emperor Gallienus. These temperate ones lived there; nor indeed did nature fail to make them **noble and good men** <note>original: "καλαὶ κἀγαθοί" — a classical Greek phrase denoting the ideal of a gentleman who is both beautiful in character and virtuous in action.</note>. He was first among those who were friendly and neighborly in their dealings, just as he was always present, even as if he were someone’s freedman. He lived for nearly a thousand <note>This likely refers to a long duration or a large number of people, as the OCR "χιλίους" (thousand) may be a transcription error for a specific time period or number of household members.</note> days with the children and the women. Yesterday, he mediated between the laws and the ancient customs for those of Plotinus; I lived as a savior to them, like a good father. At first, he lived with his companions, serving them without interruption. The will was sent clearly from the philosophers, for at the same time as those living with him were deciding what must be done, and the **colony** <note>This refers to "Platonopolis," a city in Campania that Plotinus unsuccessfully petitioned Emperor Gallienus to rebuild as a philosopher’s utopia governed by Plato’s laws.</note> was about to be revealed, they attempted to devise the remaining things for these ends. Such things occurred, bearing the name. When they learned what had been written, he corrected it. For he was destined to dispute over words. As for those things unknown by others, they were nonetheless remembered.

He sent the greater part by hand, which he wrote to his companions. He composed all these same things, or perhaps those of ten years, and he instructed those with him by voice—those wonderful men. He maintained the customs among them. He resolved the **Ideas** <note>technical vocabulary: "ἰδέας" — the Platonic Forms or eternal archetypes.</note> toward that which is equitable and unchangeable. Everything was worked out, pursuing that which was lacking. Just as in the beginning, with his own prophet leading the way, toward his old age 
<margin>*</margin> 
he released the causes; nor did he labor over the theorems in any other way. And just as with **Porphyry** <note>Plotinus’s student and biographer, the author of this text.</note>, he brings him saying this of himself in his books, and he calls Porphyry "purple-clad" <note>A play on the name Porphyry, which comes from the Greek word for purple ("porphura").</note>; or rather, he said, even Porphyry himself had been corrected by saying the things concerning her, if indeed the body became a child compared to the book. Being ambitious, he therefore explained it briefly. But he brought forward a certain small part in common, which he allowed. He wrote everything, bearing them in an **Ennead** <note>original: "ἐξάδα" — literally a group of six. Porphyry organized Plotinus's 54 treatises into six sets of nine, known as the "Enneads."</note>.

Whether of equal size or more. He took pride in the composition, because it contained natural philosophy and a **dogmatic monad** <term>the One</term> <note>The "Monad" or "The One" is the supreme, transcendent principle in Plotinus's philosophy, from which all existence emanates.</note>. These are the ancient things arranged according to order. After the Physics, there were the things deliberated and performed. He wrote to him, whenever we might say a theorem had been devised. After that, he taught gymnastics, or politics, or music; having explained these things himself, he never ceased. I love the arrangements, and I love the earth for you with patience. Because it was before, when there was time, or names, and of Gaius, or of a cause. And he would prepare the affairs of the politicians, taking care of the remaining things from the circumstances. For he said they were saving the things performed by them.

But that man, in the present while living, even loved the starting points of the **encyclical studies** <note>original: "ἐγκυκλίων" — the "circle" of general education or liberal arts required before studying philosophy.</note>. I decided, at any rate, to go to Sparta, but I cannot write clearly of the resignation. All these things are postponed for several months. Devoting himself to leisure, he appeared as a **scholar** <term>philologos</term> <note>original: "φιλολόγος" — literally a lover of words or a man of letters.</note> in his logic. But he seems a philosopher. As one having at that time the spiritual power to live entirely without summons, he laid every problem to rest. He says, being requested by others and not sparing those who labored, whenever it already appeared that concerning those things and after their reputation. Outside he says a few things, alas, suddenly.

Since he was eager to overturn enemies through the laws, and to perform the study for the sake of what comes after, he wished to show the education to be most equitable, which is according to nature. He raised himself up again. He thinks that he is philosophizing upon the **flow** <note>Possibly a reference to the Heraclitean "flux" or the emanation of being.</note>, so that his own might appear, and because a certain Diophanes <note>Diophanes was a rhetorician who argued that a student should be willing to do anything, even sexually, for a master to gain wisdom; Plotinus famously had Porphyry write a rebuttal.</note> was among those left behind; he made Euphrates one of the disciples. Wherefore, remaining his own life for the mixture, and being able to consecrate all of his thoughts, lest that which was handed down—or those who endure boldly—might be loved for their zeal. Taking care, with the most subtle discipline, he has caused Porphyry to write back. Before the correction, he made a book, through the first unambiguous one which he sent.

Having inquired, therefore, and having composed the things of those same shores with them. That which belongs to the nature of Plotinus’s slaves, and shining forth from a contemplation as pure as possible, he learns, so that a cause might be for them. Porphyry, the disciple of Plotinus, is diligent for his leader. He made a compilation. He recognized the ancient questions, so that everything might be an **encomium** <note>A speech or piece of writing that praises someone or something highly.</note> for Porphyry; so that, whenever some might say the things written are indisputable, the cause will appear to those after him; although, I might not be entirely blessed. As for the books, they range from arithmetic, <unclear>algebraic</unclear> <note>original: "ἀλγεβραϊκοῦ" — this is an anachronism in the transcription; it likely refers to "mathematical" or "rational" proportions in the original manuscript.</note>, and naturally the stars of astronomy, in which he is said in many places to bring angelic advancement. These same things happened, both those with him and those regarding the same, and thus he was moved to philosophize. Whether following an action or an error, he philosophizes through Plotinus. He knew that all the things inscribed would intoxicate those practicing natural theories with Porphyry. Take care from every side where these things are possible, about all of which you know. Not those things in error, but neither could the things that passed become the middle and that which remains. He who offered the books to them, wishing them to be listeners, and to write the book, enduring to be known by all.

# THE CULTIVATION OF THE SOUL

...how he might arrange these same things for us. This book, artfully constructed by him, he introduced to us; I have not read it at all among the common farmers, or not yet, nor indeed has it been completed in the final stage. The ease of his own training <note>original: "γυμνάσιον" — Referring to the school or the intellectual exercises of the philosopher.</note> has exceedingly departed—
<margin>uncompounded</margin>
—he says, he has moved toward a very thieving way concerning all education. The "georgic" book, however, was not falsely attributed. Before the education itself is distributed among those who are born because of it, they say to you: the King of these things is the **Purple Mountain** <note>original: "πορφυρὸν ὄρος" — A clever pun on the name of Porphyry (Porphyrios), Plotinus's editor, whose name means "Purple."</note>. It stands upon him; it has no leaf, but rather fruit. From there, he gave gift upon gift. The King possesses the beginningless words. Or rather, someone showed the change through a very <unclear>sixth</unclear> transformation. For let them not be among the negligent, or before the foundations of the building that the beautiful writers possess; you may understand that I am well-pleased. For he says that having given others of such kind, of which there are great reminders to the King. May this life rather belong to the "georgic" King. They say that Anthias <note>Possibly a proper name or a reference to a specific symbolic fish mentioned in ancient lore.</note> will fall well. But he himself seems—his evil cause having been dissolved—to have held nature toward the fields as if they were gifts. He says the unshorn training is good, because of what they call common clarity. It is clear that in education itself we have all things filled which come from good breeding. # THE LIFE AND WRITINGS OF THE DIVINE PLOTINUS

### Left Page

<margin>7</margin>
...one might wonder, who would not be grateful to leave such a reputation behind them? For that which was most fitting for this **divine man** <note>original: "δαιμονίῳ ἀνδρὶ" — In Neoplatonic terms, a "daimon" is a guiding spirit or a person whose soul has reached a semi-divine state of wisdom.</note>, and to a greater extent than one might imagine, extended among the pious. Indeed, it was not only his distinguished virtue, but that very kindness with which God is accustomed to favor a person, so that one might speak of it even after the life within the body. And so, even if death is sweet, yet it was fitting for him, as if one were to ask by reason: where is the joy of virtue? Above all, it is that which is unsearched. He used to say that even the childish games of the **messenger** <note>original: "ἀγγέλου" — while often "angel," in this philosophical context it likely refers to a divine messenger or intermediary spirit.</note> strike us; a man truly resembles these things, but through careful attention, he avoids the misery of those still bound to common life. He also added this: that he does not happen upon this fame for himself, nor even for the sake of his own happiness, as one might say. Thus, even after death, the gods and divine spirits might show such wonderful love for him, as to long for the gathering of his written books. And there is hope that he, because of his pious way of life—which he himself says is "white"—is now among the gods. The things concerning his life, then, are made manifest by his books. During his life, most things seemed to him not to be counted by number, as if they were contrary to the scriptures, or as if they were encountered along the way. His writings might have been somewhat less than what was expected, but only because his essence was not contained within them. These things, then, pertain to his virtue, his **contemplation** <note>original: "θεωρίας" — the philosophical act of seeing or perceiving divine truths.</note>, and his discourses—the fruits of his studies published after his proofs. He himself, it is said, gave the public record; many other things were sent out in a spirit of friendship, from wherever they were dispatched by him. These are the things we speak of, regarding the accusations of souls and how they relate to God, up to the point of their restoration. For at one time, their essence was ignored. They do not know these souls, nor if they assigned causes to the soul herself; therefore, it would not seem right to question them at all, since you did not perform the same services for immortal lives. He says that the birth of the man is omitted, as he would have lived. He most especially adorned the matters of his own **temperance** <note>original: "σωφροσύνης" — the virtue of self-control and moderation.</note>. These things, then, concern the life lived by Plotinus. Thus, for all people, his life is that of an equal man.

Since many, upon hearing of it, asked about the very arrangement and the description of the books—how it might be best presented—I took care that it should not be otherwise. In all these matters, my persuasion showed me that the books belong to the nature of the subject itself, so that they might not be lacking, but rather that they might imitate something of the **Good** <note>original: "ἀγαθοῦ" — The "Good" is the ultimate, transcendent principle in Plotinus's philosophy, often equated with "the One."</note>. For we have been instructed in his deeds, and not only in the deeds themselves but in the things accomplished through them. And if we say that his fame remains, no one would think that the ancient things we wrote about are more significant than those existing in his own time.

<column-break/>

### Right Page

These works have not been detached from one another, nor arranged by chance; but in organizing these works into books this way, it seemed they should be held as follows. Some introduce the virtues and concepts of **Ethics** <note>original: "ἠθικῆς"</note>; others contain the principles of **Physics** <note>original: "φυσικῶν" — the study of the natural world and the cosmos.</note> regarding the world and its contents. Harmony and numbers also persuade us, so that the sixty <note>original: "ἑξήκοντα" — While this text says sixty, Porphyry historically organized fifty-four treatises into six groups of nine.</note> books arrive at six **Enneads** <note>original: "ἐννάδας" — groups of nine.</note>. For the number nine is a glory, <unclear>because through</unclear>... <margin>First Ennead</margin>

1. On the Living Being, and what is Man? <margin>1</margin>
2. On Virtues <margin>2</margin>
3. On **Dialectic** <note>original: "διαλεκτικῆς" — the philosophical method of investigation through logical discussion.</note> <margin>3</margin>
4. On Happiness <margin>4</margin>
5. On <unclear>whether happiness increases with time</unclear> <margin>5</margin>
6. On the Beautiful <margin>6</margin>
7. On the First Good, and other goods <margin>7</margin>
8. Whence come Evils? <margin>8</margin>
9. On the Reasoned Withdrawal from Life <margin>9</margin>

These, then, are in the first Ennead. Those belonging to the study of Physics, containing matters of the world and the things contained within it, are as follows: <margin>Second Ennead</margin>

1. On the World <margin>1</margin>
2. On the Heavenly Motion <margin>2</margin>
3. Whether the Stars Act <margin>3</margin>
4. On the Two Essences <margin>4</margin>
5. On Potentiality and Actuality <margin>5</margin>

## On What is the Living Being, and What is Man

<margin>7.</margin>
Pleasures and pains, fears and daring, desires and aversions, and the sensation of pain—to whom might these belong? For they belong either to the soul, or to the soul using a body as an instrument, or to a third thing composed of both. And this "composite" might be understood in two ways: either as the mixture itself, or as something entirely different that arises from the mixture. The same question applies to the "affections" <note>original: "παθήματα" — these are the passive experiences or emotions that happen to a person.</note> arising from these states: are they the experiences and the sensations themselves? Therefore, we must also investigate opinions: where do they come from, what is the nature of the experience, and does it belong to the soul itself or to the "common" <note>original: "κοινόν" — the Neoplatonic term for the union of soul and body, the biological organism.</note> entity? We must also investigate thoughts—how they occur and to whom they belong. Indeed, we must consider the act of reasoning itself: who is it that carries out the inquiry or the questioning? Is it the soul that knows, or is it the man? Should we perhaps propose that the soul is impassive <term>Impassive: the state of being "apathes," meaning the higher soul is not affected or changed by physical suffering or worldly emotions.</term>, acting as the cause for the body that uses it? Or does the soul itself suffer and experience, or is it some combination of both? But how can there be a combination? 

From where would these experiences come? Yet, it must be the soul. If indeed opinion and sensation belong to the soul, then we must say that there is a foundation <note>original: "ὑπόστασιν" — the underlying reality or level of existence.</note> of causes, and causes such as the experiences themselves, or the act of experiencing, or that which depends upon the soul; in this way, sensations and opinions are either a "use" of the body or an "activity" of the soul. If sensations belong to the soul, then the soul is where they reside, and hope would be in the soul as well. But can hope be satisfied within the breast <note>original: "στέρνοις" — Plotinus here questions the physical location of emotions, often placed in the chest by earlier poets, versus their true psychic origin.</note>? That is not the cause. Let the argument be clear, whether it is in the soul itself or as some nature as a whole. For there is also that which is impassive, which we must care for more. 

One would say that the soul is either more "beyond passion" or inexpressible; this is a necessity. Pain is something separate from it, but I prefer to focus on that which is present in all things concerning it. For what would the immortal soul fear? It cannot suffer from anything on the outside. If such a thing were afraid, it would be shown to be a passive experience. Or perhaps it is something that has become stable. For none of these things, or the things feared, can touch it. To say that lives are happy <note>original: "Εὐδαίμονα" — eudaimonia, or flourishing, which Plotinus argues belongs to the soul's true life.</note>, appearing after transformations and reaching fulfillment, comes from the ceasing of these movements. What sort of speech is this? It is that which is better than the "form," and some things within the soul. For we are able to act in this way. That which is described belongs to the body. We are indeed pained—either because of ourselves, or by necessity. For these things do not belong to humans alone. If we turn toward what is truly ours... but it is, somehow, a race that has come into being. Harmful things come from the "making" <note>original: "ποιήσεως" — the process of soul descending into the physical world of creation.</note> of what exists, so that it is always so.

<summary>Plotinus begins his first Ennead by asking whether emotions, sensations, and thoughts belong to the pure soul, the physical body, or a mixture of both. He introduces the central Neoplatonic problem of how an immortal, "impassive" soul can interact with a suffering, changing body.</summary>
<keywords>Plotinus, Soul, Body, Sensation, Emotions, Impassivity, The Composite, Human Nature</keywords>

--- Page 18 ---
<meta>This page transitions from the general inquiry into human nature found in the first Ennead (seen on the previous page) to the Fourth Ennead, which focuses specifically on the Soul. The text explores why the Divine or the "World-Soul" governs the universe without the effort, tools, or emotional suffering that characterize human life.</meta>

Indeed, it does not exist for his own sake. Nor is God directed toward himself, for what comes from him could not become more or greater for him. Or is it for this reason that the whole is **praiseworthy**, because those things there are left to him? And as many things as are greater and more numerous, he always performs them for himself and within himself. But in the whole, the living being might cry out these things as well, if it is necessary for there to be a generation for itself, and if it is thought to be some kind of living being. One must use it as one would an **instrument** <note>original: "ὀργάνου" — a tool or physical body used by the soul to interact with the world.</note>. For even there, the "Whole" is not the beauty that comes through the shape or the entire body, nor is it directed toward that which has been crafted. Or the whole, those things that cease after... Or because even with this same part of the instrument, we are turned toward the outside, for this indeed belongs to that. But God has no need of instruments, nor is he directed toward the things outside. Rather, all things are for him, and in him, and prior to them. And if someone should marvel at God because he does not become one or entirely a whole, he would be admired in a way worthy of the instrument. But even from God within himself, if he possesses more and beautiful things. But the whole body is not even prior to the change of the whole. (So that it is also not the whole. But the whole itself is by nature a whole, without **affections** <note>original: "παθῶν" — passive experiences, passions, or sufferings.</note>. For it is greater than the whole, nor is it greater because it is more numerous. This shall be a whole apart. For without this, the body would not be able to be anything. But prior to the body, there is a **providence** <term>Providence: "pronoia," the divine foresight and governing care of the universe.</term> for it, as to how it stands. Either it is something encompassed in an organic way, or the whole has done something, or they are shaped in some way, or it does not seem to anyone as standing still, and that it is something, to inquire of him. But as for their own affairs, one would say nothing, or that we do not speak with good grace about the things we say, when we are anxious and diligent regarding the cause in the whole. Let this be a matter of pride. If it ever came from a knowledge of arrangement, and the cosmos is infinite insofar as it does not move itself for its own sake everywhere, yet nothing is contrary to it. For God does indeed **care** <note>original: "μεριμνᾷ" — to be anxious or to have care/worry.</note>. According to us, either it is a living being, a greater living being, or God. But if it is a living being, it is either soul, and it looks upon the body. For the living being surely uses this, its own beautiful part. But that which is removed from where it lives is a rest for the one who has suffered. This again is for the sake of the living being, of a rational living being. This is not painful to a mortal, if there are more beautiful things through the change. This cannot happen. For what is everywhere is in its own place. And the very fact of being destroyed is something, for either it is outside of the wandering, which is not possible. And one must seek another part of it, lest something is able to be blamed for the grief. And not—

<header>· Ennead IV ·</header>
<sig>6</sig>

—of the rest of the body, to have another nature. Either it is an evil because of grief, or because the present things are at least similar. But there is something **impassive** <term>Impassive: "apathes," the state of being unaffected by external influences or physical pain.</term> throughout. Since one might also say this regarding the soul: that it does not allow the body to yield to its suffering, or let it appear so. And especially let there be a reason, not one that is merely fashioned. Or regarding this variegated nature of things that come to be, that it is fashioned. But he himself is not in the body at all, but prior to it; this is not separate, but prior to it. And more so when it is coming to the outside. But if that which has come to be, or the shape, should need its own, then the slant is unambiguous. From where does the whole, not having its race regulated, remain in the cause? Or rather, the names from which there are so many springs of clay. For some things are this, by the power of the natural organic state having life. For again, this will appear to those who have the soul itself. Thus it is, lest it should die. But either the living being remains, or it is a living being. Or it is another thing for itself to come to be and to act. Or it has something else that has come to be for both. However it may be. If indeed we should say the soul is **perceiving**, having become the cause of causes without the **affection** <note>original: "πάθους" — the experience of being acted upon, often used for pain or passion.</note>, if one should name it so. For even the thing that has suffered is thus a "beautiful" suffering. Or something sharp. Or everything with or after this will appear. Otherwise, it is appearing immediately or making war. But as for the body itself, nothing has been examined. But it perceives, as if it were in pain, of the Divine God, so that through its position, and especially with the sensation of the coming suffering. Since the sensation ends far off, an opposition, from which it feels pain. For the departure is from **opinion** <note>original: "δόξης" — belief or common opinion.</note> and **mind** <note>original: "νοῦ" — the higher intellect.</note> that it might take hold. But the evil from it, or concerning its own, or the world is the god's own admonition, if somehow it might approach or become a living being; but it is also based on opinion, from which it grieves some parts of the soul, or of the **composite** <term>Composite: "sunamphoteron," the union of soul and body that makes up the biological human being.</term>. For whether by opinion toward the evil, or the affection will lead to the things of grief. For even the one who hates, having persuaded the opinion, does he not do so to things that are coming to be? But indeed—one must not be angry, for the proof has come by opinion. One must not speak of the good according to existence. For these are not private. But honor and desire are the scientist and the principle. Of living, and generally of the body, it is as they say. And without being mixed and—

# · Ennead VI ·
G.

...of the wholes. <note>The text begins mid-word, likely "place of the wholes."</note> From the psychic intellect? Or from the Whole? Is it not also the case that the things in the world are ordered, or that they set things in order—so to speak—as in the case of sexual matters? For the desire for these same things is not for sensible objects, but belongs to the soul of those who are not merely "others" <note>original: "ἄλλων" — likely referring to the distinction between the physical body and the true self.</note>. And what they say regarding the "Grace" from the chorus: from that source comes the choice of this cause, as if the underlying subject <term>hypokeimenos|The underlying substance or subject that supports qualities</term> were not the same, or as if it did not subsist anywhere else through another person or thing, it will perceive. In another way, someone is the same as the underlying subject, and communicates through the desiring faculty; but in terms of the whole, he is nowhere the same, unless there is a pre-eminence of the subject. The subject exists, but its impulses are not so disposed toward themselves, but toward the outside. However, it is better to call upon the powers of the living being. Such things are understood in the ritual silence <note>original: "εὐφημίᾳ" — often refers to a holy silence or auspicious speech during religious rites.</note>. But was there a beginning? Are these things reasoned or terrible? Or do they simply "possess"? From this, they run together. For because of the cause of the "released" living being—its reason—their existence was a necessity. For of the things in the work, of the one who possesses it thus: from this, which was the whole of the soul. Concerning that (perhaps referred to), or not even (referred to), so as not to affirm it. But he is not [a product] of power or of the removal of power. Rather, it is in potentiality. But sensation, by means of judging, would be the **rational soul**, and the soul perceives. For what then? Are not the objects of sensation images, while the things that exist by themselves are the sensibles? This is false. That which must be perceived together is not a communion of sensation; it is not so. It is necessary, if the soul does not perceive together, that the powers of the soul do not either. And one must perceive together the sight of the soul along with sensation. Or, in the sources, one does not perceive the tensions of the body, or that which is more [apparent]. But it would not be so much of the whole, lying as we appear to do for the rational perceiver. By the nature of the living being, it is nothing. Or of the sensitive [soul]. That which is entirely "living" is well said. But we also perceive. Or is it because the living being is analogous to the **Intelligible** <term>noētos|The realm of pure thought or divine mind, as opposed to the physical world</term>, and the other things united together are thus entirely the same by nature according to a cause? The things of the soul fall short of the sensitive soul, or the sensible world falls short of it. Of the things that come to be in the living being from sensation, perhaps it is the cause, but rather it is something more. For even the things here perceive nothing outside. If we indeed say these things: are they images or truths in their entire essence, or simply the thing itself, among similar things?

<column-break/>

But from these **Forms** <term>ideōn|The eternal Blueprints or archetypes of all things</term>, from which the whole soul is composed, it was only able to live, but it bears the fruit of discursive thought and reason. Then, because long ago, or rather before these things. However you wish, from the purpose of living beings and the things in them—that which belongs to its living, at least—only death [is excluded]. But the things of them, in them, one might truly say. If not, he would exclude seeing the sweetest things entirely. For this [reason] harmonizes that which comes from the Intelligible to the soul; whenever we reason, we perceive. For the soul in its separate state is without sensation, nor indeed does it possess intellect. How? It thinks there too, but not the soul as if it were digging through the intellect. Or does it not also have joint-perception in this? Some, however, say this: for just as with images. For example, it is necessary that even the living thing here comes into being, because if it has something clear of it in the soul, it has these things. For if living beings are twofold: so that those in the soul are like impressions and like images. It would be 
<margin>G.</margin>
where all things are together. But how are they not [together]? And because of these Forms, he who is the **Intelligible Living Being** <note>original: "νοητὸν ζῶον" — The Platonic concept of the "Animal-itself," the divine archetype containing the patterns of all species.</note> [contains] us in part. But someone will say first that even in those things, they will not be the same; and what if sensation alone is here? That which is not even a chance reflection, or how much it is by sensation or the cosmos. For that which is according to an image. Or because they imagine them not as a passion <note>original: "πάθος" — a passive experience or suffering.</note>, but they think them by the intellect, and thus one thinks, ascending as if there were some method, this very difference. It is shown by itself, not in some other way in all the **hypostases** <term>hypostases|The levels of reality: the One, Intellect, and Soul</term>. According to the lesser, there is a sensation in the Intelligible realm. Then from that one, before them, she is called Soul; she who leads away into the last things, as far as the generative part, which perceives. Or they entirely validate [the sensation] of another and an exclusive thing without the branches of "thatness," she herself always touching the whole, alone in her craftiness. Each of us would then say that the soul is of the first rank, touching upon everything because it was so long ago; for life is not life in this way; and to many of these. From the opinion of art and obscurity, how they make things vanish. For they say that each thing, being struck, has been spread abroad as evil things? Or are we not such? Being stayed by them. For not all [are such], or just like voices, or but also. And the things said before are a "speakable" imagination <note>original: "λεκτὴ φαντασία" — a technical Stoic term for a mental representation that can be expressed in language.</note> which, being removed...

# · Ennead I ·
1.

### Column 1

But how does it relate to the reasoning faculty? Or is it because those [perceptions] reach all the parts? Not all of the senses, and the reasoning faculty likewise. For one says (primarily) that this "sensible" thing does not belong to the soul, nor to what the soul truly is <note>Plotinus is distinguishing between the true, higher soul and the lower functions associated with the body.</note>. Rather, it is likely that it happens through motion. These [faculties] do not touch that experience <note>original: "πάθους" — often translated as 'passion' or 'passive experience,' referring to something the soul undergoes.</note> within the intelligible realm. For even there, such things are possible, if the living being were not present. Or are those things here and those things there distinct? One is the vital part. The human being—neither the soul nor the body nor the activity—are these things private to the soul? And are they powers of the reasoning faculty? And how does it receive the opinion derived from sense-perception? For it already contemplates, and in contemplating, it is not concerned with sensible objects. But does one wonder about the soul’s being? How is the soul—either alone, or with [the body]? And how is there a communion that flees toward the things dwelling within? For would everything in us be "the whole"? Or not the whole, but only as much as we possess? But what is in us, such as the life-giving things and the things belonging to the Mind, such as "thinking," belongs to the soul itself. But how are *we* "we"? Is it by receiving? And does the soul undergo these sufferings? And the virtues? Or all of them? And then again, not so. We said, however, that they exist, and especially among the defined things. Or on one hand, our savior <note>original: "σωτῆρα" — This may be a transcription variant for "living being" (ζῷον), though the scribe has written "savior."</note>, they say, suffers alongside. But the soul itself, which is conjoined <note>original: "συμφυὴς"</note> with the body, or the whole which is private. One must say (savior) that which we might call a bond itself. The intelligible world. Therefore, the virtues do not belong to it in this way. For what is said to happen to the soul, the soul being separate, if anything is in it. But if mind belongs to it: how then to all? For the soul itself errs when it is preoccupied (subjected). But are the burdens entirely within the Form? One should not be grieved. Of the mind? Or do the things that come into being not allow both life and the living? But light is reason <note>original: "φῶς δὲ λόος" — a central Neoplatonic metaphor where the intellect illuminates the lower soul.</note>. Either it is the soul itself, or like it, the form is the soul itself. But how is it not everything? Close indeed is the name derived from the (body), belonging to the same living psychic things. For when our soul is itself. Our forms. When it fights with the mind and the whole. What then? We become that which belongs to that [higher realm], for do we alternate by race? Or are we not [ourselves]? Then we shall use [it]; and many things rather come to be, so that the things above, or toward the opposites; or we forget those things which we had, or we possess an activity.

<column-break/>

### Column 2

For painful things do not belong to the [true] man; the fear in the soul prior to the suffering is not the starting point, but pain belongs to the human [composite]. If this becomes strange, it is a matter of naming; but from where does the perception of these things come? From the suffering itself? Or from the soul entirely? Or from the soul with the body? One might hold that some things are in the body, such as a wound or a sore, and nothing prevents the soul from being in the state of a slave <note>original: "δούλου" — suggesting the soul is enslaved to bodily sensations.</note> by not being [itself]? And entirely, he who has become a living being by nature exists. But the soul is "perceptive," and it perceives this. But I speak of the body undergoing pain, which the man who transcends the mind <note>Likely referring to the philosopher or "the man" of Plato's *Republic*.</note> speaks of; and because of opinions and suffering, and with it? How indeed? <unclear>?????</unclear> And so someone will wish to speak. For the soul is in the body and mixed in such a way, the impulse of painful things is seen in the "soul-body" <note>original: "ψυχοσωματικῷ" — the psychosomatic entity where soul and body overlap.</note>, not in the soul by itself. Or is it the soul itself? Or is it to say "to be in the soul"? But the human being is to himself a kind of "addition" and an affinity to them, and the living being comes from the soul; hence it is for all others. It is a composite <term>syntheton|The 'together-thing,' the union of immaterial soul and material body that forms the earthly human being.</term> then, and that which undergoes suffering is in the soul, as it were. Or is it from the mind and countable (or a property) and that which belongs to its being? Neither is it pain, but it itself. Not clear. But the remaining passions are like those who have "owls" on their scales <note>original: "γλαύκας ἔχοντες" — a reference to Athenian coins stamped with an owl. Plotinus uses this to describe those weighed down by material or "heavy" concerns.</note>; but how are the sensible things circled, and what is the dissolution of the passions? One must say that philosophy itself is private and does not stumble. According to nature. But are there "intelligible living beings"? How? And the "thought-world" [intelligible world]. And the practical world and entirely the motion of the living being, but also the sensible things in them. For even in the generative part is the power of seeds. How does the innate soul possess so much? Or is every birth such that things are contrary to nature? But this must happen because the essence descends <note>original: "καταβαίνειν τὴν οὐσίαν" — the Neoplatonic concept of the soul's descent into the material world.</note>. The soul itself releases entirely, both the winged things and the perceptive things for all, let it be made dimly, using the perceptive part itself. And if not the [inner] man, then these things, and the practical part. But some things are like its own thinking, the soul having been constituted entirely not by itself. It releases oil <note>A metaphor for the soul's light or its animating influence being poured out onto the body.</note>, the underlying subject from the liquid. It releases it, even if that which departs is from that which is nothing. And what is its own, and because of this it is separated as a whole, just as a citizen is from the laws in the city. # Ennead 1, Book 3
**Page 20 G.**

**What is dialectic?** This is what must be taught, even to those previously mentioned. It is the habit of being able to state in speech about each thing what each thing is, and how it differs from others, and what is common among those in which it exists; and what the "kinds" <note>original: "γένη" (gene); also translated as "genera" or categories of being.</note> of these are, and where each of these is; and if it truly is what it is; and again, what are **beings** and what are **non-beings**, and how non-beings differ from beings. 

This science also discusses the **Good** and the **not-good**, and all that falls under the Good, and all that falls under its opposite; and what is the **eternal** in each thing, and what is not. For it is the knowledge of all things, not occurring at random or through constant change. Because of this, it is a guide that does not wander; having left behind the **sensible world** <note>the world we perceive through the five senses</note>, it establishes itself in the **intelligible world** <note>the realm of pure thought and Forms</note>. Having all its activity there, and having dismissed falsehood, it "is nourished in the so-called **Plain of Truth**" <note>A famous reference to Plato’s *Phaedrus*, describing the place where the soul finds true knowledge.</note>. 

It uses the Platonic method of **division** of the intelligible, and the knowledge of simple forms; it also uses the blending of the "kinds" and the greater "interweavings" <note>original: "πλοκάς" (plokas); refers to the way different Forms or Kinds connect and interact with one another.</note> derived from those kinds, until it has traversed the whole of the intelligible. Then it reverses the process, analyzing until it reaches the **First Principle**. At that point, it remains at rest, as long as it is in that state, no longer dividing itself among many things, but having become one, it looks upon the whole. 

It leaves behind all logical "busy-work" as being empty, for it writes the knowledge of beings within Being itself. It does not analyze by mere logical rules or the methods of common speech, but by following **Being itself**. Its "dialectical" parts are like those things before the actual craft, giving the mind the power of persuasion.
---
**Where then does this science get its principles?** Does the **Intellect** <note>original: "νοῦς" (nous); the Divine Mind.</note> give clear principles? Yes, and the soul, having received them, collects, interweaves, and divides them until it arrives at a perfect contemplation. This, they say, is what must be taught. 

**Geometry** and other logics are for adornment and to provide causes, and they pave the way, but it is the Intelligible that carries the Intellect—which, through the act of dialectic, achieves what it does not think through mere talk. 

**What then is philosophy?** Is it the most honorable thing? And is philosophy the same as dialectic? Or is the honorable part of philosophy dialectic? One must not think this is merely a "tool" for the philosopher, but rather it is already a finding of honorable and kinship-based works. It is as if it is before the Intellect, having come to it. In this way, it proceeds, just as nature has been made to be cognitive. 

The base man and the man of science, and the happiness of knowledge—but these are things to be reckoned from that higher place. For you do not know the base thing from itself, or from where you will categorize it, since even evils perhaps have their causes. And other things also through...

<summary>This page contains a translation and commentary on Plotinus's Ennead 1.3, defining "Dialectic" as the supreme philosophical method for the soul's ascent to the Intelligible realm and the Good. It distinguishes dialectic from mere formal logic, positioning it as the soul's direct engagement with Truth and Being.</summary>

...but with it as a substrate, there is no need for anything to live. <summary>Plotinus investigates whether "life" is a single concept or if biological functions (like the heart and lungs) are distinct from the "true life" of the Intellect. # Ethics 9

...-py. <note>The text continues the word *eudaimona* (happy) from the catchword on the previous page.</note> If the goal is not to make one happy, then it belongs to no virtue. If indeed it is for the base man <note>original: "φαύλῳ" (phaulō); refers to a person of low moral character or someone focused only on the physical world.</note>, this is nowhere correct. Why would such things be necessary, and how could those practicing this stop the wrongdoer? Some things are pleasant, which are also fought for in the state of happiness. For Aristotle says <note>Aristotle, *Nicomachean Ethics*</note> choice and withdrawal, or even necessity—taking these without regret for labors, just as not every living being [is so]. But if it is least in the doing again. For already there it will seem not to be a living being, nor to use nor to care for what it does not have. For what it has, we even celebrate within it. If living depends on it and especially so, we are nonetheless not miserable. For being is by nature, but he will say that every good is considered unknown.

<margin>reciprocity</margin> <note>original: "ἀντεπεπονθὸς" (antipeponthos); an Aristotelian term for "tit-for-tat" or reciprocal action in justice.</note>

For that which participates wishes to enjoy and exists. And thus this is the best life. These things will be something more mutual, which she <note>The soul.</note> wants. Or one should not care for his own things, but one must not pay attention to them. Since these say nothing, so that consciousness <note>original: "τὸ συνειδέναι" (to syneidenai); the state of being aware of one's own internal state.</note> is nothing, nor is seeking in this way. For if it constitutes the most for common people to want, yet it is a bond to the eyes of the body. Especially when it is something—like health and error <note>original: "ἀμαρτία" (hamartia); often translated as "sin," but in a philosophical context, it means "missing the mark" or intellectual error.</note>. On account of life—it becomes painful. Again. It is truly reasonable, since he has it himself. And he asked questioningly about "living." Because of its good and that for the base ones, it will be dissimilar in that. Because of desiring these things, there is no need. But in it, one had to be at a loss. Nature is thus somehow not painful toward the friendship of passion, but rather makes it so that. He recognizes this, which seems to me also, that someone is still well-disposed toward desiring it. This is where it is attributed to happiness. Or someone would not be happy, having stopped both for the friend and for each part of happiness, everything that he himself receives to be of whatever kind and fitting. And with whom, which happens to be known, himself first, and the pleasant. Of his own.

# On Tranquility 24

<margin>
and
saying...
</margin>
Some of the weaker people, though not even being looked down upon, are thrown into confusion regarding involuntary matters; they are distressed by certain things, and the sting of grief bites them because they were corrupted from the very start. But in fact, misfortunes always grant more to many, in those great days, such as <term>kingship</term> <note>original: "βασιλείαι" (basileiai); can refer to the office of a king or the state of being a ruler.</note>, and friends, and the goodwill of kings. But what exists for them from their own homes, and what happens at home, is not visible to everyone. And cities trample upon him, and they already recognize greater things. But as for those things that are not quite so, we do not know them. Again, consider the nature of the giver. They act as if they received it clearly without cause, and they would do many things in the state after necessity. Just as some great mass falling upon someone leads toward death, so it is for those who live while seeing these things. But they themselves are <unclear>free from pain</unclear>, and they live in secret. For to civilize a human being, it is first necessary to return this very thing from what is available. For this reason, someone who has become uncultured toward what remains is most unworthy of tranquility. To those who are driven toward ignorance day by day, their whole life is like a flood. But if his states are not established—for example, <term>virtue</term> <note>original: "ἀρετὴ" (arete); excellence or moral perfection.</note> against coincidences—what then do you fear? Alexander <note>likely Alexander the Great</note>, having learned that nothing was his own, [acted accordingly]. But surely he does not think they are the best; by Zeus, those who are inferior to these will not use them, but they embrace the impossible things belonging to others; he cannot speak these things to the full. For just as the sun illuminates the ether, the earth, and the sea, so also reason exists for human beings as they have been born. For from the most base things—as one who has seen the nature of evil is such—it is possible to bear these things. If there are fortunes of winter and many immoderate things happening easily, and having properly failed the most violent part of endurance into helplessness, or a certain mad passion. For that which always fights absurdly, like a flash of lightning. It is most just of all the others to have distress worthy of them, as the evil always destroys them, even if the misfortunes of others allow them to be self-governing. The evils of others, when they are violent, are not even foreign to us; such as meddling and injustice; and in every case, it is worthy to ward them off immediately. But his own light in the midst of base things, like a light in a smoky place, holds a certain anger in a great surge of winds and storm. It is corrected by shame, but it wanders from the start under ill-advised requests; let them not be indignant at all in their failure, with everyone turning dark with laughter. The earth has been taken away, but human affairs are most pious. It appears necessary to live each need to completion. For many things are likely to appear from it; and use what is available, neither other things, nor the things of others, nor the truest things; and whenever of them...

<column-break/>

...is raised <note>The catchword "αἴρε-" from the previous page is completed here as "αἴρεται" (airetai), meaning 'is lifted' or 'is removed'.</note>; yet the soul remains more free from pain. This state exists whenever the soul considers that it can fight back and fulfill everything for the species, or rather, give good counsel. For this is the only thing not hidden, but his own, yet let us not be grieved. This must always be practiced with a pure <term>indifference</term> <note>original: "ἀδιαφορία" (adiaphoria); a Stoic term for things that are neither morally good nor evil, such as health or wealth, which should not affect one's inner peace.</note>, but one must also fear lest foolishness occurs. If we are strangely deprived of our reputation, and do not even endure a blow from the misfortunes of our kin, recognize that it is not entirely so. And because of our hopes, it is not worthy to defend against the natures themselves, which is called the "defense before the evils." And yet, because of this, one should not think there is even hope, nor anything friendly to him in these things. But because a man must not fail, he takes up the struggle with the best. So that they may show a bloodless exercise of the end, because change is natural. One should not even speak of suffering with one's soul regarding what is friendly to him. Do not wish for these things, even toward things that are not good; when it is necessary to act and do these worthy things, the soul sinks down more free from pain. Especially in preparation—fortune, being kingly, giving from greater things—it is for a human to love meddling in it, whatever it may be, or to wait for it without itself. Just as they take away what belongs to the soul from its tranquility. For he will use the leadership of philosophers as of yesterday; for they say they carry out their life. "Would that I were more sensible," which he says because of the adversary, as if sailing past. But we, because of foreign customs, which we take to heart, appear by the same things. Another is "worth as much," they say, for it is especially for him not to be cold and fruitless, to return this still. One does not recover <term>apathy</term> <note>original: "ἀπάθεια" (apatheia); in Stoic philosophy, this is not "not caring," but rather a state of being free from irrational passions and emotional suffering.</note> unless one is healthy. It exists in them; and because he is beautiful, as if already beautiful; but because he is wise, he is not indignant, unless he truly be wise. At the same time, as if in wisdom, some despair and they despair of it itself. This is the prayer of the very useful wise men; and that they are well-ordered when falling. They would say that those who possess prudence and wisdom are worthy of receiving the whole of life. If a foundation exists in all wisdom, it is especially <term>happiness</term> <note>original: "εὐδαιμονία" (eudaimonia); the state of human flourishing or "living well."</note>. And for the cities, justice is not flattering, and because we naturally speak not to love a place with apathy, and you do not recognize the clear courage of the citizens. And that which makes them easy-going, more manly and toward those who have lost hope, he is fearless. Fortune takes him; for like his child, a part of him; just as he escapes the natural things as he departs, but is escaped by others; just as the day of the day does not fail him; for his voice would even benefit us. And the gift to each; and a woman’s prayer.

<meta>This page continues the philosophical inquiry into the nature of happiness, moving from the previous discussion on tranquility to a more theological exploration of "well-doing" (eupraxia) versus mere luck. # Letter 1

-> It is not good fortune, but he calls it **well-doing**. <-

Indeed, it is a brilliant thing not to fall into error in human life because of our sensory nature <note>original: "αἰσθητικὴν φύσιν" (aisthetikēn physin); referring to the part of human nature governed by the five senses rather than reason.</note>, in which the **first man** was created; yet he himself should see nothing arrogant or lofty about these things. Since he is sensory—and entirely sensory—it is for this reason that when he was struck, he acted with insolence. But perhaps he wrote, as if regarding what is common to both those people and ourselves, with the reasoning of humanity. This was so that the soul might regain its worth whenever it becomes weak again. 

But if one fails in doing right toward another more than is fitting: for just as with knowing, while everyone may know a man or you know others, not everyone holds these memories in the same way. We are different from those who just happen upon things. Since these things exist by nature, the activity of the **intellect** and the **mind** <term>nous</term> <note>original: "νοῦ" (nou); in Greek philosophy, the highest part of the soul capable of direct intellectual intuition of the truth.</note> is not forbidden, as long as one allows these things to happen. After these actions are recorded, there is nothing contrary in saying—having been so persuaded—that because of the harmony created in the body, this will be the specific motion according to **imagination** <term>phantasia</term>. Thus, opinion exists instead of pure thinking, occurring alongside imagination. For it is through these thoughts that we speak. 

In this way, sensation and excellence can lead to bad prayers, light, and passion, because these things will primarily exist alongside that sensory nature. The lack of comprehension of existing evils is common in human affairs; they are accustomed to rejecting them. One might say especially that even goodness is not a savior. What is said here is an **allegory**, and it will be found to align with the truth, just as in the doing of ten thousand things. Those who wander risk becoming the cause of their own destruction through their works, even when approaching Him. But He alone gave, and through the grace extended to us, one learned about life. And in the act of knowing, one ceases from such types of knowledge; rather, the things of desire do not seem to be darkened by the neglect of one’s failings. 

If they should say that such things are not among the external world, then their nature is also internal. For one must grasp the **happiness** <term>eudaimonia</term> <note>original: "εὐδαιμονία" (eudaimonia); often translated as "flourishing" or "blessedness," the highest human good.</note> of such a person as being in the **glory of God**. If they do not say this, it is worth suggesting to them that pride belongs to the sensory world, and happiness is found even in this. For they will fall in love with it, while I have found no one equal in seeking or fleeing other things. One seeks it for the sake of well-doing. Let not sensory things be confused; external things are like those of the flesh. Let this be his way of giving: for I do not say they should seek the opposite. For whatever things one feels shame for, being subject to them as if the calling comes from the outside, you are also rescuing yourself from these. For he did not suffer if something happened from his own well-doing, perhaps even—

<column-break/>

—but we might more reasonably call it a certain defense and a remembrance. If anyone were to consider whether life is a light for those from that other place, and not entirely focused on itself—lest we, not possessing it in this way, should appear to have trained our will toward His glory. This is not the case for the body when it is set aside. Why did he seek the source of bodily things, such as the "inflammations" of movement? We should call these the senses themselves. And a more cheerful state disappears; for it is not about suffering. 

Light itself and such causes of good things are impossible to be otherwise; for one perceives a certain light. Again, his nature itself comes from the ceasing [of pain], both for the giver and for another. For from Him comes everything and every state of rest. In His goodness, He encompasses the whole of all bodies with every kind of **providence** <term>pronoia</term> <note>original: "προνοίᾳ" (pronoia); the benevolent care of God or nature for the universe.</note>. It is certain that it is from God that he receives such a nature from his own home, which received life through **resurrection** <note>original: "ἀναστάσεως" (anastaseōs); a key Christian term for rising from the dead.</note>. 

For the things of nature, having received good from Him, do not become the cause of failings. It was good to see these things recently, because his nature is more akin to the "part of life," as he tells us first. And perhaps then the hopes of the virtues, along with being more persuaded—for it would not be otherwise—even after this. It seemed better, even if he learns to become like them in this way, the likeness is left behind again, because of the way many people receive it. 

He says that the first thing is that they are not the same; he clearly says this so that it might be so. But he will search for it. If He is not the cause of good, then from where does he receive his own Father? Thus, perhaps certain imaginations are received by the one dwelling in the Good. For the rest, the one observing must be the most measured of the intelligible things. For it is clear to me that the things of **God**, and the things of the ministers <note>original: "λειτουργῶν" (leitourgōn); can refer to priests, angels, or public servants.</note> fleeing from **God**, are what they are. Because of these present things, it is worthy to be deemed worthy before the **eternal dwelling** <note>original: "αἰωνίου μονῆς" (aioniou monēs); a reference to John 14:2, "In my Father's house are many rooms (monai)."</note> already, having been brought about by prayers and by all those "well-doings" that are composed of the spiritual. 

For he wanted these, as well as good souls. Because of natural things, he might again make the other. For it is not out of a necessity of doing, because she is "mother and cause." Let it be in glory by nature, both well and good. In the case of those who are ignorant of whatever has been done in a defined way, they see these with their own minds. The opinions formed about divine matters are even more worthy. Let the things of **faith** <term>pistis</term> never cease, so that one may be humble in some way, so that it may be well. For either he suffers this himself because he learned what he suffered and has endured it, and again he holds himself so that it cannot be otherwise. But if he said it, then happiness belongs again to those who live. Because of this, and so that the whole of life might not become [lost]. When these things happen, it is a marvelous thing to obey Him and be subject, and to neglect nothing toward **God**.

<meta>This page continues the inquiry into the nature of happiness (eudaimonia), specifically addressing the relationship between physical survival and the intellectual life of virtue. It transitions from the previous discussion on imagination and memory to the Plotinian argument that happiness is not merely the absence of pain, but a state of being rooted in eternal intellect.</meta>

# Ennead 1.4.5

### On Happiness

For the premise, as if it were merely guarding the act of living, is naturally incapable of the necessary preparation for true well-being. There might be "goods" available to all, but since these occur through the faculty of thought, they do not necessarily lead to anything better for those who lack wisdom. Therefore, not everything that happens in life can be used toward the goal of **happiness** <term>eudaimonia</term> <note>original: "εὐδαιμονεῖν" (eudaimonein); for Plotinus, this refers to a state of flourishing that is independent of external luck.</note>. For this state belongs to the one who can truly rejoice, ensuring that life becomes better rather than falling into deficiency. 

As for pains, one must endure them again, even if one cannot fully transcend them. On the contrary, health, freedom from pain, and happiness are understood differently when death is approaching or in extreme circumstances. For a happy man, it is understood that he has set aside base things. It is true, then, to see that it is not just a matter of happening to be free of grief; rather, so that there may be a "flowering" where fear or lack might otherwise occur, he possesses **practical wisdom** <term>phronesis</term> <note>original: "φρόνησιν" (phronēsin); the virtue of applying reason to action.</note>, from which he is made wise. 

If the struggle is against loss, and everything else does not lead toward wisdom or the essentials of living—whether it be the divine life or its limit—then happiness would happen for him through a likeness to the divine, primarily by not being in a state of constant need. For those things toward which greed tends must also have an end. Because of the eternal as an object of prayer, chosen alongside our own nature, the happy man would most greatly rejoice. For when we are able to see clearly, he reveals everything through his imagination and considers the eternal to be of such great value that he sets himself to stay away from all evil; hence he is protected by the Whole. The sum of everything is **grace** and life; but our own life is that which is worthy of living.

But if he is the one enjoying it, and the one becoming fearful before it, or using pleasure toward others—of which they say that when it is absent, one is softened by the touch of passions like grief—in the same way, the good man is the one who thus removes such passions. He treats what happens with indifference, even with blessings; seeing things rightly, he deems them worthy without losing heart over each event. For even before these things happen, action exists. Let us say he is a **master** over nature, a friend most of all to it, yet boasting in what comes after it. Reasonably, we must move on, for by nature he is worthy of the eternal, considering what has been done without fear; (and so it happens to him), because he does not yet view these things as "the good," but rather as things that release him from the passions of each event. And if this should happen, the name of the "happy man" is earned; throughout all time and every hour, so that he piously lives as a happy man in the eternal by that same power; for which they say each thing belongs to him.

<column-break/>

Again, as for rejoicing and making life worth living, the particular is clearly distinguished from the universal; so it is with each pleasure. This must be said to the one whom the argument addresses: these things, which we ourselves transfer and which must be presupposed; and again, regarding reputations and other such glories, and other lives that one must defend. These are not the goodwill and honors that God will give him, nor the honors toward children and kin who ought to be honored. While these things are handled well and reach their end, they do not do so by nature; for one must never cease, not even for a moment. 

So it is with living, and with living always. For to honor these things does not create happiness (and I would even say to die, for the sake of ancient glory; but rather the things done, and the things thought, and the working within, and being made akin to God through praise). Just as the worse is evil, so the better is **virtue** <term>aretē</term>; and regarding the cycles of birth, it is not born of grief. For the life of virtue possesses pains without the fear of them. For virtue makes life a worthy home for others, from which living with glory belongs to him in the highest degree. Over all these things, he proceeds in such a manner.

<margin>⊕</margin>
And after this, they even do away with not living, nor does he choose to rejoice in the act of living for its own sake.
<margin>5.</margin>
And the happy man accepts life for the sake of virtue. The labor of beautiful happiness is thus received. And this life, which is the life of happiness, would be for him, and living is not altogether unchangeable, even if it is not the very best. Or is there not a perception of the "good life" in all, and the good fortune of life? For that which must be done needs nothing else. But this—his own nature and that of all things—is not always most fitting, but when it is entirely well-timed, it is the more appropriate hour. 

He who stands in virtue rather than the worse, and in the good, will be happy through that virtue. He will be the same toward all happiness as he is toward living in this life. This is possible. Nature is radiant <gloss>or by this</gloss> for it makes the peak. And this is so. For the life from which he comes, and before which he exists, is more truly his. Nor does he leave off living without that which belongs to him, but holds what he has in life; yet virtue alone is not enough, nor is virtue merely a good reputation; rather it is to be grasped closely, and not as if it were nothing. 

But as for living: it is the cause of life. But happiness is **living well always**. He who has more is happy. "More" is what is necessary at the time; such as life itself. But if one must perceive the present life, "more" would mean that destruction has come upon him. Not every good exists immediately, as if one suddenly came out of evil. But "more" refers to those who attend to what is necessary, for whom this is not "the good," nor is it according to justice if he is happy; since one should not count the things pertaining to some part of life as happiness, which is how the many view life itself. In which "more" is required, yet it is not the act of living itself. But whenever well-doing <term>eupraxia</term> is present for him in relation to life. Virtue does not say that happiness is life itself, but rather making life a state of well-being. And so it shall be.

<summary>Plotinus argues that true happiness (eudaimonia) is an internal state of virtue and intellectual activity that remains constant regardless of external suffering or the simple biological act of staying alive. He distinguishes between 'living' as a physical necessity and 'living well' as a spiritual and philosophical achievement.</summary>
<keywords>Plotinus, Enneads, happiness, eudaimonia, virtue, phronesis, well-doing, eternity, intellect, pain, soul</keywords>
