And here, if it is necessary to provide for wealth, one should do so simply, without excessive concern, and be ready to share with those in need. For if there is some necessity, perhaps of a kind we never even considered, one must not take from another except when there is nothing else. For what should we call such a thing? Or rather, one should leave behind abundance; all the other things that have passed away give only the appearance of gold. For instance, if people gather and make a profit from material substance, these things are for those in need or based on hope, because of the honor given to that substance and the good fortune of wealth. Or indeed, do not take what is given to me by the givers as if they were providing for a use, such as that of the present life. For there is either a need, or you are setting a measure as a rule. For the matter of need must not be for itself alone, lest the harm be greater. 

For [true] goods lead to **virtue** <term>arete</term> <note>original: "ἀρετὴν" (aretēn); moral excellence or the fulfillment of purpose.</note>. Whatever freedom is added, let the one who has become [virtuous] stand apart alone. There is a limit to such desire: to provide what is needed when it is according to the mind of the receiver. For the advantage of the individual, or similar things, are rather preparations for need. Therefore, perhaps wealth is something more. Or even that which is left by others, the giver might be able to return. But it is not only that much, but as much as the cause of those receiving. If these things are not according to hope toward what is necessary, perhaps no one would care for them at all. Or perhaps casting away a portion of wealth toward the whole... which is nothing. 

But because they cared for the body long ago—for there is a deception stemming from these things—they themselves + leave behind the whole (for to me also, and for...). Therefore, at that time, some made their expenditures a thing of wonder, as if there were no remaining bond. For the one who acts with **repentance** <term>metanoia</term> <note>original: "μετανοίας" (metanoias); literally a 'change of mind' or 're-evaluation,' often used in the New Testament to mean spiritual conversion.</note>, acts through himself. The greater word is the calling back of regret. For it is not of parents, nor a change; for there is no word for such a thing, like the last one. We might say we have not walked a new path through the common way of all, but that which the **earnest** <term>spoudaioi</term> <note>original: "σπουδαῖοι" (spoudaioi); the morally serious or advanced practitioners of philosophy.</note> do. It is right that all things which must be done as a task should happen, or be learned. 

Generally, things concerning death would not be able [to harm], nor the one in the same state. Therefore, she [Virtue] seems from her words to manifest a power that is well-regarded. Instead of that, because it is possible to give unsparingly of their own money and possessions. Thus, instead of this, the appearance of virtue arises in its generation. When the "all-good" is given, these are already the doctrines of the Divine and of divine things. Because through kind words, He made all things—the earth and the heaven—given by Him alone to be enjoyed, and to be a grace. As the cause of the whole for each individual.

...and to maintain oneself in being, as one ought. The same thing. For rather, those things that have been set apart from all his possessions, whatever useful thing they take, those are the indestructible things. Because of the man of God. He who would not only [be] alone, but the first things are for everyone. If, then, there is no greatness among those who excel in doing good, how is this not the primary element of wealth? In the **happiness** <term>eudaimonia</term> of tranquility, or in participating with it. Or the one who is stingy in nothing regarding the doing of it, [the happiness] of tranquility; thus, the taking is stingy. 

And because of this, toward the table, or the house each time. These many things reveal what is better than riches: cheerfulness and goodwill. And because of good reputation, which is also what appears beyond hope. Is it not also the passions, or that which is grieved, or everything that is useful? That which appears did not seem so great. For if there is an uplifting, everything of his is placed above. But also well-being, as well as piety and equity. Or those things not contrary to these. From where he is far from enemies. <margin>( . )</margin> Therefore long ago, for many things [were done] by many, as one might say, seeing but little, or even more toward piety. For the [nature] of these? Or the just? Or through whom there seems to be both a clear cause and their affairs. 

To continue unmoving and to be a friend to God, or happy (goodwill). Happiness can also appear to the earnest man, because of the abundance of these affairs. It is well said, then: that of the Father is for all, many things because of the good order of need. Surely, it is well-regarded also in the things according to the **Scripture**. And I am only the cause of the **Savior**. I said, not unreasonably, that happiness is of tranquility. But it is clear that He did many things in which the **saving word** <note>original: "σωτήριος λόγος" (sōtērios logos); the message of the Gospel or the divine reason that brings salvation.</note> is true. 

Since, then, this [blessed man] had to be revealed to all, through having hopes toward good things. Or knowledge again to all, and he is deemed worthy because of good intentions. This too was necessary, or to demonstrate the good order of the pious, as also the blessedness of good fortune through the things from... for those who have nothing good at each time. <meta>This page continues the exploration of the nature of the Soul and its relationship to the divine, shifting focus from the soul's presence in the body to the metaphysical origins of Justice, Light, and Life. ### Follows 4. 9. 5.

And that which is according to justice; and in all things among men; and what was <unclear>said</unclear> by <unclear>**Aristotle**</unclear> <note>original: "ἀριστοτέλει"; the philosopher Aristotle, whose definitions of justice Plotinus often interprets through a mystical lens.</note>. These things regarding <unclear>stability</unclear> and self-love, even these he transfers toward the beautiful; so that justice among men and all beings is in place of light. But what justice is in God? And what is holiness? Except, as <unclear>I said</unclear>,
of the human sort; for such necessary things are adjudicated. But what is the justice in Him? Even there, justice
is light; not, by Zeus <note>original: "οὐ μὰ Δία"; a common Greek emphatic oath, here used to stress that divine justice is entirely different from earthly legal systems.</note>, according to the justice and law in the world. For we are comparing the things of angels and of men.
For justice and the just man hint at these things through their kinship with God and light. There is
an intellectual light <term>noetos</term> <note>original: "νοητόν"; refers to the realm of the Divine Mind or Intellect, which can be grasped by thought rather than the physical senses.</note>; darkness is its analog. For justice hints at this same light; and according to
these things, the light. It is as if one were to render the light which is before the light. For justice is light;
so that even that which is before the light is justice and is light. But that which is before the light is life and fire;
and every property of fire is light. This very thing, the true Living Being itself, by that which is before the light
calling it also light; which is not so because of the same thing. And it will move all things, and thus the rest
belong to the law. Clearly it is not thus, both justice and life; so that which is before the
light is according to the law that is before [all]. There is that which is according to motion, and that which is before motion,
but even this is that which is before the light and fire. For fire possesses motion; that which
is in Him, yet He is unmoved before the motion. And it is a true illumination and all that is in Him;
and all His power is vital; all things are in Him. But the fire and that which is before the light
are the very movements; so that God is unmoved before all things. He is also light and life
and wisdom; and all such things pre-exist in Him. Thus the things in God, which is also before the
light, before all ages <term>aionon</term> <note>original: "αἰώνων"; referring to eternal cycles or the state of timelessness in the divine realm.</note>. But the things in the world, they all participate in Him. For whatever
participates in light here, from there comes the light and the life, from the unmoved and ever-moving
abiding of light, and it shines forth among all things in the world; through the ever-moving and vital fire; and
that which appears full to all intelligible things. For there is nothing without light throughout eternity, nor without life;
for all things live in Him and through Him, and are moved. So that even material things, being lit by His light,
shine forth because of His ever-moving eternal nature. For His generative principle <term>spermatikos</term> <note>original: "σπερματικός"; literally "seed-like," referring to the formative powers or "seminal reasons" that shape the physical world from divine patterns.</note>,
the intellectual illumination, is in communion and impassibility, and through Him all things are and in Him; therefore
He is ever-moving, always existing, and through Him all things are in Him; and He is all things;
indeed all lights are His, because of the Living Being in Him and all existing things; and the light. For the
light was sent forth by the Eternal itself, and through Him the light, blazing in the world, gives life to all.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Soul’s relationship to the Divine Intellect, transitioning from the nature of divine justice to the practical distinction between the higher life of the mind and the suffering inherent in the physical body and the "animal" nature.</meta>

### In the First Ennead

That which belongs to the intelligible <term>noetos</term> <note>original: "νοητοῦ"; the realm of pure thought and divine forms, distinct from the physical world.</note>, even if there is a lack of sensation, is due to a cause: namely, that there is no consent to painful things. For this belongs to life. These things which he says are not the property of the soul alone, but belong most especially to it. This soul has acquired **Opinion** <note>original: "Δόξαν"; in Neoplatonism, "doxa" or opinion is a lower form of knowledge than "nous" or intellect, as it deals with the changing world of appearances.</note>. Even if we were to become merely a dwelling place for the Intellect <term>nous</term> <note>original: "νοῦν"; the Divine Mind, the second principle in Plotinus's system, which contains all true forms.</note>, after all other things the soul is blamed. The soul becomes lesser through its passions and sufferings <note>original: "παθήματα"; these are the "affections" or "disturbances" the soul feels when it is too closely tied to the body.</note>; it suffers anger and diseases, and even remains among existing things. Whence the soul of the intellect and all the innate things within its contemplations cause the soul to regain the intellect. Instead of being alone, it possesses all things according to the intellect. It is in her to be, or it is ancient. But he says she is only in this way. Therefore he said: opinion and intellect become the soul—not of himself, but for a time. Yet here, it is not entirely so.

Greater are those things of a spiritual nature. The soul is the same by nature as that which it suffers, but it is the same as the generated intellect. Thus everything has acquired the same **Good**, or we possess reasonings. At the same time, the soul makes a search for itself and creates movement; that which it looked upon. Because the beautiful belongs to the intellectual, it is immediately either itself or the soul leads according to contemplation, not shaping the soul. These things then are as they are; life will be released. And the things in life, just as the things in the living being <term>zoon</term> <note>original: "ζώω"; refers to the composite of body and soul that makes up an animal or human creature.</note>, are lesser souls. It is not "the Good" simply because the living being is toward the intellect, nor does it remain entirely the same, even if it returns. It is never possible to turn the soul away. It is necessary to use it without appeal. For every soul is an opinion, and because of this, it suffers inflammation. But the soul itself is also the body; the reasoning becomes a living being—for that which is by nature is "labor." Its order is necessary toward other things, and it holds a station in the inhabited world, according to the commands of Fate <note>original: "πεπρωμένον"; the pre-ordained destiny that governs the physical world.</note>. How then do certain things happen as a whole, insofar as sin <note>original: "ἁμαρτία"; here meaning a "missing of the mark" or a turning away from the divine source.</note> is a departure from the present? For there is a certain virtue. One would not think that beauty exists in the slave or the servant. One cannot see it without self-concern. Otherwise, contemplation bears fruit, upon which everything is hung. Then there might be fire. Sacrifices, if they exist, are a vital faith; and one is in that which is necessary. This, then, is to live. For all things are individually better for being alive, having found happiness <term>eudaimonia</term> <note>original: "εὐδαιμονεῖν"; a state of flourishing or true well-being that Plotinus identifies with the life of the Intellect.</note> in it. How? Through a syllogism with reason. Because it is not entirely for one who has not chosen it, both good in herself and a good man. But that which is in each soul and beautiful, sinks toward the movement in the body. Either to be a living being is to be uncrushable, or it is a living being not like other animals. To be pitied for its labors. Still, there is a description of other lives. And one must consider all things beautiful as they change. For thus he makes that which he demands of himself, doing it secretly. Because it is in no way said that similar things are "beautiful animals." What of the irrational ones? Is life itself "the Good"? It is itself base and evil; not for praise, nor for enjoyment. And in the dwelling of the father <note>original: "τῆ πατρὸς"; likely referring to the "One" or the ultimate source from which all souls descend.</note>. If all these things shall be, one must remain in the city he is commanded. For if it is necessary for all to agree, it is not entirely necessary to remain.

<column-break/>

They cause pain and give life to the sensible world. Furthermore, all such animals and plants, when they cease to be, are dissolved, and a kind of death comes to them. This very thing suffers most and feels pain and is stripped away: that which is its most vital life and its actual activity. The living being possesses no greater or more manifest life; but the labor of the intellect and the intellectual is a separation from habit and toward learning. Whence, while learning, one suffers. The soul is entirely ignorant that it possesses life. So if it has life, there is pain in the non-intellectual life, but pleasure in the intellectual life. But this life is not the "kingdom" and reason, but this is from a place and with labor. So if life happens in suffering and feeling pain, it is made alive and there is no change; even if it is in the pain of life, there is no pleasure, just as it will be in the animals.

What then is the manner of it? That the intellectual lies in certain movements of its own, as among one another and the intellectual beings. The movement occurs so that it may see contemplation. This is good sensitivity. If the animal perceives, it lies outside and sees a vision and would flee the pain itself, so as not to be within it. Life should flow in the beauty of the city, not in the vintage. But indeed, life will be in the individual things; you eat and you drink, and everything is within. So if one takes contemplation in such things, we would have not pain, but a form and a fullness of life. One is pained not as if certain things are painful and grievous, but one rejoices if it happens that they are ignorant of life. For the same thing is to be ignorant and not to permit the whole. What is the living being? Reason weaves together the soul and body; I call it the "living being." For the irrational ones are animals without reason. And there is also the suffering of bodies. Most people have accepted "the spiritual" as signifying nature. The things in the soul are directed toward the bodies, such as anger and joy—all of them according to the ancient way. The rational man does not even concern himself with these, even unto the passions—though it is not entirely so. At any rate, there is life in them concerning pains, because it is a most base thing. What then is the "station" or the "course"? Or what kind of thoughts are these? For by nature, all reason had been sent upward. Perhaps reason will stand thus when we have ceased. But the passions are alongside those of the desires. Even if one does not have it, he loses another vision. There is also that which belongs to the soul toward the things spoken: the painful things in the intelligible world. We have strength, such as to no longer look upon painful things. Contemplating the soul itself, he will certainly demonstrate its life: that strength and power are the same from the beginning. But the sensible painful things are unsparing. Because the form is the beauty that flows down. How then are the passions good by nature, even if there were beauty? Opinion and writing and form—clear beauty, a beautiful form—all things are noble. And that which might become, is because there is a beginning and a generation; because even in the intellectual movement, every activity and life is **The Good**.

<summary>Plotinus explores the distinction between the suffering "animal" life of the body and the serene, contemplative life of the Intellect. He argues that while the soul experiences pain when tied to the physical world, its true essence and "The Good" are found in returning to the activity of pure thought.</summary>

# · for the sake of · 4 · H

... tree. Thus, even the act of <unclear>thinking</unclear> <note>original: "νοεῖν"; the intellectual activity of the mind.</note> is <unclear>never</unclear> forced <term>forced</term> <note>original: "βίαιον"; also translated as "violent" or "compulsory," referring to an action that comes from an outside source rather than one's own nature.</note>. For even fire would never be forced, nor would the tree. And if the tree is not, neither is the soul of the tree. For the soul of the tree is never, nor would it ever be, forced. But if the tree is not, neither is the animal. Thus, neither would the soul of the animal ever be forced. And if this is not forced, neither would that of a human; and if not this, neither would that of the rational being. And if not this, neither would that of the intellect <term>intellect</term> <note>original: "νοῦς"; the higher, divine faculty of reason in Neoplatonic thought.</note>. Consequently, neither is the act of thinking forced, nor the act of willing. Thus, even the voluntary <term>voluntary</term> <note>original: "ἑκούσιον"; that which is done of one's own accord.</note> is not forced. But if the voluntary is not forced, neither is the involuntary. And if the involuntary is not, then the forced would not exist at all. But if the forced did not exist, neither would the involuntary exist. Consequently, neither would the voluntary; and if not the voluntary, neither would the act of willing. Thus, neither would thinking. But thinking could never be forced. Thus, neither could willing. And if willing is not forced, neither is the voluntary. If not the voluntary, neither the involuntary. If not the involuntary, neither the forced. But if the forced did not exist, neither would the All <term>the All</term> <note>original: "τὸ πᾶν"; the totality of the universe or the cosmos.</note> exist. Which is absurd. Therefore, it is a necessity that the forced exists in some way. In this way, then, it is a necessity that the forced exists. And if the forced exists, both the voluntary will exist and the involuntary. And if the voluntary exists, then willing will also exist. And if willing exists, then thinking will exist. And if thinking exists, then the rational will exist. And if the rational exists, then the soul of a human. And if this exists, then also that of an animal; and if this, then also that of a tree; and if this, then also nature. And if nature exists, then also matter; and if matter, then essence; and if essence, then being. And if being exists, then also the Monad <term>Monad</term> <note>original: "μονάς"; the principle of unity or the number one, often identified with the source of all things.</note>; and if the Monad, then also the One; and if the One, then the All. Consequently, if the forced exists, then the All exists. Therefore, the forced exists.

<meta>This page transitions from the logical proof regarding voluntary and involuntary actions into a deeper psychological inquiry. Plotinus is now examining whether the soul itself "suffers" or undergoes change when the body experiences "passions" (emotions or physical sensations). This continues the theme of the soul’s independence from material compulsion.</meta>

# Ennead III.7 | Ennead III.8

Is it then from the **intellect**, or perhaps from some **form**? Or let us say it is from some kind of intellect. These matters were investigated by many of those who came before us, and always in very different ways—though they might seem to agree on the same opinion. However, I would not say quite that. Instead, our discourse must address what this soul actually is for us, and how we might describe it as something clearly distinct. Is this not what we are seeking? Or rather, are we seeking the things within it? How should we describe it, or the things belonging to it, or the things that come from it? And then, in this way, we must always seek the things that pertain to us. 

If this is so, I would not say the soul is "in nature" in the sense of being entirely within this world. For the nature within this world bears witness to this. It is not simply the soul in the world, but rather that the things within the world belong to the soul. These things follow nature and specific natures. But these, in turn, belong to the soul—not according to the nature found in the body, but according to the soul's own nature. For that which is "according to nature" <term>according to nature</term> <note>original: "κατὰ φύσιν"; referring to the inherent blueprint or proper functioning of a thing.</note> in this body is not the same as that which is "according to nature" in the soul, nor is it the same for the perceptive faculty. 

If this is the case, would the things belonging to the soul also exist in this way? First, there are the things that belong to the soul in itself. Then there are those belonging to sensation, or those belonging to desire, or those that are "according to nature" within it—as if a living being <term>living being</term> <note>original: "ζῶον"; can refer to a physical animal or the metaphysical concept of an "Animated Being."</note> came from the Living Being. Or what sort of living beings are they? Or do they only seem to be so? What, then, are these things in themselves, just as the things of the intellect possess a soul? Or is it not like that? How then shall we speak? Is it because they are also in this perceptive realm? Our discourse rests on this hypothesis: does the soul receive things toward itself according to its own nature, or does it receive things from itself? Or perhaps it receives the things from itself that are already within it? And will this also be the case? 

Why then is it like this? Or would we not speak of the soul itself? Is there also a perceptive part? Or is it not within the soul? And because it is a living being, how could it be? For if the "Living Being Itself" is not there, then the things of the soul do not exist. How then are they primary? Is it that the soul is not itself a living being? Or is the living being merely an opinion? Or are these "forms" of the soul? And the soul itself—is it not impossible for it to be a specific soul, or a life-giving one? Or is it that the "Living Being" is a whole? In that it is a living being, it also belongs to the soul. Indeed, it belongs entirely to the soul. But these are also forms of the soul. Is it because it is within it? Or is the whole faculty of sensation a single thing? Or is it because the soul is "in a body"? Is the living being then formed this way? Or is it not a living being? Or is the soul itself the living being? Not this, but rather the "Primary Living Being." Or are these again things of the soul? Is it not so? Or is the soul not directed toward it, or toward the things of sensation, or toward the things of desire? 

And is it so then? Is there **movement** within it? Or **activity**? Or the state of being moved? Or how is its primary part? And is it the same for the things that truly exist (for these are moved)? Or in the soul, how are the things within it? And is it the same? Or is it not moved (for those other things are moved)? Or could the things in the soul that belong to it become a kind of movement? Or is it not a movement that "suffers" <term>suffers</term> <note>original: "παθομένη"; from 'pathos,' meaning to be acted upon or to experience a passion.</note>? This seems clear. For through its own "passions" <term>passions</term> <note>original: "παθῶν"; affections, emotions, or states where the subject is passive.</note> it says that it is a certain living being, or a soul that suffers. Or is it that we are this way? Or that the soul itself suffers the things belonging to the body? Or do both experience these passions?

<column-break/>

And is it moved by the body? Or does it receive something when the body is moved? But neither is the case; for it must not be this way, so that the "other" part is not moved, nor is anything turned, but rather the whole must be transformed. It is necessary, then, that this be either an "outgrowth" of the one who suffers, how should one say, or a "birth." 

But **sensation** is not a passion; it is an **activity** <term>activity</term> <note>original: "ἐνέργεια"; a state of being in action or operation, contrasted with being passive.</note> of judgment regarding the passions. I am now speaking of the sensation concerning the body. For sensation itself is not "suffering" <term>πάσχουσα</term> something in this world, but it possesses a "work" or "function." This is most vital: we must not suppose that **judgments** are passions, but rather that they are activities. The soul itself does not suffer; even if it did, it would be a kind of activity. And if one were to trace this back to the same point, sensation has not "produced" the soul, but rather judgment and sensation exist within the soul. 

Most of all, one must think about the passions in the soul as if they were something else, namely **movement** and **activity** within it. For one would not be wrong if they were to call the passions regarding desires or appetites—or even the "desiring faculty" itself and generally everything concerning the body—passions. For nothing moves us except impulses or movements. But to say that these things "happen" to the soul, or are certain movements or passions, is not even so. Rather, it is that "whole" of the soul by which we exist. And the primary things of the body are like this: both **pleasures** and **pains**. Or is the desiring faculty in the soul, within the perceptive faculty itself, or is it directed toward the body? 

What then? Is such a movement "according to nature" or "contrary to nature"? Perhaps the one is in the body, but the activity itself is in the soul. And it is the soul itself. Now we must also posit the opposite: that there is a certain "nature" of the soul, just as if one were to say there is judgment within it, or movements, or the sensation of these things. Or even its own movements or appetites. Since there are changes or appetites toward what is "according to nature," and again pains—though the soul has nothing of these itself, they are in the body. As for the passions, one would not call them "forms." Thus it might be said that the soul lives in a certain way. However, it does not change because of this. 

For even among external things, some have a perceptive faculty in living beings. Or the "passion" is contrary to the soul itself, yet it moves toward the perceptive faculty. For a **judgment** is never produced *by* the passion itself. Nothing prevents the soul from being moved because of a passion, yet the judgment is what responds to the passion; therefore, this judgment is not itself a passion. Consequently, neither the perceptive power nor the desiring power is among the "passive" things. And even if they are directed toward the body, it is not in that way—or at least very little. Perhaps they are in the body in that way because of the things that belong to the body. For we must say that these are not passions but **judgments**, just as we treat opinions. 

Such things, even those directed toward the body, do not belong to the soul; rather, they are directed toward judgments, or are like those directed toward the perceptive faculty. But even after those things, they are perhaps in the soul. They become "works," such as the things they are, or the things concerning them. Or even further, they are those things that are persuaded, or the "lives" that exist with them. And regarding such souls—lest they be "un-yoked" or again persuaded—and the things concerning the passions, it would not seem to be so. But the soul itself must be discussed: the passions are said to exist "before" it, or they concern pleasures and so forth; or they are in it as if in a certain "subject" <term>subject</term> <note>original: "ὑποκειμένω"; the underlying substance or substrate in which qualities exist.</note>; or they are like certain "natures."

<summary>Plotinus argues that while the body undergoes "passions" (physical sensations and emotions), the soul remains essentially impassive. He redefines sensation not as a passive reception of pain or pleasure, but as an active "judgment" (krisis) and "activity" (energeia) of the soul.</summary>
<keywords>soul, body, passions, sensation, activity, judgment, desire, Neoplatonism, Plotinus, impassivity, movement</keywords>

# The Enneads | Book IV

But if it also concerns this, doing something identical to what appeared, from the sensible <note>original: "αἰσθητοῦ"; referring to the world of the five senses.</note>. First, it is necessary that a sensible object exists within the universe, according to the constitution of the whole. For just as with the living being, so it is with what is in the living being. It is nothing else, but rather perceptions. As we have said: if their existence comes from the universe and provides perception, or if a perceptive faculty arises in them. For that which is implanted by the universe—how has it not given a sensible object to the living being, or something directed toward the sensible? It does not make other things, while other things simply exist. And according to the sensible object, it is an evil for the living being itself; yet it exists with the universe, and for this reason: so that it might exist and because it was necessary; but not because of this specific nature. Rather, it appeared upon the nature of the sensible. 

And it will appear itself, if it is among sensible things. So that even sensible things would not exist in living beings as mere opinion in the perceptions of the senses. For these exist so that they are like the things in living beings. If indeed forms <term>forms</term> <note>original: "εἴδη"; the eternal archetypes or blueprints of things.</note> exist outside. For it says this material thing is neither sensible nor such as to be nothing; or rather that it is the sensible, or that which is in the living being. Consequently, it says these perceptions are of sensible things. 

But perhaps the same forms are not in the sensible things which, being present, make the soul similar to them. And when they are not present, the soul imagines those very things within itself, and perception seems to belong to the living being, yet it is for the soul. As has been said, perception belongs to the soul of the living being. Since it is for the soul, these affections of the living being arise from there. Thus, perception is directed toward the sensible of the sensible object, just as external things or those within the soul; and so the universe is composed of these. But that perception is composed of those; yet some are not perceptive. What then, is there an absence of sensation in some things that follow nature? 

Nature belongs to the soul, but the heavens do not belong to the sensible. But this is because, just as these things are, those things which never belong to perception. Or the living being arises. And those things directed toward these appear. If then, from that which the living being comes, there should be some living being (the sensible is taken up). If this is the fitting thing, not hoping to say <note>The OCR "πεῖν" (to drink) is likely a transcription error for "εἰπεῖν" (to say) in this philosophical context.</note> what is in the soul, but because this man would not be according to himself, or because he is sensible, and thus a sensible part of the universe. If it becomes similar to the soul in its affections, how can there be perception again? If indeed this comes from it—itself from the sensible. So that what comes from it is sensible, but not evil. It would still be sensible in the universe. Or even perceptive. Or because it itself becomes sensible or perceptive. If it says to the living being, if indeed it is perceptive, or has perceptive faculties—none of them, if it is itself, is the whole itself. Upon all these things, it already exists. For him, every perceptive faculty is the cause of opinion. But if he is perceptive, he becomes subject to affections and leaves them behind, or even himself, from which...

<column-break/>

...from the universe, and the same, if one happens to know it from the whole sensible world—such as this perception—for nowhere was an alteration through external things admitted into the living being. The sensible is something, or a body, such as that which exists; but the sensible in the living being, or the body, was admitted because it moves itself, but the element of the imagination <term>imagination</term> <note>original: "φανταστοῦ"; the faculty of forming mental images.</note> was cast in. 

If this is so, it performs its activity in its own part; but the whole will not leave it behind. For if the sensible itself is what is left to the living being, it produces it in the whole of what belongs to it. Secondly, from all things, so as to receive the sensible, because the living being arises from the impulse from which knowledge also comes, not just the affections. If the affections are necessary for perception, one must seek the organ of the sensible because the organ is there; but if they are toward external things, it is required that they not be in one's own parts, so that we may have sensible objects as we do. 

If we have these, a similar perception requires imagination; but notions <gloss>and</gloss> the things from the perception of the living being are directed toward that where the sensible object will be. If the sensible is in the living being, the whole living being is still moved by thinking, so that not even the whole living being is always the universe; unless the living being is within it, it would not have perception. If there is perception, it will itself be a certain kind of external alteration in the sensible, and thus there is a removal of the name shared with sensible things. 

For while the sensible and perception are the same, the external things are the beginning, but the sensible in the reasoning <term>reasoning</term> <note>original: "λογισμῷ"; the discursive activity of the mind.</note> is a sensible thing of the soul. But indeed, also that which is in the body, and perceptions are affections <note>original: "παθήματα"; things that the body or soul undergoes or suffers from outside stimuli.</note>; where this [perception] might be, it is in nothing of those things in the soul. For they belong to neither the soul that suffers with the body, nor to the body itself when it suffers. But these voices belong to both. If indeed matter exists in the universe, so that for us the living being will be nothing of the universe from the sensible. 

But the rational principle <term>rational principle</term> <note>original: "λόγος"; the formative and ordering principle of reality.</note> itself is incorporeal, even if the sensible is in the universe. For the one who fashioned it should not be... and the same things happen to them from one of the shared perceptions. But she <gloss>and</gloss> herself to set aside becoming, she is imagination or apart from perception. That which is from the cause belongs to the soul. These things too are clearer. If it is still possible to grasp, it is evident that it is sought in the soul, or a sensible soul. This is what is in the living being. Furthermore, the living being—that which has suffered this—is not the whole. Rather, either the whole living being is separate, or the soul's part is separate. Whether the living being is in the rational principle, it would not possess the soul's part; perceptions are at no specific place, or even in some... but the living being is something else. 

These matters are in accordance with the philosophy from the beginning. This is so, since the living being is generated by the universe. In these things, it seems to me. It speaks many things of the soul; or at least to me, these things belong to the soul, but the soul itself is matter...

Nor is the knowledge of its own essence excluded.

The unjust man <note>original: "ἄδικος" (adikos); one who violates the law or fairness.</note> acts toward his friend with **greed** <term>greed</term> <note>original: "πλεονεκτικόν" (pleonektikon); the specific vice of wanting more than one's fair share of goods or less than one's share of burdens.</note>. The unjust man becomes unjust, but not everyone who does wrong is so in relation to the living being, but rather as being someone else. For this is the concept of the unjust. It is necessary from where he holds it, or how, that he alone is the cause of it. These things, then, are clear as parts. But this is not always the case. Of the virtues, one is oriented toward others; for it is the **most beautiful of virtues**, because virtue is not only useful to oneself, but also when practiced toward another. That which is toward another does not come from everything. # Theophilus, Part 9

->**On the Nature of Movement and the Spirit**<-

Here we ask: why is a living being able to move without any external force being applied? For it moves solely from within itself. Inanimate objects, however, do not move from themselves, but only by some external application or through a change of location, which does not belong to their internal essence. The living being <term>living being</term> <note>original: "ζῶον" (zōon); encompasses all sentient animals, often contrasted here with plants.</note> moves and grows from itself. Furthermore, it moves through alteration or the specific movement of the body. In this regard, the living being moves even after taking nourishment, and after the waste is expelled from the body. Again, this is because the **spirit** <term>spirit</term> <note>original: "πνεῦμα" (pneuma); in ancient medicine, this is a physical "breath" or "vapor" that carries life-force through the arteries and nerves.</note> is present here, due to the vital power. The spirit is the cause. For every living being possesses movement because of the spirit. 

This spirit is vaporized from food; therefore, blooded animals possess spirit. Because this spirit is the cause of life itself, it provides movement to living beings. From the vaporization and movement of the spirit, through its "outflows," the living beings appear to have movement. For he says that the outflows of the spirit, which travel from the brain into the body, occur through the nerves. And thus, living beings move. 

We say, however, that the spirit is not the primary cause of movement, but acts as an **instrument** <note>original: "ὄργανον" (organon); a tool or vessel used by a higher power.</note>. For the soul, which is in the body, is that which truly moves it. The spirit is merely its instrument. Because of this, when the soul is separated, the living being remains motionless. The spirit within the body remains for a time even after the soul's separation. Furthermore, plants are nourished and grow, yet they possess neither soul <note>In this context, the author refers to the "sensitive" or "animal" soul, rather than the "nutritive" soul.</note> nor spirit. Spirit resides in the blood. Plants are bloodless; therefore, they do not have spirit. How then are they nourished and how do they grow? We say it is through **nature** <term>nature</term> <note>original: "φύσις" (physis); here meaning the unconscious biological force of growth, distinct from the conscious soul.</note>. For nature in plants is that which nourishes and causes growth. 

Spirit is unique to animals, specifically to blooded animals. Bloodless animals do not have spirit. However, we may say that bloodless animals possess a certain spirit analogous to blood. Just as blooded creatures have spirit because of their blood, so too bloodless creatures have spirit because of their blood-analogue. For everything that lives must necessarily have spirit—but some have it in the primary sense, and others in a secondary sense. Furthermore, spirit is vaporized from food. The primary food in animals is liquid. All moisture, when vaporized, creates spirit. Therefore, spirit is in all animals. One might say that plants also have liquid nourishment, and therefore must have spirit in them. We respond that spirit, in its true sense, is in animals. In plants, there is no spirit in the true sense, but rather a certain **vapor** or **exhalation** <note>original: "ἀτμίς ἢ ἀναθυμίασις" (atmis ē anathymiasis).</note>. Even if it were called spirit, it is not the same kind of spirit as that found in animals. Furthermore, the spirit is cooled through breathing. Plants do not breathe; therefore, they do not have spirit. This has been said to demonstrate the necessity of the spirit.

<column-break/>

Regarding life, it seems that well-being is the goal of life. If this is so, it is clear that all growth, nourishment, birth, and decay occur through spirit. One might argue that plants are also of the essence of spirit. For plants live, grow, are nourished, and reproduce. Certainly. If this is so, why do you not grant spirit to plants? Certainly. But while growth, nourishment, and reproduction exist in plants, it has never been said that spirit is in plants, just as it is not said that soul is in plants. Nevertheless, the **nature** or power in plants—nourishing, growing, and reproducing them—is a spirit. For it is not without spirit. 

But what is the spirit? Spirit is a certain subtle substance, or a vapor vaporized from food. If the spirit is a subtle substance, it might appear in plants. But what of this? If it happens that spirit exists within blood, and plants do not have blood, then for this reason they do not have spirit. However, one might say there is spirit even in plants. For if plants are nourished, grow, and reproduce, and all growth, nourishment, and reproduction require spirit, then plants must also have spirit. What then? We say that spirit is nothing other than that which is **innate to the blood**. Everything that has blood also has spirit. But how can a plant have it, being entirely bloodless? 

We say, then, that nourishment and growth are not simply the work of spirit, but specifically the transformation of blood into flesh. For this reason, blooded creatures are primarily said to have spirit. Moreover, the spirit is the instrument of the soul’s activity. But the soul is not in plants. Therefore, neither is the spirit. For the power that exists in plants—the nutritive and augmentative—is not the "soul," but "nature." Even if it were called soul, it would not be so in the true sense. Furthermore, the spirit serves the soul for the activities of the sense organs. Plants do not have sense organs; therefore, they have no spirit. In this way, we say that spirit is not in plants. 

If someone should say that spirit is even in inanimate things, such as in metals, we say that it is not called spirit in the true sense, but rather a vapor or exhalation. Even if it were called spirit, it is not the same kind of spirit found in animals. Furthermore, the spirit is cooled and nourished through breathing. Plants do not breathe; thus, they do not have spirit. This is said to show the use of the spirit. Therefore, the ancients used to say that the spirit is the cause of life. And in general, the spirit in the body and the soul are the same thing. Some said that spirit was the **air** breathed in from the outside. But **Aristotle** says that spirit is not the external air, but the **innate heat** <note>original: "σύμφυτον θερμότητα" (symphyton thermotēta); a central concept in Aristotle's biology regarding the internal warmth that drives life.</note> dwelling within animals. This, he says, is the spirit, which is also analogous to the **ether** <note>The "fifth element" that makes up the heavens.</note>. Some call the soul itself "spirit," as the **divine oracles** <note>A common way for Byzantine scholars to refer to the Holy Scriptures.</note> also say: 

> "God is spirit, and the Holy Spirit." <note>original: "πνεῦμα ὁ θεός, καὶ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον" (pneuma ho theos, kai pneuma to hagion); references to John 4:24 and the Nicene Creed.</note>

But now our discussion concerns the **physical spirit**.

<note>Vocabulary: spirit, soul, nature, growth, nourishment, living being, plant, Aristotle, blood, blooded, breathing, exhalation.</note>

Senses as it perceives, because the Intellect perceives. <margin>of itself</margin>

# II. On Speaking #

But if it happens thus, so that the necessary things exist, because of the **beautiful** <term>beautiful</term> <note>original: "καλὸν" (kalon); often synonymous with "the Good" in Platonic thought.</note> and the useful... that which is profitable to the Soul, or it is necessary to rejoice in the body itself. Thus even now, for each day, in the **mire** <note>original: "βορβόρῳ" (borborō); Plotinus frequently uses the image of "mud" or "mire" to describe the soul's entrapment in the gross materiality of the physical world.</note>. Because of this, the sensation of the Soul, and that which is intended within it by its power.
Just as light—this very thing of objects, this very All—since through it
<margin>himself</margin>
it contemplates itself, through itself. Why then, the Soul being before the body, is it likely that it contemplates itself in sensation? Why does it not see the **form** <term>form</term> <note>original: "μορφήν" (morphēn); the outward shape or manifestation.</note> within the Soul, nor the image of it within itself—that of the world—but sees it outside? For the things within must not be with us. So that even if one were about to turn toward the things outside... and because that which is in nature is also in the All. Because of this, experience is sensible to us, and thus because that which is in the All is of power, to the one who unites. But if upon the All itself, for even this Soul has become essence. Since it follows essence in this way, and in this very thing
is the essence, these images so as to become, enjoying the thing in itself, in the All, by that which generates from itself and out of it. So that the uniting principle is as nature and sensation, so that the nature of the All is thus, and again the images are the better things. It is said, that Soul and sensation and nature are mixed with things, lest there be anything for it, which by that which is in it is that which becomes for the All. And the things of it are images in essence, and the things in it, but there is that which

world, and that which is in contemplation. But this is not that one. For whether it is nature or Soul,

For it has come here. And after a short while. Because of this (as if), according to the truth it even comes to be of the seeming. The others, again, it seems perhaps to divide even of him. It is natural.

For he will place these same things. Female to all things nothing greater, like a **prayer** <term>prayer</term> <note>original: "εὐχῇ" (eukhē); here suggesting an alignment of the will with the cosmic order.</note>. These things also by himself. In this way also the natures of the kings. The others, I do not say. That which is as if it were either parts or the same ones, all things are constituted. Having obtained nature and fortune. These—all things indeed the whole is seen no longer yet the whole life of the universe. The same **soulless** <note>original: "ἄψυχον" (apsychon).</note> thing of those within it, and yet by impulses. And just as if a **guardian spirit** <term>guardian spirit</term> <note>original: "δαίμονι" (daimoni); a mediating spirit between the human and divine realms.</note> outside if it were nothing. The others as greater. The others, which always has from around as if, as if a fitting equal. After the equal he lets go. That which is lacking, the same of itself is manifest. What remains is your own of nature. So that therefore the thing of the whole and the **collective whole** <note>original: "συμπαντός" (sympantos).</note> is not less, and he spares equally; nor by being persuaded by a prayer, both of the whole, and they are constituted around the whole. And the greater things of him upon the same worth. For I have learned many things. And concerning the things of the gods likewise; if also of the whole either care or grace. The others, even according to the whole. To cease by power concerning as if of the soul. The others, of those changing. For also the things because of him. He is pious in many things and not clearly. But he has of them even if he has something by these prayers.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of ethical development. Although the source metadata identifies this as Plotinus, the text is actually from Aristotle’s Nicomachean Ethics, Book II, Chapters 3 and 4. It transitions from how habits are formed to the role of pleasure and pain as the ultimate indicators of a person's character.</meta>

# Ethics, Book II

...and they are produced from the same sources and through the same means, and are likewise destroyed; and their activities will be the same. This is also the case with other more visible things, such as strength: for it comes from taking much nourishment and enduring many labors, and the strong man would be most capable of doing these very things. It is the same with the virtues: for by abstaining from pleasures we become **temperate** <term>temperate</term> <note>original: "σώφρονες" (sōphrones); describing someone with "sophrosyne," a state of self-control and balance.</note>, and having become so, we are most able to abstain from them. It is similar with courage; for by being habituated to despise fearful things and to endure them, we become brave, and having become so, we will be most able to endure fearful things.

<meta>catchword: sign</meta>

<column-break/>

We must take as a sign of **states of character** <term>states of character</term> <note>original: "ἕξεων" (hexeōn); refers to a stable disposition or habit of the soul.</note> the pleasure or pain that follows upon deeds. For the person who abstains from bodily pleasures and finds joy in this very thing is temperate, while the person who is vexed by it is **intemperate** <term>intemperate</term> <note>original: "ἀκόλαστος" (akolastos); one who lacks restraint and is "unchastened."</note>. Likewise, the person who endures terrifying things and finds joy, or at least no pain, is brave, while the person who feels pain is a coward. For moral virtue is concerned with pleasures and pains. Because of pleasure we do base things, and because of pain we abstain from noble things. Therefore, one must be led in a certain way from youth, as **Plato** <note>A reference to Plato's *Laws*, where he emphasizes that education is the process of training children to hate what they should hate and love what they should love.</note> says, so as to feel joy and pain at the right things; for this is the right education. Furthermore, if virtues are concerned with actions and passions, and every passion and every action is followed by pleasure and pain, for this reason also virtue would be concerned with pleasures and pains. Punishments also demonstrate this, as they are administered through these means; for they are a kind of medical cure, and medical cures naturally occur through opposites. Further, as we said before, every state of the soul has a nature related to and concerned with the kinds of things by which it is naturally made better or worse. Character becomes base through pleasures and pains—by pursuing or fleeing them, either those one should not, or when one should not, or how one should not, or in whatever other way such things are defined by **reason** <term>reason</term> <note>original: "λόγου" (logou); the rational principle or logic that guides ethical behavior.</note>. For this reason, some even define the virtues as certain states of **impassivity** <term>impassivity</term> <note>original: "ἀπαθείας" (apatheias); a state of being "without passion," often associated with the Stoic ideal of being unmoved by emotion.</note> and tranquility; but they do not speak well, because they speak in absolute terms, and not "as one should" or "as one should not," and "when," and other such additions. It is assumed, then, that virtue is such as to be productive of the best things concerning pleasures and pains, and vice the opposite.

<margin>G: <note>Likely a shorthand marking a specific commentary section or a "Gnomon" (rule/guide).</note></margin>

This might also become clear to us from the following: there being three things that lead to choice and three that lead to avoidance—the **noble** <term>noble</term> <note>original: "καλοῦ" (kalou); that which is fine, beautiful, or morally excellent.</note>, the advantageous, and the pleasant; and three opposites—the shameful, the harmful, and the painful—the good person is likely to succeed in all these, while the bad person is likely to fail, especially concerning pleasure. For pleasure is common to all living creatures and accompanies all things that fall under choice; for even the noble and the advantageous appear pleasant. Moreover, it has grown up with all of us from infancy; hence it is difficult to wash away this feeling that is **deeply dyed** <note>original: "ἐγκεχρωσμένον" (engechrōsmenon); metaphorically meaning stained or saturated into the very fabric of human life.</note> into our life. We also regulate our actions, some more and some less, by pleasure and pain. For this reason, it is necessary that our entire study be concerned with these; for it is of no small importance for our actions whether we feel joy and pain well or badly. Further, it is harder to fight against pleasure than against **anger** <term>anger</term> <note>original: "θυμῷ" (thymō); spiritedness or hot-headedness.</note>, as **Heraclitus** <note>Heraclitus of Ephesus (c. 535 – c. 475 BCE), a pre-Socratic philosopher known for his paradoxical sayings; the quote suggests pleasure is a more insidious opponent than temper.</note> says, and both art and virtue are always concerned with what is harder; for even excellence is better in this. So for this reason also, the entire study of virtue and politics is concerned with pleasures and pains; for the one who uses these well will be good, and the one who uses them badly will be bad. Let it be said, then, that virtue is concerned with pleasures and pains, and that it is increased by those same things from which it is produced, and is destroyed if they are not done in the same way, and that its activities are concerned with the same things from which it arose.

...he had leisure. For, in order that the first of the philosophers might not be blamed for having touched upon these very causes <note>original: "αἰτίων" (aitiōn); in Aristotelian philosophy, these are the 'reasons why' something exists or changes.</note> randomly and by chance, he spoke regarding their causes as if one could not reasonably attribute blame to them. Having been eager to care for these causes, their works were made manifest and beyond dispute. They took care for these causes, making all their own things perceptible to the senses; and through the most widespread of the perceptible things, the first and greatest matters became apparent to them. But God, regarding whom he has decided to show the **principles** <term>principles</term> <note>original: "ἀρχὰς" (archas); the starting points or fundamental origins of reality.</note> of things through all these living and universal matters, demonstrates in this way that they would not be equal to perceptible things. For this reasoning gives much weight to the **Reason** <term>Reason</term> <note>original: "Λόγῳ" (Logō); can mean word, reason, or the rational structure of the universe.</note> regarding his own nature. For the things belonging to men are not clearly manifest even to those men themselves. Those things which are <unclear>likened</unclear> to God are thus. One must look at the nature of God himself concerning the generation of the cosmos. For that which he renders along with God is the **naturalist** <note>original: "φυσικόν" (physikon); one who studies nature (physics).</note>. For this reason, all the Greeks attach the first and greatest works to God. And for this reason, they say the cosmos is a God, because it is as if that one made this world; for it was not possible otherwise unless it were in God, and through whom this cosmos truly is what it is. But also concerning causes, as we said, they wrote everything. If they did not have a cause, it would not be spoken of in this way to them. Wherefore he says even the young philosophers ought not to be content with sight alone when asking about natural things, but also with reason, so that they might be able to find them in this way. But since the name of "cause" is spoken of in two ways (for it signifies both the "that by which" and the "for the sake of which"), how then does the naturalist define it? One must say that this is the thing of which nature is the cause or in which it exists. For from where does generation have its cause, and why is the generation of irrational animals not within themselves? For this is how natural things are. If the matter is so, the **instrument** <note>original: "ὄργανον" (organon); an tool or bodily organ used to achieve an end.</note> serves this; since the instrument of each is such, for this reason it is an instrument. All things, such as this instrument, are this productive reason, so that by doing all the things he saw, they might make a demonstration from things that are clear and manifest. For in this way are the majority of works, which mostly come to be. It has been called a part. But must one call it the thing itself or some part of the soul? But also regarding being a soul, is it in matter, or is it separable? If it is matter, we say, it is not even able to be. But all things concerning contraries have this as a property. This was necessary, but it only needs its own specific nature, so as to think themselves to be causes of the fact that it is not only by not being or having the cause, that the living being is in no way able to have within itself the reason of the soul and the body. Whence there is no resolution from the things said.

<column-break/>

Nor as much as is needed, but let him who has obtained his own prize take it. This is what is fitting for God alone; among the powers in the soul. According to these things, therefore, one may also speak of the divine property in relation to the living being. For soul is not only such a thing; soul is also the **perceptive** part <note>original: "αἰσθητικόν" (aisthētikon); the faculty of the soul responsible for sensation.</note>, by which all animals exist. Of the parts of the living being, some are material, such as the sense organs, and others are immaterial. <margin>Note</margin> Concerning the **Intellect** <term>Intellect</term> <note>original: "νοῦ" (nou/nous); the highest part of the soul, capable of rational thought.</note> we shall speak again. The beginning of motion for it is from **potentiality** <term>potentiality</term> <note>original: "δυνάμεως" (dynameōs); the capacity to become or do something.</note> and **actuality** <term>actuality</term> <note>original: "ἐντελεχείας" (entelecheias); the state of being complete or in active operation.</note>. Generally, the release of such a thing seems to be its activity, but it is not. For as many things as we say have intellect come from it. And so too with matter, as it seems to be, do not seek the thing itself, or such as it is in matter. Having the reason for the sake of which, it is led back to this. If then it is so, then concerning the things said. It seems that even the things in time are perceptible. Because he who defined this world, in one way said it is this, and in another way that it is not. Wherefore they are not perceptible, but how are we able to know these things? All these things some might say logically. And for this reason many of the animals would not even have time. There are many things that come to be in sequence. It is later, and after this. But again, it is not like the natural state of each. This is like the fact that it does not even <unclear>become</unclear>, at least in this way. One part is the passive by nature. We saw, and how he himself assigns motion, and as many things as concern it. This motion is not <unclear>properly</unclear> spoken of regarding the particular perceptible things. Whence also the naturalists speak. For this generation is a manifestation of certain passions, of each thing, and of each. Whether the soul ever comes to be for itself or not, we shall say. Whatever the "being" of the soul is, each is destroyed. Each is not persuaded. It is either in the soul, and these again are specific things. The things of the passions of the soul are not so at all.

### On Sleep
<margin>Note</margin>
Concerning the cause of sleep and waking, through which each of them happens, and which part of the soul is properly **sensation** <note>original: "αἴσθησις" (aisthēsis); the act of perceiving through the senses.</note>, whether the cause is in the sensitive part of the soul or not. This is now manifest. For the other passions of the soul, such as desire, have a reason, and such is this motion of the soul. Since, then, sleeping is nothing for the living being other than to sleep or to wake, the one is being deprived of sensation, and the other is the capacity for it, as if by itself. For he who does not have it does not sleep. The activity is the sensitive one, and again, that which is sensitive. Since we saw this, that: for we perceive that we see and that we hear. For he who sees perceives something. It is necessary either to perceive by sight that one sees, or by some other sense.

# · Generation · Book 2 · 46

...not because of human nature; this must be understood in the same way. But even before his **incarnation** <term>incarnation</term> <note>original: "ἐνανθρωπήσεως" (enanthrōpēseōs); literally "becoming human," referring to the Word taking on flesh.</note>, he says that the Word himself exists in the form of God. And so, in the very being of the Divine, we find both the divine form and all the divine **attributes** <note>original: "ἰδιώματα" (idiōmata); the distinct properties or characteristics that belong to the divine nature.</note>. One should not, however, seek to find what sort or how many these divine forms are, so that we do not project human qualities onto the Divine. Rather, it is enough to know that God, who is, gives all things their appropriate forms through those things which are His own. This much is clear: He possesses a form not because of our need, but because of His own being. For even if God had not created us, He would nonetheless possess His own form. For before creation came into being, God existed and possessed His own form. Indeed, if He did not have form, He would not exist in being; thus, He possesses His own form not for our sake, but for His own.

But if someone says that one cannot speak of "form" in the case of God, they are clearly not speaking the truth. For if He does not have form, how can He give form to all existing things? For every maker creates according to his own form. God, therefore, created all things according to the forms proper to Him. But someone might say: while it is true that God exists in a form, He does not possess form in the same way as created beings. This is correctly said. For God does not have form like created things do, nor does He share the same nature as them. Rather, God Himself possesses the divine form, and He holds this within Himself. Regarding created beings, some possess form in **actuality** <note>original: "ἐνεργείᾳ" (energeia); being in a state of active expression.</note> and others in **potentiality** <note>original: "δυνάμει" (dynamei); the capacity to become or be formed.</note>. In this way, created things differ from God: other things possess form by **participation** <term>participation</term> <note>original: "μετοχῇ" (metochē); the philosophical idea that worldly things exist only by 'sharing' in a higher reality.</note>, but God Himself possesses form as His very **essence** <term>essence</term> <note>original: "οὐσίαν" (ousian); the fundamental 'what-ness' or substance of a thing.</note>. This is why the Apostle said that He "subsists in the form of God." He did not say "having a form," but "being in a form," to show that in God Himself, being and form are one. And just as His being is, so His form is: infinite and **incomprehensible** <note>original: "ἀκατάληπτος" (akatalēptos); that which cannot be fully grasped or 'seized' by the human mind.</note>. So too is His **energy** <term>energy</term> <note>original: "ἐνέργεια" (energeia); the active power or operation of God as distinct from His hidden essence.</note> infinite; for His very being is a kind of energy. If His energy is infinite, His being is infinite, and His form is infinite. His energy, which creates all things, is a kind of form, and this too is infinite. Every maker creates according to his own form; if God created all things, He created them according to His own forms. One should not wonder if God has forms or how He has them, for it is clear that He has them. If He did not, He could not have created things in their various forms. The essence of God contains every form, and thus all things are in it, and all things came from it. This form of God is not like the forms of created things—which both are and are not—but is eternal and always the same. For nothing existing in God has "non-being"; everything in God is eternal. If these forms are in God, they are eternal, and every form in God is His very being. It is not that essence is one thing and form another; rather, as His being is, so is His form. If this is so, it is clear that God possessed these forms before the ages. Therefore, the Apostle said this:

<column-break/>

that He exists in the form of God both in being, in nature, and in attributes. We might also say that the works of painters exist in a state of being. But if someone argues that painted works do not possess the nature of the things whose form they carry, but are forms only in appearance and not in reality, they are nonetheless real insofar as they are named through them. For we would say that things in an image do not appear truly in any way. We call it an "image"—a composition of different colors—even though we say it has the "form" of the person depicted. In this way, the truly real God, who possesses His own forms from Himself, does not proceed in a mechanical way. He proceeds with light—for He is called Light—having within Himself the vital and intellectual powers which are, as it were, "in His hand." For this reason, the Father is Light through His activity; and the things provided in the light are nothing other than the light itself. His form is nothing other than His light. Thus, this **Intelligible Sun** <term>Intelligible Sun</term> <note>A Neoplatonic metaphor for the Divine Mind or the Source of all truth and being, which illuminates the mind as the physical sun illuminates the eyes.</note> and its rays are not outside of Him.

<margin>but</margin>

But they rest upon an infinite form. He has nothing external to Himself that He might distribute to another. Just as the physical sun in the heavens does not have its light from the outside but within itself, so too does the Intelligible Sun. If anyone says He has no form but exists only in being thought and being known, we should not be persuaded. For all knowledge and all thought is nothing other than a kind of form of the knower directed toward the known. If all knowledge is a kind of form, it is clear that God possesses every form—not just one, but all. For all knowledge is like a form within the whole. Thus, one might speak of God as "form within the whole" or "light within the whole." These forms, then, are not essences, but forms and energies. For if they were essences, they would not be "forms." Since they are forms, it is clear they are not essences but exist within Being. Just as the rays in the sun are not the sun's essence but its energies, so in God, the forms are not His essence but His energies. An essence is defined when we assume something exists as a subject; every essence refers back to itself. But if these forms of God refer not to themselves but to their Cause, it is clear they are not essences. These are the forms of God, and one cannot say more than what we have perceived. Since this form is not essence but a kind of energy, it is not easy to say what this "intelligible form" is, or any other form in God. However, the forms in God are not like the forms in us; they are active and vital. Just as the spoken word is a kind of form of the thinking mind—not an essence, but an energy—so...

It distinguishes between the divine essence (ousia) and divine activities (energeiai), using the metaphor of the sun and its rays to explain how God creates and is known through His energies without compromising His singular essence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical inquiry from the previous discussion on opinions and passions. It shifts focus from the psychological and logical realms into the metaphysical nature of Matter (Hyle) and physical bodies, which is a central theme in Plotinus’s "Enneads." The text explores how Matter acts as a substrate that appears to have properties like size or form, while remaining inherently "indefinite" and "empty."</meta>

Is there anything left then? What is the essence of bodies? There is also a passive potentiality, which specifically exists as a principle of motion. For example, the **builder** <note>A classic Aristotelian example: a builder has the "potential" to build even when resting; the "actuality" is the building process itself.</note> has the potentiality to build. For in another way, potentiality exists, and **bronze** <note>Bronze is the standard philosophical example of "potentiality": a block of bronze is potentially a statue of Zeus, but it only becomes it in "actuality" when the sculptor imposes form upon it.</note> is like bronze in potentiality. That which comes from fire. Therefore, it is not the potentiality, as much as the remaining potentiality is the potentialities.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of generation and corruption, specifically examining how Matter serves as the underlying substrate for the shifting forms of the physical world. Therefore, it is for this reason that **generations** <term>Generation</term> <note>original: "γένεσις" (genesis); the process of coming into being or birth.</note> occur, and why there is both being and non-being: because **generations** and **corruptions** <term>Corruption</term> <note>original: "φθορά" (phthora); the process of perishing, decaying, or ceasing to be.</note> have been found to exist. For how could existing things be, if there were no generation? And if there were no generation, how could beings persist? Some things relate to one another, while others relate to different things. Some relate to different things, and others to one another. That which arises from a **substrate** <term>Substrate</term> <note>original: "ὑποκείμενον" (hypokeimenon); literally "that which lies under," referring to the underlying matter that stays the same while qualities change.</note> is such that, if it were to remain without it, I would be destroyed—this is the **Reason-principle** <term>Reason-principle</term> <note>original: "λόγος" (logos); the rational, formative power that shapes matter into specific things.</note>. Now, one thing exists in **potentiality** <term>Potentiality</term> <note>original: "δυνάμει" (dynamei); the capacity to become something else.</note>, and another in a different kind of potentiality. Nothing, or at least nothing by itself, remains in the same state; for then it would not even exist. Indeed, if there were no change, nothing at all would exist; therefore, change was necessary. If there is **matter** <term>Matter</term> <note>original: "ὕλη" (hyle); the raw material of the universe.</note>, how can it be **bronze**? In the Reason-principle, it is not bronze. Nor is it any of the other things mentioned. For it is neither the "otherness" of matter, nor the "sameness" of motion. Nor is it found in the Reason-principle, nor in the **form** <term>Form</term> <note>original: "εἴδει" (eidei); the ideal shape or essence of a thing.</note>. If generation exists, do these things come before it or after? It would be absurd to say. And it is not simply "this," but rather "how." For one thing is in one way, and another in a different way, as it could not be otherwise. Generation is a kind of **motion** or **change**; how then could it exist? When it is "more," how could it exist? We have spoken in previous sections about the **simple bodies** <note>These are the four elements: earth, air, fire, and water.</note> and how **composite bodies** are formed, and that there is a cause for generation and change. That generation occurs in such things is clear. It follows in relation to other things, and some in relation to each other. If generation exists, then other things must also exist. One part is form, the other is matter. If generation exists, then **transformations** <note>original: "μεταβολαί" (metabolai); general changes or transitions from one state to another.</note> must also exist. One part is form, the other is matter. If there were no generation, there would rather be nothingness. If, then, even non-beings exist, how could they? Because generations and corruptions have been found to exist. That which arises from a substrate is such that, if it were to remain without it, I would be destroyed—this is the Reason-principle. That which arises from a substrate is such that, if it were to remain without it, I would be destroyed—this is the Reason-principle. In these matters, they do not fail.

### On Substance or on Quality.

<margin>9</margin>
We must first speak about the **simple things**. If not, then generally about the others, and for what reason some are simple and others are composite. And how each of them exists. And through what motion, or motions, or indeed, what state.

<column-break/>

They come to be in this way, and they do not happen by chance. For the cause of the things within bodies—that it is the same, or that which was the whole long ago—if the whole were so by nature, the whole would not exist, because not all things would exist. If it is because of **substances** <term>Substances</term> <note>original: "οὐσίας" (ousias); the fundamental "what-it-is" of a thing.</note> and other things, then it is because of something else. Thus it is in the cosmos. All things are together. And all things would be, even the "other." We have the forms, and the colors, and the flavors, and such things. Those things related to others differ according to their forms. Now, the difference is that some beings are "other" and different, entirely in **substance**, or in **quality**, or some according to **quantity**. As some things differ from others, so let us speak of them, even if they are many. And these differences are called the specific properties of beings. And yet, the differing genus itself is intertwined. Other things, when intertwined, happen to be in a state of arrangement. For example, some things would not be intertwined forms if **quality** were not present. But it happens that other things are intertwined even if they are not in the whole. For the Reason-principle exists either in the **shape**, or in the **order**, or in the **position** of beings. Just as the letters **A** and **N**, or **Z** and **H**, differ by their **order** <note>The author uses the alphabet as an analogy for how the same "matter" (letters) can create different "beings" (words) simply by changing their sequence or position.</note>. In this way, beings are not merely what follows, nor what is at the beginning. In general, then, beings do not change; for not all beings are for everyone. For while the body is a necessity, it is not a necessity for all things to exist. Change according to substance would not exist if it were to come from [absolute] being; but the things from which it arises would not exist; it comes to be by substance. But even that which becomes white from that which is not-white, that thing must change. And it is not merely "this," nor "greater," nor "as much as it is." There would be generation of the whole body, and of fire, or of air. It is necessary for things to change. Beings exist, and they are altered by their shape. Indeed, they come to be from the body. In this way, beings themselves exist, and even the forms. And there are changes in relation to other things. Since, therefore, the things from which bodies are made might not exist, yet the whole body and the things related to others do change. In these things, then, he says they all come from there. In these things, then, it is because of something else.
