<margin>On true pleasure</margin>

One might ask: if **pleasure** <note>original: "ἡδονή" (hēdonē).</note> follows all things that exist according to **activity** <term>Activity</term> <note>original: "ἐνέργειαν" (energeian); the state of being "in work" or active functioning, as opposed to mere potential.</note>. This passion is brought to completion by **opinion** <note>original: "δόξῃ" (doxē); belief or appearance as opposed to certain knowledge.</note>. Such people seem to long for life. How then could pleasure—or anything that participates in pleasure without interval—come to be, or how will it come to the soul, or does it even exist? 

For the things of the **intellect** <term>Intellect</term> <note>original: "διανοίας" (dianoias); the discursive reasoning mind.</note> come to be within the **genus of becoming** <note>original: "ἐν τῷ ἐν γένει γίνεσθαι" (en tō en genei ginesthai); the realm of things that change and move, rather than the eternal.</note>; and whenever things reach their limit, they lead beyond tension. Some, even while desiring the **place** <note>original: "τόπον" (topon); likely referring to the "intelligible place" or the soul's proper home.</note>, are able to do so. And there are limits to the pleasure that pervades them, because it rested through itself, or rests upon what is said. But if its place does not follow, it is worthy for some to wish to perceive things in which hope allows them to rejoice. When pleasure arises in the present, it is a cause for him, but only if it is for all. For they speak of it together, as a certain **disposition** <note>original: "διάθεσιν" (diathesin); the way one is "disposed" or arranged internally.</note>.

# On Vision: Why Distant Objects Appear Small

<margin>On vision. Why things far away appear small.</margin>

Because of distance, things appear small <note>original: "βραχύ" (brachy); literally "short" or "brief," here referring to the diminished appearance of a large object at a distance.</note>. Even those things that are quite far off seem to have only a small portion of their actual nature with them. Objects appearing nearby, however, are seen as they truly are. Regarding those objects whose distance is not known, those things far away seem smaller because it is necessary for them to be seen through more simple parts. 

And concerning the **motion** <term>Motion</term> <note>original: "κινήσεως" (kinēseōs); in this context, it refers to the movement of the visual ray or the transition of the form through the medium.</note> of that which is far away, how it appears. Whatever matter is far off, or whatever it must be, then the whole **Form** <term>Form</term> <note>original: "εἶδε" (eide/eidos); the shaping principle or appearance of a thing.</note> is shaped as it stands apart, becoming more than it was, and yet again, it is not merely its **Reason-Principle** <term>Reason-Principle</term> <note>original: "λόγον" (logon); the rational, formative structure of the object.</note> that arrives. If the whole is a unity, in which there is a passage through and a part of the experience remains which is most perceptible. 

Within itself, it is a flat surface, so that it might know "how much." But because it requires **drawings** <note>original: "κατάγραφαις" (katagraphais); likely referring to the geometric diagrams used to explain perspective.</note> of the intersection, the space itself is never seen by it. To the extent that it is known by motion, it is known; where there is no motion, it is not. Regarding those things near the sight that have power, the difference of **quantity** <term>Quantity</term> <note>original: "ποσοῦ" (posou); here referring to the magnitude or size of the object.</note> gives rise to a puzzle. Why is this a wonder? If the intermediate things and the extremes do not occur, just as the Form itself departs from them until it moves the whole Form. 

It is not a matter of length. Or perhaps you would grasp it through **perception** <term>Perception</term> <note>original: "αἰσθόμενον" (aisthomenon); sensory awareness.</note>. As much as belongs to hearing, it is not by means of **spirit** <term>Spirit</term> <note>original: "πνεύματος" (pneumatos); in ancient science, a subtle material or "breath" that acted as a medium for the senses.</note> accidentally. To whom is it not entirely like a louder voice, as if in that place where we see? Or it is like or equal or unequal. Or many things. But rather, if it is somewhere, it also happens. Because it is intense, just as the knowledge of sweet things is intense. Or it is both. What appears concerning length, what about sight? This happens even with the first of the points. To know them. But if it is very intense, even though it is itself. And as for the multitude, all things of this which hold...

<margin>And another...</margin> ...the rest of the senses. It remains. Magnitudes are similar. In both, it is according to what was necessary. For one uses them without care, but length is the same to it. For the parts are length, proportional to the width. Clearly, the **affection** <term>Affection</term> <note>original: "πάθος" (pathos); the passive experience or impression made upon the sense organ.</note> does not come from the variegated; **internal consciousness** <term>Sense-perception</term> <note>original: "συναίνησις" (synaisthēsis); a shared perception or the soul's awareness of bodily states.</note> does not refute anything, and it does not speak fully, and many things are together or the whole. Of voices, one hears the whole rather. And the whole is timely. 

Hearing the motion. It is either length, which is known. It is near, when it is known from those things around it. All these things must appear according to reason.

<column-break/>

However much greater it appears in the sight. When the whole of what is seen is gathered at once into a single **opinion** <term>Opinion</term> <note>original: "δόξαν" (doxan); the mental judgment or appearance that follows the sensory act.</note>, it cannot be known. Whichever of the magnitudes are similar, these also appear unequal. Because the power of sight itself towards distances is weaker compared to those things not yet reached, the differences in all parts will be very sharp. 

The distant things are [seen] from nearby because the intermediate things stand together; those standing still have the same cause. For things standing on a road seem to wander for the same reasons; and the swallow <note>A common ancient example used to discuss speed and visual tracking.</note> because of the distance is not seen as a whole, if the road is bright where it is most seen. 

Those things facing the sights without width, the length seems to be an opinion as knowledge; for from the internal motions as if from the external ones appearing in a place, there are parallel regions of smooth things like a mirror <note>original: "ψυγές" (psyges); perhaps a corruption or specific term for a reflective surface or cooling shadow.</note> equal to itself and each other, or because the front is thus such as it would be. 

When, therefore, it perceives nothing of the "many" that exists, but it will be and no longer from what kind each of them is, being shaped according to the distance of the seen thing, since then the opinion is not by each of the visual attacks; for the width in the length is brought in together in equal distances, and again there will be the act of seeing. 

If indeed it is for all the composition, if both are more worthy. And either both being there, in it the one **measuring line** <note>original: "σχοῖν’" (schoin'); a measuring rod or cord.</note> or **angle** <term>Angle</term> <note>original: "γωνία" (gōnia); the visual angle formed at the eye, a central concept in ancient optics.</note> becomes as much as the sight is poured out, does it not also happen to hit upon it? It must happen in another way. If it is not, it did not take the whole, stealing away much of what happened from what appeared so that it might exist. The branch making it so that it appears, and the fact that it appears from a smaller angle of the stunned [vision], the distance must be blamed.

<margin>Note: These things are according to the geometrician.</margin>

Since, therefore, the distance of the eye and the affections have been defined for us, and the things that happened have been set. And the thing affected is nothing. But there is a certain one, and from the one remaining the nature is the same. And the same thing happening, or something else. For this too is another. When it is good, when we take it so. And when it becomes painful. Thinking this to be the nature and not something foreign, he establishes that it must happen. It is as if they are not fitting, such as the upright things. And again, because it is unshaken, and the same thing and whatever they know. So that from themselves they go to the outside. And by **spirits** <term>Spirits</term> <note>original: "πνεύμασι" (pneumasi); the airy medium or vital force believed to transmit visual data.</note>; for they are upon one another and all. For it would not happen if it were in another. Nor is it established in any one, being forced by it to be. For he is over each and stands. But this is nearby, through the intermediate things he will direct it with spirits. # On the Soul and the Intellect

Therefore, by its nature, it is not fixed in any one place within the whole, nor is it a living thing apart from the living whole; the **Soul** <term>Soul</term> <note>original: "ψυχὴ" (psyche); the animating principle that bridges the higher realm of ideas and the physical world.</note> would appear even in the universe as a whole. Or it must necessarily be **Intellect** <term>Intellect</term> <note>original: "νοῦν" (noun); the divine Mind or realm of pure, eternal Thought.</note>. A difficulty arises for all things, smaller in many ways. It remains then to consider if these things are within itself, or equal from God. Of what nature would error be? And to what does the name apply when it seeks its rest? Or even the causes of failure. Let that which dies indeed die; and let it become. But in that resting, there remains a nature through its own beneficence, generated in its own activity, which it receives in the nourishment of nature—many things. 

And from that time, it would be changed. It would seem, then, that the Intellect following it is in a certain journey. But for what kind of work? For what is the stillness of the Intellect? How, in becoming, will it be with itself? Or is it a state of inactivity? Let it be a life taken as a whole. It is somewhat less than those things in the world, for they are not even with themselves. But perhaps it is with him in release, the Soul being nowhere. But it seems to be in the soul. The Soul makes it possible to think. It knows, then, the middle ground of that which is in the body by nature. 

Because of this, the **Passion** <term>Passion</term> <note>original: "πάθος" (pathos); not just emotion, but an "affection" or something that happens to the soul from the outside.</note> of those things with them, and dying—whatever that may be—is nothing to the act of thinking. If the other thing is in the act of thinking, and the earth is not heaven, there is but one certain <unclear>ecstasy</unclear> <note>original: "ἔκστασις" (ekstasis); a standing outside of oneself or a departure from the ordinary state.</note> of unceasing activity. It might happen. For the things of the mind fall into forgetfulness. But let it cease. There is no one in whom all things are in the few. And if not, it would happen thus. Generally, that the Intellect thinks. It is an immovable necessity that this happens. But those things appear to have something more than the world. Or they were <unclear>hidden</unclear>. 

And here there is **Darkness** <note>original: "σκότος" (skotos).</note>, because of speaking falsely. One can grasp that the Intellect thinks only, and what it thinks is revealed to itself. And he will find it, or it will happen, so that by this faith, in stillness, they might no longer be hidden. It came from a moderate necessity, caused by its own lack of counsel. And when it is in the agitation from this of one another—that which it did not know was happening to it—you pull away from its power, or it grows weak; but the **Intelligible** <note>original: "νοητὸν" (noēton); the object of pure thought.</note> has itself. There is a passion, which is not of itself. Resting, yet it must be thinking. So in changing. Or it might not come to pass that it is Intellect, as in heaven the life is from the earth. But if it has those things in its sight: What, then, are its own? Perhaps animals have mind from the Intellect. And if indeed the cause will be with them, one might say that in the earth itself, or elsewhere, the Intellect is a heaven. How could they say it is of the heaven? Because it happens to be most pure. And if he said this was the cause, it was of the **Reason-Principle** <term>Reason-Principle</term> <note>original: "λόγου" (logou); the rational structure or forming word.</note>. Whenever one proceeds from what is with it, already from the becoming, the Soul...

<column-break/>

...is itself of itself. This is so that it is between that which is in passion and that which is the Intellect thinking by itself; some are considered passions. But it creates a total equality. Nor indeed is it more than its own lot. Thus must one know the things said here. For that which is in place, when it seeks itself in itself, it cannot seek. And it is necessary for it to have a specific perception in thinking here, according to which it does not belong to it. It will appear to it, that which has happened. And so its Soul will not be entirely in the life from beyond. 

For by nature it is one. And it is not possible to divide me. But when the things there are <unclear>cast</unclear> into its rest, or the ceasing. And this happens to it not as a passion, because it also happens to us. When the Soul is alone for judgment, and the passions in us are not yet at rest. The child does not have it. But because not even thus is all **Matter** <term>Matter</term> <note>original: "ὕλη" (hylē); the underlying "stuff" of the physical world, often seen by Plotinus as a void or lack.</note> dissolved; the imperceptible remains to it. By opportunity, the things of governance happen from the cause in thinking, and the turning away of the powers of drugs; such as those things still toward him, one and evil, or it will rest. 

As he says again: it is not a matter of changing; since having thought there, it does not change its mind again; but it is not poured out; it is free toward what it thinks even if it is bound. And the other opinion is before the state of being **Impassive** <note>original: "ἀπαθείας" (apatheias); the state of being unaffected by external passions or suffering.</note>. For the life of each is dissolved as a whole. So that it does not even try the things according to the body. It does not die in this way. Because either the Intellect still remains. But when we dissolve and change our station, I do not know if one could carry it away in this life. For if it were to take it along with it; but let each of them be dissolved; so be it. But it suffered unjustly. Just as not even in life is the Soul toward God. If indeed it is to live with the whole. Then what I say. As for what things it is the Soul of, let it be known. But it would happen that we became what it was for a human. And one must be wise. But if it is the same in matter, why does he speak of matter? Because even freedom and these same things have become nature. But if it is impossible to wander in nature, it knew necessity. And if not even in the divided. # On the Soul and the Deception of the World

...of the faithful. And he says to me: the **deceiver** <note>original: "ὁ πλάνος" (ho planos); a term often used for a wandering spirit, an impostor, or the shifting nature of the material world that misleads the soul.</note> says that his lawlessness does not exist; but if he has known, when the promises turn the one who has been taken by him, how brilliantly—though he did not know him—nor from the beginning, did he ever know the soul divided toward the truth. For **Number** <term>Number</term> <note>original: "ἀριθμὸς" (arithmos); in Neoplatonism, numbers are divine archetypes that provide order to the universe.</note> possesses something more than my own parts, so that it might not be counted. For why do the souls of men possess it more? Let it be revealed. For what good thing celebrates a birthday? It comes from the one who works evil. For it has come into being so that it might be honored. And they are transferring things to the inexorable child. It is under the year, whether in **light** <note>original: "φωτὶ" (photi)</note> or in **darkness** <note>original: "σκότει" (skotei)</note>, as that which once shone for us, this would be common to the struggle. From where did he bring it? For if it participated, it should receive it. But if I have it, it holds some description, if it enters, which someone writes with care; but this one wipes away the souls of each, which had their own study; from where the knowledges in abundance were persuaded to come into the sea of those very sufferings; and so it will be subject. Because of this, it has come into being: this whole **world** <term>World</term> <note>original: "κόσμον" (kosmon); the ordered universe, which Plotinus views as a living, breathing reflection of divine beauty, though lower than the realm of pure thought.</note>, so that he might one day say: this is unique because everything is greater in its same self. But the cause reveals that it did not come into being. It is necessary to find what exists, which did not come from vice or from evils. For why do you proceed from the nature of **God** <note>original: "Θεοῦ" (Theou)</note>, from which fire was created? For he for whom it became a cause for all, after the same...

Why should it be seen that the beauty of the form, having been enacted, will depart after the corruption of this **wicked theater of the world** <note>original: "πoνηροῦ θεάτρῳ" (ponerou theatro); a classic philosophical metaphor viewing human life and the material world as a stage play where souls act out their roles.</note>? Generally, it is worthy to change the argument to find something. But for we have from ourselves as much as is provided by them from the feast. And grief comes, brilliant before all, not neglecting. But it appears that he wishes to set things right, not so that he might answer to dissolve these things. He went out again from where he rather held within himself. But spare me, for the hour is the cause of us whose birth is seen through the tribunal of those who are exhausted, upon the **aetherial seat** <note>original: "αἰθέρα ἔδρον"; the high, celestial home of the gods or purified souls.</note>. But the one deceived concerning the **immortality of his own soul** <term>Immortality of the Soul</term> <note>original: "ψυχῆς ἀθανασίαν" (psyches athanasian); the core belief that the soul survives the body because its essence belongs to the eternal realm.</note>, still among those visible things, which he suffered by another, let them not be moved as if made of adamant. In many ways, the battle is joined. It is a necessity for the wise choice of our own. He considered the pious man blessed, for he is the cause of his own innocence. For the things of the soul are not always manifest, but the will to know shall come upon him, when these things of nothingness are written; the soul having come, all judgment is for them, lest the soul ever come to be, and because of this, living. For where are they not worthy to participate in life, they who look upon you, the world? For by which...

<column-break/>

...to lie among these things is a shameful soul. I have sinned much, falling away from the right path of **virtue** <term>Virtue</term> <note>original: "ἀρετῆς" (aretes); for Plotinus, virtue is the purification of the soul that allows it to ascend back to its divine source.</note>. Where for me are the things of the **Scriptures** <note>original: "Γραφῶν" (Graphon); while Plotinus usually cites Plato, the use of "Scriptures" here may indicate the influence of a later Christian copyist or a reference to "sacred writings" in a broader sense.</note>, as I sketch in writing? When, therefore, these desires enter into me, or rather these shameful forms, or the things from my own knowledge of these, that I may speak properly, and not only such things, for some say correctly that it is the best to have been separated. This I say while reading: and yet it is she through whom the world is driven unfaithfully; and the most shameful things; for it is for them to always know these things, already beautifying themselves with the unbeautiful. 

If it is not in the suffering itself that the things of the world are to be fled as common, for after the same return, he had no cause in composing, for he knows; if indeed daily, so that the souls might be guarded; for the **Lord of all** <note>original: "πάντων Κύριος" (panton Kyrios)</note> is most lover of mankind; but if he should practice by study, let the master not be lacking; but let another follow nonetheless, for whom it was time, so that the soul might prepare itself for the guard. If indeed for the souls the path is remaining worthy of the world. What is the argument to us? The things of grief will be subject, or he will delay to lead again, immortally; both immortally and blessedly. For say to the soul: you speak evil things to yourself. That which was soft, and all is for the sake of this, someone who is within late, but also again. Let the things that have suffered not be as they ought, if he determined it from his own cause; for it is not necessary to firmly lay aside grace, while growing old; for the fear of these things is among all human affairs. 

He declares himself away from the beautiful, having been soaked always as if in weakness rather than in all strength; and it fell to them to have the things of wealth’s wealth; and the things of immeasurability to seek their own **philosophy** <term>Philosophy</term> <note>original: "φιλοσοφίαν"; here, the lifelong pursuit of wisdom and the soul's return to the "One."</note>, these things I have from the entire blow; there also are the griefs and the groanings of **Hades** <note>original: "ᾄδου" (aidou); the underworld or the state of the soul when it is entirely "sunken" into the body.</note>, and the **vanity of vanities** <note>original: "ματαιοματαιότητες"; a direct echo of the Biblical book of Ecclesiastes, likely an interpolation by a later scribe.</note>, they were without glory. And it is at least the first of those things of error. But he wrote to me brilliantly, upon the lie. 

Choose the thing said in the noble man. for his part has been sent, or that which is according to the **Idea** <term>Idea</term> <note>original: "ἰδέας"; the eternal, perfect forms that exist in the Intellect.</note> in seeing the living being pass by, for yourselves you shall again always use the mind which you established. This I received as a prayer so that in him all these things of the **Master** <note>original: "Δεσπότου" (Despotou); likely referring to the Supreme Being or the Demiurge.</note> shall be beheld through you; through whom he may give back; and often choose also in your thought, it is quick or to work brilliantly; not toward this being such as that of the brilliant; having been released, that one is through the **Demiurge** <term>Demiurge</term> <note>original: "δημιουργός" (demiourgos); the "divine craftsman" who shapes the material world based on the eternal Ideas.</note>. He might say it would be painful. These things, at least, he recorded for her; and since he had it, the glory of the beautiful saved those for them, laying down the nature of the voice and that of the **blessed song** <note>original: "μακαρίας ᾠδῆς"; perhaps a reference to the "harmony of the spheres" or the soul's hymn of return.</note>.

# 48. On the Nature of the Soul and the Cosmic Drama

A multitude of **sorcerers** <note>original: "γοήτων" (goētōn); Plotinus often uses this term to describe those who use magic or material distractions to enchant the soul away from its true divine nature.</note> call upon various names, but they think they can prove their opinions through their own lack of experience. He says that the nature of this multitude of sorcerers is such that it harms itself, even though it is agreed that the Good exists; and because of this, very little is left to destruction. Nothing escapes the whole, even those things that are perishing; for the whole carries everything in this way, both the things of the universe and whatever else exists according to nature. 

But the **Soul** <term>Soul</term> <note>original: "ψυχὴ" (psychē); in this context, the intermediary between the divine Intellect and the physical world.</note> still exists. It differs in the way a soul that is naturally well-disposed participates in the divine. One must not think of it as a mere man; for it is necessary to set aside what is called "the subject" as something to be excused. And they speak worthy words regarding the **immortality of the soul** <note>original: "ψυχῆς ἀθανασίας" (psychēs athanasias)</note>. While there is a debt to one's parents, there is a greater need for the gods. 

The fact that the soul does not appear now in its usual fellowship—apart from what is known through **Number**—is because its essence will not say otherwise. For these things are found there, according to the teachings of **Plato** <note>original: "πλατωνι" (platōni)</note>. Some speak while being loosened by wisdom; others speak out of envy. For it was not necessary to contemplate toward that which it owed, to enter together with it through things that are sometimes involuntary. Instead, the pain of such things has a beginning, because of how much they will steal for themselves through the necessity of belief. Since each of their opinions belongs to them, they do not even deliberate. For they do not do these things as if they were appearing as painful things. For he would not signify necessary things concerning them; or rather, it does not appear that there is a difficulty in asserting that they are loosening themselves within her. 

Toward the things of a certain ancient time through the parents, he says there is an "ancient way of life"; and if she who sinned was not given punishment by necessity, we recognize this reasonably. But it is necessary to take these things from their own traits, having trusted that they will be tested with a promise. For there is no **injustice** <note>original: "ἀδικία" (adikia)</note> when deaths, births, or captivities occur. How can we blame the way the Soul causes these things? But if they are grieved by what they suffer, and if they bring the same conclusion to the Soul, they think again that the part comes from the whole. For it is not that it has done nothing at all. But again, neither the **World** <term>World</term> <note>original: "κόσμος" (kosmos); the beautifully ordered universe.</note> itself is foreign to it. For all these things exist because the soul is a thing of fellowship; its own affairs will be its own, but not the whole for the whole. To the one who has nothing, it will be like receiving from the whole, as one worthy of **robes** or a **brilliant lineage** <note>Plotinus often uses the metaphor of actors in a play: souls "put on" different bodies and social roles like costumes (robes) on a stage.</note> through having managed affairs well, according to the best votes. 

Because of the differences, it receives through the whole as much as these things allow; for I do not say the same reason applies to the parts. For there are differences regarding things that are not the same, and the fates will be upon them, and that too from the whole. For we are in this whole by power; but it has not just happened, for it has come into being. If indeed the Soul is by nature, or if the nature of the whole 

<column-break/>

shall be contemplated. If, on the other hand, the Cause is the issue; indeed the whole and among all things is through its **crafting** <term>Crafting</term> <note>original: "δημιουργεῖν" (dēmiourgein); referring to the Demiurge or the creative power that shapes the material world.</note>. This is not by necessity, but a desire toward itself. We, however, are subject to fortunes. 

That which is toward the furthest edge is not for itself alone, in no way; this "recanting" of the cause is to live life, and to live it fully realized. For a little flows from above, pouring out glory for all. Because it did not cease, one must seek the cause from those things that give. For example, that which is encompassed in the heights produced the whole as a living life; and from the life dwelling within, there shall be a life for each of its parts. Therefore, it is made solemn at the boundary, like a **touched fire** <note>original: "πῦρ ἐπαφές" (pyr epaphes)</note>. Through this, the whole is more than the rest; the soul is the living being. But since it is near to essence, it is not possible for it to be older than the rest; nor is the soul alone the one above. 

Nor is it possible to see the cause for each individual thing; nor will it change only toward each. He showed that as we run through the **order of the whole** <note>original: "τάξιν τοῦ παντός" (taxin tou pantos)</note>, all these things are first among the things of great haste; those things that are near are the individual things, as many as they are. We desire those things through which we act; but we do them for the sake of 

<margin><note>A small cross inscribed in a circle, likely a scribal mark of blessing or a reference to the four quarters of the universe.</note></margin>

pleasure alone. Regarding the rest, it is nature that acts, and not [human] nature. I do these things; and let action be established for her in this way. Those things which she will flee, or the ways we grieve the order of the whole; for instance, she will not learn by chance, nor does it belong to her to take what is appropriate to her in the dance. Nothing is according to nature in the order of necessity; at least nothing prevents each from ceasing. 

But when she suffers because of them, why does she suffer? She did it. These things are not from the Soul; and shameful impulse is a **deception** <note>original: "ἀπάτη" (apatē)</note>. The one who is obedient receives as many things as there are to do. Since these people suffered the things they were meant to cast upon themselves, the cause of the error is born from anger. One must say to them: what the peacemaker does out of fear makes their pleasure appear as it does to them. And it is reasonable for those who do our deeds to be persuaded, but not as those who have made a goodwill that never happened. Because of this, it was rightly assigned to the **Administrator** <term>Administrator</term> <note>original: "διοικητοῦ" (dioikētou); the divine Providence that governs the universe like a household manager.</note> from of old. 

The measure of the common nature is entirely in pleasure. But if life has been lived in such a way, it did not have life as a beginning; the one who stands beside the significations of the things within it—which are signs of life in its own unceasing unity—encompasses both essences. And that wisdom, presiding together with teaching, **leads toward the good** so that we might somehow understand ourselves. So that this, not being isolated, has its nature according to this very thing; for it does not participate in the One alone. But again, he says it is isolated, for this was to be active, and not the whole...

# 99. On the Nature of the Divine and the Path of Virtue

<note>This image shows a spread of two pages (folio 98 verso and folio 99 recto) from a Greek philosophical manuscript, likely a commentary on ethics or metaphysics. The text is written in a late minuscule hand with numerous ligatures and abbreviations.</note>

Of the natures that exist among us, he safely admits that it is not possible for the **Good** <term>Good</term> <note>original: "ἀγαθόν" (agathon); for Plotinus, the "Good" is the ultimate principle of reality, synonymous with "the One."</note> to not exist, even if it is of a more violent sort than those things. But it is not so much that it is merely "better," but that I might be **happy** <note>original: "εὐδαίμονα" (eudaimona); refers to "flourishing" or "well-being" rather than a fleeting emotion.</note> if I happen upon it. These are his own words. Regarding that which is "through himself," it is less of us to repent. For **Grace** <note>original: "Χάρις" (Charis)</note> is indeed of **God** <term>God</term> <note>original: "θεὸς" (theos); in Neoplatonism, this often refers to the divine intellect or the higher principles of the universe.</note> concerning that which is beautiful, because God is the most incorporeal of all things. Wondrous powers are under God and are not even labored for. 

If a man is otherwise wicked, he is not even a participant in this. But in another way, he is not. If he is good, which is what is for everyone, it is possible to demonstrate by the name of God how they live. And it is necessary for him, more than all living creatures, to be happy. The wicked man is not so, even after all things; so that these things, not being tripped up by the hypotheses, have come to be in that which is disordered, and nothing is at random. I say he is happy, and for all such people. Why then do they have a foundation? Or will the matter concerning **pleasure** <note>original: "ἡδονῆς" (hēdonēs)</note> be theirs? Because this is so, it is not from many failings. Furthermore, the **madness of God** <note>original: "θεοῦ μανία" (theou mania); likely a reference to the "divine madness" mentioned in Plato's Phaedrus, where the soul is inspired by the divine.</note> does not neglect happiness. 

Why then should the base not take up God through himself? For it is either himself or a generation of movement. **Human wisdom** <note>original: "ἀνθρωπινὴ σοφία" (anthrōpinē sophia)</note> is better under God. Indeed, let these things not be forgotten by man. And again: before this, it was said that God is not of such a nature, neither for a life nor a life of violence. The soul is like a woman toward that which is good—or perhaps it is weakness, or folly. To God, whatever he is said to be, he gives these things; nor even nature. It is the same thing, or rather it is himself; he did not have contemplations even in himself. To be persuaded that these things are so—how could one not give thanks with a prayer to God? Since the inquiry is of the form, by necessity in their passions, there is a persuasion of it, that the truth is not in these things. Wherefore he thinks it is without error, having everything. Wherefore if one is nourished like a vegetable 

<margin>.G.</margin> 

among the common people; but for such as these, he had nothing at all. And he understands how the rushing life is painful. Yet for the wicked, these things do not exist, for he demands these things of the **age** <term>Age</term> <note>original: "αἰῶνος" (aiōnos); often translated as "eternity" or the "eternal realm" in Plotinian thought.</note>. For it is his year, about which the man has risen. Then, but not of such a kind, it pains him that we blame God, especially when he becomes of the Good. But the wicked man happens to have an enemy of these things, to know them. If someone flees or is lessened by his labors: of the impossible, what is wondrous even for men who have become "above" with the soul, not even under a man. If it should become an **exercise** <note>original: "γυμνάσιον" (gymnasion); virtue is seen here as a training or athletic exercise for the soul.</note> or a **virtue** <term>Virtue</term> <note>original: "ἀρετή" (aretē)</note>, even the virtue in this is better. If there are terrible things, or they might become immortal and incorruptible. Further, just as it is, wherefore the greatest memory of them exists. It is agreed that there is a certain virtue and vice. But he does not have wisdom, nor does he have blame; they think praise is for the worthy, or spring into the—

<column-break/>

—honorable. And the most desolate of all is to be more dishonored. And madness is not together, but true. But even the very guidance is **folly** <note>original: "ἀφροσύνην" (aphrosynēn)</note>, or it is carried away toward ten thousand destructions. Every guide perhaps, or not of fortune, whether he will inhabit the neighboring land in a life of poverty. In **agricultural enjoyments** <note>original: "γεωργικαῖς ἀπολαύσεσιν"</note>; as a cause, in the enjoyments of those who are the best. But it is necessary for the one who is wild or shameful toward pleasant things to think that no corner of them is worthy. For just as nature is, so also is the good man toward pleasant things; it will not be by taking less, because the much greater is with him. The good in opinion, and the more life-benefitting, and the greater. Of pleasure: then he will think. Perhaps learning equally. It is clear to liken, and to suppose such a thing. But the good man would not even hope for the madness that comes from a king through himself, or to be happy after him. For either **wisdom** <note>original: "σοφία" (sophia)</note>, and living well, and reputation, and what is not worthy for them—these are the brilliant things and the **Perfect** <term>Perfect</term> <note>original: "τὸ τέλειον" (to teleion); the state of completion or spiritual wholeness.</note>. 

Thus he reveres remaining, and does much. Every man himself flees, and pursues, and cherishes holy things. And however it may be, it is a shameful thing to live in a certain way. And the female follows. If indeed there is a **love for the soul** <note>original: "ψυχοφιλία" (psychophilia)</note> of it. And it is worse than a male friend. If this is not so, it is man; from this, showing himself, one might clearly disregard it, the one who signifies that there is something strong, and for all those for whom he is best, and the worthy learner, or every man. It is thus the greater with a hypothesis, that to eat is to eat, nor does nature take the good things. Then at some time, he thinks that the one who does not participate in the Good at all is in need of God, as if in none of the good things; but if even of this, he would be himself under the passion of the soul. And it would be necessary to be on one's knees, before then. Of the things of the senses, such as water and fire. But thus for all these who happen upon the members. 

With hearing removed, the books are not trustworthy for their own sake, but either because it is always much or from the men. And the matter concerning the piety of **Tatian** <note>original: "Τατιανοῦ" (Tatianou); Tatian was a 2nd-century Christian writer/apologist. His mention here suggests the text is engaging with early Christian or Gnostic views.</note> or the **Makite** <note>original: "Μακίτης" (Makites); possibly a reference to a specific heretical group or a scribal error for "Marcionite."</note>—it is hidden, it does not make for God, but they would have burst forth, or everything. Wherefore, he is untrained not in grasping, nor in making the hope of living well. Because it will be confused itself. Just as what he might guard, we shall see from the pain that is to come even for that one, to lick the spleen upon it. Through this, the hand exists because it is wretched. Deceiving well through all men. Nor if it is something trivial, or such things does it receive again. Or that they once made us see. But that which is according to nature does well for all. If then, it is **earth instead of light** <note>original: "γῆν ἀντὶ φωτὸς"</note> for living, or the soul of it—where can it have distress in itself? Nor should one imagine that. For it is strong.

Because of this. If Being exists; if it does not; so that no one might say it of her <note>In Greek, the word for "Soul" (psyche) is feminine, and Plotinus often speaks of it as "she."</note>. But she herself, saying both things, might speak; yet she is more true than any of those who would speak for her. If she possesses herself in a divine way, she is the **Reason-Principle** <term>Reason-Principle</term> <note>original: "λόγος" (logos); the formative principle that connects the higher Intellect to the material world.</note>. It is said she is "divine." And if her **intellection** <term>intellection</term> <note>original: "νόησις" (noesis); the act of the mind perceiving eternal truths directly.</note> is carried along, or if those who attribute the voices of sensible things to themselves happen to do so. For that child in the world is capable of grasping; it was said to be above all. 

Honoring each of the two demonstrations. From this very point it is necessary that all the things mentioned should ascend. And many are the things that move the sensible world. Furthermore: "What is it?"—a prophecy of sorts, and all things were well with them. For existence is a release of herself; but rather, let it all be numbered. And what he says again; but many irrational things are in addition; saying they possess them. If it is so, the things of the whole **Reason-Principle** are divine, either it or each individual. For many are not the other things, but rather the things receiving her. For she does not have obscurity; and indeed she has it according to reason. 

We should be led as though being persuaded by those we love. Either the one who is fortunate will inquire, or he will be absent. He loves to become, instead of the feet, like the one who remains; and yet he is known by himself. For the things of friends he would deem worthy as his own. Or if he were to be in such a state. And she will not escape notice, as they say. Incorporeal concerning the act of knowing, or how is she served by all? For there is no kinship or any other part of her, lest she be praised as herself; for if she is known, let us not live, and indeed we must change. 

By this voice throughout the inner things, and indeed let him learn that she has been written, or the thought of the things of the Beautiful which I love; but those things which are beautiful to her... she took the beginning of her own generation. Furthermore, let them not be for each other. If these things are to be grasped by the infinite. For the things there possess her. For she herself belongs to another **Good** <term>Good</term> <note>original: "ἀγαθόν" (agathon); the ultimate source of all reality.</note> so as to be thus. She coincides with herself, the **Reason-Principle** extending, which is not there as one, but as a difficulty, which he stops, which is about certain things, the things of the **Soul** <term>Soul</term> <note>original: "ψυχή" (psyche)</note>. All things are intellectualized, which might have the things of **Plato** <note>original: "Πλάτωνος"; a reference to the philosopher Plato, whose works Plotinus is interpreting.</note>, the judgments written by the wise, whenever the innate ones should be established. 

And it is said that honors are altogether dissolved. If indeed these are the things of the wise, these again they say are saved in himself. Such as the same things; but the worse things she changes, speaking differently—he would not long for much, such as not thinking; but also not for the whole; the one above and the one from there. Neither has **Matter** <term>Matter</term> <note>original: "ὕλη" (hyle); the passive substrate of the physical world, which Neoplatonists viewed as the lowest level of reality.</note> come to be. Either the one of the other or another appear, but to be cautious of the whole, or she oversees, or because it will be necessary to name it, or not another. What is called "other." If everything stands thus for him. If anyone, therefore, should appear, the **ascetic reasoning** <note>original: "λογισμὸν ἀσκητικὸν"; suggests the use of logic as a spiritual or disciplined practice.</note> to take hold or to become. Those things which are incorporeal stand up, the act of thinking in her for all.

## Chapter 2.

It is necessary, finally, to drive away the errors through **Theology** <term>Theology</term> <note>original: "θεολογικῇ" (theologikē); in this context, the study of divine principles rather than religious dogma.</note>. But first, let it be understood. But where does the barrier come from? Either the things from himself and the first things; or the things through himself... such as one would say is "good"; but for himself the one who acts; since indeed being from there. Of these. For it does not seem by opinion concerning himself. And because he knows so that it may be said. But if the things spoken of are loved; but nothing which is by power, why indeed is she also boastful?

The most powerful of them in divine things; through theology, of reason once for her, not already by a mistake it had well become. Why is color a mistake, and their world, for the sake of another? If indeed the whole reasoning, or the one for her or the beginning taken, became before letting go, not the cause of reason, it would be necessary for everyone to know. Then also for whom, for the sake of friendship. But some soul, but which everyone loves... of animals. Whether for himself as such or as a whole; but becoming or it becomes, it releases the things of the many. 

And running back nonetheless; they do not do equal things, and they say they think. But that which is. What or the things from where. But if he says the whole. Or there rationally. Of these natural and generative things, the cause is equal things, whenever she might be honored. And she perceives nothing and she dares sometimes; and that which is through friendship. From honors for her to perceive. But what as once from matter and in forms all things for her. 

But if it is **Intellection** <term>Intellection</term> <note>original: "νόησις" (noesis)</note>, first when the one who is known is as many. Then it also is, and in the act of thinking, as it were. But towards that and the generation; but this, just as not pursuing another. It is said to be suspected disgracefully. But why first before and what things are becoming, how one will say to see a portion. From the things below, so that again it was well, the same as the form is for their perception. Then how, for the one knowing, she might suppose of souls or seeing many of this **Cosmos** <term>Cosmos</term> <note>original: "κόσμος" (kosmos); the ordered universe.</note>, but throughout the soul, scarcely if one or to think of them of the world, they will be without substance, scarcely to take breath, that they might be it, but through another. By necessity not perception, but the things becoming. Those things must be asked, either through himself. But "when," and it was those things with the other, and to receive **Essence** <term>Essence</term> <note>original: "οὐσίαν" (ousian); true being or substance.</note>, and nothing intelligible; but the form was of the one born again. All those things and he of themselves, but the first of the man. Why can he not but sometimes towards himself, who is all natural? Why is the world stirred well, or every land... the things becoming throughout the whole, or below; better than them. The thing according to the desirable is manifest; but for all those things to be themselves. If for her...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Soul’s relationship to the divine and the sensible world. Having previously established the Soul as a "Reason-Principle," Plotinus now examines how this principle governs the "Coming-to-be" and "Passing-away" of the material universe. # The Enneads
### On Nature, Contemplation, and the One

Regarding the **origin** <term>Coming-to-be</term> <note>original: "γένεσις" (genesis); the process of entering the world of time and change.</note> and **destruction** <term>Passing-away</term> <note>original: "φθορά" (phthora); the dissolution of material forms.</note> of nature, the world, and the parts within it, these pertain to the changes typical of the natural art. However, concerning destruction and generation, one aspect is the structural arrangement by God. Therefore, we did not know the perishable material from which the whole **creation** <note>original: "κτίσμα" (ktisma); here referring to the fashioned physical universe.</note> was fashioned as something that merely shone forth from God; rather, he revealed his creation in such a way that we might happen to see it through its use. Thus, its superior nature was established for us.

And as for these mechanisms of theirs, it is for servants to learn them. But let us speak of the gods. There is both the perishable and that which does not always serve their needs, but exists by a prior hypothesis. Furthermore, due to the justice of the powers and authority derived from the gods, **death** will be disregarded. For what would happen? Whether from the one who holds authority or from the unaccountable Cause, there is a great agreement. And why are the things that pertain to the whole named as they are? For it is either **Nature** <term>Nature</term> <note>original: "φύσις" (physis); the lowest level of the divine Soul that directly animates matter.</note>, or Nature ceaselessly producing the things of Nature, or Nature acting through difference. Or again, insofar as it is Nature. Hence also the customs regarding the gods. For she herself is the cause of the gods, and from her comes an unyielding reverence toward the ancestors. And if the **Reason-Principle** <term>Reason-Principle</term> <note>original: "λόγος" (logos); the formative, rational power of the Soul.</note> were present, it would perfect both the useful things and the rest. Either the whole would appear as a totality, or the presence would be the whole; or perhaps he did not grasp nature and the whole by these means. Which way is it? The **Spirit** <term>Daemon</term> <note>original: "δαίμων" (daimon); a protective or guiding spirit, often seen as a link between humans and the higher gods.</note> whom they say we receive—from where does he come, as if the Good were a holy thing? But it is not the cause, as if it happens to be causeless by nature. This is the same as a preceding necessity. Let neither the passions nor the cause be blamed; for that which has been witnessed is the nature of God. Every hypothesis and the act of his coming-to-be proceeds into this. And this is because he named the **Order of Love** <note>Plotinus often links Love (Eros) to the soul's desire to return to its source.</note> as something belonging to the divine.

These things are greater than our own powers and the **tunic of the gods** <note>A Neoplatonic metaphor referring to the celestial bodies or the outer "garments" the soul puts on as it descends into matter.</note>. For by a shared consent with the nature of God, he who works by his own hand holds and manages all things by his remedies. Not everything is the "form of the world," or perhaps it suffers in relation to its order; for things possess their own destruction. Let one not fear, instead of reason, the madness or the difference of generation. Wherever there might be a cause and a world for their destruction, God is the god of the body and of the works of the earth. Their souls are flames, or they are themselves the essences or the **images** <note>original: "εἰκόνα" (eikona); the material world as a reflection or shadow of the higher, eternal world.</note> of the honored gods. And the things upon the earth will be different kinds of magic, so that these things of nature may be perfectly completed, or however they may come to be. Is it from the order—not these things through us, but rather the parts of the whole? Either it is its own generation or it is already complete. For in this way, the cause seems to exist in the whole. But the world or order is indivisible; or all things happen through them, not merely by the word of the eyes of the gods.

<column-break/>

Yet it still maintains the differences between these things. Thus, it fulfills this entire **immortality** <note>original: "ἀθανασίαν" (athanasian).</note>; it creates generation and prepares all things, even dividing the types of destruction. Their power is often forbidden; or if this is not possible, those who are formed within all things find it more worthy to learn these matters from him. For this is according to a "stewardship" <note>original: "οἰκονομίαν" (oikonomian); the divine management or arrangement of the universe.</note> for them, or through that which is necessary if the perishable is to be truly perishable. For the whole is not "the whole" by its own nature unless it is immortal. Or again, because not everything is a stone; since everything exists according to immortality in this way. Or again, one might say: God now holds the mixture. Might that which we can become also remain the same? These things are identical; but when those released from the gods become manifest, is it only the whole Soul, or the images as well? For what is it? Either because there is a release of that Soul and this one, if they received it with power, or as we are able to present ourselves? And they become servants to failures and the stumbling of nature, and the things arising from it become a source of weakness. Or is it the power of the **Reason-Principle**? For it acts according to nature or contrary to nature. Thus, those who are made like him are released from all things. This means they are released from the things that came before them.

And the entire immortality of the others—for let them not be merely "serviced"—and the form is the cause, which we see even among those of us who practice philosophy. Or indeed, we have reached such a point; for the activity was there, and in this way from the beginning he showed a law that is reverent and thorough, a sympathy through my own opinions. But not everyone wonders at the powers derived from the whole. Indeed, the Good of the gods was not begrudged. For they do not possess the causes by some preparation or a noble movement of staying behind. In general, change is either an escape from violence or it receives a proof. Furthermore, their immortality remains; for it is a happy generation, and destruction is not in that place, though the dissolved parts possess powers; and this leads to folly. Or perhaps it is these things. Or as the divine spirit brings it forward, we who share in thinking are not a proof of folly. Or rather, those men who have suffered the same things and are within themselves might know why things are also painful. For what does it become? Either because it was from the beginning of God, or even earlier, if all things belong to the Spirit. This power seems to have a cause through knowing; for it is not without a cause, all that concerns the Spirit of which they speak. Or indeed, the cause is that they are the guardians of the parts. Rejoicing, the whole gave hope to the race. And in their beauty and the struggle for the Spirit, those who lead the way believe in the rising up.

<summary>Plotinus explores the divine governance of the physical world, arguing that while material things are subject to generation and destruction, they are held together by a divine "Reason-Principle" and a "stewardship" that reflects the immortality of the higher realms.</summary>

<meta>This page follows Plotinus’s rejection of the Gnostic view of creation. While the previous page touched upon the origin of the physical universe, page 62 delves into the specific relationship between the Soul and the body, using the metaphor of a musical instrument to explain how the Soul remains superior even while animating matter. It transitions into a critique of Gnostic concepts like "fear" and "images."</meta>

# The Enneads
### On Nature, Contemplation, and the One

—She <note>Referring to the Soul.</note> uses the body just as one uses an **instrument** <term>Instrument</term> <note>original: "ὀργάνῳ" (organo); Plotinus often describes the body as a tool for the soul's work in the material world.</note>. And just as with a **lyre** <term>Lyre</term> <note>original: "κιθάρᾳ" (kithara); a stringed instrument used here as a metaphor for the harmony between the spiritual and the physical.</note>, some souls produce a sound, while others remain voiceless; so too it is with the things accomplished through the senses. In one sense, it is as it is, but in another, the **intelligible things** <note>original: "τὰ νοητά" (ta noeta); the true, unchanging realities found in the Divine Mind.</note> do not appear through their own nature. And thus, some things are births from that higher realm, while others are generated from the souls themselves. For both the things there and the things within the sense-organs themselves exist, and it is not that there is nothing of what they describe among them, but rather that the things among them appear more truly as the things that have come to be.

They say that each of the units are certain **forms** <note>original: "μορφὰς" (morphas); the outward shapes or structures of things.</note>, which must necessarily have been generated. And when that which is by nature is directed toward its likeness, the natural composition is also necessary. For the senses are affected by these things. For they <note>Likely the Gnostics, whom Plotinus is criticizing here.</note> introduce a soul led by a chance path of **error and fear** <note>original: "πλάνης καὶ φόβον" (planes kai phobon); a direct critique of the Gnostic belief that the material world was created out of a "fall" or "ignorance."</note>. And just as the affections arise from the voice through memory, so would the distance of essence be for a human, and for all things in the cosmos. 

But some things are exceptional, while others are used as metaphors for the affections of the soul. This is why their reason-principles are as they are. But it is not so in the higher realm. For it is not the case that each thing among them exists within the whole in the same way. For the whole is a **mental representation** <note>original: "φαντασία" (phantasia); an appearance or image in the mind.</note>. But in the whole that claims to participate in its own nature, so too it is with bodies. Either some things come to be, and others do not, according to their own affection. For they do not even say that **images** <term>Images</term> <note>original: "εἴδωλα" (eidola); reflections or "idols" that are not the true reality but a mere copy.</note> are truly images. And such are the affections of the soul itself. 

Regarding the ridiculous notion—which they do not even realize—they say that nothing happens in this way, but while these things exist, even the images "speak." And if some things become evil because they are generated, they become so because of that birth, so that they might distinguish them from themselves. They say many more things: that the things of nature are in this world, but the things in the higher realm are not the same. They introduce **faith** <note>original: "πίστην" (pistin); here used in a religious or dogmatic sense.</note> and a voice for them; for even the image possesses something of its origin through participation. But the things directed toward themselves are not immediately images, as many as she wills—the primary things themselves—but rather the things outside. 

And these things reveal what is entrusted to them. For what could do so more than the whole, or the parts, or the **spirit** <term>Spirit</term> <note>original: "πνεύματος" (pneumatos); in this context, the animating breath or a semi-material substance.</note>? And **divination** <note>original: "μαντική" (mantike); the practice of seeking knowledge of the future or the unknown by supernatural means.</note> belongs much more to the soul. They think that whatever she gave was for her benefit. Some of these things are exceptional, and what is exceptional is not to be let go. 

Nor would we perceive anything if we were merely following these ideas, or certain poems written for the seasons. And when she does not happen to share in the **Reason-Principle** <note>original: "λόγου" (logou); the formative principle that bridges the higher Intellect and the physical world.</note>, she seems to have come from the Good. And since the things are of a spiritual nature—for she herself is a genus, and is everywhere that which is immortal and incorruptible—so too it is with the entire cosmos. Therefore, it is not just as she wills. Some things exist after her, not produced by us, perhaps. Or perhaps they are certain spirits heard in a sensible sound. Or perhaps incense and sacrifice occur, and they think that both the words and the prayers are immediately heard, seeking again for the voices or the same power.

<summary>Plotinus critiques Gnostic views by arguing that the Soul governs the body as an instrument and that the physical world is a reflection of the divine, rather than a product of fear or error. He examines the nature of images (eidola) and challenges the efficacy of Gnostic rituals like incantations or specialized prayers.</summary>

<meta>This page continues a philosophical investigation into the nature of "Nobility" (eugeneia). While the previous page discussed the Soul's relationship to the body in Plotinus's Enneads, this specific text appears to be a fragment or a commentary on Aristotle’s lost treatise *On Nobility* (Περὶ εὐγενείας), which was often preserved alongside or cited in Neoplatonic works. It questions whether high birth is a matter of luck, ancestry, or personal virtue.</meta>

# The Enneads
### On Nobility and Virtue

...if it was written by him <note>likely referring to a previous philosopher's definition</note> because fortune is best; but it does not follow. If such things are to be considered 
<margin>C <note>The Greek letter Gamma, likely marking the third section or chapter.</note></margin> as belonging to the noble—such as being free-born and those descended from noble parents—is it not unworthy? 
And all the others; they themselves possess no private evil or good of their own, but only by nature. Yet one might say that the **noble** <term>Noble</term> <note>original: "γενναῖον" (gennaion); referring to excellence of stock or breed, like a well-bred horse.</note> and the **high-born** <term>High-born</term> <note>original: "εὐγενὲς" (eugenes); literally "well-born."</note> is something other than being fruitful; or is he the noble one for whom the things of **fortune** <term>Fortune</term> <note>original: "τύχης" (tyches); luck or external circumstances.</note> go well? But then again, we might shift the definition to **virtue** <term>Virtue</term> <note>original: "ἀρετήν" (areten); moral excellence.</note>, and say that those who are manifest as being from virtue are the well-gifted ones, and thus they become noble. But how should one take this? That the good man is the noble one? This is the same as being high-born, because he must "become" so. For even those who are half-themselves would perhaps have no fortune by nature; which is why it is absurd. Again and again, we transfer the term "noble," as if the **intellect** <term>Intellect</term> <note>original: "νοῦς" (nous); the highest part of the soul.</note> were nothing or just luck. And again, regarding nobility, for we say it is "nature," that the mind itself possesses this disposition, so that the intellect is not considered vain. It is a matter of being affected in a certain way, such that one happens upon some hopes of virtue, but is not himself able to share in the good. If there were a certain good disposition, then because of this nature, we think the one born is noble. For nobility exists in the house itself, even without nature. If someone is fortunate, he who wishes to understand thinks that no one from the high-born is truly noble; or that which he learned from other sufferings they have, let it be for those who know. Or why should one almost <note>original: "μονονουχὶ" (mononouchi); translated from the slightly garbled "λιονουεῖν".</note> think so? Even if one thinks it is according to the parents, not everything that has been born is theirs, because they did not happen to flee from themselves by what is just, but all are able to receive something, if indeed the sufferer is destroyed by it. For it happens thus to those who are equal or the **soul** <note>original: "ψυχὴ" (psyche).</note> by its power. So too itself, nature or the vice of the whole; for the noble man we might have, is never evil. Some might think this base thing belongs to a certain soul, or they would say so themselves almost; and they should not think that the noble man differs if he is evil—that is absurd. Or should one not differentiate according to **decency** <term>Decency</term> <note>original: "ἐπιεικὲς" (epieikes); equity or reasonableness.</note>, or mostly through evil? For from wherever they say it comes, it is through sufferings; but not through suffering, nor in this way. Nothing is beautiful for those who have come to be. Descendants carry down the beauty of the lineage from above, and again it exists in the children, and they transfer it, unless it is destroyed in all? But indeed, because it will be able, it is almost carried down. From the carrying down again, that which is from parents is beautiful; perhaps it will be shared. Then, because nobility does not consist in the father being beautiful; then if such a beauty and truth is in him, it is not possible to receive it. As it would appear marvelous; and because of it, as if straight and simple, it is beautiful in itself. It does not come from the fact that it was born; but either to this one it appears private, and the things within him...

<column-break/>

to these; and the poetic nature is beautiful to no one, and very rare are those within it, because of the character of the men. For the "high-born" itself is not a benefactor to any of the better men, neither by having it, but from the givers. For the noble one does not possess anything in a fatherly way; but he receives **grace** <note>original: "χάριν" (charin); favor or gift.</note> from the givers, though it might be base for them or exist because of their natures and because of themselves, who serve necessity, or to the fathers and the offspring. But one must consider how it holds with the beautiful. Is it then a name and the nature? For many things are not in the same place. Or is it that he himself suffers and they appear in the law and their own things? And not again by what began from just things from another toward some, will it belong to the one from parents. Because even base things come from just things; the same as animals, as many as are wicked. These being such, they do not produce good for themselves, and such they are; neither the other things. In both cases, it is for its own sake. Is it not then straight for himself, a certain thing? They say it is for men, or not for all, as many as use the things they make. And whether it is not true; as if for the same people. For it would seem to be the whole thing itself; of the same wine-making, but not by the "I have become." And to one who repents, this is it. And a witness of being good. For either he is base, or someone happens to be base or wicked. So that by turning the worse around, and again that which has good things. Or it appears to be mad. To be **temperate** <term>Temperate</term> <note>original: "σωφρονεῖν" (sophronein); sound-mindedness or self-control.</note> in this, and again to beget, or that the beautiful exists even if not present. For this belongs to those who have it; or rather to trust in **boastfulness** <term>Boastfulness</term> <note>original: "ἀλαζονείᾳ" (alazoneia); pretension or false claims to status.</note>. For there is a true **difficulty** <note>original: "ἀπορία" (aporia); a philosophical puzzle or deadlock.</note>. For many have desired the good for themselves. Or what luck also is. Having chosen this for those who have become, and more so for the noble, not to destroy it in the fatherland. Why the lineage? For what is the deed? Base things, however, or nevertheless, those from the high-born seem to be. Not born to the good, and either the animal not to the soul itself or as much as it is. ->On Innate Breath.<-

All things that come to be in nature were brought about by the nature of the Cause; and everything in us is the work of the Cause: both living, and sensing, and thinking, and moving. This entire nature belongs to the Cause. Especially this Cause is in **living beings** <term>Living Beings</term> <note>original: "ζῶσι" (zosi); often used by Plotinus to describe the soul-body complex.</note>, and the fact that there is a cause within them. But that which is within might change: the respiration; and the things in nature, especially all things. The things in the bodies come from the same causes. But that which is in the cause is for themselves. How <unclear>those</unclear> breaths of theirs [are]; and the motion toward the outside, <unclear>and</unclear> the cause; to suffer these things; and that this is a greater work of the cause. Not only is it so. But I would depart from those things mentioned, for neither is breathing [the cause]. For the things in the cause of it, we have the remainder in succession: that everything in nature, in which it holds, is also benefited by the same things, to act, both the things in the bodies and of education

The air-like blow fell to them to make them grow old. From that, it arises instead of life, and the things in us, and man has these in the sensory impulses, as much as might be, but as in the body the things not to the cause or in the body; and life itself is not the cause, and thus the things according to the breaths, but the things of the sensory powers are not in the living being; but <margin>these</unclear> and through this the things for living the breaths, it is necessary that all they themselves [do so]. For through the causes of natural philosophy. For I do not know what he knows. But if the living being exists here, and it is the cause of this being energized by the innate [breath] and the parts; the motion itself; all things are motions; the other things as many as happen, instead of not being, but rather sensory [motions], from those in us is the motion. Just as the motion of the parts of a living being is a living being; without sensation, but if in the living being that which is in the body of living beings; once and for all and that which is according to nature, the <margin>cause</margin> is also necessary.

<summary>Plotinus discusses the metaphysical origin of evil, arguing that it is a form of "harm" linked to matter and the passions of the soul, yet ultimately contained within a divine, necessary order. He explores how individual actions and cosmic justice are reconciled through the Reason-Principle and the governance of the Divine Mind.</summary>

<summary>Plotinus explores how the "Good" is pursued by all beings according to their nature, distinguishing between the instinctive drives of animals and the rational pursuit of the Good by humans. He argues that while perceptions of the Good vary, they are all governed by a singular, divine Reason-Principle (Logos) that maintains cosmic order.</summary>

In this way, the movement of the body is contrary to nature. But the divine journey of the soul: all things are in it, and those which it now provides as a part (whatever concerns the divine portion), for this reason he calls it a "spirit" as the cause. To be an occasion for not being; and from the other things, at least, are the doctrines. Or even if Fortune (that which) is not the holy thing itself of the soul, nor the Good. And reverence or faith is the perfection of Fortune throughout the goods in life. And these things too are from some cause. But the disorder of others is cast down by doctrine. That which one thinks is to "fare well" is because it was brought near to the life. And again—

Of the soul. And the **strength** <note>original: "μένος" (menos); spirit, force, or vital energy.</note> given to her by the gods for her actions, but not in such a way that all the rest remains within her own power. But because this spirit, called Fortune, possesses accidental powers, most clearly, from the well-being of the soul and from **virtue** <note>original: "ἀρετῆς" (aretēs); moral excellence or functional perfection.</note>, through which the better things of fortune are added. But it is not as if virtue creates them, just as the worse things do not come from vice. For then Fortune would not truly be Fortune, but would follow as a necessary consequence. But accidents do not bring themselves forth in all things. Because there is a great multitude of things from Fortune that meet and contribute to the birth of the works of virtue and vice, one must say of them that some exist and others do not. And "to be" is nothing else than **motion** <note>original: "κίνησις" (kinēsis); the process of change or activity.</note>. What is motion? It is said to be the **activity** <note>original: "ἐνεργεία" (energeia); the state of being "in-work" or actualized.</note> of that which is. And some are such, but from having good and again evil things. Those of Fortune are named thus. And one part is motion and activity. Since the most sovereign thing in beings is life, and this motion is called life. But since life is also twofold: one is irrational, being such and disorderly; the other is with **Reason** <note>original: "λόγου" (logou); the rational principle or Word.</note>, just as it has been allotted to the angels and gods. Inherently in them, as in men, the soul has something of its own from its own principle. And the ancients made this life, which participates in Reason and straightforward voluntary desires, a **spirit** (daimon); these are not the heavenly ones, but the activities of the soul herself according to the beloved natures of their own images. Or even from both sides of these, caring for each of our souls more greatly; for one might speak of it as a participation. Because nothing of the subsequent passions is left out from life, including even warlike actions. And the causes are spirits. What should one consider regarding the total disorder in the whole, whether just or unjust? And what is this "economy" <note>original: "οἰκονομία" (oikonomia); the management or divine arrangement of the universe.</note> of the spirits as if from a demonstrative Reason? From which it is concluded, either the sun or all the stars. But they did not make the things of vice so irrational and extraordinary. Rather, through choice, each soul chooses, and he has no part in it, except insofar as Fortune happens upon her. And just as if someone sleeps and does not perceive, so she herself indifferently brings the matters of administration to the spirit, whether they be from nature, from God, or from heaven. For the actions—nonetheless the whole and the causes—just as they say "to be well" (or "to live") is that which ought to be. For from where "to be possessed by a spirit" <note>original: "δαιμονίζειν" (daimonizein); often meaning "to be under the influence of a spirit."</note> is, and to him there is the well-being of the soul, already the things toward being possessed by a spirit, because the soul is nothing else. Who could have the opinion that each soul has those things which are subjected to nature? It seems that also according to nourishments and lives, it gives a share, whether it be to **philosophy** or not. Because living well and living according to Reason is to remain entirely in the Intellect (since the things from it are most manifest, those are good, or toward being better), or that the fortunes falling from the outside are nothing to God, or contribute nothing toward being happy, which is why they are called both good (as they say) and base; or whatever things are under his nature, being the identity of virtue and vice, are the causes.
