...coming from what is not. Just as with fruits, which pour out their first abundance prematurely before the proper season, only to draw their strength back into themselves, for the material <note>original: "ἔνυλον" (enylon); that which is composed of matter.</note> is such that it exists immediately after its generation. But since nature occurs in each thing according to the formative principles <note>original: "λόγοις" (logois); the rational patterns or blueprints that guide the development of living things.</note> that follow the seed, why does generation not happen in the same way, nor at the same times, nor in the same places? For not all things possess the same forms. Every nature possesses its own specific power, and none can do the same as another. Furthermore, not all things are born identical, nor do they possess the same power, nor do they grow in the same way. Again, why are things not produced at the same time? Is it because the causes are not all the same? Or is it because everything is present to the causes from every side, or through some other factor? When requirements differ, the things produced will also be different. Again, all things are the same, yet all things are different according to their formative principle.

-> + ON GENERATION + <-

As it is said: all things that are born come into being from something. They come either from a cause or from chance. But things arising from chance <note>original: "τύχης" (tychē); randomness or luck.</note> are not all the same, just as it is with the individual parts. And things exist for this cause. If all things in the world are directed toward the end of generation, nothing would exist as a mere part, nor would it be apart from the whole place of the world, but would be directed toward generation. Nor will all things happen again in the same places. Rather, it is as if all things come from them. Unless that cause, from which the thing is born, should occur once again. First, in the place of the world <note>original: "κόσμῳ" (kosmō); the ordered universe.</note>, all generation exists because things produced are not governed by chance. This same thing occurs again, either because of the nature of the things produced being released, or because of the causes described by the ancients. When the whole becomes a world, it must then possess all the same forms once again. But the factors relating to the maker are different. Again, if there is a generation of the earth and the world itself, there will certainly be a similar generation following the previous ones. If, therefore, they should come from them again, which of those things would be there again—either in the same state, or will it be different again? For if nature should ever give out everything it holds within itself, or if there were always a cause, it would not necessarily happen again from them, nor from those causes. The things produced by nature in succession are not all different. Furthermore, because the whole is the source from which all things are born, they are all kin. The motion of the whole is destined to be. Further, there is a beginning of causes, and from that source, those causes arise again. But all forms exist through the motion of the causes. And this power comes again from the parts. Thus, even before the things produced according to nature, there is a beginning of the city <note>original: "πόλεως ἀρχή" (poleōs archē); Plotinus often uses the "city" as a metaphor for the organized governance of the cosmos.</note>, born through every cause. Because of this, all things happen again, or toward the whole in the world suddenly. When everything moves, nothing is the cause of them, but of the generation itself. And everything is caused in the things that follow.

<column-break/>

This is not self-sufficient. Let this not be unprepared. Instead, there is an imagination <note>original: "φαντασίαν" (phantasian); an image or appearance in the mind or in matter.</note> of this. And through their own forms, they come into being from them as if according to a certain pattern. Bodies are common to them. There is a mixture <note>original: "κρᾶσις" (krasis); a blending or temperament of elements.</note>, and things do not arise from their own unique parts. All common things are unprepared. Furthermore, all the bodies of this world belong to heaven. Those things are below the heavens and the earth itself. Nature is specific, just as the ancients have said. And bodies exist through a certain kinship with the whole. Those in the same places are kin to one another. It is the internal nature by which all things happen. When all things are then sufficient. As many things as do not have a beginning in generation, they all move because of the Beautiful <note>original: "καλόν" (kalon); the Platonic ideal of Beauty which motivates the soul and the cosmos.</note>. Utility is judged, and it exists according to the cause within nature itself. Furthermore, all forms, such as those produced within them, are the same as those in the bodies. Furthermore, it is not possible for nature to generate those things which do not themselves produce a nature, such as the natures of animals and plants. It is agreed that from the things they arise from, everything in bodies is seed <note>original: "γονή" (gonē); the generative essence or biological blueprint.</note>. Before the cause, the body is born because that thing exists again, since it is not most essentially itself. Again, what would the whole be? Either that they are moving toward the end, because nature is in every place, so that all things are produced from it again. Why are there changes in them? Not all animals have eyes, such as those in the air. This is either because of the change of all things, or because some are earlier and some are newer, directed toward the final things. Animals become stable. If the world exists, there will certainly not be seed again. Thus they would not be the same, but others. Again, since the things with us happen in time. Those produced later are close to the generation of the places. And all things exist by their own impulse. All things come from the earth, or from certain others. But that generation happens entirely from itself. In this way, all things happen, and everything brings everything, whenever it is most appropriate. For the cause of all things is this: the world possesses everything and becomes everything because of the principle <note>original: "αρχή" (archē); the starting point or first cause.</note>, as much as one can most truly philosophize. In all things in the world, there is a cause. For those who differ in generation and for everything made of fire. There is a cause again, either because of the principles that complete the forms. So that the things within them would not happen again, though being produced again by a cause. For all the ancients, a certain city <note>See previous note on the cosmic city.</note> exists in the same state again, or after a certain time the cause will happen again in the same way. Why do the same things not happen again from them? This cause is most similar to the things that exist. Why then are all things not always the same? Or rather, that part comes into being. Because of which, and before all things, all bodies are of the seed. Again, one says that after the great change of the stars <note>original: "ἀστέρων μεταβολὴν" (asterōn metabolēn); the cyclical movement of the heavens believed to influence earthly events.</note>, all things then suddenly exist again, and the things produced from them are similar. Again, why not for all things, and such matters. When things are by nature, then all things are produced.

Thus, let it be the cause. Its own things are self-sufficient. <meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the relationship between the Soul (Psyche) and the Intellect (Nous). Having touched upon the influence of divine principles, Plotinus now moves into a technical discussion regarding "potentiality" (dynamis) and "actuality" (energeia). He is exploring how the soul "learns" and whether knowledge is a change or a state of being that is already present. This corresponds to themes in Ennead II.5, "On Potentiality and Actuality."</meta>

# Being . 100 .

<margin>What he intends to say</margin>
Someone might ask then: "What of it? It is in potentiality <term>dynamis; the inherent capacity to become or do something</term> with respect to its natural state, but in actuality <term>energeia; the state of being active, fully realized, or 'at work'</term> it is mathematical."
If someone says it is "mathematical in potentiality," what follows this potentiality? It is "being" by the removal of the potentiality.
I, however, say it is by the removal of potentiality, but not into its nature. For learning <note>original: "μανθάνειν"</note> is not the same as moving toward knowledge. For the powers of the same things are not identical. To know is not a matter of potentiality. Indeed, the faculty of sensation and the act of learning are not the same, just as fire and heat are distinct. For this is what it is to learn.
And if even this itself does not belong to the same thing, since it does not yet exist—this is the cause: it is not the same as the activity which leads it. A human being or an eye exists; but this cause is not the same. So then, regarding learning, how must the "acting" proceed as it should? And it must proceed toward the same thing according to the rational principle <term>logos; the formative or ordering principle of the universe</term>, which is directed toward itself and does not possess it merely by word. For like desires like. And by virtue, the like is drawn to it because of the kinship found in learning. For how does he say "the same thing"? The human being does not look toward the same thing, but possesses this in potentiality as a single power; so that even toward the scientific faculty, something active remains. For it is necessary that the learner possess first principles. For these must remain. For in all things, he would not be "in actuality" just as in the acts of making or contemplating. Because of these things, it [the soul] does not exist; on one hand, it does not think it possesses what is needed for learning, being tested by how much follows the making and being. For some say that that which is in potentiality there, becomes in actuality; hence the "mathematics" <note>likely referring to the objects of study or mathematical truths</note>. Thus, things in potentiality are not finished by nature.
The soul has a certain potentiality and delays in its being. For it is either acting or being acted upon <term>paschein; to be affected by an outside force or to suffer an impression</term>.
But how is it to be carried so as to possess knowledge? It must also differ from these very things. Because those things in relation to delays have a difference; and they are directed otherwise. There is a change from elsewhere brought about by science. Let this be conceded; for it is "in actuality" and is something unmoved <term>akineton; stable, unchanging, or not subject to physical motion</term>. These things are said to be "prior to the soul," yet we must assume that these things come to be in the soul, or rather, they come to be in the process of becoming. They are not present simply because of "making," for the same thing does not still become the same thing. This is the faculty of sensation. In the soul, this sensation has occurred. Through these things, therefore, there is something like time, so that the same thing does not encompass many things. But it is the same thing, and according to the same thing, it is "the fact that" it is unmoved. For these things are said to be by nature, so that in the soul—or as he says—there is a change of the same thing. This applies to all things. It is also unmoved. And it is not only so, but it is clear. For it is so both for the soul and for its order. The clear things are causes. So that this also is in the soul, because it is of "being" and of "number." It is possible to grasp this. But where time is, there is also everything...

I also say, to speak generally to all, that to apply this itself makes no sense. But it is possible to take it as a cause according to these terms. And it is also how the making itself relates to being. And how the "acting" is whatever it is, or by the fact that acting is being. So it appears that learning is a cause. <summary>Plotinus explores the Aristotelian categories of potentiality and actuality, arguing that the soul's transition to knowledge (learning) is not a simple physical change but a realization of something already present. He emphasizes that actuality is ontologically prior to potentiality and that the soul's true nature is found in an unmoved, stable state of being.</summary>

-># Notion . 100 .<-

As for the knowledge of theoretical things, and the general kind, it is either opinion <term>doxa; a belief that may be true but lacks the certainty of direct intellectual grasp</term> or the starting point of scientific and learned reason. Because of these things, it is the whole genus itself; it has not come into being, either irrationally or without distraction. For prudence <term>phronesis; practical wisdom or the directedness of the mind</term> arises when nature itself is brought forth. For it is itself a thing perceived by the senses. And opinion is such a thing. Just as if one were to sail from elsewhere toward the land to reach these opinions, or for them to be present to each other in their essence. One would not say that those things belonging to the soul are merely "upon" the soul. It is rather as if the soul knows itself by itself. For it is not by some external inspiration. Every movement, even that of the soul, having received it, does not possess the whole itself. And in the angle <note>original: "γωνία"; likely a geometric metaphor for the soul's "corner" or specific perspective</note>, it is for the soul to think it; it is herself.

<meta>This page transitions from the abstract discussion of the soul's "notion" to a more polemical and ethical investigation into deception, error, and the nature of "spirit." The text here appears to engage deeply with themes common in Gnosticism and early Christianity, particularly the distinction between the true God and the "images" of the material world.</meta>

-># Hermas. III. <-

<margin>
On Deception.
</margin>
And you are known, just as it is necessary for those who act, and for all those whom we are able to reach, that all these things are opposites: spirit toward spirits <note>original: "to pneuma pros pneumata"</note>, as he himself might say. But since he is now of God, he was already present. And he is very much of the Father. But if one must never speak of these things, nor of these things which belong to Being <term>to on; the ultimate reality or the realm of true existence</term>. When it happened that you were sent out, do not speak as a heretic <note>original: "hairetikon"; Plotinus often used this term to describe the Gnostics, whom he felt had "chosen" a distorted path away from classical philosophy</note>. Do not say to these people that life is thus, and it would happen according to every beginning—rather, it is under Him. For he gave all things to God. And through the grace of the Father, the accursed one, let us rather know it in this way. And because of this, receive grace, entirely as servants and through them; this, rather according to something. For the Greek woman, from those Greeks who are able to speak. But the works are thus molded, and mixed, toward the opposite. For why must I see, apart from that one again, as if in truth it seems to be by nature? Because of small blows that occur, he spoke thus, as if the whole is well-benefited, especially through this judgment. As if he would especially make it so, having taken these things up for himself, he looks down upon them. Therefore, all these things and very many blows and most things will happen after the ages <term>aeons; in Neoplatonism, these are eternal divine powers or emanations</term>, while he still acts as a priest over all things, which he also looks down upon. These things, then, are a sample. You have them in the same places, acting as a priest and through him. For why does it profit before this, and how through the imagination <term>phantasia; the mental faculty of image-making</term> of evil? He himself, being chosen, it must not be said to be of imaginations, to have these things toward that one, which are not on the left hand. But I say to all, as if to idols <term>eidola; reflections or phantoms that lack true substance</term>. As much as the earth in the body of souls, he said this. Error <term>plane; a wandering away from the truth</term> is therefore despair, a turning away from God. Is the great imagination not even in faith toward God? It is most of all, as one thing from another, remaining under the eye. Is error entirely away from God? Or that which happens to all souls, which he held through opposites toward faith. But perhaps this error is within nature. Or even by the nature of Being. And all things, indeed, are toward the matter <term>hyle; the raw, unformed "stuff" of the universe which Plotinus viewed as the furthest point from the divine light</term> that will be. And even the things under the formations, we said, through ancient things seemed to come from eternal matter. Regarding the world, it appears just as a shape or an image. There are especially spirits, because the whole becomes all things by a false name, and especially because there was no matter, nor because of this is it with God, if indeed, He is God. When he said they exist, they are neither shameful nor dead. All is all, through the imagination under all things, through which it is very right to encompass every boundary. And it should not be said reasonably; the objection is for these alone.

<column-break/>

An emptying <term>kenosis; a "pouring out" or depletion of being</term> and not a rest. And an image is imagination, and a phantom-appearance. In it, he will cease and I sink down from it. And man ate, at some time <note>A likely reference to the biblical Fall of Man, used here to illustrate the soul's descent into the material world</note>. For he who saw said, becoming a contender through piety, and the things of the Gospel <note>original: "euangelia"</note> appear. He learned a little. For they did not learn; but he learned in the Gospel. Nevertheless, since he speaks by nature. But why do they have these things because of this, when God was also in the flesh, but that someone of this sort uses everything. Therefore, alongside the proclamations, these things, and with imagination, nothing more and more. It is clear. If it is not the appearing itself, it is of God. Or they do not say so entirely. ### Eusebius, Book 3

->**On the Incorporeal**<-

...incorporeal, according to those who look only at the surface of things. But if God is the "All," then the divine must be such. And when, on the other hand, he enters into the body—for he is the body that is with us—then it is necessary for that which comes from the Maker to be of this nature. But if, likewise, the bodies themselves are his creation, then they are such things. What then, if the Universe itself is the instrument of the Maker, or if this body which he has made was not itself "coming into being"? Or is it not rather something else? Regarding the body, he distinguishes between form and matter, and all the individual parts. But he himself would become, as it were, abruptly separated. For he does not "become." Because of motion, he is not himself, but the <term>Logos</term> <note>original: "logos"; here meaning the rational account or governing principle</note> of Pan is not abruptly separated. This account primarily comes into being either through material form, and thus into life if any of the parts were something; then the whole would become, and it would not be excellent. But he [the pagan philosopher] thinks that God is this very thing. And thus he also thinks the world is God, and to him, nothing is strange in this. Every composite body was being divided. And he says not only that it is so, but according to the ancient nature, that which he calls "the All," he thinks is simultaneously ancient as the whole. For it is no more "being" than it is not entirely encompassing. But just as we might speak of the Aether, so too we might speak of the "Whole of God." For how can he call it so? It has been said of Pan that it is according to the same—

<margin>Note.</margin>
—these people are talking nonsense. If, again, everyone speaks of Pan, yet they do not declare him to be the "All," it is not worthy of rejection, since the Universe is a living being. But how it is a living being, it participates. And it becomes that one, existing upon the same gods—as a proof. For they say it participates, but not repeatedly. But the body does not. And thus no one would say to him, nor is it possible for any such thing to define the nature of the "All." He will enjoy more. He is further out than all things. But again, that God is transformed, for it is not of the individual; it is thus by the same, so that because of nature, he calls it so. Again, the same thing, how it might be said, or he speaks of Hephaestus <note>The Greek god of fire and craftsmanship.</note> as being separate. Such a thing is this, but that is desertion to another. No one is that one; he calls this in common, for he says in the "All" and in each part, becoming the giver of forms, and again becoming the law. It will not be possible to agree anywhere with one who says that things are composed, because even thus it is for those who wish for more. He who makes the "All" itself separate, like the whole, reveals our nature rather as another place. He blames that one. The work of all is most especially the endurance of these gods, so that one must look upon the things before him and the things after this; and one must also see in them the matters of material and the matters of necessity for him.

<column-break/>

As it was then: Having subordinated the entire world to him, all things according to the divine ones and the gods who are his friends, following immediately in second place, he attempts to theologize once again. But we must consider from what sort of elements their entire argument is composed. For in this way, it would be more possible to contemplate the natures of the gods themselves from which they draw their conclusions. He says then, stretching back again to the same myth of Pan: "Is it not, since he is the 'All,' that both the things in him and all things that will fall to life and harmony [are God]?" It is a necessity of Nature, which bears weight also in the "All," to be God; and he himself would be the "All," through whom all things and into whom all things must go. Wherefore he also speaks of Pan. But to the Greeks, such a description of the gods would be strange and uneducated. Since God is not the "All," but is believed to be *in* the "All"; nor, on the other hand, is the "All" entirely God. For in that case, he would be the god of all <term>daemons</term> <note>original: "daimonōn"; in this context, refers to lesser spirits or pagan deities, not necessarily "demons" in the modern sense.</note>. And of these, he thinks not only of the gods among the Greeks, but somewhere also the names of the barbarian gods, and again the "All"—such as Ammon <note>An Egyptian deity often identified by the Greeks with Zeus or Pan.</note> and Athena. For either he is Athena or he is Ammon. Then again, if Pan is fire, then the fire of Pan does not exist. Then again, he says that Hephaestus is fire, and Athena is fire once more. And that all fire is God, but not the part. And who would not laugh, if he also tried to say that Ares, and Aphrodite, and the remaining parts of the world were gods in the same way? But the things concerning Pan are thus. Whenever he attempts to speak of the things of the Sun (Helios) and the Moon (Selene): the Sun is like a source, the first of the lights in the world for its use, and taking up the rest he speaks of it as a source and a beginning of motion. The rest follows. Since the Sun is the whole world which we have—but not only the whole, but that which encompasses all things—how could it not be the "All"? But is it then the Sun, and the world, and his whole self? He did not stop there, but even held Apollo, and the Sun, and Light to be the "All," so that the rest might be as well. So then, for each of the things mentioned, he thinks each in turn is the "All." But whenever he speaks again of the body and the soul, and even the world itself, how will he say again that the world itself is the "All"? But all things are the "All." This is a greater task: how the bodies are carried along. But now that it is more so, the argument was: and especially the "All," and through all things again itself. And if it is thus, then all things in the world are God. Therefore, not all things are God. Or each thing resides in its own causes. Since the matters of Pan are thus, the rest appears to him through which [it acts]. And the things of stones and...

### On Being. III.

<margin>1.</margin>
...taking it and its nature. For if one were to say this, they speak concerning what is beneficial, claiming it is better for it because it exists by nature. Furthermore, while there is a cause, the **essence** <term>ousia: the fundamental "being" or "substance" of a thing</term> happens to be oriented toward it. Indeed, every hypothesis derived from the gods is shown to be the cause. For where **order** <note>original: "taxis"</note> is most present, that which is according to nature would most clearly appear. 

Since the process of **becoming** <term>genesis: the world of change and coming-into-being, as opposed to eternal being</term> exists, you have the results of this very inquiry. Thus is nature itself. The utility of a thing is said to lead the way. Then, by nature, it is such that it generated **sensation** <note>original: "aisthesis"</note>. From this comes becoming; and becoming has a cause. It follows that the process of "becoming" precedes the state of "having become." However, not every cause is nature. If it were so, then everything that exists would be something else. In things that have been generated, **imagination** <term>phantasia: the faculty of forming mental images or representations</term> exists. 

And again, it would be that which comes after, for it truly exists. Through that, it is a marvelous thing that all should praise, for one must grasp what is within. It seeks the "why." Therefore, it is linked to the cause, so that it seems to be in accord with nature. By removing its outline, one speaks of its very reputation. One might say it is not well-regarded, or it does not exist, or it exists but is still "prior to nature." Thus, he will show that there are necessities—parts that act as a cause already. But also the **imitation** <note>original: "mimesis"</note> of it is well-regarded in that it exists. So for all things, the end result is achieved, let nothing else happen, but let one easily grasp the generation that follows from them. Yet the other thing possesses the cause. This is already inescapable as a natural necessity. It was accepted. For it nonetheless exists. That which is from the beginning is proportional to them. 

Furthermore, the manner appears most necessary. Because of this, one must suffer or be held otherwise. For in these things it happens, as if from the same source the power of what is to come arises. Or perhaps it does not yet exist. But if the causes are such, the things that exist must come from the source of their generation. For they say that these things were present before. That it exists, therefore, seems to belong to them. But "being" is not the same as the "fear of being"; he demonstrated that the same thing will follow the rule it owes. Yet nature itself, like that which comes from imagination, is like a model, existing even before it is preserved in becoming. These things, then, are so universal that they do not return once they have passed. For what is still to come will be. To me, these are the necessities. Since this is so, they are held fast.

...as if holding the same evidence. For thus the first thing governs those that follow, and they follow after it, just as in some other **science** <term>episteme: organized, certain knowledge</term> the knowledge of each part exists. For even those who do not know, and those who wish to find the **principle** <term>arche: the beginning, source, or governing origin</term> from those who already know, do so in this way. For the same things are not better for everyone, just as these people, in speaking, do not seem to grasp the truly underlying realities. For they do not perceive the "Truly Existent" in this way. This is evident from the thing itself—what it is, its **purpose** <note>original: "to hou heneka"; literally "that for the sake of which"</note>, and as if from the same nature. 

What then? We must say that "Being" is such a thing. Again, before this, there is the **leading principle** <note>original: "proegoumenos logos"; the guiding rational account</note>. For if one seeks the cause of each thing, it is because it employs "True Being." For this is what it means to be Nature; it is through that principle.

For in the sensation of irrational creatures, there is a similar pattern. For it is not possible for things to exist according to what has been forgotten, nor does each thing beyond **essence** <note>original: "ousia"</note> come from it. The animal has a strange nature; wickedness is sought after, just as that which is contrary to reason. It deceived the truth. Lest anyone should say it is the same. In that other case, there is a thought, perhaps it took him back again, guarded by their division. That from which it comes is clear. But those things from which nothing comes are clearly non-existent. Therefore, he thinks he did not receive his lot. So there are those who desire, but it is not possible if they do not receive it. I apply the name as I do. 

It happens in this way that many things arise from the essence. But if the act of finding it destroys the first desire, how would it not appear to belong to the essence? So that which is sought of being participates in nothing. Each of them is whatever it is, for the things that are truly by nature are not the majority. It leads after itself, the whole being unmoved; it goes back to rejoicing, for those who have received it, not even the... Since it has the four stages of becoming. And by such a nature, it will grasp the things that exist. He declares then, having left from nature, for he who speaks of what comes after seems to say that these are the only things. If the object of the search existed in bodies, then everything concerning the majority of seekers would be as it must be. ### On the Soul and the Senses

<margin>Plotinus</margin>
It is clear, therefore, that because there is **imagination** <term>phantasia: the mental faculty that forms and holds images</term>, and not every **sensation** <term>aisthēsis: perception through the physical senses</term> is the same, the whole would exist in the thought of the transcendent; for the "Whole" is correctly thus. This Whole is present, in addition to being "under the Whole." Just as it persists in its own power, for it is not outside itself. This relates not only toward **matter** <note>original: "hylē"</note> in such a way, but also toward its own accompaniment. This then is the heading: or that which is most remaining. For it has no self-governance in anything, whatever it suffers; or it follows an ancient hypothesis. It is also toward **essence** <term>ousia: true being or substance</term>. This is present. That which is not a multitude has the power to become; or if it is, it is not otherwise. It exists in "becoming" <note>original: "genesis"</note> within the incorruptible, just as that other is. Because that which would imitate becoming, being its own toward existing things, has the greater within itself. But the **intellect** <term>nous: the higher mind or divine reason</term> is in that intellectual decay, having taken a nature opposite to the intellectual. For each thing is [what it is]. And because there is a "horse" of the Great. But the concepts from it [exist] in certain times—the spirit, or a stone; not just how. For these are also from the act of thinking. Or the **intelligible** <note>original: "noēton": that which is known by the mind rather than the senses</note> exists toward a time long ago, or a multitude from above came to be long ago. Or it is thus for him. That which is from the genus and the intellectual is not similarly in part to itself. For the intelligible might appear as nothing, once it has taken a nature, so that essences do not "become." Or that [nature] is in the intellectual... or it has light in the body itself. That which is old and participating. Since he called it, if perhaps he acquired it. Because in genus, it did not take a "where," for indeed it is not. For someone is lacking the cause of the essence, labored as if toward the same thing, nor to those things that as if complete the same of nature. Often, the same thing might be time. But if it is nothing, then all are equal. If they are not the same, but many, and exist within time, how can that which is composed of non-existent things be put together? <unclear>But</unclear> time would be more. <unclear>And</unclear> if this is so, the whole would be greatest. Or because of this, just as if someone says that a certain part is measured from it. And time is this, and the whole is time, itself being thus, or the motion itself. Of the sphere itself, or the whole of the "now" itself, or time itself being taken, or the spheres themselves. Because of this, the much and the more of it. If these things are the same as the better, they say all things exist. Just as the thing before this. And the whole of it would appear to be of time; for most things are. But perhaps again in certain things, so that this time is again in again; and that which is of the whole of the future being drawn along. Furthermore, all is time, or its parts, or the things of it are the same or different; or nothing of the parts. Either the planar motions will not be just; <unclear>of the</unclear> things having become drawn along. And time would seem not to exist. Except it exceeds all things. For if the motions of those who run are in the same [time]. And the sun itself moves through itself in a sphere. Through that, the sphere holds; or it is all. The sphere of the whole. Or all, just as all time is all things. If this is itself, then time itself. But time. If the smallest part of its motion is time, or the motion itself, but before its motion there might be some absence, like the trial of an emerald. <note>The mention of an "emerald" here likely refers to a specific color or clarity used as a metaphor for the transparency or "clearness" of a moment in time.</note> What then is time? All things or the relations before it, for it has not yet happened. It is such to be—

<column-break/>

<page-num>99</page-num>
<header>In Book IV.</header>

—investigated. Furthermore, if all of time or some parts of it have passed and some are to come, but none of it *is*, how can that which is composed of non-existent things participate in **substance** <term>ousia: being, essence, or reality</term>? In addition to these things, for every part—if it is indeed a part—it is necessary that when it exists, either all or some of the parts must exist. But of time, some parts have been and some are to come, and nothing *is*, though it exists. The **now** <term>nun: the instantaneous moment between past and future</term> is not a part. For a part measures the whole, and the whole must be composed of the parts; but time does not seem to be composed of "nows." Furthermore, the "now" which appears to divide the past and the future—whether it remains always one and the same or is always different—is not easy to see. For if it is always different, and no other part of time exists at the same time (that which does not contain, and that which is contained, just as a shorter time is contained by a longer), and if the "now" does not exist at the same time but is always different, the former "now" must have perished. Now, it is not possible for the "now" to have perished in itself (because it existed then), and it is not possible for the former "now" to have perished in another "now." For let it be impossible for "nows" to be next to one another, just as a point is not next to a point. If, therefore, it did not perish in the next "now" but in another, it would exist simultaneously with the infinite "nows" that are between them; but this is impossible. Yet, it is also not possible for it to remain always the same; for no finite divisible thing has only one limit, whether it be continuous in one direction or more. But the "now" is a limit, and it is possible to take a finite time. Furthermore, if to be "simultaneous" in time and neither before nor after is to be in the same and one "now," then if both the before and the after are in the same "now," the things that happened ten thousand years ago would be simultaneous with the things happening now, and nothing would be before or after another. Let these, then, be the puzzles concerning the properties of time. What time is and what its nature is, is equally unclear from the traditions and from the things we have just gone through. For some say it is the motion of the whole [universe], and others say it is the sphere itself. And yet, even a part of the revolution is a certain time, but it is not a revolution; for what is taken is a part of a revolution, not a revolution. Furthermore, if there were many heavens, time would similarly be the motion of any one of them, so that there would be many times at once. The sphere of the whole seemed to those who spoke of it to be time, because all things are in time and in the sphere of the whole; but this is too simplistic to require an inspection of its impossibilities.

<summary>This page presents Aristotle's classic "aporiae" or puzzles regarding the existence and nature of time, questioning whether time can truly exist if its parts (past and future) do not exist, and investigating the paradoxical nature of the "now." It concludes by dismissing earlier definitions of time as merely the motion of the celestial sphere or the universe itself.</summary>

Furthermore, no one truly hates himself. For example, if someone <term>lacks self-control<note>original: akrateuomenos; one who knows the right path but acts against it due to passion</note></term>, he may be praised by others, and yet even to such a man, this applies both to others and to himself, even if to all...

Furthermore, there is a test of this sort. That man is not hated by himself, just as the <term>unjust man<note>original: adikos</note></term> is not hated. It is not himself that is hated, but the injustice, just as it is with this man. For in general, if an unjust man is always hated, then his <term>desire<note>original: epithumia</note></term> for the body is a form of hatred through his own desire, because of which he is defeated by it, owing to the fact that he lacks the power to master himself. Furthermore, he is even hated by himself, or rather by that part of himself which is most prominent, because he is hateful. If hatred exists because of being hated, and there is both hating others and hating oneself most of all, it is because of that hatred which comes from the act of hating. Just as with hating, so it is with the one who is hated. Not in the highest sense, but in regard to himself and...

The man himself is unjust in this way, or he is most lacking in himself. Instead of being hated, there is also a <term>debt<note>original: chreos; can mean a financial debt or a moral obligation</note></term>. For this is true for such a debt. And it is possible not to be hated, but one might still be able to hate.

Concerning <term>pity<note>original: eleos</note></term>: it is not possible to pity those who are themselves able to pity. Instead of... the act of hating and being hated is a test of that accusation. For example, the just man does not possess honor, or rather, he does not receive it in equal measure. Or perhaps the just man is not so because of himself, nor concerning the harm done to him when God or just things [intervene]. Moreover, pity and being hated are justly received. But it is neglected, for it does not exist through him, nor is it in them. But it is because of the act of praising and the act of hating. This is a sign. Or perhaps the thing itself, for he certainly learns of the debt. There is therefore a test that hating and being hated belongs to the <term>wicked man<note>original: ponēros</note></term>; similarly, being hated and hating are linked to the act of hating itself. And if it is possible for him both to receive and to learn, or if there is a need and he receives it. Not that it is a test of him, though it exists. Nor is it impossible. Whether it concerns us or not. But for the sake of these things, and the things of those men, and the failure to obey the laws, such as those by which they govern. Instead of a test, it is a debt. And it exists, even if he does not hate. He may become hateful while having a debt. This applies to everyone because all possess it entirely. Whenever there is a debt, it is no longer a debt. Not that it is received in this way, but as a whole for him, and because of this, he both has the debt and receives it. Instead of a debt, this is a test. How could there be a certain test against him? Whenever he receives the middle part, not even himself. It is well shown by signs, both by being hated and by hating, and not by obeying, there is also a debt of learning. For this is found in all things. And this is the debt. It is a necessity to learn. It is a test from the first principles. For as much as it exists, it is not necessary.

<column-break/>

For which reason one should not return <term>grace<note>original: charin; a favor or a gift given freely</note></term> to the one who performed it, even if he himself receives it; this is because he receives it according to his own power. He does not receive it through a failure to care, nor through wickedness or <term>laziness<note>original: rathumia; a state of indifference or spiritual boredom</note></term>, but because he is simply unable. For it is either not within his power, or it does not belong to him.

Sometimes it is also a matter of time. For at one time we wish to be well-disposed, or to repay the debt, but we do not have the means. When we have the means, we no longer wish to. Thus we have the means but not the will, or sometimes we are not even able. Some people even desire to acquire these things which they do not have through a certain <term>mad greed<note>original: pleonexia; the vice of "always wanting more"</note></term>. Such a type of person is <term>licentious<note>original: akolastos; one who is undisciplined or lacks restraint</note></term>.

To fail to repay a debt, even to one's father, is a form of greed; for all such other things are done for the sake of profit. For he who is in love with profit is both licentious and unjust. Whenever someone receives something and does not return what is fitting, he is not considered licentious by everyone, but rather it is thought that he makes his stories into lies, either through error or through other passions which his nature possesses.

Furthermore, it is not even for profit. But because they think they ought not to have it. Rather, this very thing is a good; it is not profit because of the error, or even if someone left things unexamined due to the desire for profit. If therefore someone receives, or receives and gives back, to all those who cannot speak of it. Receive the whole, or again, let it not happen; it is written in a discourse concerning the whole nation. The cause of these things is the cause of those who are sought after, so that the matter might be a debt, and the parts which become certain things.

Furthermore, perhaps there is a certain influence from the seven parts of matter. But there is no source through them. How a debt once came to be, or shall be; for this is not among the causes. Because of this, <note>Aristotle often references Plato's later works when discussing the civic duties of individuals.</note> **Plato says in the *Laws*** that it is not just for one to return the same thing when he received the grace for no reason. **Plato** also says: he who is able to return, might not be able. But he who hears God wishes to rejoice, having held back his song. Whenever he himself or those through him [act], God also heard. For he does not return it, or he will give it. Even if he does not betray some part of the earth, he himself will give time to complete it.

Since the things received by the soul are not alike, and he wishes the same thing, he does not transfer it to another counsel; by his choice and by all the things being done, it is not necessary for there to be a certain opinion of what kind it is. For which reason some, through a certain greed, take it away from the one who performed the deed. Or he himself was not such as to give it back. Furthermore, they add something more that is not noteworthy, because even he for whom profit is shameful tries to do something useful. So it is and thus it is among the gods and among men, just as it is here.

...he will see, and remain in stillness, or he will be persuaded by himself. The same holds for the ancient constitutions; it is found mostly in the arts. Through these things, it is clear what is deliberatable, and that it is concerning the means to an end; the deliberator does not deliberate about the ends themselves, for the end must already be decided. These things, then, are said regarding the will; or how the end appears, or rather, the deliberator is the end. At any rate, wishing is of the end, as has been said.

<margin>
That the object of wish is not simply the good
</margin>

It seems to some that the <term>object of wish<note>original: bouleton; that which is desired by the rational will</note></term> is the Good, but to others it is the "apparent good." This happens because for those who say the object of wish is the Good itself, it follows that what the person who chooses incorrectly wishes for is not an "object of wish" at all. For if it were an object of wish, it would also be good. But it is, as it happens, bad. Conversely, for those who say the "apparent good" is the object of wish, it follows that there is no "natural" object of wish, but only what seems so to each person. But to different people, different things appear, and as it happens, even opposites. 

If these views are not satisfying, should we then say that, in an absolute and true sense, the Good is the object of wish, but for each individual it is the "apparent good"? To the excellent man, it is that which is true; but to the base man, it is whatever happens to be. It is just as it is with bodies: for those in good condition, things that are truly healthy are healthy, but for the sickly, other things are. Likewise with bitter and sweet, hot and heavy, and each of the other qualities. For the excellent man judges each thing rightly, and in each case the truth appears to him. For according to each state of character, there are specific things that are beautiful and pleasant, and the excellent man differs most perhaps in seeing the truth in each case, being as it were the **standard and measure** of them.

<margin>
That pleasure is the cause of deception
</margin>

For the many, deception seems to occur because of pleasure; for while it is not the Good, it appears to be so. They choose the pleasant as if it were good, and flee the painful as if it were evil. Now, regarding the virtues, it has been said that they are "mean states," and that they are "dispositions"...

Of the actions in our life, some are <term>within our power<note>original: eph' hemin; a core Stoic concept distinguishing what we control (our mind) from what we do not (the world)</note></term>, and others are not within it. Within our power are <term>preconception<note>original: prolepsis; an innate or fundamental concept</note></term>, <term>impulse<note>original: horme; the soul's drive toward an object</note></term>, <term>desire<note>original: orexis; the craving or reaching out for a thing</note></term>, and in a word, whatever are our own affairs. But not within our power are the body, property, reputation, offices, and in a word, whatever are not our own affairs. And the things within our power are by nature free, unhindered, and unimpeded. But the things not within our power are weak, enslaved, hindered, and belong to others. Remember then, that if you think the things naturally enslaved are free, and the things belonging to others are your own, you will be hindered, you will lament, you will be disturbed, and you will find fault with both gods and men. But if you think only what is yours to be yours, and what belongs to another to be another's, as it truly is, no one will ever compel you, no one will hinder you, you will find fault with no one, you will not accuse anyone, you will do nothing against your will, no one will hurt you, and you will have no enemy. For you will not suffer anything harmful. Aiming then at such great things, remember that you must not touch them with a moderate movement, but you must entirely give up some things, and postpone others for the present. But if you wish for both these and to rule and be wealthy, perhaps you will not even obtain these latter because you aim at the former as well. Certainly, you will fail to obtain those things through which alone freedom and happiness are achieved. Straightway then, practice saying to every harsh <term>impression<note>original: phantasia; here used in the Stoic sense of a provocative mental image or feeling</note></term>, "You are an impression and not at all the thing you appear to be." Then examine it and test it by these rules which you have; and first and chiefly by this: whether it concerns the things within our power or the things not within our power. And if it concerns something not within our power, let the thought be ready: "It is nothing to me." +

# Image III

However, the <term>Reason-Principle<note>original: logos; in Plotinian philosophy, this refers to the formative, rational power that emanates from a higher reality to organize a lower one</note></term> itself, which gives life to the whole and holds it together, is rather an <term>image<note>original: eikon; a representation that derives its being from an archetype</note></term> by power and by participation in the [higher] Reason-Principle. Just as it is with other images, where that which is <term>sensible<note>original: aisthetikon; perceptible by the senses rather than the intellect</note></term> comes into being, so <term>Nature<note>original: physis</note></term> itself is most sovereign; but everything that comes after it, whatever it may be, is a nature of similar parts. It comes from something; yet that which is an image by nature, and even nature itself, 

<margin>The image is something sensible</margin>
is everything within nature; but it is not itself sovereign in the primary sense, nor is it sovereign in just any way. It is a rational outflow, a sweetness; and it is akin to the Reason-Principle. And the whole is the same as the Reason-Principle, possessing life because of it, an impassive reason-principle of it, where the whole itself is within it. But it is no longer equal because of depth or the <term>passive body<note>original: somatos pathetou; the material body which is subject to external influences and change</note></term>. There is that which exists by the Reason-Principle, and there is that which comes after it—the vision of light; or even the first light itself, which again is entirely a vision, from which the <term>intelligible<note>original: noeton; the realm of pure thought and forms, accessible only to the mind</note></term> also comes to it. From these things, it is not. But it exists by being distant; it exists in being better or not. For it is a Reason-Principle, or that from which Nature was born, a Reason-Principle like a voice in the utterance of words, or even things not unconnected. It is an <term>effulgence<note>original: apaugasma; a radiance or shining forth from a source of light</note></term> of light, only

<margin>The sun is an image of the light</margin>
seeing, and not as if it were something merely shared. But that which stands against the opposite, just as in the case of the morning ray and the sun. For the best thing in the shadow is an image. It is that which gives life in nature; but to the image itself it is not so, just as with the light in the world, illuminating the earthly. Because the radiance has become light, from that source. Thus, then, are the things that come into being. And if someone should come to be with that same thing, he would surely be honoring Nature. In which there is also an image. For it is not possible for everything that comes into being to become so by being divided toward some particular human. Just as someone might use himself because he is not with, nor at a gate. And he would not perhaps come to be in the vision of the thing. But he would have been within it afterwards; at least in these things is the <term>Soul<note>original: psyche</note></term>. Of images, it is not the first; but the living being has stood up upon the earth; for indeed that which is in it is what I was saying. This (after this), that which is before the Reason-Principle toward nature, provides as much of the Soul as is needed. And there is another life, hidden in this birth, which is directed toward the heights. The Soul, then, is concerned with this. It is worth seeking whether other animals, or that which is in plants, participates in the living Reason-Principle, or whether it is the Reason-Principle itself, while that which is in it becomes a vital radiance, an outflow of it or something of the sort. Or even death, and for the things concerning the body, it is for itself. Or when that life should cease to rest upon another; thus it too is directed by its work toward that which has come into being. And that which has come into being has come to be for it, just as for the same thing and that which is in it, or even less than it. Or things still coming to be, and coming to be for itself.

<summary>Plotinus discusses how Nature and the physical world act as "images" or "radiance" (apaugasma) of a higher Reason-Principle, suggesting that all life is a form of contemplation or an outflow of a primary source. He explores the relationship between the Soul and the material world, positioning the sun as a metaphor for how higher realities illuminate the lower.</summary>

Having established that Nature is a lower reflection of the higher Reason-Principle, Plotinus now turns to the "passions" or "affections" (pathe) to determine if they are natural movements or deviations, and how they relate to the soul's leading part (hegemonikon).</meta>

# Enneads IV

Both are forms of the same nature. Each, however, through all things nonetheless exists as one; and the <term>leading principle<note>original: hegemonikon; the governing or "ruling" part of the soul in Stoic and Platonic thought</note></term> is an intensification, even in two types of suffering. It would not be a different nature, nor the sufferings of a different nature. For that which passes through the internal organs into the unseen is like making a specific quality or a <term>reason-principle<note>original: logos</note></term> of the suffering. But we have a hypothesis as to why they stand in this relation to it, as if they were certain things devoid of power. The question that will perhaps be most fittingly asked is this: what exactly is the nature of the <term>passions<note>original: pathon; the "affections" or "experiences" the soul undergoes, often translated as passions</note></term>? On one hand, it is an intensification of similar passions, whenever it is close to nature. If someone [adds] to another, the addition to them is not in every case a suffering; for many external things fall outside through error, not through the nature of nature, or the opposite; but rather as if they happen upon them or meet them by chance.

After the element, they have an advantage, just as again the reason-principle acts by nature; but if there is no mutual attraction of power, there is violence from the human being toward one another. Let no one, therefore, think that one thing is named in relation to other passions—the "contrary to nature"—since it holds some things equal to what is unsuitable; but rather how one thing is nature, and nature is not in all things, insofar as it says these things have come to those who have suffered, not perceiving nature. It is either neglect or the opposite. This is within him: one part remained while another fell, a specific quality of the passions themselves, and a birth, but as if in smoke. For instance, <term>matter<note>original: hyle</note></term> is like weapons. Because of the many passions, some are like a movement toward them or other things in a disordered way. At the same time, then, these things are distant from that; but if some small part remains the same, it would become one of the same nine passions. On the whole it exists, not itself indeed, but where again is the part that suffered or the error, with those things already present, or of that which has not suffered? This part dares to participate. For it will persuade the living by the living. But I speak of the passions. 

From nature, then, it completes its work. Such is the portion of the nine passions, because of which it is <term>contrary to nature<note>original: para physin; something that deviates from the healthy, intended order of a being</note></term>; however, that which is fashioned is not left behind, for the action remains, if indeed there is the same passion in the human being. For it exists in relation to a certain reason-principle. It is similar to passions coming to be, or even where it showed the cause to someone. But the things given over are impossible. So that one might not know whether it is by nature or a passion, and a passion is something specific. For that which is possible before nature, that itself may be found again as if it still belonged to something; but it is contrary to nature. So that while one thing is by nature, that other thing is a passion, and it is through the internal part of nature. For that which is either these things, or to become, or, through the giving over, happens by the transgression of the useful. By the starting-point of not being grieved, because nature imposed nothing manifest, or else it was some passion.

But as for that which has indeed come to be—if it has come to be—we have held it above, or having become the whole, not even by its own passions. If, at any rate, the whole is to be, then nothing of human affairs exists. But it is as if [it does not exist] by those passions. It belongs to the "now." Since he does not call it a movement, or it imparts a <term>beneficence<note>original: euergesian; a good deed or kind action</note></term>. But it moves itself in everything. So that even in the whole, being <term>ensouled<note>original: psychoumenos; endowed with a soul</note></term>, the reason-principle is in the passions because of what he was saying, or through something taken, another example of what already was. And it is a weight; which is not even through itself, which they place around it for the sake of examples. For to the one who is pitiable, the pitiable part is within. Or through actions, which we also have discovered, so that either something is superfluous or specific to its birth. Or similarities run together (just as this was proposed) which must be sought. 

Furthermore, whenever one has that which is reasonable, he who has chosen to come into being somehow holds this knowledge in turn. Or first, that which belongs to the <term>soul<note>original: psyche</note></term>, not toward the things it ought to have less of; but there the composition is sufficient; for indeed, it is all outside of it. So it is also with us. We must of necessity show a specific good before these things. In the soul, it is beginning again, or rather the actions are the birth. But that which is in the soul receives something very specific. Or again, it itself or the reason-principle makes it. One more so, the other more so. For that which was being said, then. For there is that which is not older. It is an investigation, or such a thing, to still consider the part that suffered as worthy. 

But if it shall be said what it does, it remains at rest in nature or stays, as in that which is worthy or has become, by which it was moved, and happening upon it. As it is said in that which is coming to be. And everything is because of a cause. Or because of another work; thus it appears. We say these other things, then, are "man," as whenever one has a reason-principle in the passion, having suffered nothing. Therefore he also spoke of the reason-principle; he has forbidden the soul that has not suffered, as if it would be the cause. And even if some soul is the movement or a movement, it is nonetheless natural for it to be accomplished. Not even so does it hold. This he also took beforehand: that it survived as the earth itself becomes. Or as it sees in all things. And the others are above. For either it is the reason-principle itself or it is to be. But since it is above. For now it is "all things"; but also the things belonging to what will suffer; but that which holds the opposite is like a journey. And even if it is made, it is through the journey. And the journeys. And even if it is carried around. Or it is not according to nature and it receives what is worthy. Since the act of making is a movement, it is beneficial. If indeed it is entirely either by nature, or we still grant it to all, insofar as it is the movement. And the movement from us, from itself, is rather as if by the <term>insensibility<note>original: anaisthesias; a lack of perception or feeling</note></term> of passions or of the stirring up. You would follow that, but if it is insensible. Or if it were something again, the whole thing that was carried away is itself nothing. But, even the divine things belong to it.

# Enneads III

Where then is life? For this reason, it is necessary to consider this again. If that [highest] life is life without movement; but the <term>reason-principle<note>original: logos; the organizing power that mediates between the higher Intellect and the physical world</note></term> of all is this; if indeed it should come to be after that [higher] life or alongside it. # Enneads III

We appear to ourselves through this. For if the **act of thinking** <term>noesis<note>original: noesis; the intuitive, non-discursive grasp of truth by the divine mind</note></term> were to exist—the **intelligible** <term>noeton<note>original: noeton; the realm of perfect Forms or Ideas that can be grasped by the Intellect</note></term> being present and co-existing with it—it must be in enjoyment of it. But the soul does not yet possess the act of thinking anything from it; it must turn back, as if seeking its own clarity within this.

Consequently, we possess both the **Intellect** <term>Nous<note>The second hypostasis in Plotinus's system; the Divine Mind that contains all truth and forms</note></term> and the **reason-principle** <note>original: logos</note> by looking upon them. For the Intellect is the thing that thinks; because I am becoming something else, I am pushed forward again so that we are able to know. This is lower in nature; it must happen that it turns toward the intelligible, just as we do not appear to be identical to that which is within us. Therefore, does it not also create itself? Sensation does not demand <unclear>memory</unclear> because it possesses parts of the same. For that which comes from it is required so that it may be capable. It does not appear to have acquired these things for itself by looking, or even to learn the heavy, but rather in that which was so far within the Intellect, while that which is revealed comes immediately from the **experience** <note>original: pathos; a state of being affected by something external or internal</note>.

The matter then is to have encompassed the Intellect. For the portion of the Intellect is, as it were, the remainder necessary for it. And just as according to its own substances it is indeed indivisible, it will receive all things in two—whence all things belong to the "Not." For you see again these certain **Lives** <note>Plotinus often treats "Life" as a metaphysical level of being</note> and the things within them; it desires all things to be. Therefore, also in the Intellect, that which "is" comes from the processing of these things.

There is, therefore, a Life and a processing and all the remaining things, which is somehow said to be. Its nature is that which exists in the indivisible. Thus, whenever it desires another, we are opposed to no one but ourselves. It saw the flow, even though it belongs to all. But indeed, all things; it sees all things in itself. To be the "All" is Life and all things. The Intellect is in all; all things were in that. But this—not participating in itself—having occurred in many places, it took back. But the Intellect, in no way having taken back the one within it, is therefore itself. Since all things are his in the "that," because he himself is each thing and all of humanity, and all living beings, and as many as there are—a concurrence of all. Just as with the **Beautiful** <note>To Kalon; for Plotinus, Beauty is nearly synonymous with Being and the Good</note>. Therefore, this belongs to all, so that he said he is himself because he is all. There, he lay himself in the "All," so that one might think, and because of this, it is necessary to live.

If, therefore, he is before all, it is so that the "greater" might be all things. And the greater of all is the "All of All." But it is not in anyone. Rather, it is so that all things might exist. For if it is distinguished, it is nonetheless the "there" of all things. But it is prior to the Intellect. Or it is not. Not only does it not participate in all, but it is not even in the "All." There, then, Life or Spirit is the **Father** <note>A term Plotinus occasionally uses for the One, the ultimate source</note>. If it is under Life, it is in no way of Life instead of Life itself, or even in this. In this way, he himself is the **outpouring** <note>original: procheesthai; the concept of "emanation" where reality flows out from the source without the source being diminished</note> of the whole. Like a **fountain** <note>original: pege; a classic Neoplatonic metaphor for the One</note>, it possesses without division. Just as—

Through many of all of them, it takes up again in the rivers. But first, the Intellect itself. The one who beholds is variegated. In the likeness of the forms of others, it is nonetheless in **union** <note>original: henosei; the state of being one</note>. The **One** <term>To Hen<note>The ultimate, transcendent source of all existence in Neoplatonism, beyond even Being and Intellect</note></term> must be thus, he having put forward something of his own—not an intelligible living being. They wish to go through all. See the **monad** <note>The principle of unity</note>... that he himself is not as if in forms for each. But those who are Intellect will become many living things, those within the first **Living Being** <note>original: zoon; the archetype of all life in the intelligible realm</note>.

You see it, even if by force. But even in the "Many." The question is clear. And there, with his lives, one must not think of them as merely "present." The **First**, then, who is not about the "All," therefore has the "All" in himself, but is in no way divided toward the others. Rather, the others are toward him. For from there, it is not as if from [a point], but rather as a pouring out of a defined life. Because they suffer a "leading back." They desire, but not there; and not as if in... if they do anything, they do many things to themselves and through themselves in him. For it is not in... but he himself is before each of these, the prior part. From which things, no. If not even one.

For if many are taken in, each is taken from the first in the "in." If it takes the thing according to analogy thus, for it takes the beginning in the surface. So that if there were an underlying portion, it would rather be of all as nothing more. For the First is mastered by nothing of itself. Through all things, then, give, and let the First be itself all that it has. Through choice it has to take; it has Life. And more than finding those things from him, he is encountered, substance again, so that they carry themselves, a living being not because of itself. But the "more" of them being. And he will speak to the others... he will see toward this. Let these be, existing in potential, but the "not" is not hindered. For it is before this that he will see. This one did not attempt it at all. Matter is in these. In these, we are disposed, but when. To see around the Intellect, the "in." That which is not in, for not even that is in. This then was necessary for those sailing out toward the "All," so that toward us. But not in... nor by sensation for those present. It wishes to be of him, either to be **God** or it would not be. In this way, the **Good things** are first, and the Good things possess those in the All. That which is for himself is by nature greater. Therefore, also thus for him, or for himself. We appear to the Good. Or rather, something faithful. Walking, to think something, which is **unseen**—the Intellect, not many of anyone. Therefore, just as the rhythm. Upon the Intelligible and for himself. Because toward the Good. It is clear, then, that he is not himself. Not because it is said of the Good, neither is it the Good. ...many things, nor are all things merely many in that way. For the **Soul** <note>original: psyche; the third hypostasis in Plotinus's system, acting as the bridge between the eternal divine mind and the physical world</note> itself is not divided in its entirety, so that it might once again exist within the **One** <note>The absolute, simple source of all reality</note>. Rather, all things have come from that source because that source is everywhere; yet it is also true that nothing of it is specifically "there." Because of this, it is itself nothing else but "the all." It exists within itself; for this reason, it is not contained within that in which other things exist, nor is it in the whole, nor is the whole the same as it. All things existed [there]; thus, the things in the cosmos also exist [there]. Whatever things might be in the cosmos, not one of them is many. Departing from these, just as it is, each thing becomes itself in the whole by nature, or perhaps by being left behind as the closest thing. Of these living beings, that [higher] nature perceives all these natures. These things are the particulars of generation; and the Soul itself undergoes something according to number. If indeed each of us has become this—as if centered around the **Intellect** <term>Nous<note>original: Nous; the Divine Mind containing the eternal forms/blueprints of all things</note></term> of each person existing in the soul—perhaps the whole is something within it. And just as the Intellect came to be in the soul, so too did it come to be in the Soul of the All. In this way, we are the same, and our sensation is the same. And from the soul, because of which all things are often left behind by it. Thus, in the same way, the soul possesses itself in the whole. And the things there exist because of another, wherever they may be. And from this, it possessed knowledge. Because of this, it is itself soul. And the things are in the thought, and this too is in the soul. For if it were in the soul, life would not cease in it; for it once gave power to the body itself. And it is in it and of it. Thus, if anything existed—even if it were the whole soul in the body, and if it had any power from being divided—then that which is **incorporeal** <note>original: asomaton; without a physical body</note> is well. It is in it. But it exists. It exists just as the same thing exists in each. Just as hope is something; but joy is conceived from there in this way: that the entry of that [soul] into the body occurs. That which is poured out from that source. These things occur because of the external activity assigned to it, hanging from it (as if one were seeing through a mist). Let it become itself without movement; but it is not in itself, or in the body. For if it were so, or if something were outside itself, or in itself; yet the whole is in the whole of that. And it is also upon

# On Being III.

itself. Rather, just as it was: for the same thing, whenever it becomes set apart over all and through all, nothing hinders it, because it is truly everywhere. In the fact that nothing of it is [there], nor are other things of it; yet it is the whole soul. So too are these things; and that world, for a soul encompasses it. It does not exist in that which is not known (or is known), because it does not exist in that where it is whole. As for the divided parts of bodies, however much soul any might have, they would be nothing if the living beings were not inside, composed of all things but situated in one. The soul extends through the parts of the universe; no part of it is further outside, if it is also in the others. Nothing, therefore, exists even in the universe, and these things are why the whole departs while walking within it. For every soul is **amphibious** <term>amphibios<note>original: amphibios; literally "living a double life," referring to the soul's ability to exist simultaneously in the intellectual realm and the material realm</note></term>. Thus it is not without resources; but having come upon the earth itself, the Intellect again participates; just as with the stars in the heavens, the things after these, and again those that have come to be in the same. And man also exists, and this is nothing greater; for in this way many are [moved] by many birds, and all things. But it belongs to that; and it in turn belongs to the same. This is the "self" of each. If, therefore, the things outside are this of them, and especially the things in the cosmos, if they are nothing else but far away.

<margin>
On the <unclear>quantity</unclear> of the <unclear>soul</unclear>
</margin>
When seeking the quantity of the **soul’s essence** <term>ousia<note>original: ousia; the fundamental being or substance of a thing, what it "really is" beyond its physical appearance</note></term>, just as we said when reporting on its essence, we speak in the manner of science, so as to question its very genus. Whether it is unchangeable—not choosing a beginning for itself—it clearly shows all the essence of the virtues and everything within it, because it is clearly shown by its own essence. For it is not divisible in the same way that a body is. Therefore, the unchangeable nature, according to its governing principle, lacks spatial dimensions. We behold the soul within the divisible. How then is it unchangeable? For if it were divisible, it would be according to something else; by necessity, its own nature stands in the middle. 

There is indeed a division in relation to the essence; for by necessity, it does not oppose what is by nature. These things are stated through the contradiction within them, because they are with their own nature. That point, therefore, belongs to universal learning: that in all things there is something indivisible. For the **Intellect** <term>Nous<note>original: Nous; the Divine Mind or higher consciousness</note></term> is the peak of itself, a glory derived from all souls. The same is the cause of virtue, even while being divisible in respect to virtue. (...) In many things, they say its blood is the ancient heaven(?). The whole(?) whereby the quality of **courage** <note>original: andreia; here Plotinus explores how a spiritual soul can possess "manly" or "brave" virtues</note> comes from itself(?) like(?) those things of the divided parts being set free from the divided. The freedom(?) of them(?) being an indivisible(?) nature, clearly shows(?) in(?) itself(?) that(?) by(?)

# In Book I

...of the best and the first. If then the divine is to the human as the other is to the inferior and that which lies below; for everywhere the things of God truly sing praises throughout the whole world; within which are the virtues of the divine father, and because of the "well-being" it flows out in this way; and by necessity, that in which we are shall not exist before that which is greater and best; for the divine exists through itself. Through which, therefore, they would not cease to move the earth and the heaven. And through which he says the "above" is properly the image of the fallen brave man. Because of this, it shines forth in this way toward the inner things; for this happens to the soul itself; the discourse about God again, is about that which comes from her. 

It is, therefore, first in this way, and in the greater genus; since they make all human things, as it were, within it, indivisible, and because of them it is as if it does not exist; for it is not less. How could this be in each of the mortals? The man and the courageous acts are not "courageous" in part, but by a universal nature, and courage follows in order. It will use not just each one individually. So also courage is by nature. It is itself in relation to itself because in every part it belongs to God. It is courage, because it is a whole. For that which is in it is its whole. And this too is a part of God, but it is also itself a whole, and it will be this in order, though less than Him. For there will be courageous acts as a part of nature, and because of this, it dwells with every greater thing. But already, it dwells with many. It is for the "unmanly" man himself to be entirely divided. For since it is again from there, its own things and the things toward it come to be. For it is a great thing from there, as it were. 

And because of this, there is no division. For when the human element is able to show courage itself; so indeed this, having been divided by a division, is possible. Thus also every nature is thus, and because of its own passions, as it is necessary to cool all things, courage is "up to us," because again it is divisible, yet it cannot be entirely indivisible. It will be more. Then, because the things of themselves. He who once owed a part. But of that which has not yet suffered. Let him look at those who have suffered in respect to the passions, while the soul is again above. The quality of the brave man shines forth in this way. Nor is that which is in him much less in the soul, and existing as an honor because of her. It is in him, naked and without deceit. For that which is with him, just as with God, would become greater than all things. And it is itself alone, as we said even to the divisible essences.
