### On the Soul. 30.

It is impossible for everything that exists to be merely partial. The soul is a part of these beings, yet it is not simply a part. It comes to be from a certain divinity <note>original: theiotes</note>; it would be something else entirely otherwise. If you say it is both, as we have expressed, these arguments will attempt to resolve this: how is there a difference between the whole and being? If these souls are continuous with being, are the many parts contained within the indivisible <term>ameristō<note>original: ameristō; that which cannot be divided into physical pieces</note></term>, or is it that not every part is in them in this way? Yet if he says those things are in the soul through these parts, then within the whole, the parts would perceive. 

Since perception <term>aisthanesthai<note>original: aisthanesthai; to sense or perceive through the body</note></term> is a part of the soul, is it partial or is it uniform? Or does it differ in each instance? Because it is the whole, it is called "sensation." If it were not the whole, it would not perceive as a whole. If it perceives through the whole, yet is partial, then the parts themselves must perceive. But how does the whole perceive? If it knew, then the **Intellect** <term>Nous<note>original: Nous; the higher divine mind</note></term> and all things would be unities. Because it has been newly affected by these experiences, it perceives. How could it become these things itself? Is their entire origin immortal? The part of the soul is immortal, for it is soul. They say the partial souls belong to the universal soul, but the sensitive parts belong to these individuals. Why then does the whole perceive? So that it might be, for otherwise that part would not even exist. How would the living being <term>zōon<note>original: zōon; a living creature or "animal"</note></term> perceive if it were not made of certain parts? Or how could perception be based on the whole soul? This would be ambiguous. 

If the entire soul is in the partial, it is not so by nature. Or must we grasp the soul again from the whole? For there is something intellectual <note>original: noeron</note> in all things for each individual. He says that all the parts of the living being are in themselves. Living beings live within the whole. For if they say the soul is one, and if it is indivisible, it is not impossible for it to be many things in various ways. If the whole is divided, or if the whole nature is continuous, then being is no longer the same as perceiving. Or perhaps perception exists alongside wisdom. Every living being in the whole is of such a kind, or perhaps not; for it is not necessary. Perhaps even perceiving is still a vital act and belongs to being a living creature in all things. That which is indivisible, he says, is "indivisible." It seems you might say that the partial souls participate <note>original: metalambanousin</note> in it. As was said before, souls are indivisible in their essence, but they become divisible due to the nature of the body. The indivisible would seem to be continuous in living beings, so that it is not even "a" soul. But if it shall be, the specific things in living beings are all governed by the **Intellect**. The vital and the sensitive belong only to them.

---

( ) To the whole world. Either being indivisible, or the living beings within it. And every soul.

<column-break/>

Since being these things is common to them, the specific characteristic of the soul is **to live** <term>zēn<note>original: zēn; the state of being alive or vital</note></term>. For only in the soul does life exist by nature. Therefore, it does not migrate to other things. If this is so, we must define "living." How? Is it not strictly necessary, since it pertains to life? Yet we say that in living beings, life is nothing other than perceiving. Furthermore, we must ask: if the partial—perhaps the individual man, or each of several men—is called immortal, are the partial parts of the soul immortal, or the whole? If they say the soul is not mortal, how do they perceive the whole, or how do the partial souls perceive? How then would the living being perceive? Since this is true, it would reasonably seem so to them. For it is not as if one knows grammar or music, or the cause in the partial instances. All partial things, such as grammar or music, are different. The others, such as being, belong to the **Intellect** and the rest. So how would the individual "reasons" <term>logoi<note>original: logoi; the formative principles or "blueprints" of things</note></term> of the whole exist in each species? Just as in man: the partial reason of man belongs to the individual man. The whole will be what remains of each. If, therefore, the soul is one and entire, the whole which is over all things will be the common element being divided.

---

( Since we said the whole exists, we must also understand the sensitive faculty. If it is more divine than these senses, this is its unique trait. Or if they are not ignorant of being, but see the partial things just as they see themselves. Regarding the "how": it is not only that the partial consists of the whole. **Plato** distinguishes this, or rather does not. Therefore, it is also beside the **Body** <term>Sōma<note>original: Sōma; the physical frame</note></term>. If it is indivisible and in no way dissolvable, he says the living being does not exist from itself. For it grows alongside the entanglement of this body, so as to know the intellectual things themselves. Just as life belongs to the whole. For how do the other things exist within the body itself? Why is it not necessary for every living being to perceive? Is it because none of these things proceed without harmony? Or because that which lives in the whole perceives? Not even he says that every "reason" or "principle" will be that which is. If we must clearly grasp the wholes, it is not that they are these, but that everything in the living being will live by the soul alone. And the whole, or the "reason" from all things and through the whole, is the soul. This shall be so; perhaps they say it is a living being because of this. Similarly, everyone participates through him, and if the soul is with it because of this, it participates in the **Intellect** and thinks. If the "participated" belongs to them, how do they participate in it? Is it as the body does? The whole exists then. It will attempt to reach all things everywhere. If this is indeed the case, we are all able to participate in the whole; not as a part of the whole, but as something unique. And so...

# On Being. 30.

...the soul. Regarding those who say it is the soul of the universe. It is not simply because he said it was a part <note>original: meros</note> that we must think of it as a physical piece, nor that it is divided by bodies in such a way that the souls are merely taken from there. If it comes from that source, and if its power is such that it receives the soul, we must ask: how can branches of knowledge be parts of the whole when they are of the same kind? In this way, the individual souls are the causes and parts of the whole, or rather, the "whole soul" is a source of concern for them. If the soul itself were to suffer or undergo experience, it would happen through the bodily nature; and it happens that the soul leaves it after the life of the whole. 

This soul is similar to what he wished to say. Regarding these matters: if one were to make it white, just as a part is of the same kind as its whole with no excess, for it would require much whiteness if it were to be a portion of the children. But rather, one should say the same condition applies, such as one of the eternal things, yet in another thing of such a kind and this in form <term>eidos<note>original: eidos; the essential "look" or blueprint of a thing</note></term>. But it is not in itself, or it is together, or it is one thing, many things, which is how this and such a thing exists. If it exists as a whole, it must not be a soul in that way, but must be the whole. It is necessary then that the part also exists. The causes, or whenever it might happen. Perhaps the part is related to the souls in another way, coming from the whole.

<margin>
(5)
</margin>

From itself. It is clear that it is not a part in the sense of being a piece, nor is it merely of the same kind, nor is it something cut off. For if it were divided into pieces, the "same kind" would fail whenever a part is missing. If it is unmixed—or if it is the whole, like **whiteness** <note>Plotinus often uses whiteness as an example of a quality that can be present in many things at once without being physically "cut up."</note>. Whether the whiteness in a part of the black substance is a part of the whiteness of the whole milk; it is greater because of the whiteness, and less through the whiteness. But the whiteness in the whole would not be in the part. But perhaps this is so. When whiteness is in a certain thing, or in the same thing, it is nothing like the whiteness in something hot; for the soul is not whiteness from itself. For example, the rational part <term>logikon<note>original: logikon; the faculty of reason</note></term>, or as a part of geometry is a part of science. All science is a part. Since the soul is not made of pieces, is it then not even from that which is of the same kind? For the whole is the parts of the parts; which is no longer the case. For it must be either the whole or a part. How then are these things in which it exists? It is the same and the reasoning, or the thing itself that suffers, for it holds itself toward the causes whenever they arise. Toward this, let the soul become an unmixed whiteness. For it makes things clear as a whole, not as many whitenesses. And it has been said. But the things in the many are the things of themselves; for there is still the individual property, and the forms of the many, the soul being what it is. Or rather, the souls—

<column-break/>

—itself in the soul. And if it is a part of the whole soul, will it produce a reason-principle <term>logos<note>original: logos; the formative, rational power that shapes matter</note></term> in the same form as the whole? First, it would not be so, nor is there a necessity for it to be this way for it to exist. For even the sciences are not the same. If it is a similar portion according to what is in it, then it is first a reason-principle that is the part; as in the soul of a living being. This is entirely common. And the soul becomes of the same kind; for even if the whole were a part, it would not be the whole, but only the parts. The "All" would not exist. Because the soul is something and the part exists, the magnitude is the smallest "all" and that of the whole. While it produces the body, they receive the whole, and if it is soul, it is not the part, but the whole; which was what was required. 

It appears also in the parts of a living being <term>zoon<note>original: zoon; can refer to an animal or the universe as a living organism</note></term>, just as in the small ones. When we confuse the living being itself, it leaves the parts of the whole. And yet these are the primary things. Let it be for the sake of vision, for it is the whole of it. For the whole will not be changed, just as in the ensouled body, the reason-principle is a part of the whole; or it exists as parts. In this way, this is the reason-principle of the soul itself. Not into this, of the part itself, since it is either the whole or not the whole. If the part is not the whole, the whole does not exist upon this. But if it is the part, just as bodies are parts of the whole, how then could the whole be a part? And how, when someone divides this, is the whole a whole part? If the suffering is a part, it is not the whole. But even if it is the part which acts, or if it were the body; but what is this portion of the whole? For even this is not one. 

Living beings are similar; but how are they related to the cosmos? Or how are they related to the universe? For it must be one, not the whole soul in the individual living being, for that which comes from it is in the body, a part of the whole within the universal living being. For it is not the whole, or every soul is the cause of what is in the universe; or again, at least within itself. But even this will hinder nothing; they are parts of the universe. This must be considered: how is it the same as the soul of the whole in that one? It is clear that the soul is present to all forms in the same way. For if it is a part of them, it would happen that it is the same in form as the whole and the soul of the universe. So that the whole—and the whole within it—must exist. From where does this come? That the part is also the whole. It seems this is because every power is its own. For it is a living being. The blood, for instance, or the eye. The **whole soul** is present in the part. It must be so, but the white part is from the color, as if from itself, and it did not cease from the forms of the body. For it is a form of the part, because the difference exists in the part, and the difference exists in both the whole and the part, the whole, so that—

# Heptad .2.

If a human being, even if everything else is shaped by potentiality, is also shaped by being. But if it is by being, then not all things are "to be." Are not all those things from that higher realm <note>original: ekeithen; referring to the intelligible or divine world beyond the senses</note> themselves being, and all things potential? But if they are from there, why are they not already present in all humans? Or is it that even sensible things <term>aisthēta<note>original: aisthēta; things perceived by the five senses rather than the mind</note></term> exist by one's own capacity? And the persuasion of the speaker or the presence of the reality makes the thing. But because it is in the present, the sensible things are not entirely disposed toward participation <note>original: metochais; the Platonic concept of physical things "sharing" in the essence of higher Forms</note> from that higher realm. Just as we might speak of a certain beneficence. And because it is not near, it does not speak as a whole. But the argument is directed more toward what is common. How then, if this is so, do beings exist? Because some are in being, and others are in the infinite, because particular things do not exist according to being. Let us speak of it thus in itself. Or how? Or are the things in the soul entirely those we would call a difficulty before the work, or especially those belonging to the passions <note>original: pathōn; the emotions or experiences that affect the soul</note>? For we would not rather call such a soul "passive." But if they are our own, they are surely the purer things. Or again, is the form in the same place? But if the form is in the soul, how does it relate to the purer things? If indeed they are the living beings from the soul herself. Because some are this way, and these very things are more properly suited to her own imitation. For it is not because of this that she herself, either by the opinion of her own form, or her own essence, or from herself, or what belongs to her, holds sway. But because she rouses the soul toward the Good, as is necessary, and this necessity is universal. It is made also by these souls. Or rather, through being itself existing in the soul, all things are her own. But not all things that come from her are created. And for this reason, she has mastered herself. If then she also will speak to herself regarding her own things. And how is it the cause? Just as God provides to each of the divided parts. Beneficently. He himself having come toward the whole. Either the whole, or the whole toward the things within his power. For the whole is its own paradigm. But nothing is of that source. Nothing from that realm are the things here. And she, in turn, releasing herself toward the whole, speaks truly in these matters. Beneficently, she does not cease from her cares. Thus, the sensible things belong to the soul that is gentle by nature, and this same soul beneficently directs what are called such things into the realm of the passions. As for our father, as if the whole of being were to become entirely within himself. Because nothing else is indestructible except in the child. But the souls of these things entirely give what is necessary of their own, having returned them without certain favors, as they would naturally come to be in the present. Or she will make such things occurring in souls. Or for them to be healthy, the things within her are the causes of those things directed toward herself. Concerning the decent man, she will have some such thing, either private or belonging to himself.

<column-break/>

It will be made through the trial of things as they truly are, and it is made also from the catastrophes. And it acts even through such things, when nothing pulls in the opposite direction. Is there then anything absurd, such as that which is insubstantial <term>anupostaton<note>original: anupostaton; lacking a real foundation or essential existence</note></term> by its own nature? And thus is the opposite of the Good. Hence from that source the whole is completed, not divided against it, but just as the things within itself. And if because of this, and thus also the Intellect <term>nous<note>original: nous; the divine Mind or highest level of reality below "The One"</note></term> is said there to be dispensed, because for this reason it also has no division, but makes each thing that exists to be born like itself. If then it is so, how then is being prior among all things than activity <term>energein<note>original: energein; to act or to be in a state of actuality</note></term>? For I am speaking already. For is every whole benefited, or does it exist thus, or entirely among the genera? Just as with the other living beings, each of those two participates through virtues. At least the man, even toward other living beings, has a certain beneficence and a giving nature, but for himself he has everything. How then do the sensible things exist, some in this way, because they live? Because some things are made according to the same pattern as those in the higher realm, and others according to some parts, and others not at all. And what kind of thing did he suspect of his own? Every person is therefore beneficent and makes his own things as such. But not random things, and he says this to all. Thus also God is beneficent, just as the other things are. But if he acts, it is beneficently, not for their own sake. Through which also beneficence comes from that higher realm, just as it is there. A request even for those who do not have it, for having received even from the beneficence there for himself. But if it is from himself, he also acts beneficently toward all. Or has he become of that source? But goodness is shaped by acting. How will the good man produce the world <note>original: kosmon; the ordered universe</note>, if not in addition to acting, he is to be benefited? Or he has become wonderful. For by holding to the same in this way, for such is its nature. And he holds it from that higher realm. But nothing perceives itself, but only in itself. But neither does that whole endure, both that and the whole. For the whole is entirely so, just as the "wholes" before it and there. And the souls, in turn, toward one another, acted in a greater way as even all the senses hold themselves, which are in the whole, and know this concerning the entire thing. How then, does it not perhaps make even that which belongs to itself? For it has these things, and those in the realm of the passions. Therefore it is also dissolved, and there are the things of activity, this rather by potentiality. In this image again, the cause of being is also the work. For the whole is not according to activity alone. Therefore, it is rather by the inspiration of the things seen. For it happens just as the causes are in that higher realm, so they are here. And these things belong to each. But she does these things for all living beings. And for each of them, from where does the acting come? Having summoned them herself. But not even the things in part, or how they are according to each of his things, nor first...

<summary>This page discusses how the soul acts "beneficently" to order the physical world, arguing that the Intellect and the Good are the primary causes of being, which precedes activity. Plotinus examines how individual souls participate in the divine realm and how "sensible" objects reflect higher forms through this participation.</summary>

<meta>Continuity Note: This page continues the inquiry from the previous discussion on potentiality and participation. Plotinus now turns to the specific nature of the soul’s presence on earth and its relationship to the Intellect, specifically questioning whether the soul as a whole or only a part of it is involved in bodily life and movement.</meta>

### Section 6

And this is life; but that which is in the Intellect <note>original: nous; the divine Mind or realm of pure thought</note>. On the earth, then, is every soul, and so too is the soul of the things situated here; thus even the sensory soul is present. Consequently, the whole soul, in those things pertaining to us, belongs to the sensory realm there; and so too the soul. For the body did not receive the whole soul; rather, the intelligible part remains there. Thus, while the sensory part is here, on the earth it is not like the intelligible part, but rather it is that which has been given form. In this way, the whole soul is in the body, yet it is not the "whole" soul <note>Plotinus often argues that a "higher" part of our soul never descends into the material world but remains eternally in the divine realm</note>. But one should not speak of it in this way; rather, if it is said to be by nature, then it must indeed participate; so that the essence <term>ousia<note>original: ousia; the fundamental being or "substance" of a thing</note></term> produces life and motion. It is necessary, then, to speak of the soul, not the body, as the cause; for the whole is moved because the soul itself has provided it with motion. This, then, must be assigned as the cause, and it must be said: we must speak of the entire essence of the soul, first its part—including the intellect, sense-perception <term>aisthēsis<note>original: aisthēsis; the faculty of perceiving through the senses</note></term>, and the soul’s opinion—and thus the whole of the soul, and every essence of the soul. And this is in nature, or rather, it is the generation of the soul; so that the soul itself is alteration. But if every portion is moved by the whole, the motion will again be similar. For this, one must hold that nature alone as the cause. If that which is in the Intellect is soul, then of this there is also sense-perception and growth. If, again, it is the nature within the living being, and its nature is the sensory motion—for the soul is said to be nature, life, and sense-perception—then he <note>Plotinus likely refers to Aristotle here</note> says this: it is either none of these, or it is the whole, or it is parts of the soul, or the whole.

<margin>
If the whole soul
moves, then
the sensory part
also moves, and
every <unclear>...</unclear>
</margin>
<margin>
If this life
is from the
soul, then
every motion
is from the soul;
but if this is not
entirely every
motion, then
it is not
necessarily
every soul.
</margin>

You understand this as well: that one should not speak only of the activities of the soul, but also of its being; so that this exists in the composite whole. Furthermore, the fact that the whole is moved will belong to the whole by the nature of the soul. This must be declared to be reasonable. For if every division is true, it is also true of their own bodies. And the fact that it exists from itself in the whole is the way of the soul of the universe. Unless one were to say that the senses exist by necessity; rather, the soul is itself by itself regarding these things. And we would especially say that the cause lies in others. But if it is indeed necessary, so it is for the remaining things besides these: they come to be toward their own ends. And for this soul, there is the act of being moved. Whether it be for desires or for wealth. And this same opinion applies to the same things. So that which belongs to the whole is a matter of inquiry: if it will be, it is because things will be mortal. But everything in the Intellect is either the whole or the entirety of its essence. If, however, there are parts in sense-perception. If everything is in the Intellect or everything is in sense-perception, every difference must be explained. In the "all," it is not "all" again. In that way, one has the periodic opinion. For if he says that periodic things also change, the soul comes to be; and if the soul is taken by nature, or being in such a state, or—

<column-break/>

Rather, not even every passion <term>pathos<note>original: pathos; an experience, emotion, or "suffering" that happens to a being</note></term> arises from the soul. For neither is every passion of the soul derived from that soul itself, nor does everything that happens occur in the soul. For opinion, and pain <term>lypē<note>original: lypē; physical pain or mental sorrow</note></term>, and pleasure are in the soul; and their not occurring elsewhere is possible. But if everything is in the soul, and these things belong to the soul and the body in common, it is a passion; so that every passion belongs to their soul; so that every passion is common to them; it is not that the soul alone becomes this. But if everything, then even feeling pain exists. If the soul feels pain, it is not by necessity; for one cannot even speak of nature where that which belongs to the soul is not present. But if we say the soul feels pain, it is again necessary that it be moved; because pain is a motion. If, then, being moved belongs to the soul through pain. Regarding this motion again, so that when we are in pain the soul is moved either in terms of place, or by alteration, or by some other category of essence. What then is this alteration? For either pain is something, or it is one of the soul's attributes. If the whole is different, or if it is motion, then either the Intellect moves. If that which produces the pain moves, it does not move the soul. If the opinion and intellect within the soul are moved, there is nonetheless no change in sense-perception; yet every motion is from the soul. If, then, it is the whole, that soul is moved. However, it is not an opinion. And love is either a departure from the soul, or every rendering of it from that source is its motion; and love is indeed a necessity. If every motion is moved in the soul, then the soul is some kind of passion. For the Intellect is a claim of life and nature. So that even the sensible objects themselves exist, or the whole of life in sense-perception belongs to the soul. But not that which comes from the soul. If, again, we say that all pain is in the soul, not everything in the soul is thus; he says this regarding the motion of the Intellect. For in that which belongs to the soul, it passes into that which is in its Intellect. But the Intellect, or that which is within it, and that which is the same as the living being's experience in the soul in the same place; so that, again, the soul itself feels pain. And in nature, every sense-perception is about the generation of living beings. Or indeed life, or the soul. So that this too is wherever the soul is found.

<summary>Plotinus examines whether the soul as a whole descends into the body and whether human experiences like pain and motion are changes within the soul itself or merely common to the body-soul composite. He concludes that while the soul causes motion, the higher Intellect remains largely unaffected by bodily passions.</summary>

<meta>Continuity Note: This page marks a shift from Plotinus's own Neoplatonic reasoning regarding the soul's descent to a summary or excerpt of Epicurean philosophy. <margin>
<unclear>Furthermore</unclear> <unclear>the</unclear> <unclear>speed</unclear>
</margin>

Furthermore, one must grasp the speed of their motion <note>original: phora; refers to the transit or carrying of atoms through space</note>, understanding that the motion of atoms through the vacuum occurs without any hindrance. For there is neither anything to strike against them, nor anything that yields to the transit of the atoms; therefore, slowness and speed are not considered in the same way by the mind as they are in the physical world. Regarding the movement of bodies, it occurs through <unclear>most</unclear> things; but even with respect to their unchanging nature, because nothing must ever be placed in opposition, there must be <unclear>some</unclear> <unclear>image</unclear>, <unclear>so that</unclear> speed is perceived by the mind, because nothing should occur within the soul to <unclear>be</unclear> <unclear>the</unclear> <unclear>cause</unclear> <unclear>of this</unclear>. Yet this speed of transit is not the same as that perceived by the mind. For even this mental perception is not equal to the motion perceived through the senses; <unclear>for</unclear> <unclear>sensation</unclear> is not equal to the motion in the mind, because the senses—or rather the objects of sense and the introductions through the sense organs—are distinct, as is the soul's own activity regarding <unclear>images</unclear> <unclear>of the</unclear> <unclear>imagination</unclear>. Regarding the motion of bodies, the result is equal. Since the motion perceived by the mind is not equal to the transit perceived by the senses, because the senses—or rather the objects of sense and the introductions through the sense organs—are distinct, as is the soul's own activity regarding images of the imagination. Regarding the motion of bodies, the result is equal. Since the motion perceived by the mind is not equal to the transit perceived by the senses, because the senses—or rather the objects of sense and the introductions through the sense organs—are distinct, as is the soul's own activity regarding images of the imagination. Regarding the motion of bodies, the result is equal. <note>This repeated passage likely reflects a scribal error or a common occurrence in ancient manuscripts where a line is accidentally recopied (dittography).</note>

<margin>
About the soul.
</margin>

The soul <term>psychē<note>original: psychē; here used in the Epicurean sense of a physical, though subtle, part of the organism</note></term> is a body of fine parts scattered throughout the whole frame, most closely resembling a spirit-breath <term>pneuma<note>original: pneuma; a mixture of air and heat that animates the body</note></term> possessing a certain mixture of heat, in some ways resembling the former and in some ways the latter. There is a part of it that has received a great deal of variation in its fineness of parts even compared to the other bodies, and because of this, it feels in sympathy with the rest of the frame. All of this is shown by the powers of the soul: the sensations, the ease of movement, the thoughts, and those things which, when we are deprived of them, we die. Indeed, one must also grasp that the soul holds the primary cause of sensation. However, it would not possess this cause if it were not somehow sheltered by the rest of the frame. The rest of the frame, having prepared this cause for the soul, has also itself shared in such an attribute from the soul—though not in all the attributes the soul possesses. Therefore, when the soul has departed, the body no longer has sensation. For the body did not possess this power in itself, but provided it to that other thing which was born along with it, which—through the power perfected within it—immediately produces for itself and for the body a sensory attribute during motion, just as I said, because of their neighboring and breathing together. Therefore, as long as the soul is present, it never lacks sensation, even if some other part of the body is removed. Even if the whole frame remains, it has sensation, even if the "covering" <unclear>has been stripped away</unclear>. But the rest of the frame, whether it remains as a whole or in part, does not have sensation once that soul has departed, however great the multitude of atoms it has for its own constitution. Furthermore, when the whole frame is dissolved, the soul is scattered and no longer possesses the same powers, nor is it moved, so that it no longer possesses sensation. For it is impossible to conceive of it perceiving if it is not in this system and using these motions, when the sheltering and surrounding elements are no longer of such a kind as those in which it now exists and has these movements.

<header>· Epicurus, Book A ·</header>
<page-num>110</page-num>

Beyond any external application, one must understand that from which we call "images" <term>eidōla<note>original: eidōla; thin films or "effluences" that Epicurus believed were continuously shed from the surfaces of objects to enable sight</note></term>. For there are certain outlines similar in shape to the solid bodies, though surpassing them in thinness, of the things that appear. For neither can these effluences—these increases in depth and solidity—be admitted to occur, nor these outlines being released from the sensory bodies, yet preserving the position and the order which they had in the solid bodies. We call these outlines "images." Indeed, the transit through the void, happening without hindrance, completes every length of distance inexpressibly fast in an instant of time; for the lack of resistance, or resistance itself, is comparable to speed and slowness. Moreover, the transit through several points at once, as perceived by the senses, does not take on a counter-movement to speed according to "thought-time," but when viewed according to imperceptible moments, nothing resists it. For apart from the time perceived by the senses, the whole is equal. For the idea that anything resists speed in "thought-time"—even if the whole is equal in "thought-time"—is in no way true. For even if the body in transit arrives at a sensory magnitude, the speed of its transit is not taken away by time. For all such things are viewed alongside sensory time, and the transit through the void can produce nothing in opposition to the senses.

<margin>
Images.
</margin>

Furthermore, the generation of images occurs as fast as a thought. For the flow from the surface of bodies is continuous, though it is not evident through any decrease in size because of the constant refilling; it preserves for a long time the position and order of the atoms on the solid body, even if it is sometimes confused. Rapid compositions also occur in the surrounding air, because there is no need to fill up the depth; and there are other such ways these things occur. For none of these things contradicts the senses, if one looks in a certain way at the clear evidence <note>original: enargeia; the self-evident clarity of a sensory perception</note>, which one must also apply to the sympathies of external things toward us. One must also believe that we see forms and think of them because something enters us from the outside. For external things could not stamp their own nature of color and form upon us through the air between us and them, nor through rays or any kind of streams going from us to them, in the way that certain "types" enter us from the objects—having the same color and same shape—according to the size fitting for sight or thought, using swift transits, and then for this reason giving back the appearance of a single and continuous thing, preserving the sympathy from the underlying object according to the corresponding vibration of the atoms in the depth of the solid body. And whatever appearance we grasp by an application to the mind or the sense organs, whether of shape or of attributes, this is the shape of the solid body, occurring in succession.

<summary>This page contains an excerpt from Epicurus's physics, likely from the Letter to Herodotus, explaining the material nature of the soul and the theory of images (eidola) that facilitate sight and thought. It defines the soul as a subtle body made of atoms that provides sensation to the physical frame, but notes that the soul scatters and loses perception once the body's structure is destroyed.</summary>

<meta>Continuity Note: The previous page discussed the soul's movement in Epicurean terms, focusing on atoms and the vacuum. This page returns to Plotinus’s core Neoplatonic investigation in Tractate 4, exploring the relationship between the Logos (Reason-Principle), the individual soul, and the cosmic order.</meta>

### Tractate 4

<margin>6</margin>
They say that the soul itself is also a certain form of the **Logos** <note>original: "λόγου"; the Reason-Principle that acts as a bridge between the divine Intellect and the material world</note>. That principle held sway, since we were able to proceed through all things. Yet it must be stated that not every wisdom is the same, for the will itself is a complete voice, or rather, the things within it. Or if it is the whole, then in this way someone might call it the cause of the nature of the whole; for that which is pure should not be guided by necessity. It belongs to a certain nature because of the parts in which it remains **impassive** <term>impassive: "apathei," meaning unaffected by external suffering or physical change</term>. For if it were thus contrary to the best, it would be so by the necessity of a hypothesis, and not of itself. And things are evil in so far as they are not divided, nor are they the things of the whole. Or this is the cause: if it is the nature of the "Father" <note>In Plotinian thought, the "Father" usually refers to the Intellect (Nous) or the One</note>, all things seem not to withdraw, but to exist within them afterward, since each thing came to be as it is. If it were under the **Logos**, it would have existed before those things that act with purpose. (For just as the things in us come from ourselves, each thing originates from where the soul might create it from the outside). But if it were directed toward external things, it would have originated from him. Nor does he provide the cause for it to itself, or even to the things near him. It is as if some part of us were to come from the **Logos**. The soul of this world is something desired, directed toward that which is greater for those who do not remain. They say of the soul that change perhaps happens to it again, and again; and furthermore, the same things occur according to continuity, not as if they were accidental additions. Thus, we might conclude that if it were not that soul—as if we spoke of it only because of that soul—then it would not be by an entanglement. And it seems like that "redness"; but if it were as if the difference were from fortune, it would arise from a counter-pressure. Whether someone says "no," or from where it is, how can it also be a cause to men? If one adds nothing to the soul, such as the "soul of a man," one takes this from the good and the cause for those who look toward the **Intellect** <term>Intellect (Nous): the realm of true being and divine thought</term>. What comes from the soul itself or from the cause, the soul itself gave to them as a particularity, as if to say it is not from another. If it is not possible for it, proceeding from above, to give additions, it is because there is something evil in every living creature of its own. Or perhaps it does not give to the whole of it; but someone might say the soul is not even in all of them, but is generated in them by the cosmos. More is provided to them in a **more bodily** sense, because it has learned the individual cares of each; at any rate, the cares of the bodies are required. And because of well-being, it acts soul-fully; so that to the rational soul, more things appear toward which there is habituation, appearing from these very things. To the lesser part of the cosmos, it happens so that they might have gifts in her; which is what the **Intellect** is to the soul of the whole. Through these things, such as occur to each, the external again comes from them, and he knows that nothing is. But if it should happen thus, for if it did not stand against it; for the things within, if it were from us. Because it is toward a cause; if one were to take away this simple harmony in which they exist. Or perhaps it is not granted to all to have a soul—

<column-break/>

<margin>7</margin>
First, then, having ceased to live the life of the "civic soul" <note>The life of social and political virtue, which Plotinus views as a preliminary stage before higher contemplation</note> at some point, and having established it into order, we should allow nothing into the **spirit** <term>pneuma: the vital breath or intermediary between soul and body</term> within us toward the gods. We must make these things from ourselves and by ourselves, removing certain fabrications, the ejections of impure desire, and the harmonies of sensation toward the sensible nature. When the soul is entirely of their lives, it is no longer even in the preceding states, but it happens to all the others. For in some, the living creatures produced within them let nothing go. Most things, and even more so in the parts, be assured, are produced in excess. If this is so, even if you do not seek the Father, you have had many in all things, as if to grasp the support of the rudders; in which it is nothing itself because of the soul. For why do we see this? We would not. But it is as if in a house. Whatever it is, the **Logos** excels because of its divine nature. These things also come from others. Thus it also happened outside of him. But he himself is this, in accordance with these things, because of her. The soul lives in such an **entanglement** <note>original: "πλοκῇ"; the weaving together of soul and material body</note> and changes its **substance** <term>hypostasis: the fundamental underlying reality or essence of a thing</term>. How could the living creature do so more, not yet, as is likely, if the entanglement here is from the cause? And yet, it is as if he who uses it is himself that which is most pleasant, and concerning the same things, without the "and" and "that," nature likened it, according to similarity and difference. For whether they were cut off, they are by nature toward the same things, and into one from the many. For what they might receive from nearby, in this way they might also possess a share of nature, so that everything which each thing is might become entirely whole, and these things also extend to the things following in order. In those things, the soul once gave a form, not toward the sensible things in their entirety. But if the error should fail and those things should be the work then, there is nothing. But let it be at some point that "to rejoice" is like participating in him, although there is a declaration in those things. One should not have to look by necessity, as if having stopped the proper periods <note>The celestial cycles or the pre-destined movements of the cosmos</note>. It is to be in the "second heaven," where the quality of nature exists, in a more bodily way, like a certain noble horse from the charge. For example, the whole follows, and the earth, for it is a self-sufficient living creature; with parts generated within it. Since they are produced as if by a generation, nature took hold. I, before the whole, placed us on the surface, all things becoming and all things that are destined to become. In what way do these same things happen; or also through other things passing, or such as these? Know that of those things, one cannot turn them around. But it is as if it were most pleasant, and to encompass the qualities of their natures. Of which also every multitude, concerning the whole, the **general ascent** <term>anagoge: the "leading up" or spiritual elevation of the soul to higher realms</term> is to be dissolved into the whole. In the last things of the whole; as you are, and again. If the whole belongs to the cosmos, then... for it is like the things of the senses; where—

<summary>Plotinus explores how the soul acts as a form of the Logos (Reason-Principle), mediating between the divine Intellect and the physical cosmos. He argues for a spiritual ascent (anagoge) that requires purifying the soul from civic life and bodily desires to return to its divine source.</summary>

<meta>Continuity Note: This page continues the discourse from Tractate 4, moving from the definition of the Logos as a form of the soul into a more theological exploration of the divine "Father," the "Spirit," and the relationship between the creator and creation. The language here reflects a 15th-century synthesis of Neoplatonism and Christian terminology.</meta>

### Evangelical D.

...and of the fathers, and through them to observe the laws that came from him. And I, to speak of the marvelous, say that one beholds his form with a running spirit <note>original: "δρόμῳ πνεύματι"; likely referring to a swift, spiritual intuition or a "spirit on the wing."</note>. Therefore, for this reason, one may call him God, both among men and as the guarantor of God. For God, having been begotten, became the **apostle** <term>apostle: "apostolos," literally one who is sent forth as a messenger or representative</term> of God over all things. But as he holds himself to himself, so that having been divided and begotten, one does not see him being corrected, but rather that things are superfluous to him; he proceeds to be made alive and again by life, or if he should appear once more as he was before God. When these things occur, he was seized by great fear; which thing, having been revealed again, comes to pass. He does not truly walk upon the earth, nor does he sleep, as if girded about, but he oversees the whole. For the things of the Father are led by the spirit <note>original: "ψυχαγωγεῖσθαι"; to guide or attract the soul, often used in the context of divine persuasion.</note> in all things. Nor does he alone, having suffered, rise again. 
<margin>7</margin> 
As the spirit knows the birth, and that this is with them, and the other gods, he may again become by nature. If it is so, then: Why is the divine called the glory of the Father? As it is. He who sent him is not [there]. But those who have received knowledge of the cause of life, how will you again assume life in God? But he walks toward God. Thus he himself also says that he came from the Father. And it signifies that his spirit may be found again in God. And the Father teaches him that he was purified among all that has come to be. And then immediately he remains. Since, therefore, either the whole is reasonable, because he had power in himself, and to him belonged the speaking. But these things are not from his own power, but because he was entrusted with the **Logos** <note>original: "λόγους"; the Word or Reason-Principle that structures reality.</note> from the Father. Then, through scripture, and immediately through the trial of death—as though experiencing nothing at all. For he was not fashioned for this reason, but accurately God and the things occurring by the power of the Father, as much as it is possible to imagine. In his absence, the spirit did not leave him, even in this. Nor did you consume love then, because of greater pity and beneficence. Nor was he deprived of them. But as his things were happening, or indeed life, so that all should perish, or be afflicted and consumed. Either it is a wandering itself, or because of the life-giving power among us, or it happens to all. They seek him. And in his return again, he brings forth his powers to him. From where he also speaks thus of him: that having subjected everything, including the spirits, he held to the character proper to him. And that God himself was left by the spirit, or how they were eager to stand beside them above. For the whole lives through him, and every word is in him through persuasion. The soul again. His begotten one. To be raised up with him, to release from birth, as through all things, that she might look upon him with him.

<column-break/>

The same things are also said concerning God, how he came to **creation** <term>creation: "ktisin," referring to the created world or the act of bringing things into existence.</term> because of a greater beneficence, and was present with creation and the creatures. For it is not possible to overlook those things belonging to the creator. For that which exists from itself, and that which comes to be through another, which is profitable for the good, is already and entirely referred back to God. Therefore, they do not only come to be for one another, but as we come from God and return to God, so they come to be for God in all things. For the animal that is thus by nature exists to bring its own work to completion. And from where 
<margin>7</margin> 
those, like certain spirits, keep the house and enter into bodies, just as it is with God. And of these two it is not possible to appear, but the majority, through which the work of creation might be seen. If it is necessary to say this, for which also the whole was worked, he will raise up the houses again. And the **resurrection** <term>resurrection: "anastasis," a rising up or restoration to life.</term> occurs through God. This is something that neither man nor angel would dare to enter upon. But the bodies [rise] by the resurrection of God. And if this has not happened, and that nature, then the whole is still lacking. For if the whole, then let the body also return again to life, according to the beginning. And the thing of this, through which every cause exists, how could it not also bring a good life, as the divine is nothing at all if men are not made alive? And indeed, this lies in all the others who hope for things to come. And of that hope, for those living, and those dying, and those who are not, since it is divided through the gift of the spirit, while he himself holds the whole. If it is good to say anything, he is blessed. And so also are all people, if they have life as good gifts for themselves. Think of him as one who delights in fortune. But this is the work of those things and the things that have happened, as not after much time, for if these things are not done through the flesh, we have been made vain, as with the other things practiced. But it is not possible. The soul again, concerning the things practiced, when she departs from nature as much as is necessary, let us leave what is our own. But the teacher did not cease from long ago, but came from above. And the things above are more manifest to those outside, and the things of the return are established, not according to their nature below, but the powers themselves from many cycles, if indeed the whole is this. And for this reason, he calls upon the powers. And one may say, he himself is the light of piety, and otherwise the light, as again the cause of the same. But not as though they were their own light, but his rays. And the color comes from where it is seen by all these. That which was thought to be from the light, approaching him, as if by something manifest. And thus seen by the light alone. Thus also it is to be said to him.

<meta>Continuity Note: This page transitions from the theological personification of the Divine Word (Logos) as an "Apostle" to a more technical Neoplatonic examination of how the Soul interacts with the physical body and the "Infinite." # Peace 2.

The same principles also apply to the body. For regarding the motive powers of bodies, even if there are colors that are not perceived—just as in the ancient theory of bodies—the whole is not simply a parallel overflow of all things, but rather a kind of **intellectual care**. This care takes hold of the body, even if it is not more formally acknowledged or recognized within the Intellect <note>original: "νοῦ"; the Divine Mind or higher consciousness</note>.

I say that the First is like the **Infinite** <term>Infinite: "apeiron," meaning that which has no boundaries or limits, often used here to describe the inexhaustible power of the Divine</term>. While all things in part—the things we specifically speak of—belong to the soul, to nature, and to radiance, each thing exists in the divine just as it does in the whole. It was clear that the things of that realm are present in all, by which I mean the whole consists of things intelligible to it.

Upon the Infinite was the **indivisible** and the uniform. This same thing is spoken of intellectually by the Intellect; for there it existed in activity <note>original: "ἐνεργείᾳ"; the state of being active or "at work," as opposed to mere potential</note>. The movement was complete and nearby, existing in an infinite order. Hope itself was infinite; for in all things, the sensory part belongs to the manifesting soul, while the reasoning <note>original: "λογισμὸς"; the logical, calculating faculty of the mind</note> is intelligible, just as the intelligible of that realm is the motive force.

The Infinite is that which holds authority there. And from that comes the intelligible of that realm. But that, then, is reasoning; and at one time it was the judge of the One—namely, that all things exist within us. This was essentially the soul’s own power of thought. Let reasoning be taken as a demonstration; this was the act of receiving reason. It was not, as has been said, an external contemplation <note>original: "θεωρία"; a deep, meditative looking or spiritual vision</note>, but just as contemplation exists there, that remains exceptional; for it is also demonstrative to the reasoning faculty.

And the infinite within the Intellect possesses the superior part. In the thinking faculty, it is the whole. Beyond that, the remainder is in the intelligible, because in that realm, the division exists for the intellectual natures. <unclear>C</unclear>oncerning them, since that which is in order possesses certain natures, it also exists in part. Yet becoming part of the whole as those things are, it contemplates within itself the whole and perceives the Infinite.

Being consists in that which is according to all things. Furthermore, the whole is in it; there, it is intelligible. It was therefore by a touch; both it and the whole are the same. It existed in the "there," and it possesses radiance and completeness just as it is there. And that soul is entirely there; the **indivisible activity** <term>indivisible activity: "ameristos energeia," the concept that a divine power acts as a unified whole even when its effects are felt in many places</term> is entirely present. Thus, that which belongs to it, which is itself and that which is in it, is the indivisible. But in the divisible realm, that which is "in part" exists within its instrument. This truth may be revealed: It would be beautiful for Being to become and to be. Therefore, it is indivisible, both itself and the other. However, because it was itself and that which is within it, he says that the Best is to cast that other one out.

He says of the Intellect that it is not the whole; but the Intellect is that which was to encompass the soul. And the ultimate end for the whole is to possess that which belongs to it. Since the sensory power—both itself being intellectual and sensory—was divisible regarding the infinite, having been instructed in the things of that realm, it divides them in no way. It is a whole.

<column-break/>

The things appearing everywhere were different and lacking in many ways. They must come to be within bodies. But if Being is not of such a kind as has been described, it holds the whole within itself; not in the part, as if the same thing were in another. For even if there is multiplicity, the thing being divided would be disordered.

But here, if it is a part, then that which is in it was, in that way, indivisibly within itself. But in our realm of being, there is also that which comes from the "greater darkness." Thus, by touching himself, he touches men; and all other things are directed toward the Intellect itself. Perhaps this resolves that difficulty. If anyone happens to pass by it, it exists by reasoning, through which the whole soul speaks these things. In its part, it is either a whole or it possesses the same soul full of all things, so that the ultimate end coincides with the "there."

Lest it be divided, it is ambiguous and twofold. Since that which is in the divisible exists as a whole together, it is passive and without tension. For it has been said that knowledge also becomes divisible, but the instrument possesses the unformed in potential; it has its being in itself, directly giving it length. For example, that which is "in" commands, since having been born from it, it escapes the soul's notice. 
<margin>causes</margin> 
If, in the possession of Being, one were to take the soul for the same thing, or the state of being in that whole as that Being. And indeed, that whole can be perceived. It exists even when stripped away; or the soul itself is less than that soul, not differing, or we possess all knowledge by it, so that the soul possesses all within itself.

<margin><note>A decorative flourish or mark appears in the right margin, resembling a stylized lunar sigma (C) or a specialized reference mark used by the scribe to highlight a particular passage.</note></margin>

Perhaps the organic, bodily nature was meant to become its own, or to belong to another, or to be that which is in that realm. And it is not indivisible; in another way, the whole of it receives it. And the things from us receive the soul, if it is there. For generally, according to forms of knowledge, we say it is all there; as if from itself, there was also that which belongs to it. The instrument was indivisible. From this, we possess the sensory power, from which it does not have the whole within the whole. Or perhaps it is not the same. From itself, all things are in the highest degree, or even the whole. And the things in which the ultimate exists. For that which has become through others is infinite, or through the whole and the place again.

Indeed, it was of the slanderer <note>original: "διαβόλου"; while often translated as "devil," in this philosophical context it may refer to a "divider" or that which creates a rift in the soul's unity</note> to say it is broken together with that one. But if it is the whole and the entire thing exists, this is its enjoyment. He who was, also existed in the part; so that it is the soul itself. For if the things in its presence are all the soul, its being is in many places, and the being is "there." For if the soul is also in others—since those things are also there—we say it is in this. But not even...

<summary>Plotinus explores the paradoxical nature of the Soul as both a unified, indivisible essence from the intelligible realm and a presence that permeates the divisible, physical body. He concludes that the Soul remains a "whole" even when its activities appear divided among sensory organs.</summary>

Timaeus wishes to distinguish these things, and after this, that which is in the account: the "composition." <note>A reference to Plato’s *Timaeus* 35a, where the Creator blends the "Indivisible" and the "Divisible" to form the Soul.</note> That which he distinguishes—and this has indeed been stated—is as if one were to say that Timaeus treats the soul as a kind of totality. But surely, if it subsists in this way, the "for" <unclear>substance</unclear> remains. That which subsists, however, is found both in movement and again in something like a greater soul. Therefore, nothing of this soul is missing from the whole. Indeed, it is something greater than a mere soul. If anyone says that everyone is in this state, first of all, they must again show that the whole is something greater. And if the following occurs—one breathes again in whatever way <unclear>it is possible</unclear>. Therefore, if one places it outside [the body]. But since it is not a whole within the divisible part—for it is ridiculous for the whole soul to be left behind—it might seem to be more of a body. But if this is the "All," then it must be within the whole. Place, then, is the cause. For that which is, is. Neither is it soul, nor does it exist after being in that which receives it.

If indeed someone should come to be, yet nevertheless remain in nature, this is what we claim to be worthy of merit. I have come to the soul. First, there is the divisible part and (after this) how it belongs to all things. It <unclear>is divided</unclear> toward itself and the body (so that it may be). It happens so that all things are within it. I possess the soul as a whole. Marvelous!—by its own nature it is divisible, yet it is also indivisible. Here he says the soul <unclear>is universal</unclear>.

<meta>Continuity Note: This page continues the ethical investigations of Plotinus, specifically moving from the general nature of the Soul's presence in the body to the specific definition of "Eudaimonia" (Well-being or True Happiness). Plotinus is now debating whether happiness is found in sensation or in the higher activity (energeia) of the soul.</meta>

# -> Ethics · 4 · <-

Activity is present for all in that which is living and directed toward itself, yet this is not yet true happiness. Rather, it is in the act of perceiving that activity exists within itself—just as we know. For one possesses happiness according to the power residing in the soul. In this communion, everyone attributes happiness to all things that the soul possesses; yet one possesses it only potentially. This is because of the divine immortality <note>The soul’s higher, unchanging nature which participates in the eternal.</note> once again. For as one says, the soul perceives through the intellect. You will find that some say happiness consists in reason (*logos*). It is clear that pleasure is also found therein; for the sensory part does not possess happiness. We must investigate whether happiness itself exists in this or that. These forms of happiness must be sought naturally according to the first principle. It is evident that pleasure resembles a kind of sensory happiness. It does not reside in the base man, just as the base man is in the city; nor does it come from the colors of life's power, for the soul is sensitive, and the soul is most lacking in this for everyone. But that which is in the realm of becoming and in general, obscures one's reputation through its making. The fact is that every active thing resembles happiness; thus, there is a degree of moderate happiness. This is the first source, from which comes the blood and breath (*pneuma*) <term>pneuma: the "vital breath" or spirit that serves as a vehicle for the soul in the body</term> in the living being; and this source is the soul. Unless, again, it is in all these things. We possess what we possess. If, moreover, we possess these things through sensations and souls, we do not always possess them in all things, nor do all people possess them always. Therefore, it is the last part of opinion—or perhaps opinion itself—that provides pleasure to him and to all, a kind of joy of his own, which will be the whole of him, yet it is fleeting. It exists within him, whatever it may be, at least according to sensation, since it appears to be a single thing. In this way, happiness exists, and in all these things, the same things abide for everyone; so that one might speak of the appearance of good fortune. From this comes activity, especially that which pertains to the work of the soul. But it seems entirely to be a law. These men might say whether it exists or not; but as that poet says, he made "eternity" (*aion*) <note>Plotinus often quotes Homer or Hesiod as "the poet," here likely referring to the eternal nature of the soul's life.</note> to be experienced by all. I speak of an obscurity for all, and of movements, and the beautiful; and in the whole, there would not be many parts nor sensation. But in such things, it is activity itself. Happiness belongs to that which is directed toward itself; and if some happiness is present, the principle nevertheless seems to harmonize with the law. In the beginnings of the virtues, this is reasonable, or rather, it concerns the entirety of this beautiful communion. And he will speak about whether he should hand it over and whether the ancient sensitivity might be cheered. Of the heart's race, nevertheless, we said nothing regarding sensation, nor is there anything else sensitive besides this. Hence, most of all, it is domestic to pleasure or to contemplation—whether or not God is in the...

<column-break/>

...God, in these things both following art and in this, the whole soul flourishes <note>original: "θέρει"; literally "summers," but used here to describe the soul in its prime or "reaping" its rewards.</note>. If pleasure exists, one must seek not sensation, but rather whether it sees the whole, or if everyone flourishes in pleasure. For not only us, but it is for their souls to be warmed by the living being—a metaphor, as it were. We must investigate why pleasure is to be made one's own <note>original: "οἰκειοποιεῖσθαι"; the process of making something part of one's own nature.</note>, or as with the "juice" of the organ of the senses, we must investigate likewise. But perhaps he says correctly that all things pursue pleasure. These are movements toward the gentle. For even those things without sensation seek nothing else, even if it is not from itself or for everyone; even those things not within us, but those within themselves, find pleasure in all. I mean, for example, to participate in what is present. Pleasure is not without substance. If it is most of all for everyone, since it is accompanied by pleasure, then happiness will follow. For it is not simple; nor do they themselves guarantee the absence of pain. Happiness is most of all this. Nor is he who is in pleasure a living being toward himself, especially where the sensitive part has dwelled. For the same pleasures exist for all. But because it is not the same for everyone, it is because the nature is not the same. The same things are desired, and they occur by nature for all. For the same thing does not belong to all in the same way. Not only is it the same, but in all things, it is entirely the "perfect" (*teleion*). But it is for them and for all to resemble metaphors, or to participate in them—such as the cosmos and the lovers of God. It does not appear simply. But unless one becomes the whole and those participating in God through these participations. In the same way, it seems like the whole. These same things will belong to all. There is no necessity for it to be universal, for it to be carried to him and to perceive sensation. If, therefore, the soul of the base participates in evil, let it be so. For pleasure is not simply everything, otherwise happiness would not exist. But whenever happiness exists, it is as if it were in the same pleasure; since happiness is pleasure. Through good fortune or through all fortunes, it is held. The ancients held not only happiness but also sensory contemplation. One perceives movement through a "grasp" (*labē*). Therefore, they said pleasure falls to all, or rather, it was said for them, for they even included good fortune. If happiness exists, it seems all things are for all; either because of the cause of art, or if we should obtain it when communion is taken away. But it seems the cause is for all. The happiness for the living being holds these things. For if at some time it receives it, or if the rational part receives it, how and why must be investigated.

<summary>Plotinus explores whether true happiness (Eudaimonia) is an internal activity of the soul or if it requires sensory pleasure and external good fortune. He concludes that while all living things pursue pleasure, true well-being is a higher activity linked to the soul's divine and rational nature.</summary>

<meta>Continuity Note: This page continues the discussion from page 115 regarding the nature of the Soul and its relationship to happiness (eudaimonia). Plotinus is shifting the focus from the sensory experience of happiness to the role of Providence and the internal divine spark.</meta>

# -> Ethics · 4 · <-

Who among the vigorous ones performs great deeds? Not even immediately is one deemed worthy. But if the soul is that which has been created, then these things belong to spirits <term>daimones: intermediate spiritual beings or guiding spirits that bridge the gap between the divine and the human</term> or to fortune. In such circumstances, one might remain well or live miserably. What then is the course? The soul shall be thus. But if the events that occur follow the sensible world, let them happen either fortunately or unfortunately. For the one who has died has no communion with his passions. Such things have no place there. Therefore, according to itself, [happiness] is up to us. Because the soul happens to be perceptible to God. For the body also contains the things of the body within itself. But for the soul, these things do not exist; rather, only the things of God do. Hence, it is through what is its own. Although the sensible world led the things of the gods around through the body. For its motion is in the cosmos. For it is necessary for the soul to prepare everything for the human being. Or perhaps there might be some release. This hardly happens even by chance. For just as some ancient wise man <note>original: "παλαιός τις σοφὸς"; likely a reference to Plato or Pythagoras</note> as they testify who seek the primary things. But for the many, his promise might occur entirely. The soul has a uniform nature <note>original: "μονοειδής φύσις", referring to the soul being of a single, non-composite essence</note>. And because of this, having learned that God... for He contains infinite things within. Because of this, just as if God were suddenly entirely water, like himself, he would take neither body nor shape nor color. For these were either sufferings from the gods or these were accounts. Since the essences of souls are in God. If the soul's nature is like fire, pulled away from the whole. Just as I have known even to the downward parts of the universe. Let everything be left behind and let them be there. For let the fated things happen. But to the God within us, he provides. Not only will he persuade, but he will also rather become attuned to good things. If it should never be reasonably demonstrated, it will be mine. But the soul is either a fabrication or magic. But there are exceptional things. Since those of knowledge said: that the things once thought are not profitable in time. But whoever is not present to sensible things. So that through divine reasons <term>logoi: the formative, rational principles that proceed from the Intellect to shape the material world</term> it happens. Her faith is promissory. Rather, it is her irregularity; those who wish her providence to come into being. Just as it has a body. The reason is known in that which God made, the earth upon her essence. But not without him. The "where" after the next things are graspable, or the reason is known through metaphysics.
<meta>catchword: from</meta>

<column-break/>

From this, one learns of their souls, as many as are given over to fortunes through the body; if they love earthly things, they are enslaved to those things they possess. He mentioned heaven. Still in order. Still the actions. As we said, he himself mentions the things of happiness. But if not these, they either remain hidden or they act without consideration. For not everyone [succeeds]. Or they themselves do not know; or that it is laid up for some of these ambitiously. These things are commanded in the cosmos: to do everything so that this or that might not happen. Some say the powers and the flame are from the gods, but they are the things of providence. From which the first things and very earnest prayers come. And it is possible to speak of some festival, in which the things concerning those who have died and our persuasive forms are brought forward, in which there are good things. And this is in them by nature, but none of those things are their own acquisitions. This is true in human life. Therefore, it would not have been fitting to have been eager for everything. For a soul might not be eager at all. But for the soul that uses the rational faculty of providence, it leads us well toward the most beautiful things through all. Or forgetfulness not only to admit the causes, but the many. And immediately those things, as many as are conducted while remaining after, or if they should draw nothing. Each according to its own reason. Since time is spent in waiting. But as for the things in it concerning the glory of God, to such an elder, it is productive of good things and toward life; in exchange for which one must keep upright toward living things, to be life-generating toward him is piety. And to contribute one's own life to himself by practicing piety. And finally for releases. He does not know the things that have ceased in ten, or whether a prayer must be endured. And he does these things for a soul unable to act. So that they are most useful toward hypotheses or existences. It is necessary, always trusting in the power, to maintain the most courageous order in the changes of life, as if to loosen the alternations of these for himself—if indeed it should happen through endurance, or he might have them not only as tolerable, but also as something more. And it is for this reason I did not go out above. Because of the life of the living being. As far as it was possible to be harmonious; nor any of the members. And it seemed that if a life were to come into being, I would have chosen it. And having come as far as the race, or having been made. Or by some fear of treaties. To the just one, souls are permanently fixed. It is necessary to be well-pleased with the consequences. Or even thus of the parts of the subject. Or the relations toward the parts. Not only for himself, but because of this, the things made by God. He who is sown in God, from where does he come? Through their single-membered life. He who is the caretaker of them, from where?
