## -> Chapter 2, Section 5 <-

However, shall we start again, leaving aside the attempt to examine what resides in memory? But if we do, why not rather consider those other things? What, in its entirety, is the act of remembering? For remembering seems to be its own thing; it is the quality of certain things remaining and persisting, so that it is spoken of as being within its own forms—or perhaps it should be described differently. For **opinion** <term>doxa: a level of cognition that deals with appearances and beliefs rather than certain knowledge</term>, even if it is scientific, is by no means called so because of sense-perception; but the one who recognizes something thereafter, that is how it differs. Again, sense-perception is like a spring that has been constructed. And because of this—the reason why the thing we are speaking of is unknown—perhaps no one can apply any mechanical explanation to this. Similarly, memory which occurs through these things belongs to the same class as similar concepts. Anyone who has gained knowledge would grant this. Perhaps it was said that opinion is the faculty of memory, or that opinion itself created this in the intellect; but from that comes either ignorance or something more. The first principle brings a certain **love** <note>original: "ἔρωτά τινα"; Plotinus often uses Eros to describe the soul's natural attraction to the Good or to the act of creation</note> to that which is being generated. There is evidence for this, because many things in memory are more detailed in their individual parts. This applies to things perceived by the senses as well. Hence, to speak of sensible things is the work of the faculty of memory. Within it, the first part is the sensory, which is of significant value; but memory will not exist for every single thing individually, which is why this must be the case. Memory is distinct from scientific knowledge, coming from Zeus <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ Διός"; here Zeus likely represents the World Soul or the Demiurge who orders the cosmos</note>, as he said primarily regarding this. It is that which most truly belongs to things that come after. For since the faculty of memory holds the sensible object—or the sensible object that is to be—by what do we judge it through the sensory power, or is it because memory is not manifest? It is necessary to have within oneself the things grasped by the senses, and of this, the sensible object is part. Since they are in the same things, they are either of the same genus or are the same. But if both were previously in the **imagination** <term>phantasia: the faculty that receives and stores the "images" or "impressions" from both the senses and the intellect</term>, what more would then occur? Entirely so. What necessity is there to be reminded of this—was this remembered, or do both things arise from the intellect? And we have distinguished all the different things that can be remembered. Since it is not through the intellect itself that most people gain experience. We say that some use causes when they seek to remember. If some possess the thing itself, they would remember it in another way, with the sensible things becoming actualized. But again, it will be clear from that which is within, to remember just as the sensible thing itself was experienced. And it is not possible to remember nothing. But if the object of memory is common, it holds the perception as an image. In the imagination, it exists otherwise, just as it exists in the intellect. This is a matter of a few things or many. It seems as if it goes through all things entirely; or is imagination not the greatest part of the matter, while memory belongs to that faculty?

<column-break/>

And of those things which were perceptions, memory is but a small part. For memory does not exist in perceptions alone. To the **spiritual** and good beings, it is not immediately through these senses we have seen that the organ of sense exists. Memory belongs to that which has been imagined <note>original: "τοῦ φαντασθέντος ἡ μνήμη"; this is a central Plotinian thesis: memory is not in the senses but in the imaginative faculty</note>, as does the power of recollection. Therefore, if these are perceptions, this is first by the nature of memory; or it differs in the perceptions themselves, or in the actions—unless the power of memory is contained within them. And memory does not exist for all perceptions according to itself, but rather these perceptions are within it. So that one might distinguish them. It is clear that the genus of the imaginative faculty comes from the making of opinion; it will show imagination, not as something base—such as these opinions being of themselves—but rather. Nevertheless, memory belongs to the act of imagining. If not, everything would be called into question. Perhaps even in speaking of the sensible or the recallable, there is a difficulty as to where the imagination is. Why does it happen at all, and do they obey some law, as in dramatic plays? But the argument is negative, and the powers of knowledge come from there. What then is imagination? There are some who say it is one thing more than another and nothing else; both the thing itself and its quality. Therefore, regarding memory, some things seem to have been said regarding its whole, or regarding the senses. Unless something else should occur for the sake of **perception** <term>antilēpsis: the conscious apprehension or "grasping" of an impression</term>. And according to those things by which we perceive, nothing occurs. This, however, does not distinguish what might come from heaven. Но each faculty has its own power of opinion; this follows the act of imagining, whenever it wishes to remember an image <note>original: "εἴδωλον"; a representation or double of the true object</note> and shapes it again. It no longer exists apart, but it holds an icon. In this, it follows after time; for the thing itself is produced within. It is in both. It calls it imagination, either because the sensible things also come to be. Again, it belongs to the sensory power; or again to the imaginative power—there are now two. They already have much to do with one another. Since both exist, they differ because of this. Thus also is memory. Whenever it exists in an experienced person, or when the image of those things is in the imagination, he is commanded—for this too is released—correctly in the imagination; just like those who are shut away and write in the shadow <note>original: "ἀποκεκλισμένοι σκιᾷ γράφειν"; a metaphor for the soul's attempt to record truths while distanced from the direct light of the Intelligible world</note>. And as he goes through it, he cares for the signs within it. But when we do not come to it in this way, leaving that behind, it is sometimes the same. It is not taken up in that way. Because the sensible object gave the soul the power to receive. In those things where there is more, the wagon <note>original: "ἄμαξα"; possibly a reference to the Chariot of the Soul in Plato's Phaedrus</note> and everything else departs. There, not every part... itself and also the senses. For the things of memory belong to the senses. Just as if they once followed some gatherings they had taken part in. Furthermore, it is necessary, for a little while...

# · Ennead III · Book 8 · Chapter 1 ·

And for this reason, it is as it is: one must act in this way. What then? Someone might say that the **Soul** <term>psychē: the life-principle that animates the body and connects the physical realm to the divine</term> possesses **contemplation** <term>theōria: the act of intellectual vision or "beholding" reality; for Plotinus, this is the primary activity of all existence</term>; and that it does not look toward "doing" <note>original: "ποιῆσαι" (poiēsai), meaning to make, produce, or act</note> but toward "being," and insofar as it exists, it is truly seen. 

But what would they say of the soul? And of that other level? What then? Does that level also possess contemplation, but does not act while being generated? Or is it rather that it is so, yet in a way that the **Intellect** <term>nous: the divine Mind or "Spirit," the realm of pure forms and perfect knowledge</term> does not possess? What then? Does the soul, existing in this way, do nothing? Or does it not even possess an "outer" contemplation? Or perhaps not so: but rather it directs both contemplation and its "doing" toward production, just as the arts do; for while the soul holds something within itself, it also acts, and makes itself a cause. 

But when the line is finally drawn—or if it is the same as contemplation—it is because it exists in this way, more so within itself. For from that higher source, the soul is entirely contemplation; or rather, it is not just contemplation, but is the Intellect itself, though we might speak of it as being of the Intellect. Production is, as it were, a byproduct of contemplation; for **nature** <term>physis: the lowest level of the soul that shapes the physical world</term> is born from contemplation and possesses it. 

As long as it is so, contemplation will be joined to it. Or is it because contemplation is everywhere? But if there is something more, we shall come to a division. And because of this, it is not. What then? Is contemplation first? Certainly, so that it is not merely a matter of being pleased, but that which exists before the "doing" is contemplation itself; it does not just arrive, but already follows before any power is exercised. Whatever might happen in these things, or even in the heavens themselves: for there is a spring of all things, but it appeared that nature was not a mixture from that source, but rather something else. Yet, everything comes from there. 

For contemplation is everywhere. Since even to see is a kind of "co-knowing" <note>original: "συνεπίστῃ" (synepistē), a shared or internal awareness</note>, either the one who contemplates is the vision itself, or the vision belongs to the contemplator. But in that state, when they have beheld it, they wish to see it entirely; yet those who have strayed become lost. For the soul lets itself go. Contemplation and the movement toward the Intellect itself are as if someone were the things that have been generated. Since it is also directed toward that higher reality. Since it is not the thing itself. 

Then, part of it possesses contemplation, for it does not think while it acts. But if the Intellect itself is present among those who have no intellect, or if there is something in those who are as if they were with it, then it is of the Intellect, and all things are together with the Intellect. For this contemplation is whatever might be found in **activity** <term>energeia: the state of being "at work" or in actualized existence</term>. And it is of God. For those things which are in truth are nothing else. 

In the stage after this, by its beauty and over all things, it will take up its productions through participation. For this soul acts in a noble way: looking toward that source, it was affected; and in turn, it shall be the cause of what follows. For that soul belongs to the **Intellectual Father** <note>original: "νοητοῦ πατρὸς" (noētou patros); a reference to the Divine Mind or the One as the progenitor of all reason-principles</note>; and this is how things come to be. 

Wherefore, the soul is a seeker of the **Divine Life** <note>original: "θείας... βίου" (theias biou)</note>. For surely friendship would not exist if it were not from the whole; concerning the things that are not here, let them not be diminished. Or rather, let them be more and more forgotten as they become.

<summary>Plotinus argues that all existence, including Nature, is fundamentally an act of contemplation (theōria). Action and physical production are not ends in themselves, but weakened byproducts of an internal intellectual vision that seeks to return to the "Intellectual Father."</summary>

# · Ennead III ·

And one might see this through myriad instances. What then? Is that also now power and life for it? 
O most excellent friend, even the ensouled cause is involved. For every living being is not composed of soul alone and body, which constitutes it; but rather from both of these and the **bond** <term>syndesmos: the unifying link or "tether" that holds the immaterial soul and material body together in a single organism</term> between them. It is also clear regarding both fire and water, that each of these is both bodily and incorporeal <note>Plotinus is referring to the "forming principles" or *logoi* of the elements; while we see the physical water, its essential nature or "form" is an immaterial reality</note>. But these are not the only things; one must also consider their principles and nature, and also their light in this same way. For if nothing is immutable, it would be so because of the life and light within it. For these things, as if in each individual, will receive something from these principles and the desire for them. And again, someone trying to deceive themselves otherwise might imagine a "bulwark of thought," which **opinion** <term>doxa: a level of cognition that deals with appearances and beliefs rather than certain, intellectual truth</term> has rendered as life within it.

As we seek the meaning of these **reasons** <term>logoi: the formative, rational principles that emanate from the Soul to organize matter</term>, it appears to be a matter of inquiry, such as how every soul comes to be under the grasp of understanding, and from what things within it the universal parts have arisen. But it seems only to possess this and to have this power. If, therefore, it is **essence** <term>ousia: true being or substance; in Neoplatonism, this refers to the higher, stable reality of the intelligible world</term>, how would it not know? And if it is life and light and the cause of sensible things <note>Sensible things are those perceived by the five senses, as opposed to "intelligible" things known by the mind</note> to a great degree. Since the fragmented appears unstable, why would the remaining sensible parts not also depend upon it? But that would be absurd. For the things in **Being** will themselves also exist there. These things have become, as it were, its own. And if, because of this, it were able, would it then know? But whenever it reaches toward the **intelligible** <term>noēton: the realm of pure Thought and Divine Mind, which exists beyond the physical world</term> and from there to us, or if it participates in the whole, then that light, which is the cause derived from the sensible, will be established. Sharing in division, he said the "reasons" <gloss>the forming principles</gloss> were fathers and did not have the authority. 

But it is sought whether even the intelligible itself, if it becomes the property of spirits, how one must then remember it. For if, on the other hand, someone were to say that every life is of **Life** <note>Plotinus distinguishes between individual, physical lives and the "Universal Life" or the "Life-in-itself" that resides in the Divine Mind</note>. If then it is so, every soul belongs to the intelligible. For if it is according to a great abundance of life, it is necessary for each to be distinct and for the soul to be, as it were, expansive and changeable. It holds itself there, because you have remembered it. This is so that the transformation of the thing might occur. And immediately it remains present to it, though this soul is exceedingly isolated. 
But this soul, because it departs toward the heights, its course is toward the sun

And we, perhaps dealing with the affairs of living creatures, still contemplate similar things belonging to the great abundance of the **spiritual** <term>pneumatikos: here referring to the subtle, "airy" or "spirit-like" nature of the soul's lower functions</term>. One must seek this. Since all this power of the rational spirit extends over everything. If, therefore, it participates in those things that came after it, and this is the earth, it is either worn away or fleeing from the knowledge of itself; it becomes rational, or it follows along with **opinion** <gloss>doxa</gloss>, or...

### The Probable Account

Since, therefore, not only the things appearing in this world are supposed to have come to be through causes and by God, but indeed the whole itself and that from which it was made by God, what would remain? For neither does the first seem to be in need of causes, but quite the opposite, and especially so that the good and the beautiful might be assumed to be in all things through a straight path. Since then, at the beginning, what God wishes to make, and to have faith in these things having been worked out, since the present Providence is not idle; although if the **Craftsman** <term>technites: the divine artisan, often identified with the Demiurge, who fashions the material world according to eternal forms</term> acts according to the same things, he would most of all give to each what is fitting. And we say again that the nature <margin>of the world</margin> of it is established as nature, the soul again making it from the things it was made in which works, when the sun and moon and the others, have a **sympathy** <term>sympatheia: the "feeling together" or interconnectedness of all parts of the universe, such that a change in one part affects the whole</term> with the heavens. And sometimes these things being born greater from the smooth and most orderly, neither time would fail nor the whole, if it should nod, but it is necessary for them to make, because the breath of that one, the soul, goes through the same, where its rational part remains, and thus of it, and the sensitive part indeed, where all things are written together. It approached toward the outside. And after its own life, it is the cause. For even **Fate** <term>moira: the chain of material causes and effects that governs the lower world</term> is not left out of its passions, if we ever knew, and then it happened, those who seemed to sympathize with each other, and with that one. And not only the outcome. Just as privately the things in it. May it always be. Because it does not happen automatically from a base thing with happiness. So as to provoke again through a voice. For such error does not belong to the gods, especially; nor that something that has happened should harm him, which would not belong to the blessed ones. And he will say, that it does not change thus, but that of the souls of it at some time and the whole and upon his soul and all together would not happen, unless it **dances** <note>original: "χορεύει" - Plotinus uses the image of a choral dance to describe the harmonious, rhythmic, and purposeful motion of the universe under the direction of the World-Soul.</note>, if it wishes to sympathize, it will be done. And the beauty of appearing peaceful harmony, in which now the whole **chorus**, made for all of him, is wise in itself. For he also said the same thing, how the whole living being might be for them, since it is impossible for the reason to be deserted of anything with life. To one who has understood, what will it be most of all? And if ever good, and distress, but the reason is according to the soul and again a kingdom ruled the work and makes the world as a whole. Let such things be. For they are also causal, and some of the cause are already many or fewer, and to the causes these are the Fates.

# On Being (Book 4)

...a crown, because it was brought into being by him and is of such a kind that it could not have been otherwise. And these people used such **contrivances**; and it was thought that they <note>likely referring to animals or the world-soul</note> felt **sympathy** <term>sympatheia: the interconnectedness of all parts of the living universe</term>, remembering how many benefits for human life have been gained from them. Since we would not be able to perceive the contrivances and structures of living beings—such as those found in wild beasts—if the shaping of their minds were not of a certain kind, we can easily observe such things. One wonders, moreover, at everything that indicates a sharpness of **nature** <term>physis: the instinctive, creative force of the physical world</term> regarding their own lives; for example, how the earth is produced. If, then, we are not only grateful but also recognize that they are not without knowledge—or rather, that nature shapes them toward certain actions—just as in trees there is a **sensation of life** <note>original: αἴσθεσις τῆς ζωῆς</note> such that they are still living beings; even if it is not already in them to "live well" <term>eudaimonia: flourishing or the "good life" usually reserved for rational humans</term>, a similar capacity was possible. For the **disposition** <term>phronema: the mindset or practical thought process</term> within the sensory and rational faculties is sought by everyone in every way. It is not merely a part of reasoning, nor did nature grant it to them solely for the purpose of living, but rather as a specific quality compared to other animals. Whether it belongs to the lowest things, or whether they are entirely lacking in prudence—if indeed progress, or rather any progress at all, seems impossible for them—just as with us, nothing that happens is truly "nothing" unless it is summoned or appears, or if these things are happening contrary to the nature of the young, or if their own nature belongs to them. This is the exceptional quality of the **soul**; for **prudence** <term>phronesis: practical wisdom or intelligence</term> is not granted to everyone in all things. <meta>This page continues the investigation into the faculties of the soul, specifically focusing on the transition from the general "perceptions" of animals mentioned on page 121 to a formal philosophical analysis of how sensation operates. It applies the Aristotelian concepts of potentiality and actuality to understand the difference between physical change and conscious perception.</meta>

# .Being.

One must, then, recognize that every activity proceeds from a power <term>dynamis: the potential or capacity to act</term>. This power is not entirely the primary thing, for it also possesses that which came before it. As for **activity** <term>energeia: the state of being 'at work' or actualized</term>, it is naturally united with the power through which it is naturally disposed to act. But "to act" is not exactly the same thing in every case; rather, there is a certain difference between them that one must recognize. Sensation <term>aisthesis: sense perception</term>, then, before the moment of being affected <note>original: paschein; in this context, the passive state of receiving a sensory impression</note> and being moved, is not in a state of activity, but exists only as a potentiality. Opinion <note>original: doxa</note> and knowledge, and things of that sort, exist in a state of activity even before they are affected. We see an example of this in the way spirit moves through the air. Now, the senses receive the **form** <term>eidos: the essential shape or quality of an object without its physical matter</term> during the process of being affected. But the things that exist before these are already sensible objects. In all these cases, "being" is not the same, but rather <unclear>different</unclrear> in relation to the ways they are affected. The affection that occurs within the sense-organ does not receive the entire form. Rather, the form is received from the sensible objects in a specific way. This is how sensation relates to the object. Sensation, just as it was before being affected, is not an activity in itself; it is a potentiality.

<margin>t</margin>
Regarding the sensory capacity in relation to the sensible object, it has already been said that it is nothing other than the form of the sensible object itself. It is also clear that in living beings, forms are received most especially not only by the sense-organs, but also by the other parts of the body. In this way, both sensation and the form are present. However, the "affection" is not the same thing as the organ. Rather, the sense-organ is one thing, and the affection <note>the physical change or impact</note> is another. For the one is like a physical magnitude, while the other is the sensation and the **rational proportion** <term>logos: here meaning the formal definition or the organizing principle of the sense</term>. The difference lies in that by which one perceives; it is a "reasoned proportion" in potentiality. Since all sensations exist both in bodies and in thoughts, and likewise in other animals and in plants, there is not in plants anything like a sense-organ through which the reception of forms occurs. Hence, he <note>likely Aristotle, whom Plotinus is commenting upon</note> says that they do not "undergo" in a sensory way, since no such power belongs to them. For they do not suffer for this reason. In the same way, the knowledge of the senses—both that which is directed toward external things and opinion—operates. <unclear>And</unclear> this does not exist simply in perishable things, but in those that possess certain forms. For this reason, he says that some people are already puzzled as to whether even inanimate things, such as plants, might receive the affections of sensation, not in their underlying substance. <unclear>Since</unclear> indeed that which appears is an "imagination" <term>phantasia: the faculty of mental images</term>. Regarding all imagination, the first point is that it is not present in all living beings. The second is that it is not always present in the same being. For imagination is not the same as sensation, nor is it opinion. Indeed, opinion can be false, but imagination is nothing that is truly "held as an opinion" by nature.

<column-break/>

Each of the senses, therefore, receives its own form and that alone, and nothing of the underlying matter through which it receives the form. Its "being" consists in receiving the form of that object. This is what the **wax** does in relation to the **signet ring**. It does not receive the ring itself; it does not receive the gold or the iron, but rather the impression <note>original: semeion</note> that is in the gold or the iron. He says that it receives the form not insofar as it is iron or gold. For if it received it insofar as it were gold, the wax would have to become gold. But it receives it not as gold, but as a "certain quality"—as having such-and-such a form in the gold. In the same way, sensation, in the process of being affected, receives the quality of the form. It does not receive it insofar as that thing is gold or iron, but insofar as it is "of such a kind." This is why, in the case of **plants**, he says that they do not receive these forms. For "receiving" in a purely physical sense does not contribute to "perceiving." Many inanimate things are in this state. <margin>b</margin> Such inanimate things as the lungs, or most animals, or even plants—generally, there is nothing in plants like a sense-organ through which the reception of forms occurs. Hence he says they do not "undergo" sensation, since no such power belongs to them. For they do not suffer for this reason, especially since the senses do not derive the act of perceiving simply from being affected. For example, if the soul is active and looks toward external things, then there is perceiving. But plants, not having the sensory capacity within themselves, do not undergo these things in the way sense-organs do. However, in plants, it is not only in the sense-organs <note>which they lack</note> but in their other parts that forms are most received, which is a kind of transformation occurring within the plants themselves. And he does not say that they do not "receive" at all. For he says that plants are heated or cooled. 

<margin>g</margin> But he says that plants do not "perceive," because they do not receive the **mean** <term>mesotes: the middle point or balance between extremes (like hot and cold) which Aristotle argued was necessary for sensation</term>. For this reason, he says some are already puzzled whether even inanimate things, such as plants, do not receive the affections of sensation through their underlying substance—which is what sensation is—or whether these things are separated from sensation, or whether the sensible object does not affect a part of the animal. Since an "alteration" is assumed, all sensation occurs in some underlying subject that is affected. It is clear, then, that all these things are like affections and sensations. He also began to speak in this way: for the body, or a part of the body, is "receptive" of sensation. Our physical magnitude is receptive, by which it also receives smallness of parts, or some other of the forms—such as when we speak of "fear" or "dread," or because of the whole body again. An opinion is formed in the soul; both sensation and opinion. What is it? The intellect <term>nous</term> does not possess a sensible object, but an **intelligible** one <note>original: noeton</note>. Sensation, however, is not without matter. For he said that the sense-organ is in potentiality what the sensible object is already in activity. But the "affection" is not the same; the sense-organ is one thing, and the affection is another. For the organ is like a magnitude, but sensation is the rational proportion.

<summary>This page analyzes the mechanics of sensation, distinguishing between the physical organ (matter/magnitude) and the sensory power (form/logos). It uses the famous wax and seal analogy to explain how the soul receives qualities without the matter of the objects it perceives, ultimately concluding that plants do not have sensation because they lack a "mean" or a specific sensory organ.</summary>

# — Epicurus, Book 4, 30 —

And in the act of seeing there are certain **images** <note>original: eidōla; in ancient physics, these were thin films or "husks" shed by objects that travel through the air to the eye</note>, which are similar in shape to solid bodies. Yet this is not entirely the case, nor does it apply to all existing things. Since such images are mostly formed in the air because they do not require depth to be filled; and others, due to their speed, flow off from solid objects and shine through. Following these things, one must believe that sensations also function in this way; but this is not a remaining falsehood, just as the images themselves are similar. Yet none of these things exist through the soul.

Later, let us return to the beginning of the nature of the universe and the kinds of bodies—and not the kinds of all things—and the rest of the senses. Since the nature of those things driven by impulse is to be intercepted. Perceptions, therefore, occur in sleep. And if there is a sequence, and again through organs, perceptions occur. From these very things are its sense organs. Nature exists through the process of becoming. And perhaps from spherical particles, just as through the **breath** <note>original: pneuma; the vital spirit or "air" believed to carry sensory information through the body</note>, sensations are seen to occur. Among these things, one must refrain from being confused.

And there are also the perceptions of others, some being irrational in their apprehensions. Although others exist, it seems they come to be. And those men of old once made them so. For I do not know of anything unique to those who came after. And the things within them. Or let these not be the unique things. Furthermore, there are sensations. Since their **reflection** <note>original: anaklasis; the bouncing back of light or images</note> alters the things seen in mirrors. Joys, or rather, are not a grasping of the eyes. Regarding colors, the senses perceive them; and the things within the images become sensible. And we blame **deception** <note>original: apatē</note> on our **opinions** <note>original: doxais; subjective judgments or beliefs that interpret sensory data</note>. 

That which is produced by the many. And their images are imprinted. For the falling away of images occurs, or nowhere at all; for it alone does not follow, how? Both of the eyes within it and intellect alone. But in those cases, other things are appropriate heavenly, or not only opinion, or those things which are established by likeness. They are held by likeness and by the opposite alone. How do the likenesses of signs come to be? For since the first part of sensation was defined as a line. And already for me it is the same, the sensible things upon the touch. 

But since nature, which is always directed toward the same, reflects toward its own things. And he himself made the sensible things. By learning, one will gain private possession. Bodies. Beneficially diffusing such brightness to them by their sensation. And the things in sight. Whenever the soul is far away, even if it is especially of the things about to be, as if to cross over that which is of the sensibles, as if wavering. But he who <unclear>conceives</unclear> <unclear>in</unclear> <unclear>their</unclear> is under the <unclear>desired</unclear>. ### On Ethics, Book IV
#### Page 127

...and not, as is often the case, because one is wicked, but in a friendly spirit for the sake of doing good.

<margin>In these matters there is no specific name, but in its stable character it is most similar to friendship.</margin>
In these matters there is no specific name. However, in its **disposition** <note>original: hexis; a stable, ingrained character trait developed through habit</note>, it is most similar to **friendship** <note>original: philia</note>. For the person who holds this middle state is the sort of person we mean when we speak of a "good friend," provided they also possess affection <note>original: stergein; a natural or familial kind of love</note>. It differs from friendship, however, because it exists without **passion** <note>original: pathos; an intense emotion or irrational drive</note> or a particular fondness for those one encounters. For it is not because of loving or hating that such a person accepts each thing as they ought, but because they are simply that kind of person. They act similarly toward strangers and acquaintances, those they know well and those they do not—except that they act toward each in a way that is fitting <note>original: harmottei; to be in harmony or appropriate to the context</note>. For it is not appropriate to care for those one knows well and those who are strangers in the same way.

<margin>Or even in this way: causing pain to those one should, as one should, and in the manner that is fitting.</margin>
Or even in this way: causing pain to those one should, as one should, and in the manner that is fitting. In doing so, they keep their eyes fixed on what is **noble** <note>original: kalon; the beautiful or morally excellent</note> and what is advantageous.

<margin>Such a person aims, above all, to avoid causing pain to themselves, or to help increase pleasure.</margin>
Such a person aims, above all, to avoid causing pain or to help increase pleasure. This virtue seems to concern the pleasures and pains that occur in social interactions and in living together. Among these people, the one who wishes to praise everything and never opposes anyone is called **obsequious** <note>original: areskos; literally a "pleaser" who lacks their own conviction for the sake of being liked</note>. On the other hand, the one who opposes everything and cares nothing for the pain they cause is called **surly** <note>original: dyskolos</note> and **quarrelsome** <note>original: dyseris</note>.

It is obvious that these mentioned dispositions are blameworthy, and that the middle state <note>original: mesotes; the "Golden Mean" where virtue resides</note> between them is praiseworthy. In this state, a person will accept what they should and how they should, and will likewise be displeased when appropriate. This middle state has not been given a specific name, but it is most like friendship. For the person in this middle state is what we would call a "good friend" if they were to add affection to their character. It differs from friendship because it is without passion and without a specific love for those with whom they associate; for it is not by loving or hating that they accept things as they ought, but by being a person of such a character.

### Symbols .30.

The powers that always flow downward from the heavenly heights <note>original: meteōrōn; referring to the celestial bodies and the upper atmosphere</note> to the things on earth, which indeed provide matter with its varied colors and blossoms, also concern the universe, which one cannot describe in its entirety all at once. These are the things that the ancient teachers <note>original: sophistai; here used in the older sense of "wise men" or "masters of knowledge"</note> and sages spoke of through what one might call forms arising from the waters. They were known by their specific signs, by their outward appearance, and by their shape, just as leaf-bearing plants are known by their leaves. This marking of "goodly leaves" <note>original: euphyllōn</note> occurred because of a discourse—either concerning nature or concerning other men—of restoration. 

These are Symbols, such as those used by the Egyptians; and there are some among us as well, unless the doctrines <note>original: dogmata; the core principles or tenets of a school of thought</note> within them are veiled. Just as the earth is filled by a flooding river, so too did the Egyptians manage matters concerning the celestial regions. As for the universe, you yourself encompass all things; because it is contained within the world in a formless way, and whatever the shape is, we might speak of it thus: which is why it grows dim upon the disk <note>likely referring to the solar disk</note>. 

He introduces another idea, such as atoms; and we, in turn, wish to speak of the constellations by this. If we speak of composite things, such as myths, these too should be brought together according to nature within the body. Returning again to the statues of the gods: if there is anything significant, it is taken from one’s own experiences and applied again to divine uses. However, in regard to what they said concerning the sun, which indeed no one could fully describe, this is where water and the things previously written are taken. These themselves are the gods. What was signified concerning the sun, these things are external. Just as gold scattered in wine is heavy, he praises whatever great doctrines concerning the gods one might receive from them—for many of the things that come to be are like a sketch in a discourse. 

At any rate, these things relate to their causes, so that the particular parts are like things encompassing them. And while these things have been received and proclaimed, he says that first the "all-powerful" <note>original: pankration; literally "all-power," here perhaps referring to a supreme creative force or a specific ritual context</note> rises up as the most causal. But these too, at other times, involve discourses and trials—serious and excellent ones—and sometimes the forms of the imagination are but idols <note>original: eidōla; images or reflections that lack the substance of the original</note>. Regarding those things beyond reason, such as the spiritual <note>original: pneumatikos; literally "breath-like" or "spirit-filled"</note> and divine under the power of the sun, some say these are living beings and possess souls. 

It is clear, then, that these things must necessarily come into being as they do in the whole, along with the motions of the cosmos. These are the same doctrines held by the earliest of the Greeks. It is a puzzle how this is so. If one does not use these things against them, they might not come to be through them again—unless that thing belongs to those things, so that they lead into the light. Some say these are necessary things; and so is the earth. And these things will happen to them again, which should not be seen as strange, but as belonging to the thing itself once more. It is not unworthy for such things to be found in inscriptions and ornaments. If it is not the thing itself, then perhaps nothing has been said of the things that have come to pass. These things are <gloss>to be noted</gloss> as not being equal to one another, nor all-encompassing.

Next, we must consider ourselves in relation to other living beings <note>original: zōa; often translated as "animals," but in Neoplatonism, it refers to any "living thing," including stars and the universe itself</note> and view the whole in light of what has been said. The soul is one, as if it were the whole containing the parts; but viewed universally, the parts are derived from it. Every part is like a whole; for if the genus <note>original: genos; a logical category or "kind"</note> is within it, then Being itself is the genus. For the gentle principle <note>original: meilichos; suggesting a soothing or harmonious influence</note> of the whole is within itself, and so shall its life be.

And for these parts, there is a gentle influence, and for all the parts together. It has allotted certain portions of itself, as if the living beings were partitioned off. Since it was destined to be near the primary things, it does not fully incline toward "Being." And universally, it seems to have a great <unclear>likeness</unclear> to all things, though it differs and is lesser. It might exist alongside the same thing, but not because it is lesser. It discusses the transformation of the soul through grace, the role of the Creator (Demiurge), and the importance of divine love (Agape). The language here suggests a later synthesis of Plotinian Neoplatonism with early Christian thought, particularly regarding the "resurrection" and "grace."</meta>

**Love (Agape):** Divine, unconditional love.
**Epistle:** A formal letter, here likely a theological treatise in letter form.
**God (Theos):** The divine principle, here used in a personal, often Christian sense.
**Creator (Demiurge):** The craftsman of the world; in Neoplatonism, a secondary god, but here merged with the Supreme God.
**Soul (Psyche):** The mediating force between the divine and the material.
**Grace (Charis):** A divine gift or influence that heals and enlightens the soul.
**Spirit (Pneuma):** The divine breath or Holy Spirit.
**Truth (Aletheia):** Ultimate reality.</note>

# Epilogue 29 — Epilogue 30

### On Causes and the Harmony of the Whole

In part, even if one considers him, there is both a body and a seeking after discord. For it is not uniform in kind, but exists as a certain thing by its very nature. Even if this should happen to him, we must look to the causes where the actual cause resides; for choice itself is a cause, yet we must also blame ignorance as a cause, being the source of these things. Again, one must guard the bodily needs, for it did not suffer what it held. These things belong to him or occur by force. But if form is the cause, so that a creature is merely a creeping thing, then let no cause be blamed but the body itself. At least in such a case, as with those things that are prone to change. There, then, the **Logos** <note>original: *logos*; the rational principle or "divine blueprint" that organizes the material world</note> appears once more. Both are directed toward the cause. Let us seek the causes there. It reveals neither a simple nature nor mere art; for the very disposition of a cause seemed to be a creative one, like a poetic work. And nature too. Therefore, we must remember: this is how one dissolves the bonds of nature. If one wishes, you will know something more of this ancient truth. There, he remains with himself and with those others. Another thing exists somewhere; for there, except for being powerful, he is worthy of heaven. Either now, or after the One. It happens that some fall into error, being overtaken by the Whole. In those ancient times again, from which the wandering began. The soul herself, having been stained by this, especially since then. Rather, it is a trace left for men. Of that ancient power, there is a certain choice portion of the "meadows" <note>likely the "Meadow of Judgment" or the "Plain of Truth" described in Plato’s myths of the afterlife</note> belonging to the state. Upon those things, she speaks. If it should seem to be from him, such as it is, all things still follow according to the **Logos**, like stone and wood. And of another's own things, she herself wishes. You must endure that which the passions hold. From this, then, it is both practiced and meditative, so that it is not the same for everyone. Therefore, **knowledge** <term>epistēmē: certain, scientific knowledge as opposed to mere opinion</term> is both a solution and a difficulty for those ending their journey from the soul. For the **Logos** says that different lives belong to different people in the outer world. We must blame a certain wandering of ours. And especially so; for through the cause comes the reasoning. In this way, we inhabit this life. For we do not blame the living being. Nature is wonderful, and the animals that have become living things are more than they seem. Nor should we blame the change that comes through itself. The irrational things again, having made a different spirit. And not somehow through itself—let no man say this to the inhabitants, even if they are many. And here, again, nothing is placed with himself. For what remains to him is the fall; let the passions happen to him. And before these things, he suffers the rational principles, whatever it is that he knows of them. The fall is a limb of the cause of the meadow, unsparingly. Or else we blame the powers of life themselves. Since then, it still grows.

<column-break/>

To those within, from the abundance. But if not, one must seek among their own. Everything before the Whole is shown to be a distinct living being, yet it did not fall to them by lot. I speak of them, for you have woven the traditions together. By these same traditions, he himself brings faith to each man’s life, having neighbored them. For the irrational animals do not possess the highest part of the meadows, appearing bright from the Whole or from their wandering. It was practiced and has come to be, for it is not kindred to all. There, it is rather a **recollection** <note>original: *hypomnēsis*; the Platonic concept that learning is actually the soul "remembering" eternal truths it knew before birth</note>, and a part that has not been traversed. For I wander it, having rushed from the summit. Every deed is a task and a good. There are some among the **planets** <note>original: *planētes*; literally "wanderers." In antiquity, this referred to the stars that moved independently of the fixed constellations</note> who have a wilder nature. For they were known by the harms they do and by their change, looking toward one thing and then another. For they are also the causes of evils. Because it is so, the power to lead into error is its own. And a naked thing is something shameful, but those that have come to be are beautiful. But so that it might be so in many places, as one must guard for the parents, the spirit gives to them. Here again. Do you wish, then, to know the causes of ignorance from those things that seem so to me? Most of all, let the causes of his impulse be known. From this, then (but this is the cause), there is something shameful <margin>sufficiently and</margin> and again a certain temperament that governs each. But also those who mold nature. For it was necessary, even before the living being, to take up the whole without the implanted lamentations. For they called these the **Logos**. The one who molded the animals took the cause. And rather, if the animals of generation and motion. Nowhere is it without art. He showed a creative power that is better for mortals. The same one; for the same one is for each. Because toward that which is to become nature, it is not. Except for once being in knowledge, the whole being poured through the eyes might happen. For the things that benefit the finer natures are always there. If there were ranks above. And the **Logos** spoke again to him who wills, showing many things to them through reasonings. All things are thus; if in the **science of signs** <term>semiotics: the study of how things in the world act as symbols or signals of divine reality</term>, a wonderful harmony held. A catalog of all other and unchangeable things. Since this is about the glory of the old man. And the ancient account: not to be molded for all, like the food of parents, and shameful deeds in truth. Thus also the kindred. But the ensouled things are drawn from nature. These things preside over the wanderings. For in this way, all things, and those from all, are **signs**.

# Since IV.

### On the Levels of Life and the Harmony of the Soul

It is advantageous to live one's life in the same manner, whether in equality with others or among those of greater standing. For celestial grace is not more present in the heavens than it is in a child or a grown man. Indeed, let there be every kind of ambition, or let it be even greater; for it is either the **rational principle** <note>original: *logos*; the governing reason or blueprint of the soul</note> of man, or it exists within the communal spiritual principle. Regarding his mature reason: we shall not dare to say anything at all concerning his private life, for when we speak of the cause of separation, the child's reputation always remains. Yet our choices are not already like a city-state; for the many do not control our affairs, though they try to persuade us. Since those who consume the natures surrounding them claim this is a legislative power, one must look to the **principle** <unclear>beginning</unclear>. It is not only in being that this exists; in short, there would be no **happiness** <note>original: *eudaimonia*; often translated as "flourishing" or "well-being" rather than mere emotion</note> if one were to move toward harmony or, conversely, to renounce the whole in order to be saved. For bodily deception has not yet come to be.

On one hand, there is life. The life above does not "become," even if it resides with truth. But is the life above like that of a farmer? Or does it protect bodies from passions, which seems to me to be its very nature? Toward their own impulse, they feel a certain **civic love** <note>original: *politike agapesis*; the social bond that holds a community together</note>. Already the things of the intellect truly come to be, and all things exist through these creations. We have naturally said that this does not exist if it is not fashioned, or if it is not also there. And so again, one must be educated in the **virtue** <note>original: *arete*; excellence or moral character</note> of companions. They say that the **desiring part** <note>original: *epithymetikon*; the part of the soul responsible for physical appetites and drives</note> is that which directs desire toward itself. It does not belong to that person, but rather to this life. To exist is to receive the principle from above. Since there are passions and opinions of bodies, how can the desiring parts be bright? Or are they the base life of themselves? In such cases, they lean forward. For one must not renounce things along with these, and they feel love, O **Blessed One** <note>original: *Makarie*; a traditional address to a student or reader in philosophical texts</note>. For he said it never exists. Is he a child? Quite likely. For friendship is not present, nor is the friendship based on it, but rather well-mindedness. And the offspring is a kindred guardian. Or it is necessary. Is it not a wandering thing then, having its own necessities through its own cares? For either there are natural things or a certain communion with one another. Just as union comes through generation; the nurse who becomes poor has a different nature. We might then call this friendship. The pious man guards it where it is. It is not as if those things which pass through nature have a lightness toward one another. In living, these things often occur; it bears witness most of all. We deal with that person and with being, so that we may receive a trustworthy account for all who will be in that which truly is.

<column-break/>

From what has been said, the value of the whole lies in beautiful things, whether they are constructive or not; but truly, not all are of equal value. If, as they said, those on the level planes are uneven, it is necessary to be far from the **Beautiful and the Good** <note>original: *kalos kai agathos*; the Platonic ideal of moral and aesthetic perfection</note> of man. Such virtue is either apparent or exists from within itself. But I say the whole is as this philosopher taught. However, there is an **irrational soul** <note>original: *alogos psyche*; the part of the soul that does not use reason, such as instinct or sensation</note>. And indeed, there is the sensory and the appetitive faculty. And those called friendships among men, though they are **civic** <note>original: *politikas*; relating to the city or social order</note> friendships, arise according to certain principles. For the discourse concerning **courage** <note>original: *andreia*; one of the four cardinal virtues</note> is where I become part of the life in the whole. For just as things come from God, so we must demonstrate what we are about to have. Rather, every living thing is not without a share of this. These things are within us, O Blessed One, if indeed those listening are able to perceive the demonstrations—or if they are not. For we had not yet spoken according to the principle, or rather the separation. This is the soul which is with the body; but being moved, it has life, as we might say. It is a communion of motion, as you hear him say in the **Symposium** <note>A reference to Plato’s *Symposium*, a dialogue centered on the nature of Love (Eros)</note> and regarding the friendship following the sacrifice. We might say it is to love entirely, or friendship, for there is no "Symposium" without it. And so again, lest one be ignorant, there is happiness, and happiness is this. Glory receives it just as kindred praise does. Just as being like a colony among many, not everything is friendly. But one must receive it. For just as one takes the springs of the earth, those which are admittedly harmful, or the whole. It journeys together. The remaining names there are of that very thing. From that, one will not even receive the Good; but if things are softer, they would not always be so for those people. Whatever is not prepared, it is clear that it fails. For these names signify not only certain principles and causes, but the rational principle already knows its own principles there. And because many things have natural powers. Downwards, where the works of the world’s machinery exist as in a living creature. You have been at leisure for another thing without gravity. The things appearing this way according to it are still happiness. But it is necessary to turn away by this life of his. But he who turns toward the things above, he says, toward the **divine** <note>original: *theion*</note> or entirely so. For if it is not itself, it will be left about the same actions as if from a natural source, so that it is not necessary to go upon the same path.

# Epicurean Section 4.

### On Pleasure and the Wise Man’s Resolve

...through **pleasure** <note>original: *hedone*; in Epicurean thought, this refers to the absence of pain rather than mere indulgence</note>. For even when one arrives at the end of their lifespan within the primary cause, and of life itself. And regarding his **happiness** <note>original: *eudaimonia*; the state of flourishing or living well</note> and his joys, it is clear that he rejoices in what is his own. Indeed, the same <term>Alkazo</term> <note>This likely refers to a specific Epicurean commentator or a lost work; the transcription suggests a proper name or a title in shorthand</note> in the inscribed commentary says that they might say they have been insulted—not they themselves, but we ourselves. Let us see these things when they come into view. The philanthropic man finds his own pleasure in what has been accomplished. If it is within us, it is not a secondary matter. 

Behold the **voice of the wise man**: he says that **happiness** exists in death itself, and that we must make our life such that it avoids the wandering of error. For it is clear that the force of friendship makes us feel at home with ourselves. For he says that even the **memories of beautiful things** <note>original: *anamnesis*; here referring to the Epicurean practice of recalling past pleasures to offset present physical pain</note> past are a pleasure, though communal desire and pleasure can be painful. He says that among these are beautiful and right actions for all; but either our beauty is such, or it is a matter of procreativity. Some say the resurrection, others say pleasure is the peak of age. But education and life are different; for nature resists the violence of pleasure. He says further that peace is most familiar from these pleasures themselves. For there is no pain because, perhaps, there is no other door to familiarity than that we were benefited. 

He says further that all things are **indifferent** <note>original: *adiaphora*; a technical term for things that have no moral weight in themselves, such as wealth or health</note> to us, and our actions are according to our age. For all things of beauty are ours to use. For our evil is not in itself, but is caused by our own being persuaded by the **irrational** <note>original: *alogos*; the part of the soul governed by instinct rather than reason</note> if all things belong to that, or if desire in death is the pleasure of those things. The whole inquiry of nature: for the disordered release of the irrational is to be prayed for, from where the impulses concerning pain arise—where it is not even possible to receive it. But in idleness, the procreative and the familiar are merely impossible. For we do not make ourselves; his pleasure is another according to life, so that it is also the cause. But only the one who saves them, being known, is in a state of freedom and lack of pain. For the wise man will appear to us. 

Since indeed it is necessary to have **virtue** <note>original: *arete*; moral excellence or functional perfection</note>, even in death; because of the things he labored for. For the man who is happy by the nature of the ancients, his own life brought all things to it... for us it is still an evil. Behold, we are still part of how nature was, both the lowly and the earth, and the peace of the whole, and having pleasure according to age... and pleasure. And the age of the same things. But to him, not pleasure but sweetness. When it comes into view, his own pleasure is with us. And even if **prudence** <note>original: *phronesis*; practical wisdom</note> were pleasure of the lover, it was permitted to that very desire of ours. And if there is a rule of good things, how we are benefited. We are benefited in our suffering, as pleasure brings its own gifts.

<meta>This page transitions from a Neoplatonic discussion of light and participation (common in the Enneads) into a transcription of Aristotle’s Nicomachean Ethics, Book X. It examines the distinction between superficial friendships and the highest form of human happiness—the contemplative life—which aligns the human soul with the divine.</meta>

# CHAPTER: And these friendships are accidental, because the person is not loved for <unclear>who</unclear> they are,

but rather insofar as they provide something good or pleasant. Such friendships are indeed accidental; for the person is not loved for being who they are, but because the one provides a certain benefit, and the other provides pleasure. Therefore, such friendships are easily dissolved when the parties do not remain as they were; for if they are no longer pleasant or useful, the others stop loving them. Now, the **useful** <note>original: *to chresimon*; refers to practical utility or profit</note> does not endure, but becomes different at different times. When the reason they were friends is removed, the friendship itself is dissolved, as the friendship existed only toward those ends. Such friendship seems to occur most especially among the elderly (for at that age they pursue not the pleasant, but the beneficial), and among those in their prime or youth who pursue what is advantageous. Such people do not particularly live together with one another; for sometimes they are not even pleasant to each other. Indeed, they have no need for such association unless they are beneficial; for they are pleasant to each other only insofar as they have hopes of something good. Among these friendships, people also place the ties of **hospitality** <note>original: *xenike*; the traditional Greek bond between a host and a guest from another city</note>. But the friendship of the young seems to be for the sake of pleasure; for they live according to passion, and mostly pursue what is pleasant to themselves and what is present in the moment. As their age changes, the things that are pleasant also become different. Thus they quickly become friends and quickly cease; for their friendship changes along with what is pleasant, and the change of such pleasure is rapid. The young are also prone to erotic love; for the greater part of erotic friendship is based on passion and pleasure. For this reason, they love quickly and cease quickly, often changing within the same day. But they do wish to spend their days and live together; for this is how they achieve the goal of their friendship.

and he might act; for that too would be lacking among the things leading to the end, or the work of the living being. It is not like health or physical fitness, but each is to each. For such a man is not happy in the same way. Therefore, **contemplation** <note>original: *theoria*; the highest form of intellectual study or "beholding" Truth</note>, even if it be incomplete, is a form of happiness, and if it be complete, it is complete happiness. That complete happiness is a certain contemplative activity would also be clear from what follows. For we have traditionally conceived of the gods as being most especially blessed and happy. But what kind of actions should we assign to them? Those of justice? Or will they appear ridiculous if they make contracts and return deposits and do all other such things? Perhaps actions of courage? Withstanding terrors and facing risks because it is noble to do so? Or liberal actions? To whom will they give? It would be absurd if they even had currency or something of that sort. And what would their temperate actions be? Or is praise for such things vulgar, seeing that they do not have base desires? If we go through them all, everything concerning actions would appear small and unworthy of gods. Yet, everyone assumes they are alive and therefore active; for they are certainly not sleeping like **Endymion** <note>A figure from Greek myth who was granted eternal sleep to remain forever young</note>. If we take away action from a living being, and even more so production, what is left except contemplation? So the activity of God, surpassing in blessedness, would be contemplative. And among human activities, that which is most akin to this is the most productive of **happiness** <note>original: *eudaimonia*; often translated as "flourishing" or "living well" rather than just a fleeting emotion</note>. A sign of this is that the other animals do not participate in happiness, being entirely deprived of such activity. For the whole life of the gods is blessed, but for humans, it is so only insofar as some likeness of such activity exists. But none of the other animals are happy, since they share in contemplation in no way. Happiness, then, extends as far as contemplation does, and those who have more of the capacity for contemplation also have more happiness—not by accident, but by virtue of the contemplation itself; for it is precious in its own right. Thus, happiness would be a form of contemplation. But the happy man will also need external prosperity, being human; for our nature is not self-sufficient for contemplation, but the body must be healthy, and food and other care must be provided. Yet one should not think that the man who is to be happy will need many or great things, even if it is not possible to be blessed without external goods. For self-sufficiency does not consist in excess, nor does judgment, nor does action. It is possible to perform noble deeds without being ruler of land and sea; for one can act according to virtue from moderate means. This can be seen clearly: for private citizens seem to perform decent actions no less than powerful rulers, and even more so. It is enough to have this much; for the life of the person active according to virtue will be happy. And **Solon** <note>An Athenian lawmaker and one of the Seven Sages of Greece</note> perhaps described the happy well when he said they were moderately supplied with external goods, but had performed the noblest deeds, as he thought, and had lived temperately; for it is possible for those possessing moderate means to do what they ought. **Anaxagoras** <note>A Pre-Socratic philosopher who prioritized the Mind (Nous) as the organizing principle of the universe</note> also seems to have conceived of the happy man as neither rich nor a ruler, when he said he would not be surprised if the happy man appeared strange to the many; for they judge by externals, perceiving these alone. The opinions of the wise seem to agree with these arguments. Now, such things carry a certain conviction, but the truth in practical matters is judged by deeds and by life; for in these lies the decisive test. We must therefore examine what has been said by referring it to deeds and life; if it harmonizes with the deeds, it should be accepted, but if it clashes, it should be considered mere words. But he who acts according to **intellect** <note>original: *nous*; the faculty of the soul that perceives first principles and divine truths</note> and cultivates this and is in the best disposition seems also to be most beloved by the gods. For if the gods have any care for human affairs, as it seems, it would be reasonable both that they delight in what is best and most akin to them (which would be the intellect) and that they reward those who love and honor this most, as people who care for what is dear to the gods and who act rightly and nobly. It is not unclear that all these things belong most of all to the wise man. He is therefore most beloved by the gods. And it is likely that the same person is also the happiest; so in this way too, the wise man would be most happy.

<summary>This page explores the hierarchy of human relationships and activities, concluding that while friendships of utility and pleasure are fleeting, the highest human life is found in contemplation, which mirrors the eternal activity of the divine.</summary>

But when it is guided by sight, it is possible for the souls within them to possess power; for the living being thinks and inquires, so that it can seek out its various modes of life for the sake of life alone. What then? Someone will say to it: does it come from these things, or is it not so? If the things of the sea are according to the same [principles], then what is it in its parts? For it seems to possess as much as it holds of the **Intellect** <note>original: *nous*; the higher divine mind in Neoplatonic thought</note>; and because these activities are called memories within us, it is sufficient for the first thing itself to relate to the other, or for the body to convey **nervous movements** <note>original: *neurikas kineseis*; an early physiological understanding of the nervous system</note> to the mind. But if someone should be at a loss, we shall ascend as far as the Intellect; we shall ask how every sensation and apprehension shall be, because nothing is like the latter compared to the first. If it is in the soul, it is clear that it is not by being acted upon, nor by a turning; for even if one wishes to make souls through the movement of the blood, it is not as if it were a body. The soul is the beginning of the soul. If the matter is by having that which is **sensible** <note>original: *aisthēton*; something that can be perceived by the senses</note>, it would not be the same, because it does not possess color or shape. From where then comes the memory of that sensible object to them, if it occurs only there? And the things from the Intellect—he asks—are they not the same? In the case of memory, it is the same, because these things seem to resemble those others. But this is not that which would come to be. From what cause then should we search? The Intellect especially must be addressed. For just as when they are in themselves, it is clear. In life, but not in memory—or rather, in life, but not in that way; rather, we must say what this sensory power or memory is. Since these things were once spoken of most especially.

<margin>Search</margin> <note>original: *zētei*; a marginal instruction likely from a medieval scribe or reader to "look into" or "verify" a specific point of the text</note>

That which is in the body does not belong to the soul itself; nor does the act of sensing, or how the movement in the **sight** <note>original: *opsei*; the faculty of vision</note> moves toward it. Just as with a living animal, to sense the things after that, and the passive things there in it, or in the animal, these things are spoken of. Vision, then, is its sensation, yet it is what is within it. And that which is in the sensory faculty is such that the whole body is not capable of it, because it prevails over the whole body. Thus, the sensory power comes to them from the Intellect and from the soul for all things. Why then is not every **opinion** <note>original: *doxa*; belief or opinion as opposed to certain knowledge</note> clear, whenever something of itself is similar to the things outside, which is its own? Is the soul a forgetting, or is it the soul? If it is beside the things within it. For this also has been said: the thing in the soul is not a forgetting, one seeks an opinion. In the soul of the Intellect, for it is not yet the whole; but opinion is in it or in the Intellect. If it is not even in that, so that some of them are life, and as if they are unmoved in life, but the same things either belong to it by the act of thinking.

## On Sensation and Memory

When we say that sensations are not **passive states** <note>original: *pathē*; traditionally, sensation was seen as the soul being "acted upon" or suffering an impression</note> but activities regarding images, and that memories are this same thing. Those who say that passive states are an alteration introduced into the soul, not participating in an **impression** <note>original: *typou*; the metaphor of a signet ring leaving a "type" or mark in wax</note> in their coming to be, thought this was no small matter. Therefore, from where does memory come, and from where the soul? For if nothing is placed within the soul, but as each thing was from the beginning, it would never have flowed away, and nothing would remain after its entrance. But he who speaks of change must necessarily mean something else. Therefore, the **Beautiful** <note>original: *to kalon*</note> seems to be, and this seems to occur when both are sensed, from the soul which impresses upon it, or by being persuaded by that which is impressed to appear to the soul. And the things from memory would be an image of sensation, whether in the first part of the soul, or even if the Intellect carries another sensible object into it, and from it another again. It is clear that toward the Intellect, which does not have sensible objects, there are collected **reason-principles** <note>original: *logous*; the formative forces or blueprints of reality</note>. That which is in each soul is the work of the soul, because the Beautiful is present by participation in each; not through the sensory "painting" in this way. Then, how is it in the souls of animals, if it wishes to have nothing of its own? Or the things of memory, are they not of one's own, but received from without? If these things are so for all others, then there would be no place for **recollection** <note>original: *anamnēseōs*; the Platonic concept that learning is actually remembering truths the soul knew before birth</note>, if it held the things of sensation, but the things of the soul are in the soul. But they would not even be in the body, if the sensory power is concerned with things outside. If opinion is not within, how should we say that even that which they let go is there? The same arguments apply to it not being so. When we are about to see from whence it is for us, how is it not necessary to grasp it? It is directed toward these things, or it is that which is after them, seeking nothing toward the outside. Why then are there memories of good things, if not by being colored by another, or the work of that which it received? Or is it not even so, that it will be, not all things, but the same things concerning **becoming** <note>original: *genesin*; the world of change and physical existence</note>? But our vision is so that they might participate, not moving the sensory power, nor the animal dwelling in it, as if they see what is within. For by having the thing, the soul is not led in, nor does it ever come to be in the soul because it is not in it. Consider then that it could not be accused of being equal. Opinion and thought are a search. If it exists, it is by not being in God, but the whole, toward which it is necessary, and each again is the whole. That which memory holds, which it did not even have, but especially those things, so that there may be a vision. If it is the whole, what is necessary? Either the whole toward things not its own—for this has been said—or the other things according to the soul. All that is in the soul is [there]. For it is sufficient that the things of the soul are in the form of the soul.
