# To Be Something

...to be marveled at. If it is not entirely likely that it has this wondrous cause, then perhaps it is because one assumes—due to an unwillingness to possess it, or to contain it, or to see it in its proximity—that perception is the dominant factor. In every way, this thing produced by nature seems to be such that everything truly within it remains hidden in its design. These things being so, as many as are the causes for the whole of the experience of the **vital reason** <note>original: *zotikou logou*; the rational principle or "form" that gives life and structure to a living being.</note>, such as perception...

<margin>2.</margin>
->Regarding the resting of souls.<-

The quietude once directed toward the things of nature—either to guard them or to share in them with the senses or the imagination—does not merely exist, but belongs to the soul itself. That which is often more in accordance with its nature is, again, like a cause for its lack of living. But it is as if it is in the soul itself. If life is that which is proper to the soul, or entirely that which belongs to such a thing, it must not only be an **activity** <note>original: *energeia*; in Neoplatonic thought, the actualization or "being-at-work" of a potential, the soul's outward expression of its inner nature.</note> of the soul, so that it might come from it. 

Thus, if it exists in activity in this way, there is no "resting" of the reason, unless perception shows this to be cyclical, returning to where it began. Furthermore, the self-subsistent thing might appear through itself. This is evident in the way the **image** <note>original: *eidolon*; a reflection or lower imitation of a higher reality, often used to describe the body's relationship to the soul.</note> is stored within the part. If this is the case, it would not be unclear that everything exists by nature, and that the greatest part is a greater **power** <note>original: *dynamis*; potentiality or the capacity to act.</note> for generation. For it is necessary to say that even the small things in part must have something of the whole, and the senses possess it entirely. For it is established that nothing exists without the **reason** <note>original: *logos*; here meaning the organizing principle or proportion that governs the universe.</note>. For either something is close to being divided, or again, they appear to do something. The powers of our soul are those which are active. If not everything, then they might hold for a certain time, and then cease because of what remains. 

Because of this, the reason seems most sovereign, or the whole exists before the parts, such that the living being exists. It is not that one part has its being through the soul and the other through something else, but the whole is like an instrument. If indeed the body itself exists for these things, it has such a nature. But the reason of this is entirely full of riddles. Generally, one part is in the body. In the body, let nature itself be present, and its power be sovereign, or the composition of souls. By creating a composition, it is the cause of the living being. What kind of reason is in the living being is necessary. For there is a life in the soul which is its greatest part, making a choice for the soul's nature. If this is so, the existing body, or its essence, or each body of a living thing becomes water, or whatever it may be. How then—indeed, fire or water? If the living thing is that which lives within it, this being the earthly part. Or the whole is not in the living thing, so that there might be life even of the living. For fire exists in fire; if it were entirely soulless, let fire be the vital element for all.

<note>Signature mark: Zeta (7)</note>

***

And this being so, even those things that are not "life" are something. And again, such bodies are something. And it is clear that it happens in the multitude, or in itself, that life is either soul or water. But because it is fire, no life of it is perceptible; the whole is the living thing. If indeed it is of the vital things, or rather in number because of being, there is a natural union with the living thing, and with those things that are so vitally in the same place. If one must also observe the generation of nature in many cases. So if it should happen thus, other things would flow into the living being. 

The soul, on the other hand, exists either because of its being or upon the living thing. If it is a living thing, it is instead a power or powers; if it is something in power, it is either of life or not of life. For generally in the body, whether it happens not to be through the whole, or the whole body from the beginning, or thus the whole is a certain body so that it becomes what follows it. If it is a human, let there be a mixture in the body. Similarly, it is so of the body; so let there be more things simply having a nature relative to each other, or those relative to the whole. 

We have all such vital things toward every nature, such as "living," which is that which appears more throughout the whole **world** <note>original: *kosmos*; the ordered universe.</note>. For the world, which is in the whole, is deprived of more of its own life. And again, perception of the whole would be fearful. Toward everything, either the soul is the cause of vital things and their causes, or the whole is the cause for the world. And the same soul is the cause of life for the living thing in the realm of life. Or again, the power holds it. Either it is more of the living things, or of the souls by the power of those having a bodily nature. For thus in the living thing, there would be something "soul-like" even here. For if it has something of its nature. But it does not cease, since things would live, and nature would be by the power of their own soul. So that this might also be for the other wholes, and life belongs to it most of all because of its coming into being. 

But it is likely that such things exist, and thus are the cause of that which encompasses them. Again, all life appears, and is not more in the body, just as nature does not lead all of them, or the cause shall entirely be by composition, rather than of the soul itself, to participate in the order of the whole, as if by necessity following along. And I shall be again. How can there be an experience of the life of all things, or why is there no "good" because of the whole, while in the whole, life is the cause of bodily things? For the greatest part is the whole. This reason is clear. Either the whole, or toward the cause generally, if indeed the living things are any of the things belonging to it. And let it be for each part of life, so that the power of all things might be through the whole (as one might say) so that the whole might live.

->### Eusebius, Book 30<-

<margin>The aim</margin> is established. And because the rational, knowing, and prudent man never sees the nature of the soul as having been allotted these things <note>referring to the defects of matter</note>, it could not arise from a whole of such a kind if it were not <unclear>becoming</unclear> so. Nor is the Good equally ungrudging. Except that even the begotten thing, like its own <term>logos: the rational principle or forming power</term>, does not become better than its source; for the spiritual world must provide for the soul-world. But the whole of the All, and at some time it might even become <note>original: "estaurōmenon" — crucified; here used metaphorically for the soul's entanglement or "stretching" within the material realm</note>. For there is no "angelic world" or "world of powers" that floats infinitely above the earth and water; rather, these things must have been made as they are, some in the heavens, and some in the regions around the earth. Hence also the souls themselves. Let it be said before and after these things that they also come from those sources. For the departure from the earth is the means to the highest happiness, just as it has happened; or rather, the rational world which comes from it is not an evil thing, as it is the cause of many goods. Nor indeed should one think of the soul as being in the world like a slave, but rather as having care and judgment over the whole. There are many established laws and much happiness; a certain "wholeness" of the All is preserved, nor could the world be full of <note>imperfections</note>, for it was not likely that they existed before the parts, according to the law of divine beings, upon which all things depend. And the soul itself will be a part of it, yet the whole soul would be one; or rather, it is in the entirety of its arrangement; yet it alone shall be whole. And the spiritual nature as well. In its being, it is in the world, and in its being in the All; or even in the whole. Which indeed should not exhaust every power. Like a <term>great animal: a Platonic concept of the universe as a single, living, breathing organism</term>. Unless it is something without beginning, or spiritual. For it has the indivisible All as its cause. How then can it also possess the entire age? For it proceeded <note>as a vessel</note> sailing in the order of the ages; at any rate, the causal God knows the All and guards it; and He makes it according to Himself. Because of this, these things exist. But things are never from the whole; <unclear>since</unclear> in generation, by the fire of the present; and the present moment is happy. But when the soul knows and perceives together with <note>the Intellect</note>, it might perhaps only seem to be labored in some part. For the wholes occur also in the Mind of being and persistence, and death; so that <margin>the begotten</margin> is its being, but the other is that which would be so. It acts better than that which is the All; it perceives. But if the All is "before," it is not the Good. But if things are not "child-like." It makes the part. Or even of itself. For neither the All, nor that which is in the All, is in the "begotten"; and virtue shall cease. But for that to always be; and it is lesser, yet being necessary, or that which is its child. And as for us having souls, it must be shown that the soul is not a slave, but returned close to the place from which it set out. It has the power to do what it must, and the things of decay as though of the things before the sun. And to know envy itself, secretly and in the present.

<column-break/>

...of that which participates wholly in the All. It is reasonable that it participates in the whole of life and intellect, because of the divided nature of the All being contained and stretched together. For its power is taken away; or rather, it is the same thing that possesses kingship. And in the same thing, the things of the earth. They make a portion, not that of the whole, for the All must possess the parts; which indeed has nothing above it, yet something of it might be surpassed. Whenever indeed the "too much" is worse than the <note>average</note>. It seems so, perhaps. But I would say this. Since even the portion of not coming into being. It calculates more or less for each. Since where indeed could it be if not in the region of the whole? This leads toward the Good. Or it appears in some other way. They wish clearly, because of the things in life, that these things were entirely played out <note>original: "epaixen" — a reference to the Neoplatonic idea that human life is a theatrical play staged by the World Soul</note>. For everyone who is captured. But he who participates most in the divine, and as if one were to say the things outside of having it. It is either being itself or that of the whole. From which either a concession is given to him at some time in weakness. Or in the part belonging to the All, he receives it as a fulfillment. # Ennead IV

For those who have wandered out of themselves into their bodies <note>original: "ἐξὡρημένοις ἑαυτῶν σώμασιν" — a metaphor for being "lost" in physical sensation rather than intellectual contemplation</note>, believing that the soul is merely the body, it is not easy to assign it to the divine. But for those who hold that the soul is something else, a different thing within the universe, it is not a matter of doubt whether all souls come from a single one. For the soul itself, as it is, can exist without a body; and if it is not a body, it would no longer be subject to division. This is how it stands with souls: that one single soul is their progenitor. There is no difference between the soul that exists in the All <term>the All: "to pan," the totality of the cosmos or the World Soul</term> and the soul that exists in a part. In the **Beyond** <note>original: "ἐν τῶι ἐπεκεῖνα" — referring to the Intelligible Realm, the higher level of reality where the Forms exist</note> all things are present, and all those things are within us. But since that soul receives its origin from there, and flows from there into what follows, our soul and the soul in the All appear as reflections. One must not doubt that the same thing can be both a whole and a part; for it must reside in something. Its superiority consists in the fact that it is not all the same. For just as in our body, even if the soul is hindered by some organic suffering, the soul itself does not suffer; for its body does not perceive entirely through its own power. In this way, the soul is encompassed as it was, and is naturally diminished by having a more passive relationship toward external things. Thus, the soul in the living cosmos is many; yet in the **undivided** <term>undivided: "ameristo," the state of pure spirit or intellect that cannot be split into pieces</term>, it is one. It ought not to differ within the cosmos; yet it is not solely with us, nor around us, but remains within itself, just as it was.

---

->**On whether all souls are one.**<-

Is it the case, then, that my soul and yours are one? And indeed, the soul of everyone? And if it is in the All, is it still one in me? For it would be irrational for my soul to be one, while the soul of the cosmos itself was not. Or how else could perception occur if all things did not possess the same nature? And if the Living Being is one, then when it is in that realm, it is in all. For all things within it are also living beings. Again, it must be both in the whole and in the part. But if the soul in the All is one in all things, then if we experience something, the soul of the All should perceive it; and if I suffer something, you should suffer it too, and another person as well. And the whole All should perceive it. This seems **absurd** <note>original: "ἄτοπον" — literally "out of place," a common term in Greek philosophy for a logical contradiction</note>. Furthermore, if it is in the whole and in the part in this way, how is it not something else? For even if it exists, it possesses something distinct and different in each individual. Then all things would exist together, but not according to parts. Since everything would suffer in such a way that another suffers too, what is the mechanism? For the thing in me to be in you, and to have identical experiences, it is not necessary for the whole to respond. It is like if my eye saw something, and your eye saw it too, even though they do not share the same stream of vision. Or rather, perception was one. And since there was not the same

<column-break/>

body as that other body, yet in the body of the All there was a certain unity, and in each individual there was that same nature of all; or rather, the same thing will again be present in each individual. So, whatever experience I have, the same will belong to the soul, for she is the same in the All. It would be necessary for the perceiving power to belong both to the whole and to each individual, and for each individual to belong to the whole. But it is not so now; yet it ought to be, unless the soul were **indivisible** there. Furthermore, all souls come from her and are many. For the soul in me and the soul in you are not one in such a way that they are not in each individual, being of the same soul; yet they are distinct again. Since they exist through us and in the All, there is a division that does not truly pertain to the body. This is because it belonged to the soul. Both the whole and the parts exist in each individual, and the same whole is also in us. For just as if what happened in me happened to the soul itself. That soul possesses all things; and that which was in the All, being something, did not exist otherwise than through the boundary it has according to the body. In this way, one thing and another in the All are not different from one another; but since they are distinct, the whole is present as a single unit. But it was not necessary for the whole to be in each individual as a whole. For in that way, the soul would no longer be divided from itself. But both the soul in me and the soul in you, and in each individual, and in the All, are in the same soul and in another, in which each part of her will exist, since she is indeed present. It was necessary for everything to belong to her, and for the soul in us to exist; then everything in us would be dear to that soul. But the others are held as one. This happens through the fact that the nature of the partial soul is the same as the soul in the undivided state, so that it comes from there. And that which the soul in the part suffers, the whole also suffers, since it was in the same All. Someone might explain more clearly whether the essence of being is again within her. Since all her parts have become distinct. Everything that was one—how could it still be? Perhaps those in the All would say that the whole will be there, and indeed it is there. For they draw souls there, that soul herself. And through them, each nature might never be destroyed. And again, there is that certain one who will belong to himself, and all things that have happened to the soul. But in the case of the purely **partial soul** <term>partial soul: "merike psyche," the individual soul as it functions within a specific body</term>, it fears that it might belong to itself as it was there; since then it will no longer be the most partial thing, namely, soul and animal. — How then, if it were not still as it was, but was entirely dependent on her? And that which belongs to her in the part, let it not depart into anything else, even the soul; which holds all those things there. —

He addresses the "absurdity" of shared sensation—why we don't feel each other's pain—by distinguishing between the soul's higher nature and its bodily limitations.</summary>

# Ennead IV

It seems, then, that unity appears not primarily in the sense of sight, but in the disposition of the soul. The things we have discussed happen to it. **G**oodwill <note>original: "Εὔνοια" (eunoia) — a state of wishing someone well, distinct from active friendship</note> resembles friendship, yet it is certainly not friendship itself. For goodwill arises even toward strangers and can remain hidden, whereas friendship does not. These things have been stated before. But neither is it affection <note>original: "φίλησις" (philesis) — the active emotion of liking or loving</note>. For it lacks intensity and desire, which are the following characteristics of affection. Furthermore, affection involves intimacy, while goodwill can arise suddenly, as happens in the case of athletes; for spectators feel goodwill toward them and share their wishes, though they would do nothing to help them. As we said, goodwill arises suddenly and people feel a superficial fondness. It seems to be the beginning of friendship, just as the pleasure through sight is the beginning of erotic love. For no one loves without first being pleased by the form <term>form: "idea" or "eidos," the outward appearance that reflects inner beauty</term>; yet he who enjoys the appearance is not necessarily in love, but only when he longs for the person in their absence and desires their presence. In this way, it is impossible for people to be friends without having goodwill, yet those who have goodwill do not necessarily love. For they only wish for good things for those to whom they bear goodwill, but they would do nothing to assist them, nor would they be troubled on their behalf. Therefore, one might say metaphorically that it is an "idle friendship" <note>original: "ἀργὴν φιλίαν" — friendship that does not act</note>, which, when it persists over time and reaches intimacy, becomes friendship—not the kind based on utility or pleasure, for goodwill does not arise from those things. For he who has received a benefit returns goodwill for what he has suffered, doing what is just; but he who wishes someone to prosper because he hopes to gain wealth through them does not seem to have goodwill for that person, but rather for himself, just as one is not a friend if he cares for another for some use. In general, goodwill arises because of virtue and some form of goodness <term>goodness: "epieikeia," a sense of equity or moral excellence</term>, whenever someone appears noble or brave or something of that sort, just as we said in the case of the athletes.

...in the act of doing good; and this is sufficient for goodwill. For since it is not the beginning of friendship, or rather, the one who feels goodwill must exist first. Because of this, it is not found among the many. Because of this, it also involves goodness. For goodwill is not a general thing, for they feel goodwill toward him, yet they are not necessarily friends. For he speaks of goodness. If it is a virtue. Since it is not the completion of the whole, or desired by all. If it were a passion. But it would not be returned upon demand but in the act of feeling goodwill. Or it is the underlying state in each excellence it possesses. If it is also a kind of goodwill. It exists, however, in all things that remain hidden. If all things are felt with goodwill. Whether it is learned by the bow <note>The "bow" (toxon) may be a scribal error or a metaphorical reference to aiming for a mark</note>. Through what you say, they feel goodwill toward the benefit of all. If some prefer the well-being of others more than themselves; if indeed they also give from their own. If he also returns it by providing a mutual exchange. It would be easiest for the contest to become hopeful because of this, so as to wish good things for the one who is prospering; but he does not say he feels goodwill for him personally. That it might be loved, or that which is idle becomes so by lasting through time. These things generally show that goodwill still exists. And that goodwill is indeed a kind of friendship.

# Ennead V

Already, and human beings in general, are a certain selection from intellect and reason. Therefore, the cause of evil for the soul will be set down as audacity <note>original: "τόλμα" (tolma) — a pivotal Neoplatonic concept referring to the 'daring' or self-will of the soul that leads it to separate from the Divine Unity to seek its own independent existence.</note>; and if we consider the underlying subjects, it is not certainly due to the cause itself. For it is clear that it is given to them as well. Thus even animals, those that are more numerous and often stumbling, make choices. We attribute sin to those who are falling short, by which one might become more incorporeal; for the subsistence <note>original: "ὑπόστασις" (hypostasis) — the underlying reality or substantial existence of a thing.</note> in the body is the cause. And if there was some ancient cause, it has been cut away.

Of the things before this, error gives an account, announcing justice upon it. But they seek in nature, because the place is evil, the cause of doing badly, by ignorance of what was before this, to know the things that are. Further, the things especially within them are not evil, but rather are to be known in relation to them, such as what she [the soul] has within herself. Since never otherwise than as a heaven, which is as the peak of each of them appearing, as the manifestation of the whole, its peaks, so that the things of the same kind as the whole are the kin of each. But for the whole to have another was heralded.

# Ennead V

It is clear, then, that I have spoken of these things from the beginning. The assignment of the cause has occurred in relation to the being of the present reality; it is the cause itself which also belongs to true Being. Whence it is possible not only to assign a cause to Being, but also to its existence and its persistence. But there is also that other thing—this very thing in itself, as we said—which the power gives entirely to nature according to its impulse <note>original: "ὁρμὴν" (hormēn) — the innate drive or urge of a being to act or move toward its purpose.</note>. Because there will be a generation <note>original: "γένεσις" (genesis) — the process of coming into being or the physical world of change.</note>, that which will be has also come into being, though not all things arise from its presence, through which that cause exists. Such is the grace that follows after. For that cause is not only the reason for being, but also the cause of life. And generation is a kind of making for the sensible world. For from the mixture of matter <note>original: "ὕλης" (hylēs) — the raw material of the physical universe, often viewed by Neoplatonists as the limit of existence and the source of potential 'evil' or lack.</note>, everything has been interwoven in the process of becoming. This also applies to the movements; it is entirely concerned with them. That new thing is the same, and it relates to the other things as well. For there is a difference even in these.

<margin>
For
the first
nature
is not
the same
</margin>
This, again, is generation, and it is clear that it is not a simple thing. And indeed they say that the one part is above what has been generated, while the other is something else. This account, then, is far from the principle of the activity <note>original: "ἐνέργεια" (energeia) — the dynamic actualization or 'working' of a being's nature.</note> within beings as a substantial existence <note>original: "ὕπαρξιν" (hyparxin) — the actual reality or subsistence of a thing.</note>, or it concerns the whole of nature. For it is not the thing itself—and how could it become one? he asks. How then does the one who has been acted upon become? That which he himself is, this thing becomes entirely. Or he himself belongs to that which is. And again, it is clear. For he who sees rightly does not see what he has undergone <note>original: "πάθος" (pathos) — an experience, passion, or something 'suffered' or received by the soul.</note>. And these things were becoming a state of passion; and again, the things of the nations have come to be, where it is necessary to show how they are causes—a demonstration must be made. But when that soul looks, having seen the whole, she sees as one who has come to be with it. And even further, those are the names. These things belong to each individual; they are not the things found in sense-perception. But the health within us is in the one who is caused. Yet that [higher] one is that one. And this is both a principle and a reason. Whence it must be analogous, along with justice, the reasons being within. But one must show the whole and the parts of beings as they are taken.

But he who looks upon the things of God is there, because He is infinite. For as if mimicking generation, he sees within himself. The testimony has been heard, as far as the things that produce. But as for those things, as the one following after or even at the beginning, it goes forward. Thus it is also clear that they are within Being. And both for Being and for existence in general, and as it concerns us, so that it may be divine. One must already know their things before these: the angels <note>In this 15th-century Neoplatonic context, "angels" (aggeloi) often refers to divine messengers or intermediary spirits that bridge the gap between the human soul and the high Intellect.</note>. All their things have been taken away, and yet you must know those things too. And the things which are about to be are within their rational principles <note>original: "λόγοις" (logois) — the formative, organizing principles of the universe.</note>. It is not just any way. Because all, because also, because looking upon it, he was brought away to discourse on divine things <note>original: "θεολογεῖσθαι" (theologeisthai) — to treat of or study the nature of God and divine realities.</note>.

<summary>Plotinus explores the causal relationship between the higher realms of Being and the physical world of generation, arguing that life and existence flow from a divine source and are interwoven with matter. He emphasizes that the soul must look toward these higher, infinite principles to understand its own nature and the divine order.</summary>

<meta>Continuity Note: This page continues from the previous discussion on the causal link between the divine realm and the sensible world. Having established that all life and being flow from a higher source, Plotinus now investigates how the soul and the Intellect (Nous) participate in this divine presence through knowledge and the metaphorical "light" of the Father.</meta>

# Ennead V

### .. Being . 5.

It is necessary for that one, who is to participate in all things, to learn them; and to share in those things which he could not reach except from the indweller <note>original: "ἐνοικοῦντος" (enoikountos) — referring to the divine presence or the Intellect that resides within the soul.</note>. For it exists once for all; and this is especially true for him to whom knowledge <note>original: "γνῶσις" (gnōsis) — higher, spiritual insight rather than mere data.</note> is not a matter of necessity. But he does not act through the same power by which he was made, but from that power itself; so as to lead even himself back toward it. For the Beginning <note>original: "ἀρχήν" (archēn) — the source or first principle of all things.</note> is nothing else. Wherefore it is also spoken of in harmony. For those things which are spoken of are most numerous when they admit of offspring, and he admits many of them. For the same Reason <note>original: "λόγος" (logos) — the rational principle or "word" that structures reality.</note> has come into being, just like the light of the sun. But it is not that sun itself. Therefore, it is not light in an absolute sense, but there is some other sun beside it. Just as the eye is "sun-like," and the earth in turn is illuminated by the sun, and the sun is an image <note>original: "εἴδωλον" (eidōlon) — a reflection, copy, or phantom.</note>, and another has spoken of it in a literary way. It is a sun laid up, as if not to be used; and this is done immovably. And it is not without substance, but is the power of all things. For there is no power which does not belong to the radiant one, for knowledge is like the first light of the right moment <note>original: "καιροῦ" (kairou) — the 'opportune moment' or the perfect timing of divine action.</note>. It belongs to that of the soul. Whatever we might say its essence <note>original: "οὐσίαν" (ousian) — the fundamental nature or "beingness" of a thing.</note> is—the essence of the radiant one—is that it is not like the immovable light itself. But it was necessary for it to shine forth from the indweller himself. For it is a part of that essence, and from that it must also exist as kindred, and indeed it has become so, and it is by nature entirely dear to it. And so it acts upon it, because it is both divided and undivided. It was necessary for the works to be:

> because the Father is greater than I, he says. <note>original: "ὅτι ὁ πατὴρ μείζων μοῦ φησίν" — a direct quotation of John 14:28, used here by the Neoplatonic commentator to illustrate the subordination of the Intellect to the One.</note>

For all things are good to us. For the Father is in form and in the Good appearance. He alone is within. All things are as many as are in his own thought, just as those things are in the Mind <note>original: "νῷ" (nō) — the Intellect or Nous.</note>. He made all things in which this shall be; and these are all his own. For they are not outside of himself. For all things are there. And it is necessary for this one to be like a tongue, just as he took from us. Certain people called her Athena, which is the Mind <note>original: "νοῦς" (nous)</note>, and she takes a certain form of the act of thinking. Seeing this form having come to be, the Mind was struck with awe and wondered, and at the same time wondered if the first divine light became light because of him, and already all things have become radiant. For the Reason is its own world, making it divine and like the indweller himself. And just as all beautiful things again had their own limit. <margin>(.·)</margin> Neither changed back again, nor should it grow out and depart. For as it will be said among the sensible things <note>original: "αἰσθητοῖς" (aisthētois) — objects perceived by the senses in the physical world.</note> that come after it: how does he seem to become one of the things after him? The generation again held its place. The inward growth was near to union <note>original: "ἕνωσιν" (henōsin) — the mystical "One-ing" or reunification with the source.</note>. This union, appearing most beautiful when it occurred, meant he no longer held a bare thinking of the mind. <insert>+</insert> So as many things as are still written, so are the things in the Reason.

<summary>Plotinus uses the metaphor of the sun and light to explain how the Intellect (Nous) and the Soul derive their essence from the "Father" (The One). He identifies the goddess Athena as a representation of the divine Mind and emphasizes the unity between the creator and the created world of forms.</summary>

<meta>Continuity Note: This page continues Plotinus’s critique of those who misunderstand the relationship between the soul and the divine. He moves from discussing the "light" of the Father to a defense of the soul’s dignity against those who would equate it with irrational nature or mock its origin.</meta>

It is irrational to compare the wild beast and the God; yet these people, through their "divinity," claim a victory over Him. But He has shown that He is not inferior to them, as if in a contest; indeed, He laughed at both the man and those who fathered him. They act not through wickedness, nor through good order, but—I say—through a stroke of good fortune born of senselessness. Regarding this, one should not even trust the name. Furthermore, if he possessed light from the beginning, he held it unseasonably; or, by the Earth, it is not present among us. The shameful is always more accustomed to appearing than the Good, since he seems to be talking nonsense about their lives. It is said that He appeared to the ancients as something exalted <note>original: "μετέωρον" (meteōron) — literally something raised high or celestial; in this context, a sublime or transcendent reality.</note> and that the soul itself possesses antiquity. Therefore, everything is grasped just as it is received. 

Indeed, the most intense of these things come from Him from of old—not because of "all things," for he says to the King <note>A reference to Plato’s Second Letter (312e), which Plotinus frequently cites: "All things are around the King of all."</note> that all things exist for Him and by His laws. Since this is the case, it is not unworthy of God to reach toward that final portion, for He is the cause of all other things. However, their reasoning <note>original: "λογισμόν" (logismon) — the discursive, step-by-step thinking process.</note> is not the same, for so great is the soul in them that even their movements are governed by it. Because their movements are such, even Homer says they are always fixed upon the same things. Truly, in such a state, the truth itself would not be found. Thus, one who is always about to sing will never arrive at justice for all. Such is the hypothesis of the soul. Indeed, no rational account could come to be, nor could anything remain hidden. Rather, her opinion is such that she remains ignorant of the Reason <note>original: "λόγον" (logos) — the underlying principle of order in the universe.</note> within us, which is how these terrible things have come to pass. At least, this is not how it was spoken of by some of the ancients, specifically in the writings of Plato. While this is the greatest matter, and there is hope and opinion, it is generally impossible to save it. If this is not so, how does the same thing not happen to everyone, both now and in the future? Or is it not worthy to be spoken of? Our means of salvation, as one might say to all, have been spoken of for the sake of the good, or for one such as us.
<margin>(symbol)</margin> So greatly is he occupied. Because everything concerns us, or rather, because it would not happen to him in this way. Yet Plato himself writes that, and for this reason, he would not hold to those things, though he says much. Rather, concerning all things that have been said, he speaks accurately and with a just love. Hence, from that place, the one who speaks of them—since he will live among them in the future—appears as he might be even in the friendships of the gods. Enjoying these things, even beyond that future, it is just to say so, as he himself would. We should hold to this: they will be persuaded by the most ancient of practices. If justice is not for all, it is because they hold a cause against all. These same things are the objects of love; and I dare to teach all of this. It is just: for friendship is within the soul itself, so that it belongs to all these things. But concerning them, it is said to us that we should never expect this separately.

<page-num>138</page-num>
<header>. On Wellbeing . V .</header> <note>original: "Εὐθυμ" (Euthym) — Likely an abbreviation for Euthymia, referring to contentment or the "well-being" found in the Fifth Ennead.</note>

You speak of those who have been earnest about this, yet who once yearned for those other things. They are as much lower than us as one might say the Earth is to the Heavens. Since there is both body and soul, those things that are short-lived remain on the earth, but the soul is eternal, possessing Reason and a divine peak <note>original: "θεῖον κέρας" (theion keras) — literally "divine horn," likely a metaphor for the highest point or the "summit" of the soul that touches the divine.</note>. If, therefore, the things on earth are honored in this way—and not only the whole earth and sea are filled with these strivings, but even the source from which they flow to us—then what could one say about such a thing? What else, but that one must approach it not by coming with the feet, but only with the eye <note>original: "ὄμματι" (ommati) — the "inner eye" or spiritual vision.</note> and the intellect <note>original: "διανοίᾳ" (dianoia).</note>. Thus, we are in expectation of the presence of God; just as in the universe there is only one World <note>original: "κόσμος" (kosmos) — the ordered universe.</note>. Since this world seems to manifest itself, we should not ignore their value too much, nor fall away; for thus the earth and the things in it have been mixed with bitterness for me. 

Therefore, you will provide proofs for him. If it were unseasonable, do not cease your efforts against their violence, for they were not learning. Furthermore, through you, it is for all who are earnest. For those who are concerned with the remaining things, their senses are held in such an opinion. Thus, when they are asked—seeing that no one could call anything greater than the heroic preparations of God—they would say they love all things in the contest. But they feared to gather the fruit for themselves. One must not speak of them, but of the Reason. But if we should speak of both (for the substance <note>original: "ὑπόστασις" (hypostasis) — the underlying reality or "person" of a thing.</note> is clear), it is because we are not the only ones who know that these things are worthy, having spoken worthily.
<margin>2. Question</margin> Furthermore, as the Reason now says to all, this belongs to those who are earnest.
<margin>3. It is not</margin> It is not possible for you to depart. For our entire nature is not able to be so,
<margin>9. Toward whom</margin> not mastering itself by nature but by contemplation <note>original: "θεωρίᾳ" (theōria) — the act of spiritual looking or divine meditation.</note>. For she thinks that everything from us belongs to her. These things would happen to her in all cases. These are necessary, since they are directed toward true opinion. For the same Reason will teach us, so that all souls in this life are within that which preceded us. Our earnestness in these matters is to speak worthily somewhere, so that our whole nature might be preserved. That nature of ours, which once was, does not even consider itself capable of being dissolved. Whence, it reasons for all. He who does not think his soul is [lost], from that source the reasoning of the rational soul <note>original: "λογικής ψυχῆς" (logikēs psychēs)</note> finds the Good. Therefore, one could not speak otherwise than to say that it is impossible to bear fruit in nothing, or to do so apart from my soul. I also consider that which happens according to nature, but it is clear to all how to reason. But let it now be sweet for all.

<meta>Continuity Note: While the previous page discussed the soul's relationship to the divine in a Plotinian context (likely from the Enneads), this page transitions into a technical Aristotelian analysis of the senses of smell and taste, following the structure of *De Anima* Book II, Chapters 9 and 10. · On the 5th · 2 ·
<sig>b</sig>

...smell is destroyed; and likewise for the other senses. So it is clear that the animal is not by nature so destructible by odor in all cases, but only in those where the sense of smell is most acute. Whether this is also the case for other animals cannot be said for certain; or rather, it is so in those where it is most developed, such as in birds and four-legged beasts. Regarding the differences in the objects underlying smell, there would be no specific genus, just as there is among colors. But there are species there as well; just as there are smells. For some were sweet, while others were bitter, to a greater or lesser degree. But as we categorize flavors <note>original: "χυμοὺς" (chymous) — often translated as juices or flavors; the liquid quality that carries taste.</note>, so too do we categorize smells. For we describe the remaining smells in this way, such as pungent, harsh, acid, and oily, corresponding to the smells produced by flavors. But as we said, some smells follow the differences of flavors, while others do not—such as the scents of flowers. Those floral scents that are like this are more akin to colors. Thus, there are species of smells, but they are more distinct than flavors, though not in the same way as the species found in colors. Nor are they simply categories of smells, but rather the fragrant and the foul-smelling; nor are the species strictly attached to them. But sweet smell—since I have spoken of it—is not perceived in the same way by all. We perceive sweet smells in bodies; for if the fragrance of those things is not based on flavors, then neither is the pleasure or the pain derived from them. In other cases, however, the fragrance exists in and of itself. This might be a unique characteristic of humans; whereas the smell based on flavors belongs to other animals as well, as has been said. But this is especially true of other animals: that which gives them pleasure or pain is perceived only incidentally <note>original: "κατὰ συμβεβηκὸς" (kata symbebekos) — an Aristotelian term meaning "by accident" or as a secondary attribute rather than an essential nature.</note>. For since the smell is in the food, we rejoice when we are hungry, but when we are full and in need of nothing, we do not rejoice. Nor do other animals rejoice, unless their sense of smell experiences some other passion according to the smells of the flavors. It is the same for humans; but the fragrance of flowers contributes nothing toward nourishment, nor toward desire, nor the opposite. Rather, it is simply fragrant. But it is clear that smell exists because of the breath; thus the sense organ is not necessary in this way. But that which is perceived through the air and in the liquid is known as a distinct property. It would be rather strange if the other sense were always perceived instead; for every sensation is also a form of cognition.

# On taste, and what is the sensory power of these things: -+

<margin>Note that the object of taste is something tangible <note>original: "ἁπτόν τι" (hapton ti) — something that can be touched; implying taste is a localized sense requiring physical contact.</note>; therefore, it is not perceived through an intermediate foreign body, for neither is the tangible. The body in which the flavor resides—the object of taste—is in moisture as its matter; and this is something tangible.</margin>
The object of taste is something tangible. And because of this, it is not perceived through an intermediate foreign body, for neither is the tangible. The body in which the flavor resides—the object of taste—is in moisture as its matter; and this is something tangible. Therefore, even if we were in water, we would perceive something sweet if it were thrown in. But the sensation would not be through the medium between us; rather, it would be by the flavor being mixed with the moisture, just as in a drink. Flavor does not act like sound or smell. For we perceive nothing in the way those things act. Regarding things perceived through a medium, we do not perceive them by being mixed with them, but by the medium being affected. Color is perceived in this way; but flavor is not. In moisture, the object of taste exists as in its matter, just like the tangible. The body in which the flavor resides—the object of taste—is in moisture as its matter; and this is something tangible. Since nothing produces the sensation of flavor without moisture, it must possess moisture either potentially or actually—such as the salty. For it is easily dissolved and acts to dissolve the tongue. Just as sight is of both the visible and the invisible (for darkness is invisible, yet sight judges this as well), and also of the excessively bright (for this too is invisible, though in a different way than darkness), so too hearing is of both sound and silence. Of these, one is audible and the other inaudible; hearing also perceives a great noise, just as sight perceives the bright (for just as a small sound is inaudible, in a certain way a very great and violent sound is also inaudible). "Invisible" is used as it is for other impossible things, and also for that which is by nature poorly suited to be seen or not at all, such as the "footless" or the "pithless." In this way, taste is of both the tastable and the untastable; the latter is that which has a small or poor flavor, or one that is destructive to the sense of taste. The beginning of this seems to be the drinkable and the undrinkable (for this is a type of taste; but one is poor and destructive to taste, while the other is according to nature. The drinkable is common to both touch and taste).

<meta>Continuity Note: The previous page concluded a discussion on the mechanisms of sensory perception (smell and taste), likely drawing from Aristotelian commentary. This page (186) transitions into a more characteristically Plotinian metaphysical investigation from the Enneads (specifically Ennead IV.3.30-31), examining how the soul perceives through the "mirror" of the imagination and why physical matter like flesh is unsuitable for reflecting the higher intellect.</meta>

### Image II.

Whatever the soul learns, it does not truly know as it knows itself; for it is not those things. It is through the beauty of knowledge that it knows these things better, yet it does not know the knowledge of itself through itself. Rather, it knows through those things by which it perceives. Those things are not the soul itself; and that through which it knows is mediated <note>original: "ἔμμεσός" (emmesos) — meaning acting through an intermediary rather than by direct contact.</note>. It is not the soul itself. Because everything is given to the soul, all knowledge follows from it. And the truth is found in those things. But as for the faculty of sensation itself, let it appear here alone. And it is the nature of the animal to possess a form that is not itself sensible, but which stands before the sight as an image <term>eidolon</term> <note>In Neoplatonism, an "eidolon" is a reflection or secondary representation of a higher reality.</note> or a product of sensation. 

Perhaps in the <unclear>mortal</unclear> animal, the act of perceiving is that by which it carries itself around. This occurs through the relationship between sensation and imagination <term>phantasia</term>, following each sensory act. This was not the only thing left behind. Therefore, in this animal, we do not possess the primary desire; since for an animal born this way, its powers and all it encompasses are such that its recognition of existence is more mediated and not according to its true nature. And this exists only upon the matter. 

But the one who investigates says what the soul recognizes; and why it is in the soul. It neither possesses such things, nor does anyone receive them. Rather, it is within its own vessel <note>original: "σκάφει" (skaphei) — literally a hollowed-out bowl or hull, here metaphorically referring to the structure of the imaginative faculty.</note>. What it knows, it knows as the same. And it is contained within the same. This is not like the earth, as when one holds clay in the hand to feel its smoothness. Rather, it receives their nature in this way. Nor should a sudden smoothness become the center of the imagination, or it might still happen that one becomes angry with oneself. 

When the image is further down, the reflection <note>original: "ἀνάκλασίς" (anaklasis) — a technical term for the breaking back of light or a reflection in a mirror.</note> is somehow according to that very vessel; not the whole, but some part outside the whole. For those who represent the form did not believe it was destroyed, but rather that the reception of the form appeared through the unsuitable matter. For the "suitable matter" <note>original: "οἰκεία ὕλη" (oikeia hyle) — the proper material substrate for a specific form.</note> consists of flesh and bones. For those for whom it is not suitable, it is the soul itself that has given the forms to the clear <note>original: "διαυγές" (diauges) — a state of being translucent or crystalline.</note> or the transparent <term>diaphanes</term>. Or as much as is different from the earth, such as air; and it should not be adorned by its own domestic parts. For sometimes images are produced. And after the colors there is a form, though not the one it truly possesses. 

But if the form is poured out, not even the images in the imagination remain; or that by which it is good, just as a good sensation resembles sensation itself. But God is good. Or because of the same, it is not the soul. And every faculty of desire seeks the good. For the Intellect <term>Nous</term> and all good things exist. And they shall call upon some angel-like <note>original: "ἀγγελώδη" (angelode) — pertaining to a messenger or higher spiritual being.</note> sensation of the process of becoming. And the heart of the soul is this. And the soul knows that it is through itself.

<summary>Plotinus explores the nature of self-knowledge and perception, using the metaphor of a mirror-vessel (imagination) to explain how the soul reflects higher truths despite the "unsuitable matter" of the physical body.</summary>
<keywords>Plotinus, Soul (Psuche), Sensation (Aisthesis), Imagination (Phantasia), Intellect (Nous), Reflection (Anaklasis), Matter (Hyle), Translucency</keywords>

<meta>Continuity Note: The previous page discussed the soul's relationship with sensory perception and the "mirror" of imagination. This page (137) moves deeper into the internal workings of the soul, specifically focusing on Ennead V.3, where Plotinus investigates whether the soul knows itself directly or if self-knowledge is exclusive to the higher Intellect (Nous).</meta>

# Being V.

Therefore, he says: is it the soul itself that knows itself, or is it we who know? And since the soul itself exists in its reasonings, all these things, looking toward something else, are already discursive thought <term>dianoia</term> <note>Dianoia is "thinking-through," the step-by-step reasoning used by humans, as opposed to the immediate, total grasp of truth by the higher Intellect.</note>. Discursive thought is nothing if it does not truly exist; if it lacks the Intellect <term>nous</term> <note>original: "νοῦς" (nous) — the divine Mind, the realm of pure forms and absolute knowledge.</note> within itself, it will fall into error. But if it belongs to itself, would the things outside not also belong to it? Or does it merely conceive of them? For if it thinks of things outside, it does not yet think of itself; it has within itself only the impressions of things as if they were experiences. If sensation is involved, it is not because of the many, but because the soul itself has the power. But if it is not the object of thought, and if it is not the faculty of thinking, or if the reasoning faculty is not there, how can it receive the fruit of the Intellect? It becomes beautiful in the soul through the Intellect that comes from it. Either, then, it is the soul, or it is the soul within itself. The soul is such either by nature, because it belongs to the nature of the Intellect. If these things do not exist in discursive thought, either looking upward or toward the things of God, then it is not even the soul that we already know, or it is our Intellect that comes to be. Because of this, we are admitted into it. But if the things that come to be are discursive thought, then our Intellect knows itself, or it is the object of reasoning. Because we will experience knowledge, or it will be produced by itself for itself. But if it is ignorant of itself as it is, then it is also ignorant of us. If it knows us, and that which knows itself is something of ours, then we are also known because of this. If we are the ones who perceive, and discursive thought is ours, then if we think, we are also the ones who reason. But if the thinking power in discursive thought is ourselves, then we are also that. But what does it perform in thinking—is it itself or us? For on the one hand, it is seen by discursive thought. But the Intellect is either ours or from us, and it knows that it is nothing; and how, if it looks at its own Intellect, does it know itself? Through discursive thought, it makes things its own; and is this not the greatest blessedness? What? What would it become if it were not itself? In what way do we use the object of reasoning? By not contemplating the soul itself; even if it does not persuade us. But if it does not look, it would find us in relation to ourselves. We see our Intellect when it says nothing according to itself. Or I already know as the Intellect has truly written. Or because from all sides it sees the causes, or we see those who know through discursive thought and Intellect. It knows itself; such things come to be through revelation. And I am able to know this by knowing her, having learned her name; or to think. Let it be; just as one knows the blessed, or such things. Or it also knows the nature of the soul and what kind it is. Or it knows the Intellect. And does it know itself, or this intelligible man? And would it know its own Intellect, or even itself?

<column-break/>

It knows, even if it does not know itself as another, as we said just now; and here, this does not follow for us. Furthermore, when it is impossible for us to grasp the same thing by itself, it must already be distinguished here. Since, therefore, it is the gentle assertion. It is either that or this. But if it is such as to make the same thing according to the same order, its being is its existence. If it were not for reason, it would be as if a man were to conceive of himself, and thus he would not be. Nor would his ceasing be. But how is it that he exists in this? Nothing is easily caught with which evil could exist, nor would anything bad or anything that has been created receive destruction. Nor are there any images <term>eidola</term> <note>original: "εἴδολα" (eidola) — reflections, shadows, or lower manifestations of a higher reality.</note> in this way. Their reason is not such, nor is the power above directed toward that, and those souls that know themselves are beautiful; nor would they be so most blessed, so that everything is laid out for us even in him. For by being known by those things, it is also thus from birth, because many are the causes of existing things. Furthermore, through sensation, it is part of itself in this way, or it is this; but it is by itself. Therefore, it does not even conceive; but just as it is, so a part of it has passed away. Since there is a composition, but rather the Intellect. And that which is above it. Coming to be from it, it seems to differ in no way even if it is itself; so that in thinking, both belong to it, and it perceives itself. It differs in nothing if it is somehow itself. But to fall is an absurd thing to bring upon it. How can it be through the Intellect? How perhaps is the whole that or this to itself, so that it may see? For its own image is entirely in the power of its own contemplation <term>theoria</term> <note>original: "θεωρία" (theoria) — the act of looking at or contemplating divine truths.</note>. That which exists by the power of the like. For its own was thinking of things being completed in contemplation. Some will know and some will not know themselves; for it is not when they appear that they are completed; but we have known how to have the whole in those things; we have known the object of knowledge to be of itself; in a single word, let it know itself. But knowing is the same as being. Thus, these consequences and the things known are one. From where the things according to reason come; then it is surely joined to him. So that being is around him, or he has another. For if being known is the same as contemplating, or being known is the intelligible. And it is the same. Therefore, the first thing known was not at once each of them. But as many as are causes. Therefore, to the same. And it is necessary for the essence.

Plotinus concludes that at the highest level of contemplation, the act of knowing and the state of being are identical.</summary>

# Ennead V.

...leaves this form behind. It is in need of something, or of that which is necessary. If, then, the first principle is in that state... If the First Intellect <term>nous</term> <note>The "Nous" is the Divine Mind or second level of reality in Plotinus's system; it is the realm of pure, eternal truth and the Platonic Forms.</note> existed for the sake of beings—or rather, for its own contents—it would be secondary. But if it appears as ignorance, how then is it not said that he who knows, learns; and it is as if it came to be from that which is there, through them, like the things that come to be in this world. And it is directed toward the beings, and not the objects of thought <term>noeta</term> <note>The "Intelligibles"—the eternal, non-physical realities that the Mind contemplates.</note> by some providence; for if it were not prior to these things, it would not be the cause by which he thinks. How then are these things present? Or since it is of the intelligible, it requires life; and the thing produced meets it, as if it were no longer directed toward itself. It became a necessity, potentially, for those who exist to be a sort of "susceptibility," as has been said, and to call the thing produced from there by whatever name is appropriate. And it is necessary, having known the produced thing, or all things; already there; both the things in which it is and how it is. For it is entirely a matter of power. It produces both lives and life. Each is alone. From which through them and from his own opinion. All of it. If then it was necessary for the things in the beginning to be theirs. If they should know the activity <term>energeia</term> <note>The state of being "in-act" or fully functioning, as opposed to being a mere potential.</note>, or the susceptibility of the things produced. If then thinking is through themselves. The one prior to him. Because even before this, these things were produced, or came from the beginning. If then all that is directed toward... or all to them. And because "being" there is the Intellect itself. And indeed in its nature; or even all through him, he himself. For it is from this, or toward, or he himself. Just as it will exist in him. Or does he not think being? It is the same. But these things are directed toward the Good. In those things that are all-embracing to the soul. Furthermore, just as not everything, because he himself, or such as he himself. And to live; and if all that is in him. If it is not the same to be in the "opinion" of God, he himself had to be. If it is, and if the things in him are his own. Toward the activity, or thus entirely. Just as but toward God. Because of having things similarly; and, all that is "all" to God were likely there. Or necessarily so. And the things through them. For if toward him? If not even toward. If there. But he seeks again these same things we think most, or the things for the sake of seeming to be him. If, or there is not some, or no nature or thoughts in God. If it appears that he will give life to all; for not nonetheless, in the same of them. Or it was said. And thus

<margin>one hints at a riddle</margin> <note>original: "τις αινιτται" (tis ainittai). Plotinus often uses the language of "riddles" when discussing the mysterious way the soul relates to the Divine.</note>
he signaled that the things coming to be should happen. <insert>Clearly, for if it happened this way, there would be much excuse for the soul.</insert> One might seek then for that to be present, or even a certain work. Every [part] then also teaches our soul how it might possess their nature. And the Mind of God teaches the soul all things, so that it may learn the things that are with Him.

<column-break/>

<margin>7</margin>
If indeed these things agree with our innate ideas, where is the cause? Or must one meet the difficulty concerning it? These things, then, coming to be, would occur, and since the Intellect sees things coming to be. If there is something that is "itself," and unmoved in itself, produced from it and moving outward. What then if, in itself, it existed as if being produced? From which, not possessing it, but ascending toward it into nothing more than what it was, and thus being praised, when did it receive it? Either when generation began, or the things of generation according to itself. It passes then from that toward the beginning, as if all that is produced is through it, but as that in which, or how the things there are divine. And because it is not possible for it to possess any of the things in this world. So that by some "opinion" it had to be still in being, and this by the "opinion of God," and it is, from which it would not even seem to be; it is necessary then for it to have knowledge. But if knowledge is in it—and knowledge and thinking are the same thing—then knowledge belongs more to that nature toward it at some time. But he who does not look at the thing produced... To me it is not safe, or according to us knowledge is a "knowledge of knowledges." It is necessary to know, since that which knows through itself also knows itself. He then who does not know, would in no way seem to have the "fruit of being." Perhaps it was not necessary concerning him, who alone exists, to have knowledge of his own, but there is knowledge of certain others. As indeed his life should not be thought of as "opinion," which would be lowly; but it is not so. But it is necessary to have the same from which he comes. And would it ever happen to him to be ignorant of himself? It does not follow that the Intellect itself did not have to know. And if not all is already knowledge. If there is something, but also all the things in us and near. If the difficulty is this. If the cause exists before the thinking—or rather all the things said of him. Thinking belongs to the one who thinks. Even if it is his power, he thinks. If also the thought is he himself, having become that. If it is not possible to think him? If he is ignorant? And so that we do not have a problem toward him, which must be brought out for him, what is that? These things are especially to be said to him, so that God himself does not fail, or if thinking follows there, if it is not from that. By what would his thought be said to exist? Or not, but rather the "thoughts" themselves. For there is no life in them. But so that the whole is thought... to say all from the other by power. Since if it seemed to those in us to be without mind, and he took away their lack of sensation; let us ask if living is a power, or rather the activity. And it is indeed activity. If also the acting is concerning it. Therefore it thinks itself, or if concerning it, are these the same as being?

<summary>This page explores the metaphysical relationship between the Divine Intellect (Nous), Being, and self-knowledge, arguing that the Intellect does not learn from outside itself but is identical to its own objects of thought. Plotinus asserts that for a divine being, thinking and existing are the same activity, and the soul learns by looking toward this Divine Mind.</summary>

# Ennead V.

· Peace. Book 5. ·

Since these things belong to the Intellect within itself, they are from itself; therefore they do not come from the outside. Whatever beings existed within it were in agreement with it. But as for the nature of these specific things—such as the things nearby, or the self-wrought form of fire—the Intellect possessed their rational cause <term>logos</term> <note>Logos here refers to the formative principle or "blueprint" of a thing.</note> and a manifestation for all. For indeed, one can see the divine laws <term>thesmous</term> nearby. This applies also to the soul <term>psyche</term>, so that its intellect <term>nous</term> is not somewhere else, such as "above," except in a secondary sense. The soul does not see things through the "self-vision" of the intellect, yet the things directed toward the interior are more sufficient—be it the moon or the whole universe. But the soul will not be one simply by being "sweet"; rather, the entire nature flowing out from man exists so that all things have a generative power. All things through the first principle <term>arche</term> are equally divine in some way and participate more in the things near the beginning. Even the lowest things do not neglect those that came before them, so that they too may see their own internal depths. If, then, the present is considered—or if one seeks life <term>zoen</term> and the intellect as a common possession among all things or treasures—it follows that they are either present or according to their capacity. The soul, hoping to hold all its honor in itself, happened upon this by nature. When examining a man, he seeks to follow his own nature, from which the intellect also proceeds from the first principles. It is near him, and the similar soul is near to this. I myself seek within this soul; let it become itself. From this source, each thing has its own being instead of just being "itself." This appears in another through another. For since the living animal of the soul dwells within, it was discovered through the honor of man; therefore it sees, though it may be seized by deception. Everything that comes to be in itself is something other than that first thing, stretching away from the beginning in a kind of departure. If it is solitary, it will have its own character, like a satisfaction or a longing. Who then is this "living one"? We must have intellect. And we behold the vision as light; or rather, as they say, the vision is light. It must be so; and why not? For the intellect itself is not from the outside. Indeed, **all light is born from light** <note>original: "πᾶν φῶς ἀπὸ φωτὸς γέγονεν" — This is a central Neoplatonic metaphor for the emanation of reality from the One.</note>. Therefore, light comes from God. Because of this, that which the soul contemplates suddenly <term>exaiphnes</term> <note>A famous term in Plotinus and Plato for the moment of mystical insight that happens "all at once."</note> appears; this is what it means. Being alone within, let us see how they say the things above are in it; as if someone, having received a trace of the light in the soul and having experienced it, learned on the contrary to believe it comes from the one who bestowed it. Thus, appearing alone, the inhabitant is revealed. It is because this light shone, whether living or not, that the soul becomes truly upright and alive.

<column-break/>

Τουναντίον δὲ ἑκάστη τῶν περὶ ἑαυτὴν τὴν ψυχὴν· ὃ πείρατά τινά· ἀνά-

On the contrary, everything concerning the soul itself reaches certain limits. By necessity, there are causes for these wonders; just as the image <term>eidolon</term> <note>An "eidolon" is a reflection or imitation of a higher reality.</note> is not the thing itself, so the soul looks upon its source. How does it receive vision from the cause, whether by some mechanism or like the fire there? It must be said that the soul has a life that has been made into an intellect, or a life derived from Life. For even the earth itself participates. Thus, if the living being possesses anything, it does not merely suffer light, but is fulfilled by it. From the bright color, you shone forth! It comes from the impassive **Intelligible Father** <note>original: "νοητοῦ πατρὸς" — A Platonic term for the One or the Good as the source of all being.</note>. Just as divine fire is different from other fire, let it be so. We seek this source within. We seek the knowledge of it to happen within itself. It is as if sight itself said it does not belong to itself, but is a flashing forth from there. There is a forgetfulness of reasoning when the soul is perhaps more truly itself within. Thus, it has other lives. There is the Father who is prior to the soul. How can that which comes to be belong to itself while also belonging to another? Let us consider these things in ourselves, observing how many things are lacking in a man who cannot see. Through that which is above, how does the representation <term>apeikasia</term> or image occur? Whatever part of the soul is in agreement, let the soul be as itself. Whatever is most intellectual in the soul is called so in order that it might most truly be "Intellect." Perhaps it might even become so through virtue, leaving passions behind. The soul, being rich in this, or contemplating the sensible things alone... we still contemplate. If its light is entirely directed toward the Intellect alone, then the reception in it is this: the Intellect becomes manifest in it, defining the light of that source. It is like the **sun** <note>original: "ἥλιον" — Plotinus often compares the One to the sun, which illuminates everything without being diminished.</note>; a sphere already bright from itself. This is not a light confused with the soul, but its own. It is as if one wanted to look at the terrestrial sun, yet sought to benefit from the appearance without the vision being dissolved by the excessive brightness. For the light is not something external; when the soul is alone in itself, it saves everything.

<summary>Plotinus discusses how the soul receives its light and life from a higher "Intelligible Father," arguing that true vision and knowledge are internal processes where the soul reflects the light of the divine Intellect (Nous). He uses the metaphors of light from light and the sun to explain how the soul participates in divine reality without being overwhelmed by its source.</summary>

-> # Ennead III <-
-> ### On Nature, Contemplation, and the One ### <note>Original: Εννεαδ. γ.</note>

And all things that come to be upon it are a whole. If we were to posit that "making" and "thinking" are the same thing, then **contemplation** <term>Theoria: In Plotinian philosophy, this is not just "looking" but a creative, visionary act of the mind</term> will exist alongside thinking. For the essence of the **Intellect** <note>original: νοῦς (Nous), the realm of pure, divine thought</note> and its contemplation is something more divine. Those things produced in this way are the result of contemplation. **Generation** <note>original: γένεσις (Genesis), the process of coming into being</note>, on the one hand, is like a form of necessity or judgment; yet if it is like a **Reason-principle** <term>Logos: The formative power that translates a higher idea into a physical form</term>, it still performs an action. 

Indeed, that which comes into being before the Reason-principle itself is weak, or merely a shadow of that Reason. If, therefore, "making" and contemplation are united in a single Reason-principle, then that which acts according to **Nature** <note>original: φύσις (Physis)</note> is also a form of contemplation. And if one were to say that the whole is according to this Nature, just as "making" exists prior to the Reason-principle, it would seem that Nature is many things in order to hold the Reason-principle within itself. Or perhaps it exists after the Reason-principle, as it truly is—though I know not from where. 

It follows later: how can "making" be anything at all if it is nothing in itself? And how can it be, if it does not possess sight? What, then, does it see within itself? It sees that which it holds according to its own being; or rather, it holds this within itself, derived from itself. This is how it exists. For if it is a kind of Form, and if that Form is not within it, why would it seem to grasp it? If it possesses something, it must be within itself; and thus it acts. 

Knowledge belongs to those alone; but indeed, if it appeared to have certain virtues that have come toward it, then even the future would be written there. But the Intellect is not merely the Good itself—not essentially—but it is also Mind. It is given to it, both in itself and not. Thus, what remains once again are the things directed toward it. And what is the witness of the internal? Perhaps it is the things now being thought by it; I know not how. 

If, again, the things following those should be; for where the whole from this is present to all. Truly, regarding these things and what follows them: if it is indeed in itself, then the next in order follows this. It was there. But Nature, again, is not found where there is a **serene Intellect** <note>original: γαληνὸς νοῦς; a state of perfect, undisturbed contemplation</note>. Yet this is clear to some, especially to the one who has reached it. But the things received within it have a certain persistence, neither of a specific quality nor in the same way, for they have come to be; nevertheless, hold fast to this. To each, a limit is set by how much is placed before it. Nor is it the body of anything else, but it might hold onto a phantom. It revealed other things it had taken; within it, therefore, many things exist easily. To exist is to hold many things. Either the following things are ordered within it, or that which was many came to be easily, and just as it was before it came into being. 

One who is ignorant does not know this at all. To such an extent, perhaps, of whatever kind it may be. For those who have pushed toward generation produce nothing on their own, or only from it. Because it is not total; for one does not exult in having received such a share of insolence. But I came into being according to analogy; and the things of that realm are near. Because they are true; for these things have stood firm within this. I have gone through this sufficiently. But as for the "where"...

<summary>Plotinus argues that "Nature" is not a blind force but a silent form of contemplation (Theoria) that creates by looking inward at its own Reason-principles (Logoi). He distinguishes between the higher, serene Intellect and the weaker, "shadowy" action of physical generation.</summary>
