...by thinking. Through these very things, the first of the sensible objects arise; though they do not exist in the same way. These things are clear. But people are ignorant of that from which each thing comes. Yet it is necessary to consider the first. If there is indeed something before all things, then it must be so. For it is itself [the source]; since all things exist, and those things which are its experiences. And indeed, that which is most truly itself is not something outside of itself. All things there are centered. That one is **before all things**. That which is even before the **Intellect** <term>Nous: The Divine Mind or second hypostasis, containing the archetypes of all things</term>. And it is so in its being. Or does it not act as the same? Not by **Reason** <term>Logos: The formative principle that organizes the cosmos</term> then, nor does it signify if it were the smallest of all things they see; but it is before all, as it might be named in its entirety; for I have said that it is many things. If nothing is divided from it as a whole before it is itself, then it is everything, or rather the **Good** <note>original: ἀγαθόν (Agathon). In Plotinus, the Good is another name for the One, the absolute source of value.</note>; or all is in that, or it is the Good. And these were also the Intellect. And this is likewise without its own **hypostasis** <term>Hypostasis: An underlying reality or distinct substance in the hierarchy of being</term>; but it is also **Essence** <note>original: οὐσία (Ousia)</note>; but the essence is of the Intellect. Or it is itself the cause. And all things above are all things indeed, but not there; rather, those things which are not before all, or which are coming into being. But the first is an emanation of it. But also the things in them and the things in it, are of them, yet that is in it. For as one might say, it is either all or it is not; it is sufficient then concerning the essence of the first things. But if he has said it himself. Either these things mentioned are not of it or of all, or this was its generation. As if increasing. This belongs to the Intellect and to not having forgotten, as if it has left itself behind; either the earth or before all things. And those things concerning the **Essential**; or that it is necessary, from which it is. The whole is either before all things, or by itself. But every **Love** <note>original: ἔρως (Eros), here referring to the soul's yearning for the source</note> they say is thus. Seeking the source. It is none of these things, which might be sufficient before them. Thus it is most truly that from which all things come. Or it must necessarily be that the source is without extension. To be above does not signify to each whatever happens to be there. But either everyone or this one of the others. By nature and by proximity to the **One** <note>original: τὸ ἕν (To Hen), the supreme, indivisible source of all reality</note>; from which, however, it is at a loss regarding the famous things there. Or even all. Just as the solitary joys with which there are the hypostases of the sense-organs. The hypostases are such as their own from which they are. While that itself remains. And it is not even that one from itself who is more happy than Ascandros. If indeed such things are so. In these things, that which is becoming. And that which is becoming. And so indeed it is either the things of that which is becoming or these things are said and spoken of. Either all is in it, the Intellect of the intelligible. For of itself, he has spoken of no essence among those according to it. Both it and again that which is made. For it is another thing. For again the things in it are not even of it when it is awake. And if also, either the cause or to explain this. Either the "again" then and the Intellect and that which exists in it as Intellect. The first things with it are all the works generated of the...

<column-break/>

...becoming. How then can it be divided? Is it because that which is from it, and again that which is of that, and of which the first things are. In general, also because its **hypostasis** <term>Hypostasis: The distinct reality or "subsistence" of a being</term> is directed toward that which is from it. And because what their essence ever is; but indeed also its own self-imparting. While it remains, there is something of the same, not a hypostasis. For from which another hypostasis again, or an essence of another standing below; that is everywhere; you might see it. And again this is indeed with that, and in that and through that, or all to complete its **activity** <note>original: ἐνέργεια (Energeia), the active expression of a thing's nature</note>. Not only was it so; and becoming; but also that which follows upon impulse. Or do we ask the cause of the first essences having shown them here, **as light from the sun**? <note>This is Plotinus's most famous analogy: just as the sun radiates light without losing its own substance, the One radiates the Intellect and the Soul without being diminished.</note> They come to be; it partakes and light is shown upon it, and let that which overlaps it be of it. To rule over it, and so also the other things; from it, or another light which follows after it. It will show it to be a servant, remaining and being such. For it is an offspring; which indeed follows all and is of all. It is given to all, whoever might receive it. It is for all; for it is so. But also nearer to itself. Since they come to be; because it is not different from those; the genera were seen; but since that one is entirely, and that, how it comes from that. Instead of being and saying that he is coming to be in it. For not in another alone. But neither is this of the Intellect; if indeed it were also toward it. But also by that which is from it. And toward it. Wherefore also first in truth. Because before it, what ever is this activity itself. And it is clear what sort it must be, for if to everyone the touch upon them is not itself; either that which knows, or by being seen they call him eyes; but by signifying to ourselves, but with him. Thus he himself is at a loss and whenever then of himself. What he said indeed was not only of him. The Intellect is for him. Of that one having been seen, because the things that have happened, either of a cause, or a state upon the essence. But the things becoming themselves from it, let it be known, or let it be known in them. Or the Intellect itself. But again the **father of the Intellect**. <note>Plotinus often refers to the One/the Good as the "father" of the Intellect (Nous).</note> And it must be from a genus, that the Intellect is for him there. Not to say however altogether the Intellect, and him being in that, and not needing again in the pole, whenever some from the Intellect. Because it is upon the Intellect of Intellect. To which it seems to be a cause; which indeed upon these things too far outside they were becoming, and because of this, it is so; so as to be above. Because of this, that or then and so, he would have said. And that which is again from him, is **divinity** <note>original: θεότης (Theotes)</note> in that one, such or such for him. And if anyone is entirely from whom, so also of himself. That one again having become this. (For these things). And again as the intelligible. For the intelligible again and of what cause it is. For both by the intelligible, and by the Intellect. And how it truly is.

<meta>Continuing from the discussion in Ennead V regarding the relationship between the One and the Intellect. This page moves into the nature of true Being and how the life of the universe is contained within the Intelligible realm, contrasting the "true" world of Forms with the "image" of the sensible world.</meta>

# Ennead V
### [On Intellect, Forms, and Being] <note>Original: Ἐννεάδ. ε. While the previous page discussed the Three Hypostases, the content here aligns with the later chapters of Ennead V, focusing on how the Intellect contains all real beings.</note>

Now, all things that seem to exist in that [intelligible] world are **true**. Whence it follows that to be and to exist are the same thing, or else nothing within that world would possess a true **subsistence** <term>hypostasis: the underlying reality or essential nature of a thing</term> in itself. These true things have fallen to us as an **image** <note>original: εἰκόνα (eikona). Plotinus views the physical world as a mere reflection or "image" of the higher, intelligible world.</note>. What then is required? For the being of a human is the being of all things; for all the life of the universe is contained there. And it is so for the **Father** <note>original: πατρί. In this context, likely referring to the Intellect or the One as the generative source.</note>, because he is nevertheless happy, and most especially because he possesses that which seems to be overflowing and has the greatest abundance of life. If, therefore, it is impossible not to say that it is in itself—and that it has thought in all things—then it is already likely that he is the **True One**. Because of this, he would not have life directed toward what follows, nor would he merely participate in **Being** <note>original: τοῦ εἶναι. He does not "have" being like an attribute; he is the source of it.</note>. And it is not entirely the case that all things would be him, but that he, being already all things there, might hold them through the principle of "all." Whence it did not seem to him to exist in the **essence** <note>original: οὐσίᾳ (ousia)</note> of each individual thing. At any rate, his true subsistence is such that he would be all things, and that he, possessing as much as possible, is disposed to be from that which is. And to that 

<margin>7.</margin> which is coming into being, he is disposed toward being. This has been said by us. Whence I also say to him that the **Reason-Principle** <term>Logos: the formative power that acts as a bridge between the Intellect and the physical world</term> governs that which is coming to be. It is clear that he says the "greater" thing. For they blame the reasoning of these same things and everything in the world, as if it were otherwise. And indeed, the world coming into being according to nature is struck by the fact that it does not come from [mere] existence, but not all things, only the **Forms** <note>original: εἴδη (eide). The eternal archetypes or blueprints of all physical things.</note>. I speak of that which is in him. For it seemed so. Now, however, it is necessary again—and he was prior—that all **creation** <note>original: κτίσις (ktisis)</note> was in him. This seems almost ridiculous to say. But immediately, the other point must be stated: that the multitude and all things coming into being are as worthy as the degree to which they possess more within the same. And that which is existing belongs to the creator and his **providence** <note>original: πρόνοιαν (pronoian). The divine care or plan that orders the universe.</note>. For it could not be that all the things the **Beautiful One** <note>original: ὁ καλός</note> ordained are not. And for those not reasoning in this way, thought exists only in part. Furthermore, they blame the greatest of goods because all visible things are only moderately good. The **divinity** <note>original: δαίμων (daimon). Here referring to a guiding spirit or divine power.</note> always governs that which is 

<margin>C.</margin> coming to be. If indeed someone is not entirely satisfied with what has been generated, it is because of this. But sometimes, as we said above, I have learned of children individually, and that life, or rather all things, somehow belong to him. For in the world, the one who boasts of beauty is a pretender. And indeed, that beauty belongs to the sensible world, but there [in the higher realm] it is a law for all. And indeed, this **Reason** is the genesis of it, for how could there be a world of the whole? But it is not that; it is truly as a world of the whole. For the things according to it [are there]. But from this, as the Great One [intended], for truly it is entirely from that which is coming to be. It is necessary to set this aside. If, then, the **One** is thus, as having the first...

<summary>Plotinus argues that the intelligible world contains the true essence and life of all things, asserting that our physical world is merely a reflection of these higher Forms. He defends divine providence by explaining that all things proceed from the Intellect and the "Beautiful One" according to a rational principle (Logos).</summary>

# Eusebius, Book V <note>original: Εὐσεβ· Ε·. This indicates the text is likely a citation from Plotinus found within Book 5 of Eusebius of Caesarea’s "Preparation for the Gospel."</note>

And for this reason, to the many, so that they might find a respite through them, there is also a **Reason-Principle** <term>Logos: the formative, rational force that emanates from the Intellect into the world</term> from him; and beside these very things, the exchanges are taken away. For each thing comes into being and is then taken away again; just as things occur again and again within the **Eternity** <term>Aeon: the realm of timeless, unchanging reality, as opposed to Chronos or linear time</term>, and the things concerning him come to be. But the Eternal is not such from itself, but because of that very one in whom we saw it to be, because it is **Good**. This, in turn, completes the book. Since even in the Eternal he names something greater than itself, where truly this exists for him, because it is in the same place. And again, this itself exists through the Eternal, because of its very **Being**; but also from that one, this Being is Good. And for this reason, he is the cause of all things and of life, but not of the passions. For to whom life belongs, there is life. And there is **Eternal Life** <note>original: ζωὴ αἰώνιος (zōē aiōnios). Plotinus distinguishes between the fleeting life of the body and the permanent life of the Spirit.</note>. And these things, indeed, are the kinds [genera] within this; for the Eternal is neither life nor is it directed toward these things; therefore, the Eternal is self-generated. And as for the seeking, one seeks in all things, but how is the **Cause** <term>Aition: the primary source or the One from which all existence flows</term> also in him? For it is through repetition; so that the Good is not merely in him. For if he were there, he said that he possesses life. And again, by taking what is in this, already the Good comes from him, so that he would not merely participate in **Goodness**. But that which exists remains the same. For the line of that one does not exist before this same thing. And the writing would not be for his own sake; since he is the thing itself, for nothing of him can live [separately]. For through this very thing he lives. It is greater than... For because of this, toward and around himself and the life of that which is in him, the greater is that in which he finds himself. Beside this; since this at least is something singular for those in him, because not everything is completed. That which is defined in itself is, I say, both unintelligible and indivisible. For indeed, things appear to be held in an indivisible manner. Not in himself. If, therefore, someone says that the **All** <note>original: πρῶτον πᾶν. The totality of the Intelligible world.</note> is first, and not in the [specific], let it not appear that he possesses everything. Since neither would the calculation of the Good [hold]; but rather its opposite. But it is a certain Good. I speak of those things which are with him. And that this man might be deemed worthy to be saved. Just as **Happiness** <term>Eudaimon: a state of flourishing or well-being achieved through alignment with the Divine</term> is to him. And because each part of him thus participates and he praises the father of someone. Therefore, each of the two. The father himself and each let them be. But how shall each nature be beautiful? That nature is necessary to all of him, and it again is both the **Essence** <term>Ousia: true substance or being</term> and the honor; and the same is not life. But all of this, it is not itself. Are those who speak of the unspeakable fighting back? Or is it not that they are poor? For he learned, he would not say to us: "Become the ancient things around him," but in no way is it reasonable. For us, there is much that exists, or he practices the image concerning the great Eternity. These things indeed for us in...

<column-break/>

...it may be said, let them be obedient to him. He begets. Who then, having looked upon such **impiety** <note>original: ἀσέβειαν (asebeian). This likely refers to the Gnostic or materialist views that Plotinus and later Eusebius argued against.</note>, would not marvel? Or in all the lawless things in which they are not toward him, so that he might appear healthy; for the same thing belongs to the **daemonic** <term>daimonion: a spirit or intermediary power, neither fully divine nor fully human</term>. Since the souls of those people are also causes, to receive from him. But whenever they are greater. Just as the same thing, through the voice of those people, is virtue and law and benefit. For we were showing that as the same thing will be again, on the one hand, the image, but also that life might be loved. And I said how you will not recognize him in this, in no way as they are to themselves, which appears to be the **fountain of the good**. For to this one, the first Good is hope. And to think that some things come to be, so that also whenever the **Divine** <note>original: τὸ θεῖον. The higher reality or the One.</note> overshadows someone, there is life; and being of no one, he would desire. Worthy of prayer, the highest itself. And of friendship. For it comes. And the **End** <term>Telos: the ultimate goal or purpose of existence</term> is a greater honor, and truly that one's voice. And therefore it comes to be itself because of being more to those who are otherwise; how could this come to be, from whence all things come?

### ->CONCERNING THE ORACLES AMONG THEM WHICH THEY THEMSELVES DID NOT ACCEPT<-

These things which we say are therefore **unspeakable** and **unintelligible**, yet they are true. For one must not despair because of the mediation of words. And thus to create the **shadows and types** <note>Plotinus often uses "shadows" (skias) to describe the physical world's relationship to the Intelligible Forms.</note> within him which is called the Good. For it is both in him and in the **Form** <term>Eidos: the ideal pattern or archetype of a thing</term>. And we would say this first: for it is the earth. For even toward the paternal things... not being carried toward the paternal. And again, that which this man himself... or power. Not in this way; but it is therefore, because indeed. Insofar as he [possessed] all things from which he is. On the one hand this, and **knowledge** <term>episteme: certain, scientific knowledge of the Forms</term>. But that in which we said he has been seen. And not even of these things does he say he possesses them in a complex way. And not this one. It is indeed, but since they are signified in opposition, the first thing; and of this, of all things. For one must not act, if this is the cause. And that which is not, but rather, with whom he himself might be spoken of, this belongs to those. But that which has become, did not stand in one place. But not such a thing, in that which is from him. For also to those saying how. And in what kind it is, because the common thing has been said. For when the **body** <note>original: σῶμα (soma). Plotinus views the body as a temporary vessel for the soul.</note> comes into being, it is non-existent. And not itself. It would come to be. Let one not think it exists. But until it does not, this in turn is out of the body. But if again something, after persuasion, they say if there is disobedience. He who is persuaded has no evil. To do it himself. And the thing having happened. For indeed not of each thing entirely not. And not from such a thing. But he acts concerning this. Since also to be present. And in the body...

<meta>This page continues the exploration of Neoplatonic emanation. Having previously discussed the Intellect's relationship to Being, Plotinus now turns to the mechanics of how the higher "First" (the One) generates the "Second" (the Intellect) and how Matter eventually arises at the periphery of existence. This text contains fragments from what are known as Enneads V.2 and V.5.</meta>

# Ennead V

Or how, and in what manner, does **Matter** <gloss>original: tēs hylēn</gloss> proceed from Him? It is as if it were necessary for Him to produce it without Him being changed himself. For it is not possible to know how He might become the cause because of this. But He is, as it were, impassive in all things. And such a thing existed previously, or before the entirety of the most causal existence, she herself being a light poured out everywhere. And that which comes to be immediately from that [First] is greater, as if we remain from Him; for we are within **Contemplation** <term>Theoria: the act of vision or mental looking by which a lower reality derives its being from a higher one</term>. Yet it is not according to each individual living creature. Nor are these things merely according to nature; and not toward the opposite. But if that one is truly there, it is before the act of thought. And what He sent forth was good: the sensible world. Thus, there are ancestors of Himself; or as it were He himself, or all things in potential. For how does it have the "but"? Or what is the "but"? It is for that one to come into being. But it might have something; in other things they shape the **Substances** <term>Hypostasies: the fundamental levels of reality, such as the One, the Intellect, and the Soul</term>. Because it is necessary, it is not; but something of the gods is always coming into being. For if it is becoming, it is not necessary; if on one hand toward the "but" or becoming; if anyone should think of it. Since it is not yet sufficient that it thinks itself—that is, the act of contemplating—and not the things after it. It would be similar to how we might say the "but." And the "but" having come into being by Him, from the Unchanging. The cause of Being is the power, and from that [power] only what is comes into being. Furthermore, it is before what belongs to each. For either as if setting aside the cause; or it might come to be, for Him to endure as if toward the act of seeing. That which indeed shall subsist.

---

<margin>2</margin>
### How that which comes after the First comes from the First, and concerning the One.

---

Therefore, by a certain form; as if he even saw that form. And the **Form** <term>Eidos: the intelligible pattern or "blueprint" of a thing</term> is the things that are rooted in the One; for this truly is. But before it, it is pulled away. And life is in embryos, as a certain something illuminated by a fertile portion. For the All is a manifestation of the **Intelligible** <term>Noēton: the world of pure ideas that the mind perceives</term>; but since it exists because of Him. And that is either with it or after it as an intelligible; but it exists before the "and" and the intelligible Being. To be ignorant of oneself is greater. But it is within us, as knowledge is also before that. But if because of this he knows, let us not proceed as if knowing about each thing; but to think Him; in this way knowing; or because He himself makes all thought. And it belongs to the sensible things; since even the same thing; because even his good is himself. Neither is life Himself, who is His own offspring. Here, in this way, are the intelligibles. He seeks to become that one of his own, the "but" might become impassive. So that not even especially or because; but a participation in Him in one's own, as if of Him toward the becoming to have become. And especially the All. Since therefore there is a solitary **Substantial Reality** <term>Hypostasis: a distinct, existing nature</term>. That which, becoming, might become eternal; the **Essence** <term>Ousia: the "beingness" or true nature of a thing</term> might become before itself, as if it were a wonder, for it is before. The peak, as it were, is that which is upon Him; a certain contemplation of that very one. But that very thing is always participated in here; and because it is placed; so that even that which you endure. But if it is not placed itself...

<column-break/>

<page-num>164</page-num>
<header>Ennead V</header>

<margin>6</margin>
If one should say "once"; either speaking it, or He instilled it once in the one who experienced it, lest it ever be outside of Him. As if the Intelligible were to be. And if there is any benefit from those after Him. Or rather, in this way they come to be again. For if the Intelligible is outside, he knows that thing without possessing it. And that it is necessary to have seen it. Since it is not the case that if he thinks, he does not exist in the act of thinking it; from the contemplation of the Intelligible he held knowledge, or contemplation. For never was it a substance, nor is it possible for each of them not to be, it is not necessary. But it is truly something else; and altogether toward things that are not themselves. Since I would not be able to speak to all others, there is silence for all. But if one should say "all things," from whence all things came, the things that are will surely be; all things are, and all things are one. Or it is equal to all, whatever one might think; however it may be; and what of it? The One? Or the "not-one"? For if indeed the Intelligible belonged to each of them, it would not have it. And how of Him, supposing? Or because the alien nature is such? Or indeed still of them. Since even not seeing the alien thing is not to know.

---

### That the Intelligibles are not outside the Intellect, and concerning the Good.

<margin>7</margin>
The **Intellect** <term>Nous: the Divine Mind, which contains all truth and forms</term>, the true Intellect which truly exists—would anyone claim that it is deceived? And that it is ignorant of the things that are? But if not even this, but if it is necessary to possess virtue in being truthful, it is necessary to remain in the act of thinking. But for the one in the act of thinking, there would be no being deceived, nor ambiguity; nor would he, as it were, deny error. Oh, to have proofs of all things! For if someone should say some proofs, being at a loss himself, he might possess some whole. He says that all things are entirely. For how indeed is it possible? For the things in the "but," these things and others, or to concede to them, how will they say that knowledge or contemplation is a stone? And how is there faith for him that the Intelligibles are thus? Since the things within are to be grasped, or let the Intelligibles be to inhabit entirely one's own. Security, lest we ever suppose otherwise than this; we know, therefore, that in the last things there will be **Matter** <term>Hyle: the bottom-most level of the universe, representing lack of form</term>. But in the Intellect, in relation to the things in it, there will be knowing. For there is a certain endurance of sensible things. And senses for all things of which he says, is it not to be thought of? But the **Image** <term>Eidolon: a reflection or shadow of the higher reality</term> is in that which they do there, or to perceive is to receive. For not even again an image if we know. Or to know, to know, because of being such as the things that come to be, again (as if) to him. For thus indeed; he himself then and not knowing, or altogether he does not exist.

<summary>Plotinus explores how the Intellect and Matter emanate from the One, arguing that the "Intelligibles" (the true objects of thought) must exist inside the Intellect itself rather than as external objects. This internal unity is what guarantees the truth and certainty of divine knowledge, contrasting it with the fading "images" found in the physical world.</summary>

Certainly, even this: that "to be" is also this magnitude. How it might come from this, let it be. Or if it were such, they are consumed because of that one. So that not only the mortal and life; but so that even before this, those who speak of the things of nature well. <summary>In this passage, Plotinus examines the nature of "free will" and "self-mastery" in relation to the One, arguing that the First Principle is not subject to chance or external necessity but exists "as it ought to be." He contrasts human autonomy and the fleeting joy of festivals with the absolute, self-contained existence of the Divine.</summary>

## Enneads, Book 6

It was alone, or rather, the Intellect was within them. Nevertheless, it is not that same thing again, nor does it arise solely from its own **contemplation** <note>original: "θεωρίας" (theorias) — refers to a deep, intellectual vision or spiritual looking.</note>, but rather from the radiance of that higher principle. Thus, because of that radiance, it no longer exists as it was. At that moment, being unable to look upon it directly, it took on a **substantial existence** <term>hypostasis (a distinct reality or "standing under")</term>, which, possessing its own movement, both knows and sees. For as it holds second place to that source, it is established through its contact with the divine Intellect, not knowing all that it is capable of receiving into its own existence. Because of this, it shares in all things while being entirely none of them. In this way, it is not to be counted among all beings. For it was so even before, or rather, in knowing them, it knows them all in this way: the Intellect knows them within itself. For it speaks of things that come from God; for of God himself, there is not even "knowledge" in the ordinary sense. In that which is truly God, there is something else. And this seems to be the case because the specific nature is the cause of its power. So it is reasonable.

But since he says the Good consists in **thinking** <note>Plotinus is likely critiquing or refining Aristotle's view of the "unmoved mover" as "thought thinking itself."</note>, it does not follow that it comes from the Intelligible realm. Rather, because of the Good itself, which is its cause, it exists in that way. The Intellect is the cause of it. For he speaks of the Intelligible; for that which is like the Good in the Intelligible is the "Good-form." And this is not just "God" in some general way or belonging to another, but is like the light of our own nature shining within us. In this state, it is necessary to be within it, and this will be more so because it is especially within God, just as it is in the heavens. Since it is so, those things in the Intelligible realm are even more present. Furthermore, never can it be without a cause from which it comes. For one is ignorant when they are "unthinking." This is how it gets its name. One escapes oneself toward another. And it is not a matter of necessity that it is not voiced. But that which is "beyond-touch" appears again. Because of this, it is worthy of all things.

<margin>6</margin>
...distinguished in relation to the sun. Within the plane of the Intellect, it is already like a flame; having become part of these things, it exists in such a state. It knows the source not merely by how much light it possesses, but because it has grasped its own **cause** <note>original: "αἰτίαν" (aitian) — the foundational reason or origin of a thing's being.</note>. It is through this that it sees what has been revealed. Which is no longer merely light, but is in the "heavens" of that realm, just as it is in man. What then? Is it not the essence of something? For it is that very thing in which it resides. But if it exists in another, it is that which comes from the source. It is possible to seek this again: all that is transcendent (it seems necessary—being its own cause. But that which is with God is separate) regarding itself. You are aware of the act of **thinking** <note>original: "νοεῖν" (noein) — the activity of the Intellect.</note>. But what is that very thing—to know and to be wise—insofar as it thinks? Is it only essence? Or is it that it moves primarily within the Intelligible? It seems it was not formed by itself, but through those things. And the Intellect...

Regarding how it is the Intelligible and how it did not depart from being so, we have spoken in those other places. Or rather, **desire** <note>original: "ἔφεσις" (ephesis) — a fundamental striving or "reaching out" that Plotinus identifies as the bridge between the One and the Intellect.</note> generated thought and gave it its foundation. For the desire for sight became **thought** <term>noesis (the act of intellectual intuition)</term>; and the Good is that which it desires. It must be as it is: the Good became the "object of thought" <note>original: "νοητὸν" (noeton)</note> for it, so that the Good would not merely exist before the act of thinking. For if it were so, it would exist even before the Good. But if the Good and that which it reaches for are the same, it is for the sake of thinking the Good; and the Good is present. This would be **happiness** <note>original: "εὐδαιμονία" (eudaimonia) — the state of flourishing or supreme well-being found in union with the divine.</term>. And the act of thinking its own intelligible object belongs to it, as does that which it reaches for. For it thinks by looking through the Good, starting from the Intellect and acting upon itself as Intellect. But insofar as it desires the Good, it acts according to the Good. If indeed these things are said correctly, perhaps in some necessity a world was born, which is the Good.

But they say the Intelligible is the Good. Yet if we say the Intelligible is the Good in this way—if knowing it and being known are the same thing—then the First would not be the Good. But if it is as has been said, the Intelligible is there, so that thinking is there as well. Or indeed, both of the other things are there, but the First itself shall be this alone. Thus, even this might pass away. Or were these things not also stated? For this **Intellect** <term>Nous (the Divine Mind)</term>, which is secondary, thought itself. But it thinks the Intelligible; yet that which comes from it is Intellect. Therefore, that which is not thought becomes the "thinking subject." This "thinking subject" is the Intellect that comes from the First. Since it must be equal to the Intelligible, as is necessary, how could we allow it to not perceive? For its nature falls short by being "this way and that." For the Intelligible according to it is this very thing, and it is perceived by itself. Not only because that First is intelligible to the Intelligible, but also the things that come from it, insofar as it reaches them. For those things there are within the act of thinking, and exist through the act of thinking. But most of all, it is because the desire for Being gave birth to them. For the act of thinking made beings radiant, and revealed both **Being** and **Essence** <term>ousia (substance or true being)</term>. Being full of it, and being full in the way that it is, the Intelligible is like a **sun** <note>Plotinus frequently uses the sun as a metaphor for the Good/The One, which illuminates all things without being diminished itself.</note> from which it shines. Together, the Intellect—for I do not know what the other things are—is near. It is very near. The Intellect is near. But how could the **Soul** <term>Psyche (the third level of reality)</term> itself come to be from it? It is what it thinks. And that which comes from there is like a fire, even if it is not yet the Intellect. They are like coins and images of it. Thus, it came to be; perhaps it was the desire by which the Whole was generated.

<column-break/>

The Intellect [turned] toward itself, as if seeing these things from the One, or as possessing what the One has. And because it has been said that it is the "second" <note>Plotinus refers to the Intellect as the "Second God" or "Second Hypostasis," following the One.</note>, and the Good is like the "other." Everything is not present in the same way, because of the same contacts, and those contacts are near.

<margin>·2·</margin>
-> **How that which follows the simple One comes from it, and what those things are.** <-

If the One is all things individually, and yet is not any one of them—for it is the principle of all—it is not those things, but rather those things are "all" in that way. There, they exist in that manner. For it is not the "All," but prior to the "All." For the "All" exists in such a way that it is to be held in awe. Insofar as the whole Soul comes from the Intellect, and all things are in the "Second" <note>The Intellect.</note>, the Soul itself flows from the source. **Socrates** <note>A reference to Plato's dialogues, which Plotinus interprets as the foundation of his philosophy.</note> asks somewhere—as do others—if the One is all things individually. The spring does not have motion in its streams while being the First, for everything is within it, not having gone out as it was defined by the **Logos** <term>the formative or rational principle</term> and its outward-facing nature. If, then, the Intellect acts by a single power, it is because all things are within it. And everything that comes out from it—such as it is—everything is within it, so that in the Logos they are not separated, yet the things within it are distinct from one another, though not separated in the same way. It is like the Logos that comes from a single **seed** <note>original: "σπέρματι" (spermati) — Plotinus uses the biological metaphor of the "seed" to explain how complex life is contained potentially within a simple source.</note>. For each part was in the whole, their powers; and again, in these powers, each was not separated. Hence, the All is one within it. But indeed, the All [is there]. For the one is not the Logos and the Intellect, but the Intellect is the way the All was generated. And as for the unspoken Logos of the Soul that I was mentioning: the Soul is the Logos of the Intellect, and a certain activity of it, just as the Intellect is the activity of the One. For everything that comes from it is different from it, and the one turns toward those things there. The Intellect is that Logos, because it would not be Intellect otherwise. But also the Intellect, in the way that it is something of that First, turns toward itself and primarily toward that which is from there. So that it would not be Intellect otherwise. For nothing is such as it is, and all the Intellect is insofar as it is in it. For everything is from it; such as it is, the All is as it exists in the Logos. And its power extends exceedingly over all things. But that First is not "all." Yet all things are from it, so that it would not be Intellect. It is in the whole, or rather, it is as if it were not that; but it is not.

# Ennead V

### Page 172

**Ennead V, Tractate 7** (continued)

...pours forth, what the differences are. Since the soul itself is different, it would possess the **formative principles** <term>logoi (the rational, creative blueprints that shape matter)</term> from itself which are no less productive. Since these principles are also in the seeds—though the seeds are merely the starting point, as it were, for the matter—and the things belonging to the matter are mixed, as it were, they are productive as a whole. It is unlikely that the principles are different [merely by chance]. Or, perhaps, things that are born, such as those born in a single labor <note>Referring to twins or multiple births from one pregnancy.</note>—yet they are not the principles themselves, along with which the differences were seen appearing. Or nothing hinders any of the wholes from coming into being, even before they actually occur. It was necessary that all things exist through themselves, not according to how they might happen to be. In [the Intellect] it does not matter that all things are in equality, nor again that there are many souls differing by nature in their principles. If there are pairs—why then would there be many, unless they are not perfectly modeled on the **Form** <term>eidos (the eternal, perfect archetype)</term>? But rather, these are like the **paradigms** <note>original: "παραδείγματα" (paradeigmata) — the perfect divine templates</note>, or as many as are the same, or as many as the underlying subjects differ, or are different. For if the things in matter are many, then they have their shapes in their own habits. And how could he differ regarding all things in general? For the craftsman does not do this to himself, but rather takes a principle from himself and makes other things like it, even if these are not again the same as the art itself. But if by nature—and they come from reasoning and intellect, yet a reasoning different from ours—for that is how things are in that which is different. How then does one grasp the difference? By himself. If the soul of the whole had the principle of what it produces, it would be the principle itself. If through one soul, whichever one might heal <note>original: "ἰατρήσῃ" (iatrese) — possibly a corruption in the transcription or a metaphor for "ordering" or "restoring" matter.</note>. Therefore, it is necessary that the number of principles be defined and harmonized. For the soul does not find the end of everything, or rather its soul does; but whenever it enters into a human, it does not always produce the same thing again, but each according to its own principle. It would be necessary for the same formative principles to be applied to the same living beings whose essence comes into being. Or the movement of those in the same [cycles] towards the same [results], while the soul possesses all things. # On Intelligible Beauty: 8
<margin>Volume 5</margin>

Since we say that the one who dwells in the **intelligible world** <term>kosmos noetos (the realm of pure thought and forms)</term> and the true Idea there is beauty, we must examine this. For if there are intelligible gods, and if we grasp the examples of the Form in contemplation, let us try to see if that beauty is still in the art itself—if it is possible to speak of such things—and not just through the art. Let there be two masses of stone lying in the same place, one beside the other: one is unworked and possesses the nature of stone in its raw state, but the other

<column-break/>

has been finished by the art of man in the middle, and already possesses the image of a form—perhaps of a god, such as a Grace or some hero, or even of some god—but also of himself and of everything. If it should happen, having appeared from the art, it has become beauty, though not from the stone itself, for that would appear most beautiful. For it is not the fact of being stone that is the underlying subject, but rather that from which the form entered. Therefore, the stone did not have the form before it arrived; rather, the form exists in the one who conceived it. It was in him, not insofar as he had eyes or hands, but because he participated in the art. In the art, then, this beauty was much greater; for it was not that which was in the art that entered into the stone—rather, the art remains, and another lesser version comes from it. And even that does not remain pure in the art, nor exactly as the artist wished, but only as the stone yielded to the art.

But if anyone dishonors the arts because they produce by imitating nature, first it must be said that natures also imitate other things. Next, one must know that they do not simply imitate what is seen, but they run back to the **formative principles** <note>original: "λόγους" (logous)</note> from which nature itself derives. Furthermore, they produce many things from themselves; and where something is lacking, they add to it, since they possess beauty. For even **Phidias** <note>The most famous sculptor of Classical Greece (c. 480–430 BC), known for the Statue of Zeus at Olympia.</note> did not make his **Zeus** according to any visible thing, but as Zeus might be if he chose to appear to our eyes. But let the arts be set aside for the present. As for those whose works are called imitations, nature itself contemplates and produces, which we say is a nature that imitates other things. Thus we might say that she herself is the one who possesses what she imitates, leaving it to another to sit there upon the intelligible. Because that which produces is bodily; it possesses beauty, but it is not the most beautiful, since it is only a potentiality of that other beauty. But nature, through its relation to thought, is itself the fruit of what it might become, or that which was before it, from which it was held to appear. This will be stated more clearly elsewhere. Concerning the things of the intelligible, nature itself has come to be and exists by sight alone, just as it is. And one must say that these things are without speech, producing what it possesses as an imitation of itself. As many things as they produce towards themselves or each other are not equal, and that which is in matter, so that it might finish what it wished. Thus it became so by power. For whatever greatness one might see in it, it comes from that [higher source]. It possesses it, and there something is coming to be; or as the first Intellect of all does not know. But one must receive what is sought by these reasonings, and that it is not possible to properly assign causes for particular things; but rather that which belongs to **Aphrodite** <note>Used here as a personification of beauty itself.</note> herself. For indeed, from the whole, she is beautiful and worthy of that which is sudden.

Plotinus argues that beauty in art comes from the artist's participation in divine "Forms" rather than simple imitation of the physical world, citing Phidias's statue of Zeus as the prime example.</summary>

If there is a sun, and if there is fate, it is the activity of God. The uniqueness of the Blessed One and of the All is sufficient for this. # Ethics, Book 5

### Page 174

It comes to be by and of itself; but that man <note>likely referring to Plato or Aristotle</note> also said that the sensations which arise within it are more active. The powers of sensation are not all derived from us, so it appears that they arise only from external impressions, as a starting point. For why should the genera <note>the fundamental types or categories of being</note> themselves not be poured out? In this way, they exist within nature. It would belong to these [genera] to bear that nature, while others exist by nature. If all things were so—but they are not all so. It follows then that to be something by nature is a visible thing, which is what we call **philosophy**. **Prudence** <term>phronesis (practical wisdom or the ability to act rightly in specific situations)</term>, however, is concerned with external things. It is impossible for it to be the same as **Wisdom** <term>sophia (contemplative or theoretical wisdom regarding eternal truths)</term>; for wisdom itself is an inquiry. As a true inquiry, it is wisdom. In its actualization, it is an inquiry that is full and complete. Thus, the preparatory inquiries <note>original: "προ-φι," likely "προφιλοσοφήματα" or "προχειριζόμεναι"</note> are inquiries in truth. Therefore, there will be certain wisdoms that hold together and end in wisdom—those which we call inquiries. But not all things use wisdom; inquiry is the response. Which of the two is a mixture? It is not a true mixture when things are mingled. For some underlying things, which are spoken of poorly, might be said to be so. Or those things which were deceived into attaining wisdom itself, which was a certain good when it came to be. But it is not so. Therefore, toward these things, it is possible to hold the same view. So that, because of the cause and wisdom—if indeed the thing itself—

# Ethics, Book 5

### Page 175

-> Ethics, Book 5 – 33 <-

It has been stated, then, how the living being must perceive, and also how it perceives through each of the individual senses—what kind of **perceptible object** <term>aistheton (the object of sense perception)</term> each sense apprehends. Furthermore, we have discussed the **common sensibles** <note>These are qualities like shape or motion that are not limited to one sense (like color is to sight) but can be felt by many.</note>, such as motion and magnitude, which every sense perceives. However, **time** is not a perceptible object in itself, for all perception occurs within time. It has been argued by some that every sensation is indivisible from the others, but this is not well said. Moreover, regarding the idea that the "Whole" experiences sensation, one must say that sensation belongs to nothing other than the **sense organ** <term>aistheterion (the physical body part used for sensing)</term>. Furthermore, these indivisible sensations differ from the processes within the sense organ itself. Yet, it is also true that these sensations exist where the sense organ is located. The **impressions** <term>pathemata (passions or experiences of the soul caused by external stimuli)</term> fall upon the sense organs, but the impressions and the perceptible objects are not the same thing. Therefore, the impressions are not located purely within the sense organ, because perceptible objects are perceived *through* the sense organ. Furthermore, regarding the source of these impressions in the sense organ: while it is not necessary for the impressions to exist permanently, the perceptible objects must exist. Because the sense organ is a unified thing, it follows that the sensation, the things within the sense organ, the objects perceived, and the resulting impressions must also be treated as a unified whole. Since activities occur in time, but perceptible objects occupy space, it is necessary for perceptible objects to exist in time as well. For example, if a certain sensation is tied to a sense organ, the object of that perception exists in the "now." The impressions are also perceived in the present moment. It is not necessarily the case that the perceptible objects reside within the organ, though the impressions do. This is not entirely true; rather, the impressions reside in the **imagination** <term>phantasia (the faculty that holds images or "phantasms" of things perceived)</term> as if they were in the sense organ. These things have now been stated. Having first spoken about the sense organs and the objects of perception, it follows that we must speak about **memory** and the act of **remembering**.

<meta>catchword: Of what things</meta>

<column-break/>

We must state of what things memory consists. For it is surely not of things to come—that is the domain of **hope** <note>original: "elpis"</note>—but memory is of things that have already happened. Nor is it of things present, for that is the domain of **perception**. By perception, we know neither the future nor the past, but only the present. Therefore, there is no scientific knowledge <note>original: "episteme"</note> of the past, only of perception, as was said in the treatise *On the Soul*. For scientific knowledge is of the **universal**, while perception is of the **particular**. It is clear, then, of what things memory consists: for it is impossible to perceive even the present or the future without time. This is stated so that memory is not mistaken for scientific knowledge. Memory is not of the present, but of a specific time; it is not of that which is known in the present, but of that which is marked by time. Therefore, none of the animals that lack a sense of time are capable of memory—such as **insects** and whatever else does not perceive time. Since it has been said in the treatise *On the Soul* that the imagination is a kind of "weak sensation" (for it does not arise by itself, but through perception), it is clear that memory belongs to the **primary faculty of sensation**, and not to the **intellect** <term>noetikon (the faculty of rational thought)</term>. For memory does not exist without an image. Memory belongs essentially to the primary sensory faculty, and only "by accident" to the intellect. This is why we say some other animals remember, and not only humans; for we do not claim that these animals possess intellect. If memory belonged only to the intellectual faculties, it would not belong to other animals. Yet we see many other animals remembering, such as **dogs** and **horses** and such creatures. Therefore, memory cannot belong to the intellectual faculties alone. What remembering is, and how it occurs, has been stated: memory is like the **settling of a certain image**. <margin>Note this</margin> Therefore, to remember is nothing other than to possess an image. This is also clear from the images that appear in **dreams**. For we do not see then with our physical sense organs, but in the imagination. Furthermore, if one contemplates immaterial things and remembers them, it is not without an image; hence remembering is both intellectual and concerns the image itself, which is an activity. This is why some speak of "time-keeping" and the "impressions of death"; for while some things are contrary, a well-trained mind understands them well. Furthermore, remembering is the capacity of the intellect to receive an image. This is especially true of all things in dreams, and the imagination's own images; all these things can occur. How this is so has been explained to them. Thus, the matters concerning these things have been stated.

<summary>Plotinus (paraphrasing Aristotelian thought) explores the mechanics of perception, distinguishing between the sense organ, the external object, and the internal impression. He concludes that memory is a function of the sensory imagination (phantasia) rather than the pure intellect, as evidenced by the fact that animals like dogs and horses can remember.</summary>

...under our own specific cause, whether it be an accidental attribute or not; but the first and the absolute last, and every cause. By a new application of thought, let us see all things again: the **Intellect** <term>Nous (the divine or higher mind)</term> wandering within us, as if in darkness, led toward those things which the discourse said were cast off long ago. These are the primary causes from which the non-causes arise; it is as if we are observing a single dialogue—not the original philosophical one, as someone once said while looking on, but that same Intellect forced out of its own bodies. But we do not refer back to this, nor does the primary genus of the **Soul** <term>Psyche (the life-force that mediates between Mind and Matter)</term> lie there. The matter of faith belongs not to reason, where, conversely, we have not overstepped both the offspring of the soul and the causes. Yet again, we must consider the first principle, to the extent that we are able to use it. Plato is among us, seeing in this way, as Paul says <note>Original: "πλάτων παρ' ἡμῖν... ὡς λέγει παῦλος" — This suggests a late-antique or Byzantine synthesis where Platonic philosophy and the Epistles of St. Paul are harmonized</note>; for it is not merely some specific thing, but the whole that is referred back. Since these things are loosened [from their source], they are no longer each of these things individually, but things loosened from within. Or so it seems. This is just as with bodies; one might call the lack of it **Matter** <term>Hyle (the raw, formless potentiality of the physical world)</term>, but they would have **Form** <term>Morphe (the organizing principle that gives matter identity)</term> as a cause, rather than being the cause itself. And it does not even offer a hint. To speak of it as one in itself, never but through ambitions. What then must be hypothesized? They consider this a wandering of their own. But how should one posit a certain form as a cause for the things under it? What then? Are the Soul and the **One** <term>To Hen (the ultimate, indivisible source of all reality)</term> the primary things? And why? Because for us, things exist for a purpose; or rather, there is a "purpose" as such. It is clear then from us and from the soul. But if he who reveals the soul to them, or as much as he is himself, and to all the many things, again to all that it is truth. Plato from Paul <note>The scribe appears to be drawing a direct lineage or comparison between the two</note>. If again it is not necessary in the same place, then it is entirely so. Either simply as private things. For, being present toward the cause, they are persuaded by him in the matters sent to the talents among them. For we do not cast this mostly into the offspring. Nor are they persuaded in this way. In this, neither these things—as he says, the discourse is perhaps correcting them—it is not so, but that which is confirmed before the genera, and the Intellect is for all their own things, because it is not receptive to these. Let us see the discourse as the genera, in that which is in all things. These things are worthy to be distinguished in the hands as a whole, especially in those things which Paul said. In the essences and in being present, this is his own nature of being. But not in the fields of the seven. By position, the things said to be, and the things spoken. We saw of him that in all things the genera are specifically each thing, which hold nature together. These are specific and distinct, some more than others. And again, our [reason] being corrected. Concerning the present cause, but in itself. It is necessary for all, for all, each of these causes, or it seems to see the wandering of souls. And again...

### Eusebius, Book 15
<page-num>178</page-num>

Bodies, then, and their productions, seem to tend toward that which is lower, and are dissolved into the elements from which they were joined together; just as a house is dissolved into wood and stones. It understands, if the rest follows. By bringing out the matter of the body toward the creation of form in matter. For even if the change happens from one to another, the **Matter** <term>Hyle</term> underlies each thing. We are also seeking the **Soul** <term>Psyche</term>. Whether it is of our bodies, or whether the same principle exists, as a certain thing, or as a **Form** <term>Eidos</term>, just like that which is in bronze. Since, like a mold in bronze is the shape. I know what kind of shape he means when he speaks of making it from bronze. The remaining things are according to what is in that which has been participated in; they vanish and are no longer, since in this way he positions us. I said, the form following the rest, either as specific or as a whole. Body—that which is essence, which is also the soul. These things are not of a single form, being made from certain things. This is in the soul. For the soul and the intellect have their origin. Of the forms of the cosmos, it has its own, and of this the Intellect of the living and the Reason of the Intellect have come to be; they did not set themselves as souls and everything before, that which I said immediately: the **Intelligible things** <term>Noeta (realities accessible only to the mind, not the senses)</term>, both that and the form. For the one who receives the form of the forms. For these are not all things; themselves, and the things before. The things in her are not body; they are near even if they are through the soul. But that which is not a body, is so either otherwise or according to the form. But not toward the cause. And the Intellect is immobility. It is not by position. Either that too of the soul is the same and let it be moved. That which is fitting, by nature a field. Or all that they think, for toward the birth according to which. From where now there would be the act of reasoning, or rather immediately and necessarily, it is thus. That which is before matter does not receive [form], and again it is in the genus. Because of this, the field is helped to become, and it is made. He said. Their things, becoming thus. Having been born, not for all of those things generated, a cause concerning the essence. Those things which he saw pierced through them entirely. That which is in matter is all alike, but different. By the cause, he shapes it for each. And the soul is not in them. For they are not holy themselves. Or again, leaving behind the things of bronze, or he saw the things of the soul. That which is not in the soul, nor again in that which is as if being, and this soul being the things that are. Nor if it is able, that which is in it, either to be, or it will certainly say afterwards. As reasons having themselves, they will not leave behind the same things. And because Intellect and Soul are the things before, so that before what he said is the birth of the cause; that the Intellect also uses, being questioned by the being, and the power. But rather that which he saw to have is not receptive. To become.

The text is notable for its explicit attempt to harmonize Platonic philosophy with the teachings of the Apostle Paul, likely within the context of Eusebius's "Praeparatio Evangelica."</summary>

...acting as another and becoming centered around it; rather, it comes from that which is there <note>Plotinus frequently uses "there" (ekei) to refer to the higher, intelligible realm of divine forms, as opposed to "here" in the physical world.</note>, which is also what this is. And if 
<margin>it will appear</margin> all things should be entirely so. Or indeed even through that which is there, it is there for all. This is what has been discovered by that **Intellect** <term>Nous (the divine Mind)</term>. And it finds rest. Because it does not look toward a single thing, but toward its own self and its own **being** <term>Einai (the state of existence or essence)</term>, this is its very **becoming** <term>Genesis (here meaning its eternal emanation or origin, not a temporal birth)</term>. And becoming is within it. But if it does not see, he says, it is the cause of all by releasing them. Or if it should see, it acts, just as the whole does. But if not, or as many **images** <term>eidola (reflections or shadows of higher reality)</term> as it carries in the soul. For these things leave me. Whether rightly or not. It seems to be in the manner of the intellect. For it does not already need the present, when it is itself. But this is the intelligible and the cause. He himself leads every soul along the path. He says, therefore, that which comes from the intellect is there, if indeed it saw itself. Or every breath is that which it is itself. If the things that come to be are divided, as it seems, then it is in this way. And concerning their errors; for from where they come, they are their own. Or the whole remains in the same place. Not by will, but by nature and by **reason** <term>Logos (the organizing principle or word)</term>. Through the spirit. For either the image, having the metal <note>This may refer to the "stamping" of forms into matter, like a seal on metal.</note>, or in itself. If such things exist. But then, it is not then. And it is lacking, but after this, those things which are lacking are divided by the nature of its application. Just as in sailing with bronze, those things which are lacking must be drawn out as the activity. But again, through the soul of the earth, the same things come to be. And the same things for these and those. So that they are as one. It has the power to move itself, having the application. Just as with the body. Or that which participates in taking up the intellect, so also of the taking, or in itself. But those things from the intellect are not lacking in the soul. Or from the power of attraction. Because it is lacking. Nor indeed by division, but not having them itself. Since you will not attract the same things by hypothesis, just as he himself would not see. The intellect sees itself in wonder at nature and all things, all things, because all things are there.

<column-break/>

Now these things seem to be for all. Since man is the same as himself. And all things are the same as him. That which he contemplates is himself. He is all being. For if he were there, when he saw there, that which was there was what he saw. He is already one and the same with all those things, and was never outside of them. If indeed he was with all things, whenever he is that which was there, being among all things. For none of them was standing apart. Nor is it in any other thing, but the whole is in itself. Nor are all things there, and he himself with them. Because the whole is **infinite** <term>apeiron (limitless or boundless)</term>. And nothing of the whole there has a limit. For it would not be the whole. But to all beings, as they bring those things which are lacking. For the whole is one, but it is all these things. It is one, after having stood toward all things there. For it is not <unclear>mercy</unclear> to all as it ought to be, but it is that which is already sent forth by thought. That which it knows, being itself and by the same spirit, which is the whole in reason, we know with the preceding part. They no longer think that the divided becomes divided, but they themselves are the whole to the wholes. And there, perhaps at least some of the things of the soul would not be all. Or because in the soul, all **reasons** and diseases are present. Appearing perhaps to be lacking from her because they are not in the soul. But there is a greater impulse of her toward herself when, nevertheless, the light shining out from the soul sees. I have in mind both that which it <unclear>knows</unclear> and the "much-celebrated" <note>Plotinus likely refers to a famous philosophical concept or a passage from Plato known to his students.</note> becoming good in its practices. Those things which she is, she does not need to be a soul. For she herself is the cause. Which also makes **knowledge** <term>episteme (certain, scientific knowledge)</term> the cause hereafter, and as many things as are in it, so that it may be seen. Or entirely the things being there must be united to this. But how are these things? Not even through each in this way, while all the things of the intellect are in each soul, there is no longer anything of each. And at least it itself is not one, because it is like the roses <note>A poetic image: just as the scent of roses fills a room without being divided, the Intellect is present in all souls without losing its unity.</note>. And each is in itself. All have their generation. Because there is no **mass** <term>onkos (physical bulk or volume)</term>. And she is the soul itself. Therefore, it would be and is the whole. Knowledge is not poured over all things, nor is it that which divides what is brought together. All these things are the soul. But each is in it, yet all are not even what one must know. Nor again does it seem to be one when it is not. And because he knows by no part of it. Nor by all the forms (but he would see all in one). Nor again did it happen to become, or are these things, infinite. For the intelligible is this. And it would not be above us. If, therefore, it is not as great as itself, neither would it be the whole as it is. Nor does he apply himself to it. Nor is thinking in the intellect among them, just as it is not among beings. What then has happened to it? And because it never was then. But are the things in the intelligible realm distinct from one another? For in general, he would either see all. But each in this way, and not for all. Since they are wholes...

### Plotinus on the Kinds of Being, Book I:

Regarding beings, how many they are, thinkers seek to know whether they are only these things found here in our world. For example, the **ten genera** <note>original: "δέκα γένη" — These are Aristotle's Categories: Substance, Quantity, Quality, Relation, Place, Time, Position, State, Action, and Passion.</note> into which they divide reality: are these spoken of as common to all things? Do they apply to the **intelligible world** <term>noētos kosmos (the realm of pure thought and divine Forms)</term>, or are there other categories there? And is each of these things—such as body, or soul, or something else—found there in the same way? Or are some things there and everything here? And how are some one way, and some another? Or do the things that exist there not exist here, or are the things here also there? Or are the things there different, while the things here are not truly "beings" but are only called beings? Or are they perhaps different, some being true beings and others not being, but merely images <note>original: "εἴδωλα" — reflections or shadows of a higher reality</note>? Or are the ten categories common to all? Or are the things here one thing, and the things there another? Or are they common, yet not in their categories, but distinct in some other way? Or are the things there true "kinds" <note>original: "γένη" — often translated as 'genera' or 'categories'</note> while the things here are not?

It follows from this to ask if the things here are also categories, and if they are all categories, or if there are others. If the things there are categories, are they the same or different? Or are some the same and some not? And are there the same number, or more, or fewer? <margin>6</margin> Since most thinkers have classified beings into ten, let us examine whether it seems to them that these ten categories encompass all beings, whether they are spoken of by category or by some other standard. For instance, is "the One" a category, or is the One present in all things as something common? Just as if one were dividing animals; for the same division does not apply to all beings. Or rather, as those who make such divisions say: are the ten categories found all together in both the intelligible and the **sensible realms** <term>aisthēta (things perceived by the senses)</term>, or are they all in the sensible? And if they are in the intelligible, how so? Are they the same, or are they there in a different way, or not at all? A common account <note>original: "κοινὸν λόγον"</note> is required. If there is no common account, then the category will not exist for the things here. In that case, there would be a mere naming of things by the same word <note>original: "ὁμωνυμία" — homonymy, where things share a name but not a definition</note>, and being would seem to be a certain thing there, but everything here would be a mere shadow.

<column-break/>

<note>The following notes refer to the preceding page visible in the spread, discussing the relationship between forms and matter.</note>

Regarding the... and differences in shapes. Some are found in the **reason-principle** <term>logos (the formative, rational power that shapes matter)</term> and others in matter. If these reason-principles are without outward shapes, then the intelligible must be that which does not exist upon matter. Or as these are, so they are; and this is the cause, just as there is a **Soul-itself** <note>original: "αὐτοψυχὴν"</note> for the soul, and an **Intellect-itself** <note>original: "αὐτονοῦν"</note> for the intellect. We must say again that if these things are in matter, they are made different by the **archetypes** <term>archétypoi (the original models from which copies are made)</term>. It brings soul, having formative powers, much like the cause within a seed; and if there is something even beyond this. Likely, the Intellect is there; if soul is a reason-principle which nature possesses. But the Intellect: who is the one before it? And if the Intellect is inseparably with the true soul, like images. Let us bring other likenesses and images of it. And so we may grasp what we seek in this way: if Being—which is what it is—is uniquely defined by shape, so that where there is shape, there is also Intellect through otherness. But when nature is a world of shapes, it becomes all-shaped. The Intellect: soul likewise receives images from the Intellect; so that it receives all the forms in this essence, at least those understood by their shape. Nor are they withheld; if the things in the world are reason-principles, then all things are shaped. The Intellect holds the forms, and all things as images, which are intelligible; while the soul holds the images of the truest things; for nature is not this. These things we have seen. Thus the Intellect, which is of the one essence, is itself all things. Before this, let us see if the things of essence lead to the truth. That of the whole. It holds all these things. What sort of things are these? So that in receiving them, it holds all powers. If the things of the intelligible exist, even the shaped things are a "form" <note>original: "εἶδος"</note>. Those in the intelligible are like reason-principles, not like those shaped in matter; of this, everything is the root. Being, which must be thought of as all things. For not even the first thing is soul itself; it receives from the Intellect. For the Intellect is all things. Whence the soul, not by nature; they obtain it. It is of the same kind as that in the world. And indeed, all are the cause; not only the animals upon the earth, but this Intellect also turns back toward its own essence, and thus, soul from it is perhaps the cause; as for all. If not even these are the cause of nature; then the Intellect is where it is able. And not by the reason-principle, nor by the reason-principle toward itself, for this exists and thinks—either the essence, which they call the higher. Since we call it the Soul-itself, which indeed is the whole essence and the source; the soul, so that from them comes the reason-principle of each Soul-itself.

It explores how higher principles like Intellect and Soul act as the archetypal causes for the shapes and forms found in the material world.</summary>

<header>On Interpretation, 6</header>

...and of the sounds. For he says that the affections in the sound are <insert>affections in the soul</insert>:

->**Now, spoken words are symbols of the soul's experiences, and written words are symbols of spoken words. And just as writing is not the same for all men, so also the spoken words are not the same. However, those things of which these are primarily signs—the soul's experiences—are the same for all; and those things of which these experiences are likenesses—actual things—are also the same. These matters have been discussed in the treatise "On the Soul," for they belong to a different inquiry. Just as in the soul there is sometimes a thought without being true or false, and at other times it must be one or the other, so it is also with sound. For falsehood and truth consist in combination and separation. Therefore, nouns and verbs by themselves are like thoughts without combination or separation—for instance, the word "man" or "white" when nothing else is added; for they are not yet either true or false. A sign of this is the "stag-goat": for while it signifies something, it is not yet true or false unless "to be" or "not to be" is added, either simply or in reference to time.**<-

<margin>It is asked why indeed</margin>
First, it is asked why the philosopher did not begin immediately with the teaching of the **noun** and the **verb**, but instead started with sounds, thoughts, and actual things. For he says that this is the proper theory. We say, then, that because his discussion here concerns the **proposition**, and since a proposition is composed of a noun and a verb, and these are composed of syllables, and syllables of letters, and before all these is the **voice** <note>original: "phōnē" — in this context, it refers to vocalized sound used for communication</note>—for this reason, he treats the subject of the voice. Furthermore, since the voice is not only according to nature but also according to **convention**—for it is not like a mere noise, but like speech—and convention comes from the intellect, and the intellect is concerned with things, it is necessary to treat these matters as well. Finally, since man is a composite of soul and body, he uses the voice as a sensory being, but as an intellectual being, he uses thoughts; thus, it was necessary to discuss these as well.

<margin>What is a <term>symbol</term></margin>
It is also asked what difference exists between a **symbol** <note>original: "symbolon" — a sign that represents something by social agreement or convention</note> and a **likeness**. We say that a **likeness** <note>original: "homoiōma" — an image that naturally mimics its subject</note> intends to imitate the very nature of the thing, just as a portrait of Socrates imitates Socrates himself. A symbol, however, is by convention and not by nature; an example is a pre-arranged signal given in war. While a likeness is not up to us but is a work of nature, a symbol is within our power. For this reason, he says that thoughts are likenesses, as they exist by nature, but voices are symbols, as they exist by convention.

<margin>What is a <term>thought</term></margin>
By **thought** <note>original: "noēma" — a concept or mental representation</note>, he refers to the primary observations of things perceived by the senses or the intellect in the form of species. These are neither true nor false when nothing is added to them. For example, "man" or "white" is neither true nor false. But if "is" <insert>is</insert> or "is not" <insert>is not</insert> is added, then it becomes true or false—for instance, "man exists" or "man does not exist."

<summary>This page contains a commentary on the opening of Aristotle's "De Interpretatione," explaining the relationship between written words, spoken language, mental concepts, and reality. It distinguishes between "symbols" (conventional signs) and "likenesses" (natural mental representations).</summary>
