<header>Ennead 6.9</header>

<margin>Not non-being in an absolute sense, but that which comes after the soul, just as there is that which comes before it.</margin>
But the soul, in turn, tended toward non-being; for in this way it also proceeded. Not into non-being in an absolute sense, but into that which is after itself. Just as, again, it moves toward that which is before itself. For that which is before it is not non-being, but something different from non-being—rather, it is that which is before Being <note>original: ὄντος (ontos). Plotinus distinguishes between "Being," which refers to the realm of Intellect and forms, and "The One," which is so pure it exists above the category of Being itself.</note>. And this is none other than The One. Having departed from there, the soul will come to nothing other than itself. And being in nothing else, it would be in no thing, but in The One. For such a state already exists: so that not being in another, it is in itself. But being in itself alone and not in the realm of Being, it is in That [the One]. To be such is not essence <note>original: οὐσία (ousia). Plotinus argues the ultimate source is "beyond essence."</note>, but beyond essence. In this way the soul communes with That. If anyone, therefore, should see himself having become this, he possesses in himself a likeness of That; and if he should go from himself to That, as an image to its archetype, he would reach the end of his journey. And even if he falls away, if he is raised up again through virtue and moves toward the Intellect <note>original: νοῦς (nous), the divine mind where all ideas exist</note> and through wisdom to that place there, he would again possess such a state. And this is the life of gods and of divine and happy men: a release from the other things here, a life without pleasure in the things of this world, a **flight of the alone to the alone**.

->THE END<-

<header>Ennead VI. 5. 1.</header>

<margin>Regarding Plotinus</margin>
Of the indivisibles <note>original: ἀτόμων (atomon). In this context, Plotinus refers to the fundamental, non-material units of reality or "beings" that cannot be further divided.</note> from which the world is composed, some exist to a greater degree, and others to a lesser; some participate more than others. Some participate as a whole in the whole, while others participate more or less. And that which participates more is greater and more abundant. For instance, consider fire: because it possesses a power that is not always the same, it participates in power, life, form, and the Reason-Principle <term>Logos: In Neoplatonism, the rational ordering principle that reflects the higher divine mind into the material world.</term> of the whole. Thus, the Whole itself possesses more life and beauty than the other individual things within the world. Since bodies also possess more, yet Being itself <note>original: τὸ ὄντως (to ontos) — that which truly exists, as opposed to mere appearance.</note> does not define itself by plurality. But this is also true of incorporeal natures. For just as the soul is not only one but many, so too fire is not only one. If indeed the Whole exists, it would not have just one Idea, but many which constitute that Whole. Those realities at the furthest edge of material mass participate in such things as if in place of forms, or instead of form, since nothing is entirely without form. It is necessary, then, that this Whole and all beings possess power, for the greatest power exists alongside the simple, and according to the rational. So it is that those things which participate more are greater beings; those whose relations involve greater virtue are similarly more rational. Those things that are not such are still powers, and the more numerous things are found in his more numerous parts, and some less so. Is it then just as bodies or beings are lacking, so too are places? Something flowed forth, more to be hoped for than to be nothing. Because it is not fire of that sort, and it seems not to have received the greater life, yet these natures are more so—these many things and those lacking in power, whose strength exists, or all that exists in the state of being forms. 

Do animals have a Form <note>original: εἶδος (eidos). The spiritual blueprint or "Type" of a living creature in the realm of Intellect.</note>? There is a cause for this. But some have a cause of life and power, others of beauty, and others of strength or health. Are, then, the things within the One and other things altogether wondrous? Or is it that some things, and these among them, are lacking to all? But what prevents the Reason-Principle from being many, spoken of together, and yet being itself as if in a single disturbance, and in every part of the creation—more and less—or even in nothing? Or according to quality, or the lesser things? So that these things are themselves all things potentially. And the Whole—but some have the power of each thing in the same place, and some more. Then Being is thus. And the One also exists because of Being. But this, whatever it may have been, has been clearly shown instead of the many. Is it then the Whole that exists before Being? But it also exists because of potentiality, and the Reason-Principle is the most abundant. So that even if it is a genus, it is Being, just as it is Existence. For example, it is one because Being always uses the Whole in a wondrously manifold way. And divine form—

—there is some difference within them. And the One is able to appear in many places. From this, indeed, the things within it relate to the One in such a way that they even exist in it as bodies. For either the One of those things is together with all, or again, the many are powers that hold existence toward what follows. Because whenever there are powers that look toward it, but someone having once taken what is most of all the cause, they seek the relationship toward each of the things from them and collectively the point upon which they exist. # Virtues 6

...but they are called six different qualities. For each of them has its being in the soul, as if in their underlying subject. <note>original: ὑποκειμένῳ (hypokeimeno). In ancient philosophy, this refers to the "substrate" or "subject" in which properties like color or virtue reside.</note> How then does Plotinus say the virtues are not in the soul—and likewise pleasure? Or is it that the primary things are forms, while those that come after are activities or qualities? But he himself says they are not a subject. Or does he say, which is true? Is it the form, or the highest peak? 

It must be said that correctly, the virtues are in the soul. But these are like the shapes of objects being gazed upon within the soul. The Intellect <term>Nous: The Divine Mind or Intellect; in Plotinus's system, this is the realm of eternal Truth and the second "Hypostasis" or divine level of reality.</term> is the highest peak; truth most resembles these. If they exist in something, where must their being primarily reside? In the Intellect; for it is there that truth originates for it. For as knowledge is analogous to the Intellect, so too is it clarified—one part concerning sensible things, the other in the Intellect. Contemplation exists in the Intellect; or else it is matter. But the soul also becomes individualized through it; for surely things are not the same for everyone. Knowledge, then, is that which is in the Intellect. The truth of things in the soul comes from these. One is in the Intellect, from which its own truth comes. 

For indeed, Plotinus says: to place virtues among other virtues, or for there to be a certain virtue of the soul, is not possible; since even form is not rationalizing. Or perhaps these virtues, which exist in themselves, are the differences between the formal types. And it <unclear>generates</unclear> their rational principle. The best is the virtue of the Beautiful. Again, he extends the "goods" toward the act of seeing. Such will be the perception of the principles of bodily things, like a sound in the ear. Because of this, there are differences in such things. One kind is in the soul as a gaze resulting from universal motion, while the other is in the Intellect as being itself. 

It is worth asking how Plotinus, in his difficulty, places the virtues either in the Intellect or in the soul. But if they are truly in the soul, how are the virtues known? Perhaps because one kind is the "social" <note>original: πολιτική (politike). Often translated as "civic" or "political" virtues, these are the practical ethics—like justice and temperance—required for living in human society.</note> virtue; for this and those following it are the social ones. The most authoritative seems to be the "exemplary" <term>Paradeigmatike: The "paradigmatic" or "exemplary" virtues. These are the divine "blueprints" of virtue as they exist eternally in the Divine Mind, before they are mirrored in the soul.</term> virtue. And thus we have within it the nature of what their power must be. Because of this, the most authoritative is that of power, either through acting or through being. In this way, one is greater and the other lesser. The greater is of the sort concerning which Plotinus reasons. Behold, such it is: the virtues themselves must have their being as a whole in the Intellect. Either the power is for acting upon another, or within itself; such then is the aim of Plotinus. 

9. One kind is to be that thing itself; yet the social virtue is productive. Contemplation is within him, and he is the Intellect itself; or because the contemplation of the theorems from the Intellect is arranged for others. 9. Perhaps one kind, while the other is toward those of the...

### Eusebius — 5

...in which, having manifested this cause, he did so not without cause. For he said the cause was **labors** and our estrangement from external logical causes. <note>The author is discussing why humans are moved by certain arguments; "labors" likely refers to the effort of thought or the struggles of the soul in the material world.</note> However, one must examine how he said it exists. For he claimed the cause is **persuasion**—specifically, to persuade in such a way that the result follows through the act of persuading. Following these points, he proceeded to explain the primary argument, once again mentioning the success of the discovery. He said that its reputation was marvelous. <note>original: εὐδοξίαν (eudoxian). This can mean glory, good repute, or a favorable opinion.</note> And having addressed the causes—and if anyone else did so because of the matter itself—he says this cause is found in **rhetoric**. <term>Rhetoric: The art of persuasion; in late antiquity, philosophers often debated whether rhetoric was a true science or merely a knack for manipulation.</term> He says it is absolutely successful if it consists in persuasion. 

Having said these things, he brought the argument to the third point; for as he himself says, it is possible for persuasion to exist in rhetoric. For everything that is persuaded according to approval is like a form of persuasion itself, and such a thing is esteemed alongside persuasion. He says this is either praiseworthy or blameworthy. It is what is apparent. So it is concerning this and all other causes of the rhetoricians that they find success. He marks the utility of these things, as they are intensified toward greater or lesser ends. And if someone says they intensify within persuasion, then they persuade in such a way as to turn toward the greater part. 

<margin>☉</margin> But **refutation** <note>original: ἔλεγχος (elenchos). A logical cross-examination intended to reveal a contradiction, famously used by Socrates.</note> would not have the power of induction, for it is not persuasive. It has been said that their fairness is what counts. For the "worse" part persuades. In opinion, however, do not be overly serious with oneself. (For even if it were in persuasion, do not ask "how?") having spoken... <note>The text here becomes fragmentary, suggesting a transition into technical logical proofs or shorthand notes.</note> ...for some. And they would not accept those "feet" <note>Likely referring to the "feet" or steps of a logical argument or perhaps metrical feet in speech.</note> either. And such a manner is clear to no one. But if even before the appearance, and the rest, or that of the multitude. For men, it is just to believe that the cause does not happen to be the persuasion of the worse; or rather, that [word] is the cause through which one practices rhetoric. He says this because it is thought that one persuades, but if one were to persuade of *that* [the truth], it would be so.

These points were subsequently set in opposition to **Porphyry**, <note>Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234–305 AD) was the student and biographer of Plotinus who edited the Enneads and often debated the practical applications of his master's philosophy.</note> as he says they receive these causes in turn; and after this, they reasonably reach agreement. For there, the cause appears to be its existence in rhetoric. But persuasion is such that everything is reasonable. In general, he created the rules for things within persuasion. But the argument... for it is not from writing. Since refutation might ask if it happens by agreement. Not everything would appear. Things would not become softer. Some are soft, not because they are not persuaded. He marks this too, if indeed persuasion is to wither away. But he does not want them to be softer. Yet someone might say: although from what was said, the labors might become soft, instead of them he answers—or how, if indeed, there are spirits <note>original: πνεύματα (pneumata). Can refer to breaths, vital spirits, or rhetorical "airs."</note> in rhetoric. And this, the arguments.

### Conclusion 6

At one time it receives wealth, at another time later, or even earlier, it receives **poverty**. Others, looking at present circumstances—or the descent from heaven, and the things within these movements, and the changes, and the things happening in such places—believe that earthly matters have their cause there. But this **holy teacher** <note>This likely refers to Plotinus himself, or perhaps a commentator like Porphyry or a Christian interpreter, given the "holy" epithet.</note>, having contemplated the mind of the prophet, or rather to say the spirit which speaks through him against us, thinks that one should look at everything in relation to the **need of the soul**. For present things are nothing to the soul for its own sake, whether they be profitable or harmful, which appear most clearly concerning those who are wealthy or those who wish to be wealthy. From this, it becomes easy to assign no cause to evils or to goods, unless one attributes this to **choice**. <term>Choice (Proairesis): A fundamental concept in Greek philosophy referring to the moral will or the internal decision-making power that determines character.</term> For this teacher does not believe that painful things are such by nature, but rather by the judgment of those who receive them. Therefore, he even says that **afflictions** are the causes of happiness, or rather, are happiness itself. For through these things, there is a **turning back** toward God for humanity, so that even wailing and such things would not happen, except through ignorance; or rather to say, through bitter habit. For it is not that wailings are evil, but that no one is a praiser of them, except perhaps when a king or a ruler is involved. If someone hears these things from others, they will not immediately blame the afflictions or the labors for this reason. For those who mourn are not entirely unhappy, nor are those who rejoice miserable.

Or one must run back to the beginning. Since we were speaking of it—how, and in what manner, or why—and we did not use it. He says it is proper to contemplate the whole of this. For all such things concern the **body**, not the spirit, in which sensation exists regarding the things it perceives. For sensation belongs to the sensible world alongside the act of sensing. We ourselves—the act of sensing itself, or everything from that source, and that which is in sensation—do not act in this way, or so he says about them. Then, why concerning the need, or that we are the soul? Others might say, how do these afflictions come to be? For it is reasonable. Either from **sin**, or for the sake of a trial, or a temptation. So that even according to our view, God—before those days in which He said He would destroy man—not only did this, but also gives patience and **repentance**. <note>The text here mirrors Christian theological language (sin, repentance) being applied to Neoplatonic providence.</note> But to those others He did not give it, because of their lawlessness in deeds; as much as they held toward God, it is possible to say, and this is what he seeks to teach the prophet. If we have anything, it is clear that it belongs to sin. And from this, the cause of them is also clear. But also of what sort they deem worthy for the punishment of the wicked. So that some say they flee even the punishment itself. Thus, having seen well how God the Father demonstrates the need, or the punishment, or whatever comes from the cause. Then the sins, and the difficulties, or the injustices—those caused by their own errors; and so, rather, and through a few words, thus toward their own circumstances, and how they truly are. If indeed they are not painful. These things, then, before the—

### Ennead VI

The causes of nature’s **gestation** <note>original: "κυήσεως" (kyēseōs) – referring to the process by which nature "breathes life" or brings forms into being.</note> are found here. There is, by necessity, a presence of **Intellect**. <term>Intellect (Nous): In Plotinus's system, the second hypostasis or Divine Mind, which contains the archetypes of all things.</term> This is an affection shared among all living beings. Or it is not the making. For as many things as are base, there are also some for those. At the same time, there is a wandering for all. But into a voice by a breath. What then? His at some time, and the rest, as he thinks. But not so. The writing, or his own. Both would become hopes. Let him use life at no time. <meta>This page continues the investigation into how the Divine Mind relates to the physical world, specifically focusing on the paradox of how the "All" (the totality of Being) can be present in individual parts without being divided. ### - Ennead VI -

That it is indeed inferior; for if it were not the whole, it would not be the "All," if it were nothing at all. But if it is the All, there is nothing within it which is not also the All. Or, if it is entirely the whole, it possesses all life within itself. And if this is so, the All cannot come from anything other than itself. How then could the enumeration of each individual part occur, whether by coming into being or otherwise? If someone were to say, and fashion a world in a primary sense, as if from another world—and so it would be from those very things. The All exists, and each part is a part of itself, or it is not; or rather, when we speak of the All in relation to itself, each subsequent thing is directed toward the One. Nor is it entirely in potentiality; for if the All is the All, then every part of it is like the limbs of a living being. <note>original: "μέλη τοῦ ζῴου" — Plotinus frequently uses the "Cosmic Animal" metaphor from Plato's Timaeus to describe the universe as a unified, living organism.</note> For it would not be the All unless the whole were in all the parts, at least in the sense that they are members of it. It remains then that it is more like a **reason-principle** of knowledge; <term>Reason-principle (Logos): The formative power that emanates from the Intellect to shape the material world.</term> so if the whole is not in potentiality, how is it not absurd, and how is it misconstrued, when it is shown that the whole soul is in the parts? From where, then, does the measure of life come to a man, or the complete likeness? But we are no longer able to hold it. But the **Intellect** is everywhere. <term>Intellect (Nous): The realm of true Being and divine thought that exists above the physical world.</term> And even if someone were to announce it; no one who is ready and willing can possess the whole of knowledge. For not even <unclear>that</unclear> <margin><unclear>seek</unclear></margin> seeks all things, it meets them in each whole. I say, then, that the All is always by itself, but all things are also within the All. But if anyone should ask how, it is because the All does not have anything else, nor is it something different. For that would be inferior, as if it were not present by joining with the stone. <note>This suggests that the divine presence doesn't just sit next to matter like a stone, but permeates it.</note> Just as we might <unclear>grant</unclear> what we imagine, or as has been stated further. Nor is it a part, such that it must necessarily be affected. But it is the All. The All would come to be in that which is below, or the All is there below. But because it is in the same state in the All, it is from nowhere. Rather, it exists in the absolute One. For it is not in the "Other." These things perhaps stand thus. We are seeking the All as a whole. The Intellect becomes everywhere, both in the things beside it, and in those that possess it, and in all those that participate in it, just as with water or something else; and perception makes use of it in all things, whether on the earth, in the air, or in the entire cosmos. One might grasp many things. Near to them, not in them, or that one who brought the All as a corrupted spirit. — And others say, even the ancients say, and those who have hoped. — It has been sought, what it is that exists within it. Let it be said, then, that nothing is outside of it. Nor indeed was there anything but that which was the All. It was in a similar state. Let these things be said concerning the cause of why the many appear in all things. Either becoming or <unclear>possessing</unclear> a generation.

<column-break/>

Having recovered their whole life, wherefore it also seems to be the principle which is completed in its ancient self. That one, therefore, before the others, is not in another. It is set before, not for itself, but because it is itself. And its nature, as in the forms, is that in which it is one, or however much it might receive from the others. But if it is also toward the same genus, or its own, there would be more in **Matter**. <term>Matter (Hyle): The underlying "stuff" of the universe which Plotinus views as a shadow or a lack of Being, receiving forms from above.</term> Since this is no more so, then, than itself which is not in the All. In that case, it will not give of the wholes either to all or to any other. So that the All is also in the **Monad**. <term>Monad: The "Unit" or "The One"; the ultimate, indivisible source of all existence.</term> Its essence comes into being. But nevertheless, all that is Matter. For because of having it toward itself. Not only would one say Matter, but in the All or in Matter it is possible for that which is so present. Since it might also happen. Rather, the things toward it are nothing of it. An **image of essence**. <note>original: "εἴδωλον οὐσίας" (eidōlon ousias) — A key concept: physical reality is just a lower-density reflection of the true spiritual essence.</note> All other things. Either they are not in it, or that which is the All, or at least the All, or to be the All, as the All is thus, even if. But the Intellect, possessing everything. Everything that contributes moderately to such things. And it is placed alongside Matter, and one part it keeps in itself, while the other it gives, through that which we indeed call "the whole." Generally, Matter participates in it, which is in potentiality, and on the one hand in something like fire or earth, and again into such a thing. Since we also say that the soul enters into the All. But how is it that which is said not to be upon the essence? Or by being present to its essence. But not as if it were the **actuality** itself, <term>Actuality (Energeia): The active, manifesting power of a thing, as opposed to its mere potential.</term> nor the All of it. But if not of it, then not even that which is by essence toward itself. It is therefore possible for the same thing to be in each. For if the All is that which is in Matter, it is necessary. For otherwise it would not be; for where would the All be? Or the All as a whole? Or the All in a primary sense. Therefore, the All is not in Matter. But in all things by means of actuality. There indeed because. — All things being itself, even Matter. For in the body there is no Matter. But that which it was. Upon all things, to be the All. The All as a whole, its part is for itself. — But their actuality, or that in Matter, is truly joined to the body. But all is the same in each. — Both the All and generally Matter still possess. In each. And either possessing the All. Since it is in no way entirely here. — But either from where, nevertheless, what is called the All is Matter. For not even all that is Being, which he speaks of in parts, is left behind anywhere, both itself and in all things, or as a whole. — It is toward the things that are becoming, and indeed the All. — How then the All. And the things after it and the things...

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of Being and Substance. Having previously discussed how the "All" resides in its parts, Plotinus now turns to the problematic nature of Matter (hyle) and its relationship to extension and the categories of existence defined by Aristotle.</meta>

# — Ennead VI — · 8 ·

The problem is resolved. If matter is essentially that which constitutes extension, then the form belonging to matter must be this very extended thing. Rather, it would become **magnitude**, though certainly not a sensible one, in every instance of union; for even this is a form of union. But whatever it may be, it is reckoned in such a way that it happens to matter when it arises. Let it be, then, that each difference is itself a substance, being unchangeable, while magnitude is different. Or does it become a **body**? <note>original: "σῶμα" (soma) — Plotinus is debating whether the addition of magnitude to matter is what creates a physical body.</note> And how could that be truly real? If it is "Non-Being," is there not a difficulty? Is it something other than the things that do not participate in it? Or is it by affirmation? The cause, then, belongs to those things; it might happen to this or you might agree it happens. Furthermore, why is "place" associated with this affirmation? These things happen to all that are not mere "affections." In one sense, it is by **accident**, for it is not the thing itself, but is in a place. 

Substance, having a different nature from all other genera, also differs in being "somewhere." And it is through these principles that they grasped what pertains to these matters. If it becomes infinite, then it seems to be of the infinite. For that which exists through itself is not "out of place." The cause of matter must be either matter itself or that of the body. But as for matter, or rather not every body—then is it a state of persistence? Both might be true. For that which does not belong to each, if it is the same thing, many of them lie beneath. Then the things that are transferred to them are the same. In one way, it is that which happens to itself, having become itself; it is not **subsistence** <term>Subsistence (Hypostasis): The underlying reality or distinct substance of a thing.</term> in itself, but that which is the substrate along with matter. To what things is it a substrate? Not as the underlying subjects of that which participates, but of the things enumerated—those which are called "Non-Being"? Or is it Being itself? But for my part, Non-Being is the same thing. Or as a substrate, **Substance** in the primary and proper sense is the substrate, or this in relation to matter. For it does not possess a measure in this. But if it relates to its being and comes from there, but does not come to be along with "being," it would not be for one who is departing. Thus, this exists apart from the things that are. 

It can be a certain substrate. But that which pertains to "affection"—for it is not division, but the substrate for bodies. If the other things were the same, either what is left would be thus, but not in the substrate of the producer, or it would be something else. Rather, the other things have been spoken of generally. If it is also necessary for it to be in matter—thus that which is Non-Being is necessary. Or if the other things should come to be, that which will seem to be the substrate. But matter is not like that. It was only matter. This itself was not even matter.

<column-break/>

# — Ennead VI — · 9 ·

It is so, or in this manner. If it is by accident to the others. If it is necessary to speak of "being" in this way, it would not be "toward being." Nor indeed toward that which is not toward being, but only by "Otherness." <note>original: "ἑτερότητι" (heteroteti) — A Platonic category referring to the principle of difference or being "other" than the One.</note> If it is not even matter itself, it is not "toward." For it does not truly exist; and if it does not even exist, the things toward it or upon it would not exist. Consequently, the things toward it would not exist either. But for us, these genera of beings have been stated; the cause of each will be shown not only in themselves but in each particular instance.

->· 9 ·<-

One might first raise a difficulty regarding the **genus of Substance**. <term>Genus of Substance (Ousia): The highest category of being. Plotinus is questioning if "Substance" means the same thing when applied to the divine and the physical.</term> What is common among these things? And first, is it not the "common" that is substance, but rather that each is a cause only according to what is common? If so, we shall also place the substance of the **Soul** within it for this reason. But if Soul is a genus, it would be that which receives. How does matter differ from the others? For in this way, it has no subsistence. How could they be "matters"? For it becomes the thing itself. From it, Soul and Intellect are "matters." <note>Plotinus uses "Intelligible Matter" to explain how higher beings like Soul and Intellect can be many while remaining divine.</note> And these would be, when all those souls and intellects are the "All" in many ways. But neither is the Soul... And Substance and Soul are not the same, even if Soul is by nature as much as is in the genus. 

But if the things in Substance are many in this way and have the same subsistence—and if all of these are the same, not in species but according to genus—then the things that exist, the natures and their causes, or the things through them, are not left behind. If, again, someone makes it a genus, it will not be common but will become a cause or a genus itself, since it is not heard as being separate. Things thus separated are either genera or the same. Not being entirely afraid of the other things, we think we have such a difficulty through which... for the genera in the genus would not truly be in "Being," if one says they believe in being. Both by opinion and by permanence. If it is necessary, or each thing alone, and one sees it. But if this is so, how are they "beings"? And what are the things in relation to others? Some are by substance, others are in those. Or the things that exist in common, the **Forms**, following those, they follow as being more "real" than that. Or that which is according to species. Or those Forms which are quite prior, and especially the whole "All," in Being and the things there. 

If indeed the **Reason-principle** is the subsistence of that—rather, how could it be that? For every body is a particular thing, or even every substance entirely. For what could the things in "sensible substance" be? The things in relation to others, or even the things in them. And the things that are not substance. If one does not take these as well, one might be at a loss, for they too will have come to be in this way. If they are not called "the things themselves," but are "upon them"—or even if they are not in substance, where are the things in relation to others and the causes of those things? There is something related to them in opinion. But not even the...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of ethical action and the soul's agency. While the previous page examined the nature of Being and Substance in the context of Matter, this section shifts toward the moral implications of these categories, specifically the distinction between voluntary and involuntary actions—a subject where Plotinus engages deeply with Aristotelian ethics.</meta>

# — Ethics — VI — · 2 ·

If indeed choice is something voluntary, and these passions—which for these reasons are put forward as causes—are capable of being such; it follows that even if someone acts through ignorance of certain facts, one might again be found to be doing what is unjust. And yet, that which is done through ignorance is [in a sense] voluntary. So if a person is ignorant, they are not necessarily "unjust," but they are nonetheless involved in the **act of injustice**. And yet, why is it that he does not commit injustice at all, if he is doing something unjust? It is because the error is not [inherently] "injustice." <note>Plotinus is distinguishing between the external act (the "unjust thing") and the internal state of the soul (the "vice of injustice").</note> For just as not everyone who strikes another commits an act of **outrage**, so too not every involuntary act is an **injustice**. <term>outrage: *hubris*, a technical term for a blow intended to shame or dishonor the victim, rather than a mere physical strike.</term> That this also occurs through ignorance is clear not only from what has been said, but in other ways as well. For while every unjust man does unjust things, it is not the case that everyone who does an unjust thing is already an unjust man; rather, they may be so **by accident**. <term>by accident: *kata symbebekos*, meaning a property that is not part of the person's essential character or intent.</term> Just as one might speak unjustly, yet not be an unjust man, because he is not motivated by injustice. So too here: one person does an unjust thing, while the other does not [commit] injustice. For the one who knows what he is doing performs unjust acts; thus, if he acts without knowing, but through ignorance, he does not commit "injustice" [as a vice]. He is, however, involved in the **doing of injustice**; and this would be a kind of injustice. Or perhaps not; perhaps it is not that other kind of injustice which is a specific virtue or vice. For the actions of that vice are voluntary in every respect. Furthermore, every error is voluntary. That it is also through ignorance is clear, not only from that source, but because voluntary actions, as we have said, consist of the specific circumstances of the present case. For things ignored are equal across all cases. If we were seeing, we would ignore nothing in which the action consists; so even if one happens to strike in ignorance—because he did not know it was an injustice, or because he did not refrain his hands, or for some other reason, or in the manner of one having caused the death of some through his own actions—[the act remains complex].

---

<margin>· 2 ·</margin>
If, then, being in the state of doing injustice is not always the peculiar mark of an unjust person, and if doing injustice while ignorant of certain things is altogether different, all unjust acts are equal [in category], as we say regarding other things, but it possesses a **proportion**, just as the whole does with bodies. <note>original: "ἀναλογία" (analogia) — Plotinus often uses the harmony of the physical body as a metaphor for the structural harmony of the soul and the cosmos.</note> Bodies, according to proportion, preserve their own organs. In this way, injustices also have their equalities, so that either the injustices or the virtues—if these exist—are either in a part of the soul or in the whole. Thus it is in genus, in species, and in number, because the action is the same in all; and virtue is not in one place while injustice is in another. For errors are **naked**. <note>The term "naked" (*gymna*) here suggests that errors are exposed for what they are when stripped of the actor's intent or justifications.</note> For a person does injustice when they wish to "fare well." All virtues are directed toward the good. This we have stated everywhere; thus, they will not exist alongside injustice. In this way, sight relates to sight; and indeed, regarding those forms that are diseased, it is necessary for them to become so. For there are some things which a person does unjustly without being ignorant, yet they are not truly "in the state of injustice." For there are things which are truly unjust but not "injustice," which one might say are **involuntary passions**. For...

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the causes of human action, transitioning from the legalistic definitions of injustice on the previous page to a deeper metaphysical inquiry. Plotinus is now exploring whether the ultimate causes of our world are visible or invisible, and how much influence the celestial bodies (the stars) exert over individual human choice.</meta>

Do you wish, then, to say first that not everything that acts is visible? In these cases, one might not grasp what is happening. For it is true that every active cause is not seen. Both the things that act and the causes of one another are clear in themselves. For not all things are causes. For they are aided by the **moving spirit** <note>original: *pneuma* — in this context, a vital breath or force that permeates the physical world.</note>. And these same things tend toward death. Let us see then what this means: so that even the things that complete the movements of animals, and those of trees, or those through which the generation of each occurs, are driven by **invisible forces** <note>original: *aphanon*</note>. There is no perception of this at all. Furthermore, it is not the same thing. For a man would not move, nor would there be perception at all [without these forces]. Furthermore, it is not the same thing. For he would not move, nor would the causes leading to action exist—such as those following falsehood and the nature of causes. How then, having taken the reasons for this argument, could those who seek in this way fail to grasp what they say? But if it happens that the influence of the stars is the same for [us] and for the cattle—since the things concerning us also [depend on them]—how then would the things from above be masters over our own choices? And yet, even according to these [influences], we have our food and drink and the rest. It would be absurd if the things destined to happen were not according to the things above, and were not of them. But let it be God. So that through them, they are causes. And perhaps these alone are not the only things, nor is one thing the cause of another in a different way, but each is toward the rest. So it would follow that there is a cause for each individual thing. Or is it that things happen without a cause? Each thing has a nature that preserves its cause. It holds the laws from him, not even toward what is necessary. Therefore, there must be **choice** <note>original: *hairesis* — often translated as "preference" or "deliberate choice."</note>. If indeed the things concerning us are to happen, but the Whole and the remaining causes must be presupposed. Because every cause has a single **activity** <note>original: *energeia*</note>. It is a wonder to both. Or even because the non-cause from the whole existed from themselves. If, however, one must say that nothing is a cause, it would not be needed through them. But it is through them. But seeking to presuppose the things concerning us. If we are born otherwise. For instance, if one takes the causes from themselves, how would the other hold? This is what he says of the stars. And generations occur also in particular cases. Except that either this work has a certain purpose, and it is most beautiful. It is necessary that each kind, in relation to those things that exist, should be the cause of everything and the rest, but he himself would not have it. It exists for all in the infinite world. But many and different ones do not exist. Because all things are each their own. But if even all things were to happen—the multitude of particular things—nature is **reciprocal** <note>original: *antapodotike* — a balancing or responding nature</note> to generation. And it holds the future as a foundation and the whole. Leading it toward the cause of the whole. And these things are a word toward the other. How does he not think that

# — Eusebius — Book 6 — Chapter 2 —
193

Previously, becoming [so] voluntarily and through choice. And sometimes not voluntarily, nor is he defended, and not **the Good** itself, but the works themselves are as they are, which was everything to him. And those things leading toward **happiness** <note>original: *eudaimonia*</note>. But it is not even very possible to have it by virtue. Looking at these requests. And nothing of the particulars. But the equal is to be among them. If indeed you should say this very thing. If then it is this very thing, the second must also exist, so that the rest are not under [it]. Because of all the things in order. And indeed this belongs to their order. How then could the **causal essence** <note>original: *aitiati ousia* — a being that is the result of a cause</note> be that through which it is a **monad**? In it, by being all things. And in the visible part of bodies, the parts are at their greatest extent. But the body will have power from there, which is both a sensory expense and its own movement. From where then does this come, and from what causes is it carried? In this way then, in a single **interweaving** <note>original: *symploke* — a Stoic and Neoplatonic term for the "web of fate" or the interconnection of all things</note>, it would necessarily happen. And because each is a cause according to the same principles. Therefore these causes. But if someone should say that all things are interwoven. It is not possible for him to grasp the cause. Nor to take it in this way, nor as something foreign to this, so that it is again in whatever happens. Just as it is. But if there can also be a choice of such a kind as those in the Universe. It is possible to work many things individually through themselves. Apart from those of their kind. But wherever these things also become separate, it is because of a cause that not all particular things are in the same through themselves. Or not even the whole, just as each land is, and of which those who are alone say not by the things happening, but those having another cause and still being ignorant. This again could be in excess. For if the things toward the living being are through themselves. This is also to live. But what if it should include that which he does not have, nor causes? Some of those being brought to life and their causes. Or if even their kind should pass over to all things. The non-cause interweaves the kind with them, which exists above. And that if there is no choice and the **pre-choices** <note>original: *proaireseis* — intentional, moral decisions</note> of the causes. From every cause, then, that which is becoming, or the whole in every way. It will be a necessity that what has happened is as if from a cause. And they would not even happen through the unchanging, so that if the cause after him did not happen, through which nothing was before those who stumble, both his time, or even that which is nowhere, its kind itself not providing that it should not even be. Altogether, then, perhaps the things through which they are causes will be causes of causes and of others. But nothing of it. And there is a word of it. Each is one nature, and each one thing toward **quality**. And this itself was of itself, and no longer able to do anything. Which will appear as many things happening according to [it]. How then can some not be from which he would make it, and the cause of all things not being one? For every part of it, having become **temperate** <note>original: *sophronesas*</note>, all things are in each.

# Ennead 5

It is posited* <margin>*</margin> that all **generation** <note>original: *genesis* — the process of things coming into being in the physical world.</note> is a form of **immortality**, because it was necessary for the universe to exist as a whole. But even though these things are by nature parts, they are intended to be one again. They were placed toward the same end, and therefore the cause that is to come brings them together into the same identity. For the part is the same as that which is in the whole. And in this way, it came to be, more as a unity. The cause within them is neither the part itself, nor is it found in the physical form, nor in the mere portion of the whole. These things are indeed similar to the realities found *There* <note>In Neoplatonism, "There" (*ekei*) refers to the higher Intelligible realm, while "here" (*entautha*) refers to our physical world.</note>. And if the things spoken of exist anywhere, they exist *There*. It is the causes themselves that brought about the distinction between the part and the whole *There*.

For *There*, nature possesses what it wills; it is as a "whole of wholes," or belongs to the whole to which the part also belongs. It is always being divided into part upon part, yet it remains as it is, and the things that follow it are as they are. It is not a part that is separate from its own being. Furthermore, it exists as a nature within the whole, when it is in its own true thought, or rather, it is all things. For this reason, it is similarly present in the [Intelligible]. These same things are divided here as well, and their existence here is according to their nature. But in their true essence, they would become what exists *There*. Furthermore, if these things exist in the **Soul** <note>original: *psyche*</note>, they exist *There* again and as one. Even if a difficulty should ever arise in the nature of the absurd, even those things are *There*. Therefore, that which is *There* belongs to the things of that realm; it is either a whole that is one, or it has reached those things. It belongs to them and to itself, either in the part or in the Soul. It is divided by the distance of the **rational principles** <note>original: *logoi* — the formative forces or "blueprints" that bridge the gap between the divine mind and material reality.</note> concerning generation *There*, where nothing is lost. One has learned this. Then, since everything exists in the same place and in the [Intelligible] realm, we agree that it also exists in the Soul. But there is a distance between that realm and this one. In the Soul, the remaining things also exist. Since, then, the Soul encompasses the rest, being divine, it has turned toward all things; this is a perception derived from the **divine education** <note>original: *paideias tou theou* — the process by which the soul is led back to the contemplation of the divine.</note> and all things, just as much as she needs from God and in Him. And for those to whom being belongs, whenever they are in the things of God, those things are the Soul. She herself is also within the universe. But for the Soul, nothing exists except as a distance; she receives all things as a result of this education. These things, therefore, surround the Soul, just as we are surrounded by the reason of the **Mind** <note>original: *nous* — the higher Intellect or Divine Intelligence.</note>, so that we may rejoice in what is *There* and in Him. And this is indeed a very great thing.

<column-break/>

This greatness belongs to them. Since the Soul encompasses the rest, being divine, she has turned toward all things, toward God, by the education of God. And she holds all these things *There*. It is best to speak of this year by year. It is less from itself, so that one learns in this way, or by likeness. As for the things concerning the distance, they are as great as they are. But here, God is not among the things that have come to be. As He is the cause, through the total sovereign cause, all things are the affairs of God. What they do or possess, this is also in nature. What then is the First? He is the cause of the things that come to be. Those things are themselves the same, and the **rational principles** are His. And there is for Him a reason and a benefit for the whole. In His presence, only the rational principles exist. This thought is the salvation of the whole. Many things in the universe are in the Soul, or are at other times divisible. But again, she receives this from the cause. Ascending herself to the point where never... all bodies are suspended from Him.

It is so that all things are directed toward His **Intellection** <note>original: *noesin* — the act of divine thinking.</note>. He escaped these things, as I was saying, in a similar way to the Mind. For all men, it is either the same, or it is because of a cause, or because one seeks how much **chance** <note>original: *tyche*</note> she possesses. Either from the outcomes of chance, some things are one because of those very things *There*. It is either by the cause, or less than another. This has happened to the nature of the Soul, and in the things where she is lacking, or in the things of the Soul, it is from our own nature. It is so, just as a thing is white, but only in its quality. This again also pours into our soul; it is not in those things that remain according to him. It is according to the **reflection of God** <note>original: *emphasin tou theou* — the "shining through" or manifestation of the divine in the material world.</note> that those things exist, but not according to their own essence. For Intellection is present. Either the whole is *There*, even in its substance, but it acts according to the reflection. Instead of the whole. Furthermore, its being is in the same place as Himself. As he says, to think is the same as to be. Therefore, it is also something else. Rather, all things are what He is, from them. Since, then, the being is in the same bond, it is one, as one might say, or as if it were in Him. It is so. As again, that which is in the Soul. These things, then, belong to that Soul. Either they are His own from the [Intelligible]. What I call the head of the investigation—for what it is, it is. But also why it came to be in the universe, in the midst of the painful and the infinite. Or in that Soul. It is because she has a reflection in the same place. It is His. And why then... in the One. And this would be entirely in the portion of the Mind. Let us assume then that all things are in Him, the same. Just as that which is from the Soul is within. And the same thing is present in the same place. The Soul is the cause for him to say much. For it comes to be...

He emphasizes that all things are ultimately suspended from a single divine cause and that the Soul’s journey is one of "divine education" back toward this unity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Relationship between the One and the Many from page 192. While the previous page focused on the invisible causes of action and the physical universe's link to the Soul, this page moves deeper into the metaphysical architecture of Ennead VI, specifically exploring how the "One" can be present in all things simultaneously without being divided.</meta>

# Ennead 6
### 193
**b**

Regarding the **One** <note>original: *to hen* — the ultimate, simple source of all reality in Plotinus’s philosophy, which precedes even being itself.</note>, he says that since this must necessarily be **indivisible**, why should you marvel if he says it is present among all existing things? For it has been shown that Being is always "all at once in all things," and it makes no difference if it is present in something small or within **Life** <note>original: *zōē*</note>. Life is dependent upon the One, and is the source of the whole of life and of the **Intellect** <note>original: *nous* — the realm of divine thought and Platonic Forms.</note>. All things in Life and all things in the Intellect are in the same source; for it is not as if one part is in Life and another part is in something else. Life will be like the One brought into being.

Even in the act of **Intellection** <note>original: *noein* — the process of pure, non-discursive thought.</note>, it is the One that separates these things. Or rather, that which is a "whole and motionless life" is what you were calling "self-sufficient." The specific nature of life and the whole within it belong to this source. Or, since we say it exists in the same thing, it is according to the "division." Yet how could you not remember the One? It is present in all those who think upon it, and Life especially is not separate from it. For this is how it always belongs to it.

If Being is, and if the act of "having" is removed from "thinking," then that which remains is either not always of the One, or that which is allotted from it becomes that which comes from the One itself. In this way, the One has allotted those things There <note>original: *ekei* — referring to the Intelligible realm, the higher plane of reality.</note>. He posits that even there, the "many" belong to it. It is the **cause** <note>original: *aitia*</note> and the whole. If things have come from that source, then from the same source those things and the One are by nature a single unity.

And that which is each of us individually is not a separate thing in the whole. In such a state, it is not as if Being does not exist, but rather it exists separately because it is alongside the One. But everyone, as he says, must be present to it. For this reason, it is necessary to be present to the cause. The nature of that which is **Beyond** <note>original: *epekeina* — a term often used for the One, which is "beyond being."</note> is the cause. Rather, the One is all things to those things There. In this way, the whole is shared. It clearly takes on the role of a cause, just as he himself possesses knowledge in all things. For those things There have come to be, and because of the **Principle** <note>original: *archē*</note>, they are an image of Intellection itself.

If, as you said, it is still within the **Reason-Principle** <note>original: *logos*</note> in this way, then Life belongs to the whole that is unmoved. It is the very thing they might call "that through which." For such as it is itself, it is just in this way. Or it is only by having the whole that it possesses a portion of the One. Life is its way of being. For it holds it from that source. If you were to imagine a **chorus** <note>original: *choros* — a famous Plotinian metaphor where individuals circle the One like dancers around a conductor, only achieving harmony when they look toward the center.</note> standing around the One, they would have the One, even if they are two things in each case. It is through some intermediary, as if through the One itself.

<column-break/>

And if anyone among us should apply their **Intellect** <note>original: *dianoian*</note> to the whole, they would see that for these reasons the One is both "all at once" and "all things together." It is not as if everything came out of it or is merely inside it, but rather that things exist alongside it. Each of the things **Beyond** exists in this way, according to every opinion and every **Abundance** <note>original: *aphthonian* — literally "lack of envy," a Platonic term meaning the divine source does not hold back its goodness.</note>.

This same reality is found in another. You will ask him about his difficulties, and these things are clearly agreed upon. He will be those things where they belong to him. Everything is together There, especially from the source. In this state, Intellection is sufficient and holds a portion of the One. But it is more—or rather, it is the whole. Everything is There. This same sufficiency will come from that source, for it is the same everywhere.

Or perhaps the "worse" part belongs to Thinking, while everything There is whole. Wherever it may be, the other thing is there too. It is not as if one is looking at the One as a separate object. For one sees neither an **activity** <note>original: *energeian*</note> nor the One as an individual thing, but rather that which was allotted from the source. For that which participates while not being Being will not cause harm.

That which is directed toward the **Beautiful** <note>original: *kalon*</note> would not cease; it would be strange if it were far from the cause of the Intellect. But just as in all things, the **Infinite** <note>original: *apeiron*</note> is all. Some would call this most venerable. All other things belong to that nature. Let it be so for each. But it will stand over each. The Intellect is also within Intellection. Not only we, but all things must have Intellection. To know those things There, the One is equally all things to all, as if it were within itself.

Thus the whole is held. These things are not for all by a specific identity, but the **Light** <note>original: *phōs*</note> of Life There has come to be. For all things in the whole are equal to the others. He who is "by himself" is the same as all things. For that which these things are—of which there would be an Intellect—is not like the **form** of a body. Nor is it held in a confused way. For the Intellect is not like a **bee** <note>original: *melissan* — Plotinus uses the bee/beehive metaphor to explain how the Intellect contains many distinct Ideas without being fragmented or "confused."</note> that must be over the whole. Each is where that Intellect is.

What are these things? Each one, because of its **simplicity** <note>original: *haplotēta*</note>, possesses them. For those things There are always present to all in the same way. The Intellect holds them. All things are in all if the One is in all. The One exists if all things are in it or from it, and all things will become one in what they possess. For it is necessary that these things have a portion. For the whole is in it, and the Intellect is all things. For the objects of sense come from Intellection, and the whole is necessary. For the whole exists for the whole.

<summary>Plotinus argues that the One is an indivisible source present in all things (Life, Intellect, and Being) simultaneously without being partitioned. He uses metaphors like the chorus and the bee to explain how multiplicity exists within a unified, simple source in the Intelligible realm.</summary>

<keywords>The One, Intellect, Life, Indivisibility, Participation, The Beautiful, Simplicity, Intelligible Realm, Metaphysics, Neoplatonism</keywords>

# Enneads, Book 2

What then, if anything is the same, it must exist in difference. And the "other" must also exist in the rest of things, which it is not necessary to perceive. For either all things are beings, or the One is not a specific individual, nor is it the "self," nor even the One [as a defined object]. Rather, it is like the "One being," or the "others"; for it will not be in the future. For that which is the One itself would not even be the One within itself. For it is not as if the One consists of many parts. Therefore, the One is not something that "becomes." It is necessary that beings do not exist in any other way. These things could not be, for some are the majority, and others exist within different things. For it is not necessary for it to be in each individual one. But the One would not be in the One itself, so long as it is in each one. 
So then, is the "same" in each individual one, or does it not exist? If the One, which is also the same, exists in none of the remaining things, then the One would not exist at all. But if beings <unclear>in</unclear> perceptions exist before one another as part of the things that exist, then each one will be all things in their **substance** <note>original: *ousia* — the essential nature or "beingness" of a thing.</note>.
Therefore, every substance is in a state of continuity; these very things are the same. But it is different insofar as there are many. Children. <note>original: *paides* — this may be a metaphorical reference to "beginners" in philosophy or a specific rhetorical address.</note> For the One is also both of the things that exist. But in what way is each one so? It is in the **participation** <note>original: *methexei* — the Neoplatonic concept of lower realities "sharing in" the qualities of higher ones.</note> of the One. So the One in itself is many; but the "same" and the "other" are not within it. In the case of substance, the One is in this way, if it is something that can be participated in <unclear>in</unclear> something. For in one way it is not the One for that thing, but in another way it is also everything, just as it is not the "other," but everything and the One. But the One and the whole are the things <unclear>in</unclear> each of them, or the One is the whole. 
For in this way, the One is in each thing; but in relation to the many or <unclear>in</unclear> in the One. For each thing is always many, not by being the One, but by being in the One <unclear>itself</unclear>; because of these things, it comes into being. For it is necessary that beings exist for each thing; and these in turn exist according to themselves, so that what appears exists in themselves. Whether they will bring a cause to themselves. If indeed one throws away each thing again, he will return to them. For if they were to exist, even if he did not wish them to be, so too would each of the things belonging to others.

toward the same part. For every praiseworthy activity is for the sake of virtue and praise and for the sake of being well. We fall short in all things. But in the case of involuntary acts, there is also pain, which leads to force and the involuntary. Those acts done through want and pain cause grief because of the labor, and they fear things that are not everything. Now, what courage is, and how it relates to the voluntary and the involuntary, has been stated. For every activity and virtue, and the having of...
<margin>courage</margin>
Since courage is a mean <note>original: *mesotes* — the "Golden Mean," the virtuous middle ground between the extremes of deficiency and excess.</note> concerning confidence and fears, in the terms already stated. It is not, however, the same in both, but is rather concerned with fearful things. For he who is undisturbed in these and holds himself as he ought toward bold things is more courageous than he who is merely as he ought toward bold things. By enduring painful things, as has been said, men are called courageous. Therefore, courage is also painful, and it is justly praised; for it is harder to endure painful things than to abstain from pleasant ones.
<margin>moderation</margin>
After this, let us speak of moderation <note>original: *sophrosyne* — also translated as temperance or self-control; literally "sound-mindedness."</note>; for these virtues seem to belong to the irrational parts of the soul. We have already said that it is a mean concerning pleasures; for it is less concerned, and not in the same way, with pains. In these same things, profligacy <note>original: *akolasia* — the vice of excess regarding pleasure; the opposite of moderation.</note> also appears. Let us now define what kind of pleasures these are. Let them be divided into mental pleasures and bodily pleasures, such as the love of honor and the love of learning; for each of these people rejoices in that which he loves, without the body being affected, but rather the intellect. Those concerned with such pleasures are called neither moderate nor profligate. Likewise, neither are those concerned with other things that are not bodily. For those who love stories and are prone to narration, and who waste their days on any chance subject, we call babblers <note>original: *adoleschas* — gossips or idle talkers.</note>, but we do not call them profligate; nor do we call those who grieve over money or friends [profligate]. Moderation would be concerned with bodily pleasures, but not all of them; for those who rejoice in things seen through the sight, such as colors and shapes and paintings, are called neither moderate nor profligate. And yet it would seem possible to rejoice in these things as one ought, as well as in excess or deficiency. Likewise also in the things...

# Ennead II. 4

### On Matter

It takes something of another along with itself within its own **form**. But there is a difficulty <note>original: *aporia* — a philosophical state of being at a loss or facing an unsolvable contradiction.</note>; he says again that it was not found in any direct application. And since this is not a proof, we shall take the reception of the **form**, as though it were not in itself, to be what produces the form. He will show that the form is **infinite** <note>original: *apeiron* — meaning unbounded or lacking limit; a central concept in Neoplatonic views on matter.</note>. Whatever happens to be of the same nature occurs when the form is absent. For it participates in form because of itself, since it is infinite; and that which is stable belongs to form, though not as a promise, but as it exists within the forms; for that which is upon it...

Indeed, he says that this is the case: that not all living things participate, in which there is no **being** <note>original: *einai* — the state of true existence as opposed to mere becoming.</note>, but rather there is that which made things together with them. This does not create a type <note>original: *typon* — an imprint or stamp, like a seal in wax.</note>; and they are not so called; they are infinite when neither one nor the other exists. But it is within; the reason is that it participates in **formlessness** <note>original: *amorphia*</note>. Some things are everything. Some things are impossible. Others, again, are **otherness** <note>original: *heterotes* — the principle of being "different" which Plotinus uses to explain how matter recedes from the One.</note>, not even the things that are impossible. Of these, some are accidental; again, they are the same. Or of what kind? Because it is not form itself. But because it is everything, it is itself. Or it is all things. Others, again, are what follows.

In that which is **matter** <note>original: *hyle*</note>, there is also the fact of being in these "angles" <note>likely a geometric metaphor for the specific positions or constraints of physical existence.</note>; for instance, not by the "not" but by the "different," or by the fact that not even the differing things, or the same things, exist. Or that, again, it is all or what follows. For that which is in these is not from itself, nor in all, nor in the whole, nor in a "where" that is not even a whole, but rather it is the things within. For the **rational principle** <note>term: *logos* — the formative, organizing force that flows from the Divine Intellect into matter.</note> is in the form. And there is no "still more," such as the things within being. But it is necessary for all things, even those without form within the form, to be the offspring of others or as much as is needed. But in the **infinite**, it belongs to the form.

There is, again, a reason regarding **matter** and being. That when what is in it is not there at all, they would neither possess essence nor would they **shine** <note>Plotinus frequently uses the metaphor of light: matter is a dark mirror that only "exists" when the light of the Forms reflects off it.</note>. But upon which it neither is nor exists, whenever it comes from motion or exists according to itself, or is not even as is likely. Individual things do not exist by being the same, as they are at a loss. Either the being of the **accidents** <note>original: *symbebekoton* — non-essential qualities that happen to a substance.</note> within it, or not even itself. But again, it is always becoming infinite. The remaining things of each. We might hold these ourselves. Those things which follow it suffered, and are created. Some will exceed; to have the same things; see how he always says: that...

The reason of **essence** <note>original: *ousia* — the true substance or "being-ness" of a thing.</note>. For if it is because it is into the most things, then the quality of good order is entirely something similar. Still, there is the matter of being left behind. It makes everything. It was said that it is either by the **reason** alone. He might say. Or since that which possesses that, how did it come through that one? Neither will those things be. Nor is it for all of them. Nor for those still upon them, because, and entirely. (As if both were everything; again it produces motion. Or to be entirely there as well. How, or where, or for all. Or where then will it be; because. Or how, or entirely. For what kind of things are those in the form? And will there be certain things of it, just as there is **matter**?

The text appears to be a Neoplatonic commentary on Aristotle’s *De Anima*, specifically the famous definition of the soul as the "first entelechy of a natural organic body." The author uses classical Aristotelian analogies to explain that the soul is to the body what sight is to the eye.

<meta>This page transitions from the general discussion of "imprints" and "qualities" in the soul (from the previous page) to a specific technical analysis of how the soul acts as the organizing principle of the body. While the manuscript is attributed to Plotinus, the content here is a rigorous commentary on Aristotle’s *De Anima* (Book II, Chapter 1), likely following the tradition of later Neoplatonic commentators who sought to harmonize Aristotle's biology with Platonic metaphysics.</meta>

# · On the Sixth ·

...by means of an instrument <note>original: *organon* — the Greek word for both a physical tool and a biological organ.</note>, we refer to the lives of the soul, such as the **perceptive** lives and the others which are **intellectual**. For it is in this way that they participate [in life]. For if it were not so, how could such lives be considered "organic"? He will say that every **form** <note>original: *morphē*</note> is distinguished before the creature is actually alive, and these forms include the perceptive and the intellectual. For every form, by virtue of its specific kind, creates an image of itself within the underlying **matter**. Prior to the life of the soul, there would not be any other form by which the body could be given its essential being.

Indeed, this is all the more true since we say the soul is an **incorporeal reason**, a power, a **form**, and an **entelechy** <note>original: *entelecheia* — a technical term in Aristotle meaning the "completion" or "full reality" of a potentiality; the soul is the "actuality" of the body.</note>. Observe how the form belongs to the matter, and the instrument belongs to the form. But the soul does not belong to the matter; it belongs to the **body**, and specifically to an **organic** body. Form, on the other hand, belongs to matter.

How then is the soul a form? Is matter then distinguished? No, but rather matter, having life as its form, cannot be life unless it is organic. If matter possesses no other form, whether we call it "being" or "shape," how could there be two forms? For the form which makes the body organic does not leave the matter. How then is the instrument prior to the form? We might say it exists as something already generated. Having stated the cause regarding that which is generated, he moves toward the generated thing itself; this exists in the whole and also in the part.

There is a form, as it were, in the part, belonging to the generated soul; and perhaps it exists by turns in the generated part. And this applies to the whole, as in the case of the **body**, and to the part, as in the case of the **eye**. "If," he says, "the eye were a living creature, **sight** would be its soul." <note>This is a direct quote from Aristotle’s *De Anima* 412b18-20, explaining that sight is the "essence" or "soul" of the eye.</note> Since the "being" of the eye is sight, if sight should fail, it is no longer an eye, except **homonymously** <note>original: *homonymōs* — meaning it shares the name but not the definition, like the difference between a real eye and a stone one.</note>, just as we speak of a stone eye or a painted one. If this holds for the part, it must hold for the whole body; for the cause is the same. If the body were a living creature, the soul would be its entelechy—that is to say, the **perceptive life** of the body—and this is the cause of the body being alive. <gloss>is distinguished</gloss> the forms before it is a living creature, insofar as it is perceptive and intellectual. For by this, the soul is thought to be the form of the organs.

<column-break/>

Having thus stated the cause of it, he says one must speak regarding the individual parts. It is as if one were to say of the **serpent** <note>original: *ophis*</note> that it is not merely a "length" simply because it lacks hands or feet. Having said this, if it were not so, the same logic would apply there. He caused the distinction of this to emerge: it is not a serpent because it lacks hands or feet, but because it possesses its own specific form. Having said this, just as **sight** is to the eye, so is the **soul** to the whole living body.

<margin>( 7 )</margin>
And this is how the matter stands: one part concerns the specific member, the other the whole. Again, sight comes from a power, while the whole soul comes from the whole body. And just as in that case, if sight is lost, it is no longer an eye; so here, if the soul is lost, the body is no longer a living thing, but is so only **homonymously**. Just as a stone eye is not an eye, neither is the body any longer a living thing, but a **corpse** <note>original: *ptōma* — literally "that which has fallen."</note>. For the corpse is not a body, except in name; for it no longer possesses "being" insofar as it is a body.

<margin>...</margin>
And again, the living body is not that which has cast off the soul, but that which possesses it. Now, **seeds** and **fruits** are bodies in **potentiality**. The rest has not been said; or perhaps there would not be any other form. For being is not left to the matter as a form, insofar as it is organic. And indeed, if he were providing the distinction by which the soul belongs to the body—namely, the forms of the body themselves—then it would be distinguished in this way, just as it was before the form was introduced. He mentioned the **serpent** as a reason drawn from something else to provide proof of life. And if its form is such, then it is the forms themselves. For in this way it would be distinguished, just as it was before bringing in the form.

No one would say the whole [definition] is sufficient. He said also in the sense-perception, casting away the definition, and no one knows what it is and the differences themselves.
