# ## On Being VI

What constitutes a **quality** <note>original: *poion* — the category of "how" a thing is, its characteristics or traits.</note>, and does it reside in states and affections? Someone might already suggest that the training itself is knowledge, or learning, but that it should be called a quality. But does this apply to the productive art or the thing itself? It does not signify. The **differences** <note>original: *diaphorai* — the specific characteristics that distinguish one species from another within a genus.</note> between intermediate things are proper to their not being a single genus. For example, "white" seems to be an opposite to "black." Every other thing is an opposite, for not all things are subject to the same genus. Furthermore, when one takes a quality before a genus, it is as I say: in **quantity** <note>original: *poson* — the category of size, number, or magnitude.</note>, things are grasped by knowledge. But those belonging to that cause are grasped differently. These differences follow it, and according to the hypothesis, they follow the quality. If it is no longer possible to differentiate by that generic difference between differences, it would be false to take it so. But where is the quantity equal, since the unequal is by means of the equal? Things are said to be **similar** by nature. Or let it be said partially. If they are called similar, it is because **similarity** is a being "alike" in quality. Perhaps in this, it belongs to the intermediate things.

That which is similar to it, quality itself depends upon. It was necessary for all quality to be in it. You must predicate "similar" of the thing itself. But is there an image of quality within it? One must do otherwise, for it is not equal to itself. If someone defines these—for example, surface and property—as belonging to those genera, where does quantity have a quality? If a person taking "similar" participates in quality, it is insofar as the differences are in it. Generally, not all things have **completing differences** <note>original: *sympleromatikas diaphorai* — these are "constitutive" differences that make a thing what it is, essentially forming part of its substance.</note> of the "different"; there is an appearance when the difference is a rule. If one wants the **accidental** <note>original: *symptotike* — a contingent or non-essential property that "happens" to a thing but does not define its essence.</note> nature of the **substance** <note>original: *ousia* — the fundamental "being" or "essence" of a thing.</note>, it might be in one thing and not another, or by accident. These things are indeed accidental, and one will not grasp them by negation. But they complete the substance, in a certain way for them. But these things were hidden. For the sake of acting, we receive a certain quality. And that seems to bear witness: that equal things in quantity should not be sciences. And in all things signified, [one looks] to the "where" or the "out of place." So that quantity is a certain something, universally a property. But the "similar" comes upon it from those things and
<margin>concerning quality</margin>
does not have its own property. What sort of quality is that quality, as it exists for them by mixing matter and fire? It mixes the difference; it is an effect. If it should seem to participate in quality, it is this. Or it is in them, but rather of the quality. And the qualified thing is whatever it is, or rather what is signified. Or it is shown by metaphor, since the sun is all of it. Or being is transferred to "acting" by being in nature, or altogether—

<column-break/>

—not the definition, what sort of thing it is to be. And the same things belong to the "acting" of being a certain thing; the same is true of a painting. It is said to exist in colors themselves, being mixed with them. This exists in life, universally and continuously. The "more" is continuous. It has something from the temporal. It is able to have it by my saying it does not participate. And to speak of this, it is an unchangeable **reason** <note>original: *logos* — here meaning the rational principle or formative force.</note> of the "always," and it is predicated of itself. These things are so, nonetheless. Each thing being taken, apart from certain others shown by the logical process, is a quality. As for being in a pattern, if indeed it is. From where it happens. He says that they differ in themselves. If, as if from where it is clear, it exists with **virtue** <note>original: *aretes* — moral or intellectual excellence.</note> itself. For it signifies an easy **character** <note>original: *ethei* — the habitual disposition or moral nature of a person.</note>, and yet not even from that. It appears that nothing is in the "white." But I speak also of that which is in quality and quantity. For nothing [is there]. Or it completes the "visible." And yet, according to the things that come to be, or ever will be. If the whole belongs to the **soul** <note>original: *psyche* — the animating spirit that Plotinus views as the bridge between the material and the divine.</note>. Because of itself, it is another quality. But if the same thing is in the soul or present in it. Or even in itself, it does not "act" as a quality.

The same thing, by its existing state. For example, if there is an existence, for some time, to give them back. Like cases in the [soul]. There are **affections** <note>original: *pathe* — passive experiences, emotions, or changes undergone by a subject.</note> in matter, where there is some pattern under them. But when they have it so, it is from those things. For example, concerning the affections. For they are separable. It is an appearance of the soul, or the soul itself. These are **sensible things** <note>original: *aistheta* — things perceived through the senses as opposed to the intellect.</note> in light. Or even they themselves are individual substances, but in no way does it wish them to be disordered. Unless, as in the opposite, it is against the will. But not itself—the [qualities] of those things before the **body** <note>original: *soma* — the physical vessel of the soul.</note> or clearly. Having been illuminated, that thing is itself, through having understood, and those things in that same quality are hidden. It grasps those things of the soul itself, alongside the **intelligible** <note>original: *noeton* — the realm of pure thought and the Forms, accessible only to the mind.</note> by those underneath. And indeed, in the middle, the nature of all things is causally directed toward **happiness** <note>original: *eudaimonia* — the state of flourishing or supreme well-being.</note>. Those [qualities] of the soul, being ignorant of bodies, the **immovable things** <note>original: *akineta* — the eternal, unchanging realities or Forms.</note> arrive. Therefore time restrains them, or they are ensouled.
<margin>it is indeed</margin>
But especially, because even the "beautiful" seems to be, in the same quality, universal. There it is not perhaps there, so that an irregularity is established in the presences already as **political** or **practical ideas**. At any rate, the one who entwines the soul. It is also well-reasoned, because each must be presented according to the [reason]. Of a life that has been lived, an **alteration** <note>original: *alloiosin* — a change in quality rather than substance.</note> must necessarily occur. And through this, evil comes to it. They follow more by our will upon them. Let it be the soul and the things of the body. For not even if there is a reason is it glorious to change position, or to not have being. But it always seems to be before the body.

<meta>This page continues the examination of Plotinus’s "Ennead VI," specifically focusing on the second and third books where he critiques Aristotelian categories. # ## On Being VI

...are **qualities** <note>original: *poiotetes*</note>, they can immediately be distinguished by their **forms** <note>original: *eidesi* — the specific types or "species" that define a thing's nature.</note>. For we cannot say that qualities are common merely to the heat of fire, nor again merely to the coldness of snow, but rather that every quality happens to be in the **underlying subject** <note>original: *hypokeimeno* — the substrate or matter that "stands under" the qualities.</note>. For the cause is not divided into parts as if it were a single indivisible quality, but one part of it is in the fire, and another in the subject.

There are many qualities, and it seems this is why they are not all the same. If one were to ask what kind they are, one might say they are "the same." But these are not the same as those which are **accidents** <note>original: *symbebekota* — properties that happen to belong to a thing but are not essential to its definition.</note> of the subject. Hence, there are not even the same powers in those things which can be common, among which all the qualities also belong. Among these, it is said, there are such things as **psychic** and **bodily** <note>original: *psychikai kai somatikai* — referring to qualities of the soul, such as virtues or knowledge, versus those of the body, such as health or complexion.</note>, as one might call the qualities.

It is reasonable to call qualities from **substance** <note>original: *ousias* — the core "being" or essence of a thing.</note>, so that we might name qualities both individually and universally. Indeed, they place qualities within substances. But they name only the **differences** <note>original: *diaphoras* — the specific traits that distinguish one species from another within a genus</note> as such. It is clear that every quality is a difference, but it does not follow that it returns the nature of substances to their causes. Such things are clear. Therefore, he spoke clearly, saying: it is possible to seek the differences and the qualities, and how many the differences are, since the term "qualities" has been used, whether common or proper.

In another way, the matter seems to say that the differences are held in this way and are either joined to substances or separate. But if the same qualities are in many things, how could one speak of the "one" being present in many, or how could there be some that are common and some that are differences? And indeed, quality would again be a certain **genus** <note>original: *genos* — a broad category or family of things.</note>, since it is not substance itself, but a "substance from substance," yet it belongs to substance again. There are both "bad" and "good" qualities. For they accept every use, even if they are the causes of qualities. Wherefore he said the differences are linked to these; it will be the magnitude of the difference itself. But do not let this be a **sensible affection** <note>original: *aistheton pathos* — a feeling or physical change perceived by the senses.</note> because of this.

But if someone were to speak of two qualities, through which on the one hand there is a difference, and through which on the other there is an opposite multitude of qualities, these will be disputed if anyone seeks their source, or if you are to be of a certain mind. For there will be again a difference of form. But if someone asks, how is it not necessary? Because not every quality comes to be, nor could it perhaps be said. Some say this is substance itself, while others say these are the qualities. These are not strictly sensible, but are derived from those things which are "of a certain kind." It is possible, then, to produce **knowledge** <note>original: *epistemēn*</note>, just as one might speak of the comparison with affections and powers, both those from which and out of which the "quality" arose, just as the **reason-principle** <note>original: *logos* — the formative, rational force that organizes matter into specific shapes or types</note> takes up their differences. One must use it, and instead of reason-principles, establish the thing itself. And before the genus stands the **Soul**.

<column-break/>

...sprouting out from their opinion. For that which is common to all, to those... And all things are thus in a way the things that differ toward the first things and the causes. And if indeed many things are supposed to differ because of this. But even more things exist. But not the same things apply to the results themselves—I mean, for example, that it is necessary to take the differences in **blood** <note>original: *aimata*</note> separately. The reason-principle is for the sake of the differences, if we speak of them. For because the **flesh** <note>original: *sarx*</note> belongs to that, there is also the "all-ness," nor is it possible to take the qualities of the difference in this way. Except that they also differ in their souls. Whence also the same opinions are in their power. Whence, again, it is not possible for the differences to speak or to speak in vain, as if because of opinions. But not even because the opinion is here, and for them, in that way.

For either it is not the same thing to speak of substances, because this too is substance. But it was also necessary for the parts to produce the differences. For he, these men are the causes and produce such things. And to immediately speak of qualities. For not every species is one. Whence there are as many things as one might find in the qualities, they will be even more refined and the "all" exists. But how is it possible to see them? For this appears: every difference might become every sort, for instance... to cause pain. But it seems to be said, toward the same and the same, the differences of some things come to be, or even as things that have not been produced or are partial. How? For many things come to be from certain souls. But not from partial ones. There is an agreement whence differences do not arise even in the many. These things of the difference and this substance, or those things as the same.

But if these things are said from this, it was possible for some to act in this way. For instance, what kind of quality? For he might have spoken recently. And indeed toward the affections and the things, let it be said. So that other things might become quality, qualities do not differ. For power appears there to the things of the difference, not to be a quality. But he calls the difference "quality." Because the **sweet** <note>original: *glykys*</note> is broad, while the **bitter** <note>original: *pikron*</note> is harmful, the same man says this is the difference. By nature the sweet is thick, for which reason one would not call it greater. Because the "sweet" is not even a property of this. But because it is sweetness. There is, therefore, a cause of the same reason-principle. And not everywhere is there a certain position of difference of quality, not being qualities. In this way every substance also. Nor is the producer a quality. For either it also produces the difference in the living being. Or the body in this way. But they differ by the greatest amount. For how could the difference produce a substance for them? But not even to produce anything in qualities by a partial difference. At least if he also called other things causes. By quality conversely, but as if he produces it by taking it as a whole. Or thus he spoke of the cause. Whence...

# ## Ethics, Book VI

Excellence in deliberation <note>original: *euboulia* — refers to the quality of deliberating well to achieve a good end.</note> is not the same as opinion <note>original: *doxa*</note>. For everyone would be in control of the same things about which there is opinion. One also brings conviction <note>original: *pistin*</note> through reason <note>original: *logou*</note>. And all otherness is complete and distinct, whether in the causes or elsewhere. Furthermore, order exists for all things, both the universal and the particular, and these relate to one another. This again relates to cause. This is so that the universal does not, as it were, separate one lack of sensation from another, but remains within those things. The lesser, which does not signify anything else, will show everything that is. But if the difference exists only in the cause or in the objects of sense, it is itself simultaneously a voice. <meta>This page transitions from the ethical considerations of practical wisdom into a technical ontological investigation of motion and change. While the previous page drew upon the Nicomachean Ethics, this text analyzes the physical and metaphysical definitions of movement, likely engaging with Aristotle’s Physics to clarify how the soul or intellect might be said to "move" compared to physical objects.</meta>

->### Contemplation 6<-

<margin>6</margin> Self-motion <note>original: *he ex hautou kinesis*</note> is a transition from something into something. Furthermore, while there are many kinds of changes, motion is not identical to all of them; for generation <note>original: *genesis* — the process of coming-to-be</note> and corruption <note>original: *phthora* — the process of passing away</note> are indeed changes, but they are not motions. For to change is not in every case to move. If it were, then even "non-being" <note>original: *to me on*</note> would be said to change. However, it is "being" that moves, or that in which motion occurs; but non-being is not "in being"—that is, it does not exist in the state of being—and therefore it cannot move. Nevertheless, all change consists of that from which the motion begins and that into which it moves. What then is the "whole," if it is change but not entirely motion? As he says again: that which passes into being from a state of contradiction <note>i.e., from not-being to being</note> would not be motion, but generation. Indeed, things that are in the process of becoming are moving, but things are not in motion *before* they have come to be, such that there would be an underlying subject <note>original: *hypokeimenon* — the substance that persists through change</note> which was formerly non-being.
Nor would this be a simple negation, nor a partial contradiction. Let it be, then, that things which change are "changes" in a certain manner. But a change into non-being would not be a motion toward non-being, but rather a
<margin>7</margin> certain corruption; or it is a transition from one contradiction to another, where one is generation and the other is corruption. If, therefore, non-being
does not exist, how is a change of motion judged, and does motion remain among the things that "are"? Since, then,
motion exists among beings, it is necessary that the existing motions be of three kinds: those according to quality <note>original: *poioteta*</note>—such as the changes
of the passions <note>original: *pathe* — internal states or emotions</note> and their avoidance or decrease. For some say that motions, from which beings arise,
are the clear manifestations of the generation of things, or at the very least, they take them to be "substance" <note>original: *ousian*</note>.
<margin>mark</margin> But why is there neither generation nor motion of substance? For those things which are
capable of motion lie parallel to one another, and all changes belong to them, except for substance itself; this is what is said concerning substance. Some argue it
has no contrary. If motion is toward that which is "not the whole," and everything is its opposite, then what of
substances, or the differences of quality or quantity? For there are certain objections;
<margin>all</margin> either there is a change of motion, or there is not. Some also say that there is no generation or
corruption of the underlying reality <note>original: *hypostaseos*</note>. But these two occur when alteration <note>original: *alloiosis*</note> is outside the underlying subject, and they do not
<margin>according to</margin> occur in the whole body but in something else. For in that way, it would be generation. But the change
of these things by <unclear>absurdities</unclear> or being generation—it is not through them <unclear>to be</unclear> toward the changes, because
some exist, and because things according to nature are different, either toward the greater or toward the worse.
These things, as if they were themselves, do not exist in those things where they are found. They say that things according to the passions are "alteration,"
treating the passions as being against nature. For change itself, and being altered toward—
either of men or women. Furthermore, there will be the characteristics of motions; and further, those of change according to another,
each of the passions being against nature. Or rather, it does not exist toward the same thing in that which possesses
the other without being able. Doing nothing manifest, but being a motion according to the whole;
for the things within it admit of changes; for the same part <unclear>is not able</unclear> to be. But certainly
not upon the motion, when they are not present. For neither is there generation, for otherwise it would not have come to be.

<summary>This page analyzes the distinction between "motion" and "change," arguing that while all motion is change, processes like birth (generation) and death (corruption) are not motions because they involve the transition from non-being to being. It further explores why substance itself is not subject to motion, which instead occurs in the categories of quality and quantity.</summary>

And indeed, the matter of chance—as we have already stated—arises because nature acts spontaneously <note>original: *automaton* — referring to events that occur of themselves without a deliberate purpose or final cause</note>. For the majority bear witness, even more than the individuals, that there are more things beyond nature's scope, and we must ask if we can speak of them in the same way. This quality is common, not merely in the sense we described, but in the cause behind things that occur by chance. For there is a cause through which things happen to us, either by some impulse or otherwise. What these are, they have clearly seemed to be: a stroke of good fortune <note>original: *eutychema* — a successful outcome attributed to luck rather than skill</note> comes to be. We speak of chance or "good fortune" as the highest kind of success; yet a stroke of luck does not necessarily follow the things that accompany it, so that chance might exist again and again. But for "to happen upon" <note>original: *tychein* — the verb form of chance, meaning to hit a mark or succeed by luck</note> to be directed toward serious matters, and for the sequence after this to follow, one must grant that hitting upon serious things provides a benefit. These things, then, are considered strokes of luck in relation to what is serious; for chance is a kind of action. But hitting the mark is to be "fortunate" among the things mentioned. Yet, due to the removal of fortunes, the grace of God <note>original: *theou charis* — divine favor or providence</note> brings many things along with it, or far from them, as the things arising from them. # Ennead VI

**Column 1**

If, therefore, every nature is in its order among the things within the One Being, and in its powers it is always placed as if it does not belong to itself, then it does not exist at all. But if something were left out among the parts of Being, and these parts were not the same but individual, yet the whole was in all of them, then it would certainly already be Being. According to its entire order, it would be wise, and it would be the same as that which has come to be in all the things of Being and in all things; it is placed everywhere. And so it seems to me that it remains in each other <note>original: *allēlois* — Plotinus is describing the interpenetration of real beings.</note> according to what is necessary for Being itself and for the whole, and it exists everywhere. For it is not diminished. But now it is separated from itself. If, therefore, it is a wonder how it is in all things, it is because it is already in this way. It is not "inside." Therefore, those of old advise us to live according to sympathy <note>original: *sympatheia* — the cosmic principle that all parts of the universe are interconnected and "feel" together.</note> with Being in its kind, but perhaps as a whole. Nor is Being itself before itself, but with whom would it be? It would seem like a pouring out. For the rest, every part of it is as if wandering. 

Marvel at Being, for it is not in a place, yet everything in a place is not without it; it is a whole wonder to them. If it were separated, it would not be in all things before it was "not," alongside that which is in a place. But if it becomes the reason <term>logos</term> <note>The formative principle or "blueprint" that organizes matter.</note> for all existing parts, it is not necessary for it to be proportional in all things, more as a whole than as a part. To everything, it is the whole, as if to an infinite whole. If it holds itself, or is with those things, it is not by being divided. For if someone were to look above, every part remains. You will not divide life, but life itself remains, and the part is a second life. One does not think with a part, but with another <unclear>...</unclear> but the whole is within him. But whether it is a part or a whole, one does not know. What then if it is divided again? For if not even one is as it was. Is it a part or a whole? But if it is one, is it not the whole? Is it not the whole in every case? According to the body. But many things are equal to it, but not as if it were the whole; therefore they are not truly beings. It dwells within; and there are many souls, yet it is a whole from it, and they are not of the same form. It is a marvel; and yet it is indivisible, according to the ancients. And all at once in this way, there are more than seem to be, and if not, what would it be of those things that are absent? It is a necessity of the art, or of some other education. # Euclid, Book 5

->**Euclid . 5**<-

If it is possible [for something] to be not rational in itself, but in such a way that its powers are rational. But again, this is not the cause. Rather, since opinion <note>original: *doxa* — often meaning "seeming" or "appearance" in Plotinus’s thought</note> follows what is by nature, it is clear to us that one might consider things according to their surface appearance, from which the cause of this perception arises. So it is that we participate in the formative principle <term>logos</term> <note>The rational order or blueprint that governs the physical world.</note>, and each thing does not fail to possess bulk <note>original: *onkos* — a technical term for physical mass, volume, or spatial extension, which Plotinus contrasts with the soul's non-spatial nature.</note>; yet to the left it is possible to see the things from it, either as a waking reality or by its influence. Neither are those things which exist through bulk moved in a circle, and one bulk will shine through toward another bulk in front of it. Similarly, as a cause, the images <note>original: *eidola* — semblances or reflections that lack the true reality of the source.</note> are strong, but even so, this is not their own property. For when one rather considers the things prior to the passion <note>original: *pathos* — here meaning a physical sensation or "being acted upon" by an external stimulus.</note>, say that the remaining things are neither in the soul nor outside the body. Regarding how bodies belong to the soul, or if it colors bulk through bulk, it will appear as the same lips of the thing itself. But as for what remains of the bulk, when it has come to be, sensation <note>original: *aisthesis*</note> does not possess bulk. Behold, that body has lost its form. Either it never had it, or it belongs to bodies that have been affected. But if the eyes are condensed by sight, the cause of the body of these same souls is seen toward itself, and these are the lights of the soul. But the lesson, or rather for those who have been affected: how is it then that they are not produced even after the act of sight? Of the images, those affected within the bulk, or that which is the same as the image, so that the sensations are different. If these things do not belong to both, the difference is grasped. So it is not something in motion; thus it is less. And that which is less, just like motion, seems to be about the images, both the shape and the things that exist. For they say that symmetrical images belong to one another. But if the "whatness" is the same, then bulk is in that thing and in the spirit <term>pneuma</term> <note>In ancient optics, *pneuma* or "optical spirit" was thought to be a subtle substance that traveled from the eye to the object.</note>. But beyond the limit, he says that sight says the same things about the passions. And the image is ensouled. But the reasoning might not grasp this. This is the cause for both. In many places, the reason says that when they are situated thus, they do not have the bulk of passion. He said that these things are not so in themselves, but rather they act. And how are they themselves from it? This remains: how he likened it to grasping oneself, when nothing acts upon him, being intertwined. In itself, sight is upon sight, dividing the bodies of the things there. But many things also divide. Here, nothing is necessary. And that thing is toward the sight after them. It will appear as the sun’s, so that these same things, when light is upon the whole earth, are from the sun, not looking at the sun at all. But nevertheless, the lights educate. Because of this, a bright myriad is brought down, or rather not, from where it has come, or what is left in the form. From which, the power remaining upon the sights gives color, and it is light, whenever light is upon all. But how then is it sight? But light is always everywhere in each, it is not; it is disposed with it and toward the sight. It is like light. So that the sight of light, as if being molded by the sight, is neither because it is where it is. It is impossible that it exists, unless it were to become light. Thus also the light, having suffered from light.

The good things were left for him. Or rather, and even more truly, the divine will is by nature directed toward good things, proceeding from such gods. And by apportioning it, and the one who divides it—these are among those who participate. Or nonetheless, one clearly participates in them alone, yet they are not participated in by Him. For it must be through another again. When, therefore, it remains in others, it does not become a whole; but some of His gifts, and again in those things of His, many divide Him who is undivided. # · Concepts ·

<margin>(6</margin> This account, and this reasoning regarding the soul, he says, comes from the ancients; yet following his own path rather than theirs would be more fitting. For nature did not grant such gifts to the mortal. If the whole is established, and belongs to the universal living being <note>original: *zoon tou pantos* — the "World Animal" or the cosmos viewed as a single, living, ensouled organism</note>, then either all is in all, or if my soul is not in all, what kind of soul is it? Or what is this that draws the weight <note>original: *baryteta* — gravity or the physical heaviness associated with material existence</note> of the universe, or attracts it entirely? It must impart itself from itself. If, therefore, the soul should encompass the whole through some superiority, it would be the living being itself. But if the whole itself lacks nothing, but is the complete whole, it would happen that it is diminished by that from which it happened to be. Thus, it seems he who restrained the causes of all virtue being pleasing to God to cool down was raising it from the opinion of wisdom. When he transfers the cause of these goods and refers them elsewhere, there is no defense. And why was he ever present in the causes? That too had to be; but if it were not, nothing would be necessary. The goods of the better are "evil" only because the higher might be left behind by not always carrying the better. If, therefore, the whole does not happen to be "evil," then this [evil] exists in the mortal nature just as it does in all the individual parts. Thus, it is not the case that the part is always the whole. For one part of this does not serve the other. But regarding the individual parts, in which all things live and yet nothing lives, they act for themselves. Only those things among which there is preservation exist as the whole does, as if by nature. From where does the release come, unless as a good for oneself? There, from where it was generated. Nature is a necessity, since the existence of evils occurred, if this was the state of the soul’s being; just as wealth appears as a universal good to all, being a cause for itself. But it is to live the life of another, that one’s life. In this way, the whole being from the soul exists through the necessity of philosophical doctrines. It would not be so beneficial—those things which are not due to nature but the individual parts and their reasons. For it was likely profitable. They follow their own nature according to law. But if he extends himself as a good toward the same as the whole. ### VI: On whether Being, if it is one, is at the same time everywhere whole;

That each individual body <note>Note: the Greek text here uses *soma* (body), though the treatise title usually refers to *on* (Being)</note> is everywhere present as a whole is, as they say, a common notion <note>original: *koine ennoia* — a Stoic and Platonic term for universal truths inherent in human reason</note>; when all people, prompted by the god within them, say that the God in each of us is one and the same. But if one were to demand the cause of this doctrine, how and in what way are there "gods" by this doctrine? And again, through the false. Or is it not that God is this to the whole? Now and again, if it is not so, how is the whole joined together? He who seeks its unity also knows this. And among all, it is the most firmly held opinion, or even itself

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s metaphysical inquiry into how the One or the Good can be present in all things without being divided. While the previous page touched upon the soul and the nature of "evil" as a lack of the higher, this section shifts toward a more abstract discussion of Being (Ousia) and its relationship to space and participation. It corresponds to portions of Ennead VI, specifically Treatise 4: "On the Presence of Being, One and Identical, Everywhere as a Whole."</meta>

# . Ennead VI .

<note>This text contains numerous complex Byzantine-style Greek ligatures, which were common in 16th-century printings and manuscripts of Plotinus's work. These often compress words like "estin" (is) or "kai" (and) into decorative symbols.</note>

...is, it is especially for all things to belong to it and to need it; and if you should wish it so, all things participate in it at once. For wherever one might grasp it, it is already there, and it does not stand apart from itself. It remains for itself, not as if it occupied a place <note>original: *topon* — Plotinus is emphasizing that the Divine/Being does not take up physical space like a body does</note> where it was, or as if it were sustained by itself, but it is in that in which it exists simultaneously. Since that source also comes from itself, it is nowhere; rather, it is, it is, it is <note>original: *esti, esti, esti* — this repetition emphasizes the eternal, unchanging existence of the primary principle</note>, whoever it may be. It does not exist in a localized way; just as we might say even now, <unclear>editorial: illegible ligature</unclear> I mean it is like a bloom within us, and we are grown from it. 

The one that is in all things would be known in this way: if it is truly the Good <note>original: *to agathon* — the supreme principle in Neoplatonism, often synonymous with the One</note>, it enjoys its own state. It is its own will not to be confined to a single thing, nor to undergo even a single change, even while being in many things at once. Insofar as it belongs to itself, it is not "everywhere" in the sense of being scattered across itself; rather, it is in many things simultaneously. And this is not like a face <note>original: *prosopon* — here meaning a mask or a singular appearance</note>, which presents a single appearance to itself; rather, it is in all things that very thing in which it exists. It is a unique characteristic of that source not to be shared out in pieces. For that which acts as a cause from that very source provides both itself and the things it creates. Since it is One, it must necessarily follow that it is there too; for the One is at once nowhere outside of things, because it begins alongside all things, or rather because it does not originate from anywhere else. 

Each thing is like true Being <note>original: *to ontos einai*</note>, and the furthest reaches of reality are present as well. But if the furthest reach stands still, not participating in the whole, then it is not the whole, even if it is simultaneously with all things. If no part of it were separated, then nothing would be lost. 

If participation <note>term: *metéchein* — a Platonic concept describing how physical things "take part" in the perfect eternal Forms</note> meant taking away a piece of something, then the same whole could not possibly be in all things. But he said that the Good is separate and yet divides; it is from there that this simultaneity arises. For he said that the Good is not merely in another place. And from this we see that it would not be the Good if it were not so. The whole would not be whole, or each thing would be a whole, or a part. But it is a part not in the sense of the nature of the whole <note>original: *physei*</note>, because nothing is truly a part there. 

If each thing is a whole, or if each thing participates in Being so as to be, it will cease to be a whole if it is not possible for it to be everywhere. Because it is a whole, it will be attributed to Being itself or to Essence <note>term: *ousia* — the underlying "substance" or "reality" of a thing</note>; it would not exist if it did not belong to that nature. And now it seems this is also the case within Being. 

Under the One, nothing would appear to exist separately. If someone were to forge an axiom, as it seemed, wherever they might speak of it, they would be speaking of it in that same Being, not as things existing everywhere. In this way it would appear, and it would perhaps seem to be so. For he would say: it is not that which is divided. For one would not perceive the infinity <note>original: *to apeiranton* — the unbounded or infinite nature of the Divine</note> of that same self, but rather the same thing which is in all. It itself is here and nowhere else; but the former view regarding the "many" cuts off the simultaneity. Since it is this way, the whole was not in Being in that [divided] manner.

<summary>Plotinus explores the paradox of how the Good and true Being can be present in all things simultaneously without being fragmented or diminished. He argues that participation in the Divine does not mean taking a "piece" of it, but rather being connected to a whole that remains unified and infinite.</summary>

Folio 220 contains the opening of the treatise traditionally titled "On the Presence of Being, One and Identical, Everywhere as a Whole (Part 2)." The previous page established that the Divine/Being does not occupy a specific location like a physical body; this page explores how multiple things can participate in that one Reality without dividing it.</meta>

## ## On how Being, one and the same, is everywhere whole.

If, then, the same thing is incorporeal, and if in the heavens that which is perceived by the senses <note>original: *aistheton* — the material world available to our eyes and ears, as opposed to the purely intellectual world</note> is a state agreeable to it, we must nevertheless consider it to be the same, and that the same thing is everywhere whole at once. For each individual thing is a participation <note>original: *metoche* — a key Platonic concept where material things "take part in" or reflect a higher ideal Form</note> in that whole; because of this, some say that the parts are one, or that they ought to be. But if nothing participates, then it does not truly exist. If it does participate, it nevertheless exists, and generally, Being is whole and one. For that which is truly called "above," the One, would belong to itself. If it did not come from the One, it would not exist. That which has come into being is therefore connected to each thing. From that which participates, all things participate in that which they have received. For it is not among the things that do not exist, but among the things in Being; for it is necessary to be persuaded that it is like a single sphere. If it were separated from its centers, it might receive something of those things drawn to it, but it is necessary that they be of the same kind; wherever they have participated, it is placed in the whole of everything. For even if it is for the sake of something, as if in many things, or as is the custom in cities. How is it also placed in lines? And from where does it have its nature from of old? The lines are together, these places, to speak briefly, and according to the same thing, they are not entirely separate lines, because they are bright. If, then, the One exists as Being, it does not participate in opinion according to a single part, but one must say they are incorporeal <note>original: *asomata* — things without physical bodies, such as thoughts, souls, or mathematical truths</note>, and it was necessary to say all these things are the same, in that they exist everywhere entirely. But which of these are the written things, and which are the beings within the written things? For indeed, they are gods and all things. For a long time such lines have existed, and some of them are raised up by themselves, or left to each. To each indeed, but what? Or must we believe in each for all? Because of this, that which is cut off participates in the first One. It is necessary then for these things to exist, and to be at the same time. If, then, all things and the sensible things—all beings—are in the One, and are persuaded to be distinct, it is one whole; or some appear through the lines, so that they might come into being from it, but in the same place, and these lines would all be together as one thing. It has an analogy: since the first nature is not clearly seen, it is a great wonder to all. This is great or primary. By position. If, then, all things are what he says. If it is many, it is the one which is on the surface. If, then, these things are so. Since regarding the whole again, I contemplate power <note>original: *dynamis* — the inherent potential or "energy" of a thing</note>, together with the whole. It is said to be a part of it, which we first found how to measure. But the whole is left behind. It is like that from which the One, the whole above, which is not itself Being in relation to generation. From where he himself is in the whole, from which the parts are around the whole, and he makes a certain whole.

<column-break/>

This same thing is in all things and in itself. It is "one-all" <note>original: *hen pan* — a famous philosophical formula suggesting that the universe is a single, unified totality</note> in this way, because nothing is as if from the outside or apart from it. It is itself toward itself. I contemplate each thing. The whole uses each thing for itself. But in that the whole is in it, having participated from it. Just as if something were Being, having something for all. And if the soul <note>original: *psyche* — Plotinus views the soul as the bridge between the material world and the higher Intellectual realm</note> were to suffer something, the whole would suffer it. Because it is in all. It becomes one being and in every thing. But if the One participated primarily, it would not be so. But if it were present to itself, those things which were infinite would be distant. But it must be one, which is in all things, and that which follows it. If indeed this also belongs to Essence <note>original: *ousia* — often translated as "substance" or "being," the core reality of a thing</note>. He says both participate in one. That is for him. Just as they shine for him and in all things. He releases them as wholes to him. Thus we say it exists, that which alone is first to itself, and all things are with it. Nevertheless, in being in all things, it is itself; and all things would be in it. For it is not indeed limited, like a line, from which the One is as a whole. This whole is all, and from where these things would be among all, and all these things in turn. But if it is to him as a line, either in this way, or the things belonging to it are entirely separated, they say that he is seen. From where the souls are whole. But that which is through itself exists. Which then he will not show, and they themselves are in all, like the lines from a center <note>The "center and radii" is Plotinus's favorite metaphor: the One is the center point, and all beings are lines radiating out, still connected to the source</note>, and these same ones from many are separated, as can be seen. Primarily, if one were to say this is the whole. Again, all being would not be studied, but rather would have the trust of the argument. If indeed what is in all things is of it, or to be taken away. It is reasonable to be silent nevertheless, and with the whole, in all, and even if it were far above all, from which the One was present to all—what then is the cause of it not becoming or what kind of participation is this? Why then is there the infinite in the whole by power; whatever is carried along. And yet upon this, having participated as partners. One being that which is presided over, not by distances; but also with a word of courage being indeed, it nevertheless becomes, as he says to them the words of the apostles <note>original: *apostolon* — This is an unusual word for Plotinus; the scribe may be using a Christianized term or referring to "messengers" of the divine</note>, what is the cause for all. But he also gave her whole things. Or even where the things following the whole are. Again, making it by power, or it does not go at all, being alienated, because they are parts. It is necessary then, speaking somewhere of infinites, not because it is, as one might measure, nor is the One in all. But again in itself it is whole for all; for all upon all. It is itself a certain whole from every side, or its parts are not for him, if again it is clearly toward the Form <note>original: *idean* — the perfect, eternal blueprint of a thing in the Mind of the Divine</note>, as all things were for him in all, and those in the neighbors; the whole is at once also the parts. From where it has not participated.

<summary>Plotinus argues that Being (the Divine Reality) is an indivisible whole that is present everywhere at once. He uses the mathematical metaphor of a center and its radiating lines to explain how many things can participate in the One without breaking it into pieces.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Folio 220 regarding Ennead VI.5. Having established that Being is not a physical body restricted to one place, Plotinus now investigates the paradox of how the "One" can be present in many things simultaneously without being divided into "parts."</meta>

# # Ennead VI

Through which the One extends through the entire whole. It is all things, yet it remains itself alone. If that which is not in the whole exists—such as a body situated in matter—it does not possess <term>participation</term> <note>original: *methexis* — the philosophical concept of a lower thing "taking part in" or reflecting the qualities of a higher Reality</note> in the sense of taking a piece of it; rather, it is a matter of the One becoming present everywhere. It is not that the One moves to a place where it was not before; for that which is directed toward the One is, in a sense, directed toward itself. Thus, if anything comes toward that Reality, it becomes part of it. For the <term>Logos</term> <note>original: *logos* — here meaning the formative principle or "Divine Reason" that organizes the universe</note> is there; and from both the Logos and the thing itself, the object is formed.

It cannot be that the whole is directed toward only one part or toward something severed from it. For equality and inequality do not apply here. If a thing were severed, or if the whole were divided, how could one truly "behold" it? If the whole were merely a sum of parts, or directed only to each individual thing, the One would be mocked as a mere fragment of itself. It would become equal to its own parts. But if it is said that the whole is present through itself in every part, it would be more accurate to say it is not divided. If the whole were split into the parts of that which receives it, it would no longer be a true "whole." If the same thing is divided because of the things it resides in, it would be as if a human being <note>Plotinus often uses the "universal human" as an example of an Idea that remains one even though many individual humans exist.</note> were no longer one. Nor does it happen that a part is educated here and another part there, as if knowledge itself were chopped into bits; rather, the one who is being educated attains the whole, or else another person attains it from that same source.

Therefore, the cause must be visible to all, as light is held together and shines forth. If you were to teach the whole in this way, would each person participate in the whole itself, or only in a "part" of the whole? We must state the cause: so that the instruments themselves are not something else. All things that come into being, even the most distant, are the same in relation to that which moves them. Or must we say that each thing possesses its own nature? Or does one part receive one thing and another part another? If every part were its own whole, it would appear as many. Both are true of it, without being disconnected. For again, many things exist because the things in both "climb up" to be the whole. Rather, it is like a sphere's power being separate from the sphere itself. But the sphere as a whole encompasses even what is far away. For if the sphere on the earth is the whole, or if life is in us, then a "part" comes to be, yet it is experienced as a single sensation. Therefore, regarding ourselves, we say that the soul itself is present. By imagining that these are equal, they also come from that other place. All these things are within it, as we might say. If it were a matter of a name, that which exists would be the foundation, not spread over all things. Rather, it is a wealth of being within itself. It is a Form...

<column-break/>

...was such that it does not fail. But because it is revered from everywhere and is everywhere, it is in the whole. And Plato says there <note>original: *Platon d' ekei* — likely referring to the *Parmenides* or the *Timaeus*</note>, that as long as things are not of a certain lowly nature, they participate in the gods. For this is dear to them, and it does not come from the gods as a mere shadow or an image. It exists through perception, as if reaching toward certain things. From many things, one might grasp it unclearly, enjoying it as a whole, yet not being separated from it. This is so that one does not accidentally encounter only bits of it, or something else entirely, but rather comes from the source itself.

Because the One wishes to go toward all things, it reaches the whole. Yet it lacks nothing, not even a single thing. If it were present through a part, that which we strive for—the possession of a certain state or habit, or being in a body there—would be unclear. But if it is perceived from this source, it is present as a vision for those who can see. For all things possess something of it, even things that seem contrary to nature or <margin>the</margin> there in the beautiful, should something terrible occur. Even if one does not possess it entirely, one has it through this. The abundance of things comes from this. This abundance is not the "whole" as it appears to the individual; but rather, it is as if the things that are nothing in comparison to these do not participate in them. It is like someone recognizing another; through that recognition, they complete the connection. But when it is present to him, it is not possible for it to "become" his through a mere taking; it has already come to be in that which was already the whole. From these things, it does not come from "this" or "that," but from everywhere, so that it might possess more. It is like its own position in relation to the others. 

None of them should be left behind by it; they should enjoy its grace as it remains with them. This shows that from the Being which is the whole, from that which is <term>indivisible</term> <note>original: *amerei* — without parts; a core concept that the Divine cannot be split into pieces</note>, it is not in a "part." Nothing, therefore, is brought into it. It is one and from there <gloss>Genesis 18.</gloss> <note>This gloss may be a later scholarly addition comparing the text to the appearance of the three angels to Abraham, a common Neoplatonic-Christian synthesis.</note> it is joined together, and previously toward itself, as that which is owed from the hearth <note>The "hearth" often represents the center of the soul or the center of the universe in Greek thought.</note>. It is not possible to stay in such a way as to remain outside the whole. Having grasped the genus, as if in participation with it. Because of this, one should not say that it is held by the whole. It returns, it comes to be. It does not remain. It is there; it is the whole. Like a flow, which they nevertheless possess, so is that Reality. Because of this, the whole is that upon which he looked, whenever he happened to come into being; for it was present. So that it might be the whole for all. If it is for one, it is the whole for all. Therefore, it is for one; for again, nothing has been left behind. For that which is a part within itself, from which all things will be the same, we shall cease. We shall be in that place, from which all things are equally the same for them and for themselves.

<summary>Plotinus explains that the "One" or "Being" is not divided among the many things that participate in it; rather, the whole of Being is present to each thing simultaneously, much like knowledge is fully present to every student in a classroom.</summary>
<keywords>The One, participation, Logos, indivisibility, Plato, omnipresence, metaphysics, soul</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the investigation from page 221 regarding the nature of Being and the One in Ennead VI.5. Plotinus is exploring the difficult concept of how a single, unified source can be present in all things without being fragmented or diminished by the multiplicity of the physical world.</meta>

# # Ennead VI

### 222

...a just balance. It seems to me to be impossible that whatever exists—and the causes of opposites <note>original: *enantion* — the fundamental polarities in Greek philosophy, such as Hot/Cold or Motion/Rest</note>—and yet how could you speak of it, if nothing regarding the nature of opposites were to exist? It is necessary that, if the causes exist—such as motion and rest <note>original: *stasis* — a state of stability or "standing still," often paired with motion in Plotinean metaphysics</note>—they are directed toward themselves; or the whole <note>original: *to pan* — the universe or the entirety of Being</note> will be just as it is. It follows, then, that one thing is the cause, while others are already participated in <note>original: *metechomenon* — the philosophical concept of a lower thing "taking part in" or reflecting the qualities of a higher Reality</note>. Or perhaps that which is prior in order is as <term>Being</term> <note>original: *ousia* — substance, essence, or true reality</note> itself is able to be; but also that which is such by nature, and in this way, but not if something were to be within another thing. 

On the other hand, the <term>Forms</term> <note>original: *eide* — the eternal archetypes or "Ideas" that serve as the blueprints for everything in the physical world</note> do not possess this nature... or because the whole is, and because these things are beings; therefore, those things which remain. But among those things where the "above" is necessary. For the second thing is not a beginning <note>original: *arche* — a first principle or source</note>, but is always from the source; therefore, for the second thing, participation follows immediately again. 

If, however, someone says that the First exists in this way, then those things which do not participate are equal, or like the second; they would not even seem equal, as if one must deny them to all things. Yet the <term>Genera</term> <note>original: *gene* — the broad categories of Being, such as Sameness, Difference, and Motion</note> are near, and one must count them toward the one; or provide no cause for any of them; but the One is its own cause. 

But things in substance are divided. If, therefore, each thing remains in the same state, it is not necessary to have the <term>infinite</term> <note>original: *apeiron* — the boundless, undefined, or unlimited aspect of reality</note>; it happens because it is born under the One, and others use it somehow, but in being left behind, because there all things are under the infinite and the things that are capable; for they say the Forms are absent, as are the shapes. 

If number exists, these things must be numbered equally to their orders, back with the One; but besides the whole is that which is "under," from whence it would be. What then is this substance? Is it after the genera of the race <note>original: *phylou* — here referring to a class or kind of being</note> are divided, and thus it is participated in by all in this way? Or is it that which is in all, or besides the whole, over all beings? Or is it an inability of the <term>underlying subject</term> <note>original: *hypokeimenon* — the underlying "stuff" or substrate that receives form</note>? 

This genus belongs to all, but it is not the genus itself. Will the One not make many? And it is not itself the cause for another, from which the things in the whole derive; but if the genera were not principles which are equal; and Being comes from it. Because it does not participate in matter in all things; but rather in things foreign; and either the whole is about the things... but certainly not upon itself and about the things; but about all things of the genus; or the whole is nothing else. Regarding this: what is it then? 

And the qualities too. For either it is especially of something within Being. But if the states of bodies appear common. For if the whole were not to be, and those things following what is capable, because it is not acting; but then the <term>Reason</term> <note>original: *logos* — the formative principle or Divine Reason that organizes the universe</note> is the whole, and thus a choice appeared to it from all of them. If it is in matter, as many things as are divided did not thus stand together, unless by action, or those things not utterly impossible as if nature stood together itself, a simple nature? Or of the infinite, which is not in itself, such as under the living and the <term>animal</term> <note>original: *zoon* — a living being or the concept of the "Cosmic Animal," the universe as a living organism</note>.

<summary>Plotinus examines how the primary "Genera" and the "One" relate to the multiplicity of the world, arguing that the source of all things remains undivided even as it is participated in by many. He questions whether Being is a shared category or an underlying substance that precedes all division.</summary>
<keywords>The One, participation, Genera, Being (Ousia), Logos, Infinite (Apeiron), Forms (Eide), metaphysics, unity and multiplicity</keywords>

# # Ennead VI

### 223

-> ·Ennead VI· <-

It was as if something were shining forth, or radiating, or most of all, as the One. For there, the many are one; for it does not exceed measure, lest the measure not be fixed, as is said of things here, the "how" <note>original: *to pôs* — the specific manner or quality in which a thing exists</note>. Or it does not fall short there; but everything is as it ought to be, or rather as it came from Him. For it does not possess a "how," or a "this way," or a "such-as," from where it came: it is the cause. Since it does not come into being, but by looking at the cause—though not seeking what is prior to the cause—everything in it is by nature. And there it remains with Him, in being the measure of its own things. Or just as Form <term>Form</term> <note>original: *eidos* — the eternal, intelligible blueprint of a thing</note> was not always "somehow"; the beginning of "somehow" is being "in a certain way." And being in a certain way is how it is in a certain way. But because the First is itself first, it is not after another, or in another way, or in such a way, or the "how." But it is as it is; because of which, it is as all being there is. For it is not the "how" of each thing by addition, but the "how" itself. Who might it become? If everything there is what it is, and the things from Him, or rather Him itself; therefore, He is the cause of Himself, from whom He is. And the whole turned toward the beginning, not being released from Him, or from Himself. And the whole turned toward Him, just as it turned. And the cause, or the cause is, or for itself just as it is. Therefore, because He is the cause of Himself, He is also the <term>Essence</term> <note>original: *ti ên einai* — literally "what it was to be," a term for the core essence or definition of a thing</note>; for He is not another; or perhaps not even Essence, for He is the First. This is what often appears: that one must only be in these things and look; and not that He is not, as the many say. Let them turn away their sicknesses; if there is authority in them, they no longer dispute. But the cause exists in itself, and holds toward itself while remaining in itself. Or if after that, through irrationality, they are at a loss regarding the end. Since Being exists; but that which is beyond beings exists—

### -> + On Number : + <-

<margin>·5·</margin>
**O**ne might wonder about the gods concerning Number. If it is necessary that beings be associated with numbers. How is number something countable, and is number bad, or is it something in itself? This is what I am considering. For example, a multitude <note>original: *plêthos* — a collection of many things, the opposite of the One</note>, having many in one, such as a body or it remains itself, taking up spaces from the earth or another. For even that which is not countable, either in the matter of beings, or for it is written, from those things above; what other part of it was labored upon? Or because of its becoming by use, both a part and destined to become. But that which is not with Him, but did not take. The one? From itself that which is becoming, upon which to care for by another, or upon itself. Or besides that in the matter. But to live? Or because of living of what sort, and how, or a difficulty? Rather, they did not obtain a lot there. Or to live without that which is not with; but it is from itself. Or it is a wonder, the first indeed. Or it is an exception, and that which is after, they are truly ignorant of what is after. Since it does not exist, it might become; but that which is through Being /

<meta>catchword: but what he says about it</meta>

<column-break/>

but what he says about it, which he made clear. Or how it must not be. Or a mother to what is born. Or being kept for himself as it seems; that which is before all things being, whatever it may have. But since it holds the whole. For it is not itself, but all things that are not even toward itself so that itself when necessary in not after. It becomes, then, through a lack of care. Upon this great thing, that which lies upon Him. For it is not Soul <note>original: *psychê* — the animating principle that connects the divine Intellect to the physical world</note>, nor is it itself. And what ever is after that. Or because of this, they flee in sensation; she herself is the unspeakable thing there; and beautiful, or the Good. But the evil. Or himself of the beautiful. Because it became after. It appears not much, from where it is after. Or to be by nature to choose. Or the unlearned hope prevails, because it participates much in virtue. Rather it is absurd after, and most of all it is ashamed. What then is that which is participated? Or having the beginnings. But of what sort? Where is it rooted? Or that which is within. Or in the sensible earth entirely, whether even the sensible is not rooted. Or that which is rooted, the sensible bond <note>original: *aistheton desmon* — the physical limitations or "chains" of the material world</note>. But it will also be loosed or many, for those things in matter, not even these? And how is it one, or you might brighten it with bright things, or what was necessary, not vital. But one must speak otherwise. But it is not, but that from which it is taken, or no longer always such a generation, but as the specific Forms are there. Or the beginning from wealth. Because it is not rooted just as much as is there. But we are not able, we make old things being often led astray or still itself in that one, or in the neither for it needs that one, or another or it did not happen with Him. Still, as much as those who have made the lack, for whenever having him; from himself. When they have come and for. And yesterday the cables, I look away just as stars belonging to His time. Only of our passions. But it itself is all the whole, to the wisdoms it is not necessary. For that exists there, it is called number as a whole. But how then, because it is so just as, how according to what it has. Or that it is of us or himself. Or both that and the multitude to be. And all is well; how? Since it will be enriched by the year, because all is for it. It is, therefore, from there. Or as much as by being nature. But let it be a body; or it receives. But what of that, as much as it has. Or it is itself, and number is the well-being. Or number. But all these things. Or having the whole; such as to be; or it is number, and that which is, is Being. From that which has happened perhaps as in the same place. Or even in themselves.

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's exploration of the relationship between the One and the Multiplicity that flows from it, specifically transitioning into the themes of Ennead VI.6, "On Numbers." It follows the discussion of the "self-causality" of the One from the previous page.</meta>

# ## Ennead VI

### 224

-> — Ennead VI — <-

These things being so, if it should seem so—but as has been shown—it is not among those things where there is a proportion <note>original: *analogia* — a mathematical or structural relationship</note> between the greater and the lesser, or even of the equal up to two. For this is not possible in itself. For what does the One need with multiplicity <note>original: *plêthei* — a crowd, mass, or numerical plurality</note>? But the One is not the multiplicity; rather, it appears that this is to say it is "one thing." But the One is two, so that for it, it is a kind of essence <term>essence</term> <note>original: *ousia* — fundamental being or substance</note>. And the One, in its Reason-Principle <note>original: *logos* — the formative principle or explanation of a thing</note> and its essence, could not come from what is not. Because of this, when something else is said of it, it is "to be"; and for this to be, it must be established. For where? And where would it go to become one? But its creation is not there. For it was said of infinity <note>original: *apeiria* — the boundless or undefined</note> that it is the form <note>original: *morphê* — the outward shape or defining limit</note>. But it must have matter. And does the authority lie in attaining it, which is here called "within"? Or, having taken both, for the two are called places. For the one is "there," the intellect <note>original: *dianoia* — discursive thought</note> being around the same place, even if there is more. Why then should it not have the power of thought <note>original: *noein* — the act of intellectual perception</note> itself? Or do you have a need for "being" to simply come to be? But if "being" itself is required, it is not necessary for it. For it exists along with harmony. For there comes to be a vision <note>original: *thea* — a spectacle or contemplative sight</note>, a vision and a "how much"; for even the "nothings" possess a Reason-Principle according to their accounts, for it is no longer one as a number is. But it is a monadic one. So that it both acts, and these things are for it an image <note>original: *phantasia* — a mental appearance or representation</note> by means of being acted upon. Since, therefore, it has been limited, and however many are more or less as in a Reason-Principle, it is nonetheless disturbed. But in the multiplicity, for it is as some say. But it is neither so great, nor is it "all things of every thing," being many times over, it would be so again. For each thing is this because of the One; but for all, it is "all things." Or this is its nature, according to the world of appearance. Where indeed the appearance of these things is, this is it. But if it does not receive it, it is a thing private to itself, not even if it is a good and an enjoyment. For it does not leave behind what is worthy, or did it know because of this? And motion, to me each of those things that have come to be, would be a genus. Thus having it only for me, it might say more.

---

And concerning numbers: when we say in the progenitor that which is not all things for you from things made, so they are placed, or from the persons of the whole; for instance, the "individual" being the individual, as that necessity, to compose great things. If indeed it was awakened by how many are in the "ones," through which they already are; and thus each of the others would have it from which some come. But it was composed for each as one; for the same is that one, a monad. And through the mathematical way on the road, if the "of itself" belongs to you. From where then do "two" come, one might ask? Or suddenly? It will give back how "two" somehow appeared as truly being. But if so, all things are made above, or have come there. Nevertheless, it is known.

<column-break/>

The being of number, and of the One which is left over, is first toward all the first things according to itself. For the One was generated from it among the remaining things that come to be, for the things numbered <note>original: *arithmêta* — the objects being counted, as opposed to the numbers themselves</note> do not have their participation in essence through the number itself. But it is generated from it, so that it is nothing for men to participate in it in this way. For in the "not even one," because one cannot say this is not, when they are said to be in no multiplicity themselves, but in another. Just as the multiplicity perceives itself with it, in the saying of "one." Just as when one says this most truly. For when one speaks again of existing things according to opinion, as speaking of a "numbered number." In the soul, it is toward the soul itself. But through it, the things in that one. For the whole is not these things that have been made, of the essence of number. It would come to be by its nature. However many multiplicities there are, he announces them to Being. As if it were something else, such as another. And again: that which is, or is not. When all those things are the things that "are." Since number was given from Zeus <note>original: *Dios* — Jupiter/Zeus, often representing the Divine Mind or Demiurge</note>. Since all things are for him. In which all number is, in Being itself. Even if one were to say the lesser is prior, if it is upon the One. Since it is infinite in its ending, not also the "all" as in those things which are "all." And again, all things would come to be by coming to be. But he who has conceded to things not coming to be, just as the One is there, or wherever the intelligible is held there. Not only the number of those things. For again, all things are certain things; if they are, those things are. It exists nonetheless. But having placed the multiplicity of the intelligibles <term>intelligibles</term> <note>original: *noêton* — things grasped by the mind rather than the senses</note> toward bulk, it nevertheless holds the number of these as a definition, and the Reason-Principle. For even after everything, the "two" are also arranged correspondingly. And further, one must speak of "every." And so we also speak. But when from the things that come to be, they are "one." Each as "two," and two by two. It must show by its substance <note>original: *hypostasei* — the underlying reality or "person" of a thing</note> that all things have become for him, and she herself becomes visible, where that "all things" might become for him. To be under the Reason-Principle of the spirit <note>original: *pneumatos* — the breath or vital spirit</note>. Thus again, because it contemplates the body, it belongs to the spirit, nor does it become itself. But number is not that of thought. But that which is in the spirit, how it is one, that thing holds likewise, I say. There is a substance in the same, and it is not under the motion of appearing to happen, as if more beside itself. Or it seems to be that [essence] entirely. But what is accidental <note>original: *symbebêkos* — a non-essential property</note>, for as this also happens to be and is indivisible; nevertheless, since some things are by nature from it, as if to lead astray. Which multiplicity—even if you have ceased, but it "is"—must not be refused. For one would not suffer anything, if it is from the whole because of itself, but when it is from itself, and where it still is. Euphony.

<summary>This page discusses the nature of "Number" as an essential, intelligible reality that precedes the physical counting of objects. Plotinus argues that while the One is beyond number, the intelligible realm uses number as a defining principle to organize multiplicity into Being.</summary>

...of the animals; and concerning those of the earth again. One should not cease from seeking causes, so that the "well" <note>original: *eu* — refers to "well-being" or the "good" of a thing's state</note> might be understood. If one could grasp the cause, the "wherefore" <note>original: *di' ho*</note> would be found within the "in which." It is not that there is a cause of the animal which is separate from the cause of its existence. For the thing has its cause within itself, so that the cause is found within the "in which," and not as something acquired from outside; nor is it simply the cause of being, as they say, but the Earth is the cause of the animal. For the being of the animal does not come from that alone. Nor could it happen merely according to the timing of its birth, nor should they blame this. On the contrary, it has not been made that way; since one cannot find fault in the other things. Or, if something happens against nature, it is among those things that occur incidentally, but not in the very act of coming-to-be. Just as it happens in matters of health, if health itself shall exist according to its own nature. Nor would well-being <note>original: *eu*</note> vanish or happen by chance because the cause is found within us. Thus those things also exist, and it might happen that the very existence of a thing is something specific; nor would the cause of its "well-being" ever cease, nor would it cease itself, because the cause is there. For otherwise, it would not even move. But regarding the rule <note>original: *kanonos*</note>, it is not because of its own specific Form <term>Form</term> <note>original: *idea* — the eternal, perfect archetype of a thing in the Divine Mind</note>

But why? It acts for its own sake, and it is itself. Because the things produced from the earth come into being, even the old man shall not exist; but in happiness, just as with the causes. And happiness exists because of the things for which nature is the cause. Since neither <unclear>...</unclear> what remains is the earth being a cause for us, and often so. I think, therefore, because of the causes within us, as some say, that if anyone—if someone should become like those among us who carry a resemblance—this earth being what it is, its foundational substance <note>original: *hypostatikon*</note> is not merely earth. For either because they were coming into being, even if life itself were to be a good for it; and it would not be so if all earth were in all things—perhaps it is not. Either by not being this for itself, or by the seed, or it does not exist except through the offspring of the Intelligible <term>Intelligible</term> <note>original: *noêtou* — the realm of pure thought and being, accessible only to the intellect</note> as a whole. They come into being in it, or it is its power. Nevertheless, knowledge <note>original: *gnôsis*</note> is that around which each of the intelligible things exists in the same place, if indeed those things are existence <note>original: *hyparxis*</note>. But if the prior state in this constitution is not wandering, it would be able to act, leaving nothing behind, or being as it ought to be. For what is it, other than that it might become a cause within living beings, or that which has taken its own cause? This is the thing itself; perhaps one must grasp it like that other thing, from wherever he might find it. If indeed

<meta>This page continues the investigation into causality and the "reason-principles" (logoi).
