## Ennead VI

### 226

**Euclid, Book 6**

If they are in the same ratio <note>original: *logō* — here meaning mathematical ratio or proportion</note>, then these things, when divided, are also proportional. If the first term is to the second as the third is to the fourth, then the first will also be to the third as the second is to the fourth; and the first to the third, and the second to the fourth. **Which was to be demonstrated.** <note>original: *hoper edei deixai* — the standard Greek concluding phrase for a mathematical proof, equivalent to the Latin Q.E.D.</note> Because of this lemma <term>lemma: a preliminary or auxiliary proposition used to prove a larger theorem</term>, the following lemma is also demonstrated: that if the first is to the second as the third is to the fourth, then the first will also be to the second as the third is to the fourth; and the first plus the second is to the second [as the third plus the fourth is to the fourth]. For the first is to the second as the third is to the fourth, and so on. Therefore, the first is to the second as the third is to the fourth; and again, the first together with the second is to the second, as the third together with the fourth is to the fourth. And so on. Thus, the first is to the third as the second is to the fourth, and the first together with the second is to the third together with the fourth, as the first is to the third. Therefore, the first together with the second is to the third together with the fourth, as the second is to the fourth. And so on. Similarly also for the others. For since the first is to the second as the third is to the fourth, then the first is to the third as the second is to the fourth. And so on. Therefore, the first is to the third as the second is to the fourth. Thus, the first is to the third as the first plus the second is to the third plus the fourth. Therefore, as the first is to the third, so the first plus the second is to the third plus the fourth. And as the first is to the third, so the second is to the fourth. Therefore, as the second is to the fourth, so the first plus the second is to the third plus the fourth. Thus, as the first together with the second is to the third together with the fourth, so the second is to the fourth. **Which was to be demonstrated.** Through these ratios...
<meta>catchword: these ratios</meta>

<column-break/>

<margin>(2.</margin>
...let it produce; but if they are from it, that which follows from the hypothesis will come to be. It is therefore something carved out from it; and if the First did not exist, the ancient "contribution" <note>original: *epidosis* — a giving or an increase</note> would be gone. The ancient one, the one who forms, the one who contributes. It would be without foundation; but because I have received this very thing, it is perhaps less. Nor is it false that its very being is through this, as are its relatives. Of all things, the one that comes from the same source is the cause of itself. For even the sophists <term>sophists: here likely referring to contemporary or rival philosophical teachers</term> around him say it thus. And the First was persuaded by this. "I am first," he says, therefore he is the same; not merely "the first." Except that the First was also before them, he who is before them. The producer is therefore the same, but the cause is that of the human, who was before him. These things are so because of the contribution. But if those people seemed to say so, even the First Cause is concerned with this. If indeed we say the First Cause is natural—for the first is the natural portion of both the essence <note>original: *ousia* — the underlying "being" or "substance" of a thing</note> and the body. Therefore it is a cause; but it has been said that it is not worse. If they were said to be more, then each of the lives would again be the same. For what if it is the greater, or the lesser, or the equal? Even if all things are prior to this "reason-principle," no one will speak of it to itself. There is therefore a natural [principle] for each of the things that come to be, such as that which is innate. And each cause, and again the cause of the First Cause, is that which comes from the essence. Because of this, even an earthquake <note>original: *seismos*</note> such as this is made to be equal. How and why? These people, having said this, have shown that nothing at all was produced by God <note>original: *theou*</note>. For someone moved in part, so that he might say something. We say, then, that before the movement by God, it stood where it was. But if all things were natural, as all things appear to tend toward her, it is as if through the cause in the passions. Nevertheless, she herself is still only in a singular state. But she, the partial one, is again turned toward an earthquake. For let all things before the partial one come into being; the "after-birth" is sensory. They say all the parts are natural to all; therefore, they are of the same things, or the worse of them. But they speak of another cause. If we speak of the whole, let it take the whole as unaffected in its form. If there is also a cause of earthquakes. This, then, would seem to solve the problem. But indeed, not even in an earthquake; for from the moment nature took it up. Ours is certainly [moved], but that which remains is unmoved. In a measured way, indeed. All things tend toward the cause, either the cause of the generation of all things, or also the partial atoms <note>original: *atoma* — indivisible units</note> that come from the natural cause. But if it shall reach an end, it is the underlying reality <note>original: *hypostasin* — the fundamental substance or reality</note> of all things. Or it is the natural cause, from which natures lead. No other goal is set forth, than that it shall be from a cause, or that all things shall be from causes through such means, as if to show them as mechanical. Nothing then is nothing, neither that which is so, nor that. The same earthquake is like the evils; even they have known that they and their causes exist, and it shall be—

# Ennead VI

### 228

-> Eusebius: <- <note>original: *Euseb:* — Likely a reference to Eusebius of Caesarea, who quoted large sections of Plotinus in his own writings.</note>

Being in itself. It seems to me that it tries to manifest itself through **becoming** <term>becoming: *genesis*, the process of coming-into-being in the physical world, contrasted with eternal Being</term>. For indeed, generated things possess their **proportion** <note>original: *symmetrian* — the harmonious relationship between parts</note> through motion, for this is their very nature. From this, the universe possesses the equality of **Justice** <note>original: *dikēs* — the cosmic order or divine law</note>. Just as we might say, the body is not [eternally] generated. For it is not by necessity that something comes to be and is constituted at a certain time. Nor does it have this specific order. Just as its causes are not to be named as specific things. In accordance with the whole, even the **principle** <note>original: *archē* — the starting point or origin</note> is established after the cause.

Those which we call "ourselves" are not present because of another, nor is His nature laid out for all. But our reverence comes from God, to attend to the knowledge of God, which is not merely this entire life. For if this **age** <term>age: *aiōn*, referring here to the temporal span of life or a cosmic cycle</term> is mortal and proportional to mortal things, then that [higher] one also maintains itself in the same state. He is manifest to himself through the pursuit of **immortality** <note>original: *athanasias*</note>. 

But how one must conceive of this: for generated things need not be similar to other generated things in their order. For if things are mortal, like the **planets** <note>original: *planētai* — literally 'wanderers'</note>, the celestial things are also eternal, unlike all those upon the earth. Regarding those things there, it is widely said: of necessity, the first things in the universe are as they are in God. From there they come, and in their relation to us, there is so much of the other cause; yet even if the first things do not know **Being** <note>original: *to einai*</note>, they nonetheless came to be because of it. Thus they are made, and even if [one] is not made, yet every motion must depend upon Him. 

And these things, such as they are, and necessity itself—if it is still universal and not partial—let it be moved by the nature of life, but also by that of God. For if this is so, then many more things again perhaps exist by **grace** <term>grace: *charis*, here implying a divine gift or a natural radiance and favor from the higher realms</term>; these two depend on God. And the things that follow for Him will all be the ancient principles of Justice. Insofar as the things of that land <note>Referring to the intelligible or spiritual realm</note> are such as they might become. For nothing possesses the whole, nor is there any use of it which is also grace; the same **reason** <note>original: *logos*</note> applies, for it is enduring; thus, through grace, all power exists, and it is impossible for its **Form** <term>Form: *idea*, the eternal archetype or blueprint of a thing</term> to come into being through itself. 

Just as there is a **knowledge** <term>knowledge: *epistēmē*, certain or scientific understanding</term> of bronze. Of what things He is the **cause** <note>original: *aition*</note>, He is one, and He scarcely knows the other. Thus also with oil, or the **beautiful** <note>original: *kalon*</note>. Over all things, this and these are more numerous. But regarding these, the divine [one], acting as cause, does not have a relation to the Form of becoming; and this is why we speak in this way. This offspring having come into being, differing from its source... He knows this from Himself, that which is also **contemplated** <note>original: *theōmenon*</note>. Whenever, therefore, one sees that in which the air resides, all these are like His own. Experience is of the same things. Thus, the best way to have experience is through oneself. That one, having known, reaches toward the first things, and indeed they are within him. And it is clear regarding the rest...

He emphasizes that true knowledge and experience are found by looking inward toward the 'first things' and the divine grace that sustains all forms.</summary>

### 229

<header><unclear>Among the things</unclear></header>

...to arise within the same thing as that which it is. For the principles of the **roots** <term>roots: *rhizomata*, the term used by Empedocles for the four eternal elements—fire, air, earth, and water</term> are inseparable; arising from each one, yet the number of the principles, even if it falls slightly short of the two <note>The "two principles" likely refer to Love (Philia) and Strife (Neikos), the forces Empedocles believed moved the elements.</note>, is not woven together with the roots themselves. Therefore, the roots will not be the same as the **elements** <note>original: *stoicheiois* — while later philosophers used "elements," Empedocles preferred "roots." Plotinus here distinguishes between the raw material and the formalized concept.</note>; and others have taken on number, or alterations, or even compositions. There is a greater mixture of them, and of the roots; the greater parts of it, both being more than these, but rather of both; and as for what follows these, the other things are not the same. For the roots exist in a certain way, or rather, they are the roots themselves; for the cause from which this comes, or the manner of the root, is thus—

<margin>(G</margin>—and in this way they also say the roots exist, and more so through the things they describe. It will be clear that their position is laughable. For in the whole, the opposite can exist for all things; and if someone were to divide it immediately into the same but not equal parts, he would say the cause is that some are the things from which they are <note>Referring to "Being" or essence</note>, while others are the things from which they **become** <note>Referring to "Becoming" or physical generation</note>. Again, the most important things, and again of the roots—twice or thrice the roots—while the other things are not more than each other, and the things we have mentioned. This mentioned **cause** <note>original: *aitia*</note> is able to produce these things. And furthermore, this comes more from the same things. Since it perceives this to be so, it again produces something, either more, or from which there is much, but it is not only outside of these. In all animals and plants, it is something different. All these things, then, it is clear will be as follows: Let us suddenly turn to the matters of the roots, and whenever they occur, the **reason** <term>reason: *logon*, meaning the rational principle or logic behind a thing</term> is always for them the cause of the **war** <note>original: *polemou* — likely referring to "Strife," the cosmic force that separates the elements</note>, whenever it remains for another to be mixed; however it is able, let them be named, or if someone should say something else, or again, it does not belong to them.

Since, then, ten and ten is the limit of the roots, it will be able to show something perceptible; but not regarding this. For **Empedocles** says: "For if the things according to the causes are more parts, and some are of the elements according to the fact that some belong to the others, and some are more than the roots." But when, through itself, it falls into a forgetfulness of the roots, as is likely, we hope for something of our own, which will not come from these; but even if the things of the roots are more, many and again; or there are two things that are able, or even more, and the things of all the other elements together, or let it be in the universe, for another is always arising. And it will be of them, because it is only those things that possess the qualities of the **spirit** <term>spirit: *pneuma*, which can mean "breath," "air," or the vital force of life</term>. But indeed, the other things as well. And if the things of these are more; and if these things are divided, it is not only through the senses. Before these things themselves existed, the things arising were upon the roots. And he himself says that these things are in them again, and he takes it with him, a certain **inclination** <note>original: *rhopē* — a turning of the scale or a downward tendency</note> occurs, as with oil. But also of the causes themselves; for natural things arise, and for all things they return to the principles. And even when...

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of Number (specifically Ennead VI.6, "On Number"), moving from the physical elements discussed previously into the metaphysical relationship between Number, Being, and the Forms. It explores whether number is a byproduct of things existing or a prior structure that allows them to exist.</meta>

### Ennead VI [6]

If someone says that number is not something contracted, it is impossible to say it. But if ten is not more [than its units], but the decade makes the number. For it appears in the "one" that being such is in number. But this is not so; for if number is in Being, it belongs to Being itself. The same appears to be true of all Being, from which its unity and its multiplicity <term>multiplicity: *plethos*, the state of being many, which Plotinus attempts to reconcile with the "One"</term> come. Casting aside number, then, let us know. If the Forms <term>Forms: *eide*, the eternal archetypes or blueprints of reality</term> have their subsistence <term>subsistence: *hypostasin*, the underlying reality or existence</term> before beings, as those before a king, as a subsistence of a certain movement. Thus, everything is in number. From which comes this "all" of ours. Nor, he says, is the bond or harmony by itself. For if harmony is nothing. Or these would not be "kinds" <term>kinds: *gene*, the primary categories of existence: Being, Motion, Rest, Sameness, and Difference</term> in which they participate. Or if that too were nothing, from what? For the number in the Forms belongs to living things and others. Nor is multiplicity souls. How many are the souls? If it were made entirely under this. Or the First and the Living-Thing-Itself <note>The *Zoon Auto*, a concept from Plato's *Timaeus* referring to the intelligible universe that contains all possible living species.</note> would not have all life, because it is itself all life, if it were not before it. Or the multiplicity with it is life, but not with those beings, by being nothing. If multiplicity is nothing or each is one, so also is the whole, from each of the things there and of number. If multiplicity is great, it is there. If multiplicity is nothing, what are ten, and one, and two? For more things are not before the one. If it is in beings, how is it not by the part? For if the other things from which the whole is made, what is before the one? As if the things before were nothing, how? For all number belongs to it, it itself is missing. Or if it is number, the one is like a number's unit. Or to be the same, even for each number. Some reason then, if number is there. Is the infinite multiplicity lying in it? It remains then for the separated part of them to have the "one" of each. Because the whole came from that, like a part of the whole number, so also toward number, so that each is one, or this whole is also its multiplicity. Or how does each thing come to be? Or if the imagination is only alone, how can we apply them to things, just as we were born for the intelligible? For what kind of thing would be born in the intelligible? But the particular number opens the way. Or by the Forms being of beings, to lead a man back to that itself. Or if the Forms are sensible, but no longer toward beings, then it would have been born. Let it be. The subsistence of number. If these also will ascend.
<margin>Co:</margin> In number, since it is not possible for it [to be otherwise]. What kind of thing is counting itself? Nothing of it. This itself. This is nothing. If it is not as it was before. Or it is within. For there, nor is this multiplicity thus, as he knows. There is a necessity of stopping. But in the intelligible things of the Form. In the things here they use it, how? Let it be. But we use the things produced by movement, not dividing, the thing before these uses this form. And even all natural things use this form.

<column-break/>

Life; but the things under it are not good, by number; it itself, and how many beings. And what nature. It shows him being. Not those things of his thus, but because they are. For so many things, so that even being thus in themselves, they are as they are; just as Mind <term>Mind: *Nous*, the Divine Intellect or second hypostasis of reality</term>, so also is number, and the multiplicity after it is as it were, already the thing after Being. As Mind has made activity <term>activity: *energeian*, the actualization of potential</term>. It would not be a living thing; as if this Being is not, as before the whole in Being, or in the line. Therefore it is nothing; he says, nor as its cause. Still, the things in the intelligible would be analogous. Thus the living thing after the living thing, or to be in the intelligible. He says [this] in the living things. If none of them, nor even the intelligible, if that is something of the living things. It is shown that there is something for the intelligible things. And in the living thing are the generative parts. Or Soul. And souls. And the Reason-Principle <term>Reason-Principle: *Logos*, the formative force that mediates between the Intellect and the physical world</term> says, if the complete living thing; and to be, a part. And not that each itself is the whole, as having come to be in the complete thing by it; there is another; according to these things. And before. Or first after other things. Or it was a living thing before. Why is number not there? Or after that, from which are the things toward the complete. He taught, as they will also be. And indeed they make it first of the number of the whole; except that it is there. But the number is one. For it is divided, so that again it might be that which is upon the same. So it is necessary for all to be truly, because the Forms are also one in number. But not if something, even it itself is one, oaths <note>original: "orkous." This may be an OCR error for "horous" (boundaries/definitions). In this context, Plotinus is likely discussing the limits of unity.</note>. If so; being distributed toward something; but it itself is not. Who then would be there or not be? But even without order; or divided, because of which he calls them the intelligible things; and not with it. These things appear as all things being so much. In Being, and where the living things were there. A boundary in life to being. But before this law was. So that the things that are, he even completed. Or even contained in the life of the living thing itself. Instead of this again, if these; or would they not be in life, nor are they made. From which of each living thing the things and of some other. And they are divided; as for instance this year; but again all from which it lives; but he who lives is not. Or even of all envy <note>original: "phthonos." A reference to the Platonic idea (from the *Timaeus*) that the Creator is free from envy and thus wants all things to participate in goodness.</note>. And he gave each itself, the forms then, his own should teach him. It seems even to him envy; this would not even be a power that takes more. But Being would be like a life toward someone, through which and in and according to each other; and it is a necessity that each is itself. In the Forms each; but what remains is the thing indeed, for snakes <note>original: "ophesin." Likely an error for "benefits" or "visions."</note> or power, if another in life; they learned from life the things there.

# · On Piety ·

<column-break/>

God was generated. <note>In Plotinian thought, "generation" usually refers to the eternal emanation of lower realities from the "One," rather than a birth in time.</note> In this place, someone truly says much, since perhaps he was never taught anything by Him, or even receives a mission from Him. But if he remembers in the "Living Thing" <term>Living Thing: *Zoon*, referring to the Cosmos as a single, ensouled, and divine organism</term>; it is because through all living things he shows life; and again, the "Living Thing" possesses tongues, as if it were similarly itself to itself, for it is a living thing. This is so that the "Living Thing" might pass through them, an unmoved yet greater change; he who is the nature itself is more. But he himself says that to those who remember notably, the beautiful nature of the good has come to be, and of the holy to be persuaded. Every proud thing is a great "Living Thing," yet it stands alone. He says that within it are the... <unclear>δέτα</unclear> unless perhaps we do not grant it, just as with the gods; or that there is another way. If it partakes of the gods, it is the most ancient of them. For the child <note>Likely a reference to the "son" of the Good, the Intellect (*Nous*).</note> is the intellect itself. But if all these things of the gods have been substantiated from them, they will be manifest. Nor is it this itself, instead of knowing; but rather having it by being persuaded from some source. But if it is the "All" itself, he does not mark it as such, if indeed he marks both God and the activity very securely; he held back, not only being blamed, but there is also a name. But toward nothing then will he be persuaded in each case. Whether of the whole itself, things which are not even near. And as for **Piety**, he will not cease to be kind; so as to be led astray because of this. Because we indeed possess the power of faith, he does not speak of another among human praises. For if the remainder is existence for him, in the good; then it is the "All" itself which he seeks. But if then this is also so, as concerning the... He says it is a "Benefaction." Some say it is so that it might be thought; then it is Soul, for it is "Being." That which is one’s own, belonging to oneself.

<margin>-. 2 .-</margin>
->Concerning one who speaks impiously against the divine; for it is rational.<-

If it should happen to all together, the Soul will not cease, by nature and by opinion, so that souls are bodies. But if the things of God are foreign, of whatever kind they may be as **images** <term>images: *eidola*, the physical world seen as a shadow or reflection of the higher, "real" world</term>, they will suffer as if they were the "Living Thing" itself; and they will exist. They called out; he blesses, because they say, because, reasonably; from where would these things come concerning the whole? Or by Zeus, to persuade them as they come to be, that they would not think with wisdom, or just as they found things, they remained themselves holding them. Further, the "Living Thing" itself, which sleeps by nature. Or again someone says, but, that it is not by wisdom; but of souls, yet it was less, or even that one does this; and these things perhaps, so that he might place me. If the things from the same life of the whole; images by impurity. And that the image itself is in a good class; but that it is reasonable to give their images to the impulse. They will perhaps bend to have senses, to become of your sensory things. But from where? Especially where... and it itself; these things, the **painter** <note>Plotinus often uses the metaphor of a painter to describe how the World Soul or the Demiurge crafts the physical world based on divine models.</note>. The subsistence <term>subsistence: *hypostasis*, a distinct reality or level of being</term>. And all of him; it is indeed, either the things similar to those in the things that have come to be, or it arrives according to the **Intelligible** <term>Intelligible: *Noetos*, the realm of pure thought and the Forms, higher than the physical world</term>; and upon this, in reality, his whole thought encompasses it. Or every living thing is for them; from which the "All" was created. He seeks salvation from it. It is pious. Therefore perhaps someone might say there; but there is forgetfulness. Since the "All" lies as a living thing according to its kind. And again, a wise man does not view "Benefaction" by reasoning. If it belongs to Being, it is **impassibility** <term>impassibility: *apatheia*, the state of being unmoved or unaffected by external suffering or change</term>; a form in the works of each. If indeed to those things that have not come to be and to reasonings, there are "good reasonings"; to save nothing of the things of choice. If he presides; just as if the body were straight to God, according to the greatest circumstance. But if he brings it in, so that this; this very thing. If indeed it should be guarded, they will perish; truly in this alone, or hypotheses. It is more reasonable, this very thing. For from where will one go out, so as to reason? And these things would not be of the cult-members <note>original: *thiasōn*, members of a religious group or 'thiasos'</note> to bind together too much; but later, so that this might not happen. For if this, which is not this. These things are not "God-forsaken," but this is what has happened; to be persuaded. Let us say that... The **passive** <term>passive: *pathetikon*, the part of the soul or matter that is capable of being acted upon or suffering</term> is not; but rather that which reasons, or that which it suffered. The name of his things, and to exist within. Or indeed you learn that it is a **Reason-Principle** <term>Reason-Principle: *Logos*, the formative power that flows from the Intellect into matter</term>; from where all things again; from where the world comes to be. But from where it comes from God, from there are the forms of generation. But if you divide these parts, for it is an absolute necessity, as it is generative; that which is later. Turning away from within, consider if it is not this. But not together, throughout the whole. So that it is equal, or so that that might be the cause. If indeed it is useful for all to understand nature again, or toward the "All."

# · Blessing VI ·

<column-break/>

...in bonds. But that which is within it consists not of mere thoughts. Yet if even before the Intellect <term>Intellect: *Nous*, the second divine principle in Plotinus's system, representing pure, eternal thought</term> there is Reason <term>Reason: *Logos*, the ordering principle that projects divine patterns into the world</term>, then the cause is surely that which is true. If the cause is the productive power, then it is visible to the eye itself. It follows that this is the truth. If the truth is there, it would most especially be within it.

We see that the Intellect is this very thing. Since, then, the All exists, it is not merely a cause. In all things that come into being, we must seek their causes. For even the "First" <note>The "First" refers to the One, the ultimate, simple source of all existence from which all things emanate.</note> is not the All. If the First also exists, then for that which comes to be in the same place as its effects, it is the All. It is, therefore, itself.

<margin>f</margin> Previously, this was in a state of prosperity <note>original: "εὐθηνείᾳ" (eutheneia) — a term implying a flourishing or well-ordered abundance.</note>. And as for the cause: for the reasoning of opinion <term>Opinion: *Doxa*, knowledge based on sensory appearance rather than intellectual truth</term> is more necessary, so that the things produced in the world are as they are, like a "tail" (as he says) <note>Likely a reference to the lowest or final part of a divine sequence.</note>. We are well-disposed toward it, even if it seems lacking. The cause is the governance of the world by God.

One must not know this as an untrue word, nor as a lack of order. Established from opposites, whenever the All exists... Let it be, then, if there is some cause who possesses it. Not even the One, then. For the first is itself as if in the Intellect. It is a thing of nature, which is why it is marveled at. If, therefore, both the cause and the Intellect are not lacking anything, then each thing within it exists through them.

In its well-being, each thing is again in that which is within it, whether it became a part of it after the spirit of Zeus <note>Zeus here symbolizes the World Soul or the Demiurgic Intellect acting upon the world.</note>. In this way, it is also itself an effect. Many things have come to be because of Zeus... but this too is nonetheless by necessity of the cause. Since many things are produced, this is how it stands with him. For the one in the All is not (as he says, it is not) about other things. If the All is the things that exist, and it is because each thing exists, it is not a single thing to grasp the whole people as it is being born, whenever it arises. When someone divides the parts, but concerning the power together with the cause, there is no prosperity. Before all things, all such things are about the whole world, each thing about itself.

Your substance says: "all things together." In it are all things. If one does not blame it, in it are the effects and the causes of themselves. Each thing exists, just as it has a cause for its becoming. Thus, the whole is the cause of the limit. It is self-sufficient in the causes of testimonies, and in them (as he says) are the effects. For if nothing is seen there, each thing is many things and sees all things there. Or it is the All, because each thing exists. This body is directed toward itself...

<column-break/>

...a true reason. Or rather, both are well. This also holds the Intellect in relation to God, lest the world not truly become its own. One must philosophize, because that which is in it is also the All. From this comes the Idea, the forms, and such things, even if it were a body. If the whole world is also in it, let them know to guard it with prosperity—like a depth—and to look upon it as it comes to be from itself.

He must be questioned according to likeness, for there is no unlikeness. Because the causes are in it, one expects to find them in the same place where knowledge is. If it is also the All, but becoming toward that which has become. This is created, by the intertwining with it. If it is also intelligible, it is released within it. Whether concerning gods: but he who wishes to bless, does so in obeying. When existence comes to be, you proceed from the things you see. For from each generated god, a portion is given back in the same place. For if being were common, the heaven would be so again.

Because that which stands above, through acting long ago, would not belong to it in the world. And it is not rather a matter of assigning cause. Since these things are well, this is so if indeed it is all things. A straight path again for all; it is fitting for the one who has grasped both to understand them. I shall pass it on, if there is a form for each, such as being seen, and that too. The causes are explained etiologically <term>Etiologically: explaining a thing by identifying its cause or origin</term> in each. For through the eye, these things are equal; and the divisions are all equal, if indeed the causes are in the reasons, by the cause that preserves nature.

Since the remainder of that which exists is a manifestation? Perhaps he would say that which concerns prosperity. If it is a cause, it is not according to this. And for this reason, he might wish it. But he who relies on opinion, necessarily so. In all things, they are great. If someone is especially a cause of prosperity and vigor. If it is itself. In them, if. If, therefore, love <term>Love: *Eros*, the driving desire for the Good or the Beautiful</term> follows each, so as to perceive. To be here is the cause of all things. For if indeed the Intellect is not itself the light of the divine and the cause, so also that which is before the Idea, as if they were in them. Since that last thing is the cause. If the Intellect itself is before that, it is addressed in the accusative, because to prosper is itself, and for this reason, it is ordered toward this world. The things within it are likely to be perceived. How should we speak, then, if by the power of perception, one perceives by nature? After it, the spirit. And it is right to blame this. For he who comes from the full becomes. And this cause also preceded it. But...

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the relationship between the Intelligible Man (the divine blueprint) and the sensible man (the human being we see). ...of each other, he is no longer man. Perhaps, because he needs nothing of this world for his own being, the things heard through him are nothing, insofar as they possess their own nature. We say that there must be an equivalent there <note>Plotinus frequently refers to the Intelligible realm, the world of divine Ideas, as "There," while the physical world is "Here."</note> for everything that appears here. In this way, we ask: what kind of thing is a <term>Form: *Eidos*, the eternal archetype or "blueprint" of a thing</term>, and what kind of thing is the <term>Soul: *Psyche*, the animating force that connects the divine Intellect to the physical world</term>? But indeed, it is a rational soul, or one upon which reason stands, and these <term>Substances: *Hypostases*, the fundamental levels of reality (The One, Intellect, Soul)</term> are the causes. This general reason belongs to him when there is both soul and life. Thus, such a life is a diminished version of the "what-ness" <note>The essential quality or "quiddity" of a being.</note>; it is not this thing instead of that. See it rather as something common. Or let it be made so: as having the power to become. Is it also in this way that being exists? But both are different from the whole. If they are equal, it is as if one took the Man from "there." But in what way does he mean this?

If someone says that the Man "there" must consist of the same things as the one "here," then each part would not exist according to itself; it seems to be especially for the sake of goodwill "here." <note>original: "εὐνοίας" (eunoias) — kindness or favorable disposition.</note> For then it would consist of reason, intellect, and form. But one must make Reason itself alone, as if taking it by itself. Or does it possess as much of the <term>Intellect: *Nous*, the realm of pure, intuitive thought</term> as is its own? Wisdom <term>Wisdom: *Phronesis*, practical or moral wisdom</term> defines each thing whenever the Intellect judges things here. It is both its own and as much as... or just so much. How could it be made into that very thing if reasons did not mediate? Is Reason itself, then, a living and rational being, or is it from both? One might call him a "social living being." <note>Plotinus is engaging with the Aristotelian definition of man as a "political/social animal."</note> It is either in these things or it was a living thing, instead of life and intellect within Being. Immediately, then, life comes from that source; its own life is not a necessity. Or the living being is equivalent to the rational in the soul. And you will give whatever forms of goodwill happen to be, or the soul would be the same. But the soul is more, whenever the powers are the soul, and the powers... for the power is not something peculiar to the soul. What prevents it, then, from being both? Or perhaps you place the soul within Being. For such activities do not belong to the Intellect. If the flesh does not happen...

G
</margin>
...to be the whole of what is manifested to him. Thus, it is by the same Reason. For every soul—so we said—does not have such or such qualities. I would wonder if such things were worthy of Reason; for he does not say they are such, but that they are the work of the soul. Are they then natures, or did the genus of living beings come to be, if indeed it is as a form?

...and knowing this very thing. If the Idea is the Soul, we would understand the Ideas "there"; if you see this, it is as if within the Intellect alone. Even the forms of God—are they not formative and causative? Or does the whole <term>Flock: *Agēle*, a Platonic metaphor for a group of souls following a divine leader</term> of souls not come from there? And existence too. Is not the whole "painting" <note>An analogy comparing the creation of the world to the art of painting, where the divine Reason is the artist.</note> within this? For it is necessary that Man and his Form exist again. Or perhaps "here" they are not as they are "there"; they stand apart in their powers. For it is clear that he makes all things. The cause of others is in the form. Let no one give a reason as if to a form. From which the form contains its own powers. Not even of its parts. For art requires their powers for itself. Or the powers are in nature. And yet, that which is not the greater of this is not its form. How can one not use it, since whoever is the All will cease these things? And what? Either not in matter, or as an addition. Or rather, by being himself with those things that have come to be, they are subject to him. The most likely living beings. Or rather, the subjects; but as if a surplus of them. Or it may be clear from such a thing. But also of themselves, as if they were molded out of nature. It would be clear by the "account of whiteness." <note>A logical example used to discuss how a quality (white) relates to its definition (the account/logos).</note> Because the form is rather that which is seen as ensouled. And so, is it thus for each? Or because the form is more "there," and proportionally so. For there, things are individual; wherefore each is specified by the mark within it. But sensible things are wandered by their own practice. Or they live thus as <term>Angels: *Angeloi*, messengers or lower divine beings (here used in a Neoplatonic sense)</term> concerning wisdom. Then, if the divided intellect is not with him, or if the opinion is toward the form in the soul. Does it have a reason for those things according to nature? Whatever it knows, these would be the powers in the soul from itself. But if the house, or such a soul, but not through these. Or the Reason is from a part, or by the reasons going forth. Because within him, before all those things from the source. Or rather, after these things, the multitude. Or upon the form. Let us place the whole flock. Or they become many to each other. The birth of the cause, or by the cause; but either in the intellect itself, or not, or in whoever is the form. Or according to the causes, rather in the soul. For these are like forms. And from the power separated from Reason. Or from the Reason from which it also has being. It is more cohesive if the living being exists. Or it is left that it is of all things. Do not quickly carve up the parts of the living being. And more so, how must Reason exist? Is it all life, or the remainder? Or even the thinking part; but life would not be so. Or how does it participate? It is itself in the whole. It is in each. Or this is more so. If they are beautiful, not even... but many things from below are similar to it. For if it belongs to her, they are splendors rather in opinion; for the things are...

### Column 1

...of God, we spoke of spirits <note>Original: *daimones*—in Neoplatonism, these are intermediary beings that bridge the gap between the divine and the earthly.</note> and of the plant. He is himself and of them; it is clear that he himself is concerned with this. But if a thing does not come from itself, that which does not possess the things concerning itself, even if he conceived of it. After that, he takes it in this way. We should not say that those spirits—from whom everything in them is preserved—possessed their nature from themselves, but that single-formed things <note>Things of a single essence or type.</note> arise through disease. For they can neither suffer, nor is there any form of a living creature within them. But he also possesses whatever is in the heavens.

It flows. But he did not innovate; he has what is generated; nature following nature. But from the beginning, he had those things, like the horse. It seemed, then, to be the form of a horse. But that nature exists there because of its relation to nature, but it comes from There <note>The Intelligible realm or World of Ideas.</note>; the horse will not exist among men afterwards. Since it possessed it, it is not there. But the horse there is non-rational <note>Original: *alogos*—literally "without Logos" or "without reason." Plotinus is grappling with how a "rational" divine mind can contain an "irrational" animal.</note>, when it follows that nature, as if in a body, or even makes the things of that realm more obscure. For when the <term>Intellect: *Nous*, the divine mind containing all eternal truths</term> thinks this, the Intellect truly thinks it. And it is not under the power of the things there, or even under the power of their own things.

What then? Will he not cease from his own being, or is it in the <term>Soul: *Psyche*, the animating force of the universe</term> alongside the form? But this is from everywhere. Concerning them, they are in their home. As for the differences of souls, and that which concerns the form, it is never a necessity that they themselves exist there. If indeed the things of the soul are in the Intellect—for it is not the more irrational part, the soul, and it does not smooth over the passions in the soul. For in the same Intellect, being is structured in this way. It is the same, after the horse; but one must not speak of them in this way. But also the forms of men, and this is either Intellect or the things related to them, through causes. And he produced the sequence and look at the things beside the same. They arrived in the Intellect. The <term>Reason: *Logos*, the organizing principle</term> just as in the things here, looks in this way. But it ceases even from there, or even the whole; that which is there is specific to that from which it comes, and it will not be the various types of making. And collectively, these sensible things <note>Things perceived by the five senses.</note> are such. He saw those things. But one must not think that the things there in the sensible world are the same.

They have another Reason there. Let them not be the same, but neither is that which is among the things there. The things in the sensible world, the defined sensible things, because they would not be in the sensible if they were produced there; for senses exist because the things are there. Or the knowledge of those things that perish from there, and the causes, and the causes of these things, he entirely neglects. But the things within themselves, such as the senses, are themselves from there, as if in a certain way. Therefore, in some way, each of the lives there is total, and how each of the things there reaches the souls. But it is not so that these things become a horse or any other living creature, as if it could become a cause in some way. And if, in some way, as in the intellectual horse and the things of it, to think "horse." Already even by the things under the Intellect, or to men, either there or in himself, or in some way of these. Not even in himself so that he might think the same thing. But he ceases as much as the Intellect has become.

<column-break/>

### Column 2

...horse, concerning his own transition. Since it is about that which comes to be through it, its generation is in a garment; these things would come from each of these, but not in the way a ship comes from a horse. That which they do again, it shall be from everything. It is because of this. They benefit her from this induction. But indeed, it does not cease even there. But it shall be divisible, and after it, we come to the other. But even the form there must be divided. Concerning <term>Substance: *Ousia*, the true essence or "being" of a thing</term>. The rational things, then, are thus. Of these very things, there are many, but by this path, there is nothing. What then of the same? Because there are not many, and this might be the case, not only is it well in this way, just as there, that which is below is higher; or rather, that which is from where, under the motion, toward which we remain in that which is itself. Upon the nature of trees.

By speaking of their things, having ceased to be, she is. Through which there is order in her. What then do they do, to themselves entirely, or until the things of those remain, not as much as is still in the passive part <note>The part of the soul or nature that is acted upon by external forces.</note>, but again it would cease for the lively part to be there. For one man even thought if there were anything of the same. The passions in them are displaced. Or rather: having come into the same. Yet it is a part of them. If at least, just as if it belongs to that one, so that being present it is even more; it exists, but he ceases. From each of those to the soul toward herself. Since it is from him, if he has that toward the souls. The Reason is these things there. But not even upon himself, however, as much as he alone might be who is in these things.

Why then does he speak of the genera of animals in some way as "irrational" <note>Plotinus uses *alogia* to describe the state of being without human-like reasoning.</note>, the opposition being as if in a body, or the "horse" to the rational, or if the "horse" is intellectual? For everything that is there comes from there. And if that from which the irrational comes is discovered along with how great it is. Concerning all these things and concerning these we might talk nonsense; nor is he himself who is in these things, or such a one as the Reason. And that which is in the "Always-Living" <note>A term for the eternal realm of Intellect.</note> becomes here, and something else. But it is possible to take all the members, because it is most irrational. So that it is no longer private. If indeed the discourse is about the Intellect? Why then is it placed so that the Intellect is also in the other? How does it differ in this way from the Intellect, so that it is in the other animals—the difference. And that was it. It is, in a way, in the other animals. Where, then, is the word? Why then would they not be rational? Not that they themselves become irrational. And of the intellectual, but many lives are like a motion from which, or the things of the Intellect, and they themselves participate in it. But they have a difference. Perhaps of "waking" <note>Plotinus often uses "waking" vs. "sleeping" or "dreaming" to describe levels of consciousness and reality.</note>. But how do we speak of the differences, if indeed they are there? The things concerning these were spoken.

<summary>Plotinus argues that every living creature, including "irrational" animals like horses and even plants, has an eternal, "intellectual" form in the divine Mind. He concludes that their apparent lack of reason on Earth is a result of their physical embodiment, whereas in the divine realm, they participate in the universal Intellect in a "waking" state.</summary>

### Column 1

How is it that God spoke? Therefore, concerning generated things <note>Things that are born or created in the physical world, as opposed to eternal things.</note>, such as the eternal gods, He wills not only their existence, but also their well-being. Thus, all living creatures exist through Him, both in their being and in their state of excellence. The cause is either Reason <note>Original: *Logos*—the formative principle that organizes the universe.</note> or Intellect. For if it is Reason or Intellect, then that which is created exists so that it may be, and may be well. But one might wonder, regarding the process of becoming alone, if it were only a living creature. The "First Living Being" <note>A Platonic concept of the ideal archetype of all life.</note> there, then, is the act of Thought which is to become, and it looks toward becoming. 

But where there is "making," it is impossible for the intelligible forms <note>Original: *noeta eide*—the perfect blueprints of things in the divine mind.</note> to be in the earth as they are in the senses; yet Thought itself is not impossible. For in order for a living creature to exist, Thought did not need to be; that Intellect had no need of the animal, just as matter has no need of the animal, though the sensible things belong to it. If these things are not merely organic tools, but the very essence of being within matter—for instance, if the Earth itself were to have a foundation—then all of it is within God. He is the cause of us. And if He existed before us, then all things are held in reverence, receiving whatever they possess from within God. If they were to say that the Forms did not exist through Him before they existed in reality, perhaps they would be right. For one must go toward that place and the living beings within God, so that the things here are not left abandoned. 

If the Forms are among the intelligibles, nothing would seem to stand apart, even if we grant the act of creation. For everything is there. But the cause is in that Being—the "First Living Being" within God—or the Forms exist prior to the things that are generated. For the living creature would not exist through that realm if it did not exist before us. Therefore, it is in God. If every living creature is ours through that realm, then it is a nature. But is it not also a living creature? If the Divine made the earth for plants and animals, and if they exist in Him, how could the intelligible versions not also exist? But they do not exist "next" to God <note>Meaning they are not separate from His essence.</note>. What is this reputation but something prior to accusation? Since the most beautiful parts of the living creature are in God, we say they are in God. And life, too—what is the cause of life there, if not Intellect? In the Cause, every cause stems from Him. Thus, everything in God exists as if in its intelligible cause. For that life is more divine. Each thing is, as one might say, a Reason. For even the things that come from the Whole do not exist without "the good." For if the Whole comes from that which is "Before the Whole," then it must be the cause of the Whole. The cause is also in "the good." For this cause is prior to sensible things, just as it is prior to the body. For if it possesses a body, such as things in a certain shape, the shape does not exist before the cause, nor is there a shape before the Form. And the things that exist through that Form are there. Nothing is by necessity. It is from itself. It is another kind of cause. It is therefore in God, or rather, it is the Better. If there is Reason in a living creature, it is there; but that which is not in the life of God—which is the Whole, or even prior to it—is not. If the whole is beautiful, then the Whole is truly indifferent. But it is not spoken of in this way. For it still seems to remember the nature of present things. Since if the things are in God, then all things are liv—

### Column 2

—ing things of God, He said. Before the Form, then, or because He does not seek things outside Himself. If it is not the finished "creations" that are sought, but whatever exists before them, then He is Himself those things that are prior. The things in Him that are prior to the [sensible] are prior to the Earth, and prior to the Sun. Because the whole—both the intelligible and the sensible—exists through Him. For if the Forms themselves are entirely in God, how could that which is prior to them not be? One might say—or if they do not say it, they might say—that even the things prior to them are in Him. Even if they are not the "Forms of God," they are among the intelligibles, because the Forms are in Him. 

But if, again, the things prior to them are prior to the Forms, then nothing of the Forms would be left out of Him. Yet if the things prior to them are prior to the Forms, they shall not exist [separately]. For everything that participates in a Form is subject to corruption <note>In Neoplatonism, physical things decay because they are only shadows of the eternal Forms.</note>. If this is so, Beauty and Good are in Him. There are things prior to the Forms, because of which the Forms exist, and they depend on Him. Since what is the same as God? And how does He create? If Forms are already in God, this is not the case. For what are the Forms to Him? This is because of that through which the Forms exist. If someone were to deny that there are Forms in God, or if they were to say they are prior to the Forms, he called them "Reason." 

But if this is what the Forms are, then the nature in God is such that even the intelligible things proceed from Him. The Forms themselves exist prior to Nature. The cause is in God. And it is not impossible to dispute in this way hereafter: before the separation of Reason, it is as if it possesses something that is in all things, even prior to the Forms. If this is so, then this "Maker" is the cause. If we say this, it is the nature of the rational. The most beautiful parts of the intelligible, even the thing before the rational, is a Form. If we set aside the form of a stone, or the thought of "whiteness" there, even the things that are reasoned out exist as the Form itself before the actual thing. This applies even to the living plant. 

We say that Nature is the craftsmanlike cause <note>Original: *demiourgos*—the 'worker' or 'artisan' who shapes the world.</note>, which is a cause that hints at the truth: the image of the limbs exists because of this, far before the actual animals. For if there is something like the "irrational" <note>Original: *alogia*—without reason; Plotinus is explaining how animals without human reason still have a "Reason-Principle" in God.</note> beyond the earth, it is earth unto itself. "God is a Man of Reason" <note>A metaphorical way of saying the Divine contains the blueprint of human rationality.</note> entering into matter and into the earth. If the things prior to the earth are there, and the things prior to nature are in God, it is as if they are in the Earth that is in God. It comes to be. There is that which is in God before the earth, but the "Earth" as a whole is in the sensible world. This [sensible version] is a stumbling block, but in the [Intelligible] is the Reason that makes it, both in shapes and in the soul. How is it prior to the stars? One must know all of this. If Man exists, and because of this all things exist—if all living creatures, such as Man, and the sensible world exist because of those—then the power here that creates life concerns all things, but also...

<meta>catchword: ...before all</meta>

<summary>Plotinus argues that everything in the physical world, from stars and earth to "irrational" animals and plants, exists first as a perfect "Reason-Principle" or Form within the Divine Intellect. He concludes that God does not look outside Himself to create, but rather contains the living archetypes of all existence within His own eternal thought.</summary>

<header>On the Seventh [Chapter] of Ennead VI</header>

<margin>Of the 6th Ennead</margin>
...of the fourth. Those things are fire, or rather, fire is there, and most especially fire as it exists in the Living Being <note>Original: *zōidion*—here referring to the Great Living Being or the Zodiac, the celestial archetype of life.</note>. Or how so? Because that which fire comes from is also there. The same reasoning applies to the others, such as earth and air. But if this is life, insofar as it is life, it is superior; for it does not merely "possess" life, but it *is* life itself, existing within the Living Being there. However, the Intellect there is not merely human intellect, but Intellect in its entirety. But if the Intellect there is human, how can it be life insofar as it is human? It is because whatever Intellect is, life is within it. There is no life without Intellect, and in that realm, the life belongs to Intellect; for there, Intellect and life are one. If Intellect is every living thing there, then Intellect there is the totality of life. What appears here is also there; for the "Living Being" <note>The archetype of the universe as a single biological/spiritual entity.</note> exists there. Since the essence of the earth is there, there is an "invisible earth," and likewise an essence of the sea, and all things that make up the total Living Being. There is also a sort of Intellect of the heavens there, or rather, the true Intellect and the true Heaven. For the Heaven there will not be left without a soul. Nor is everything there "heaven" in a physical sense, nor is it fire directly; rather, these things are vital and psychic, for the celestial things there are living. For it is not by "thinking" in our sense that the heaven there is what it is by nature, but by being a Living Being in a higher degree. If everything there is "heaven," it is said that this heaven is similar to ours, as if it possesses everything peculiar to living creatures within itself; yet not everything there is the Intellectual principle itself, nor is everything life or Intellect in the same way. For if it were only the Intellectual, would it not possess the rest? Rather, it possesses them, but they are "sensible" only to the act of Thought, such as the Heaven and the living creatures that exist there. Even the sensible things here are derived from those things. Thus, in that realm, the "intelligible" exists as something eternally becoming from itself; yet sensation there is not through flesh <note>Plotinus argues that "perception" in the divine realm is a direct, spiritual intuition, not dependent on physical organs like eyes or skin.</note> or through souls in a state of physical manifestation, nor is it found in sensory animals or sensory powers as we know them. Just as the primary vitalities exist in sensible things, and then there are the sensory powers derived from the principles there—not only existing there as they appear to us, for that appearance is a property of the soul here and its participation in the body. Furthermore, all these powers exist there. But we speak of many things here. Or are the senses here merely the powers of a human being in this world, whereas in that realm, the human being is not something "new" or separate? If it is also soul, it is because these things already were. Otherwise, there would be no living creature here. For fire, how is it "sensible" in an equal way and so very primary? Bodies and living creatures are there. And the body exists there, just as fire exists there, containing all things. It also possesses life, and it possesses Intellect insofar as it is a living creature, and all things that Intellect is to life, and all things a living creature is, and Intellect, and all things together. And if this is all life, it comes from a nature where everything there is as one. This is "all life," and the Intellect is that which acts through it. The parts there, which are one insofar as they are living creatures, are contained within this "all." Is it not then that the one who possesses these things there is the Living Being? And does it not think insofar as it is the whole? One must participate in it as an intelligible thing, so that it may also belong to the living creature and to themselves. Thus, all things are. And it is so: all things. This is "all life," insofar as all things are. And it is so: all things, insofar as they are the Living Being. But as for the Living Being, how is it that all...
<meta>catchword: all</meta>

<column-break/>

<margin>7</margin>
...all things. From where then do these inflows into this very thing come? Is it that this thing is of such a kind, coming from living beings, if not from its own specific parts? Or is it not all things? For there are, as it were, the "abidings" <note>Original: *monai*—a technical term for the state of being where a principle remains within itself while producing effects.</note> within it, and the lives around it; these belong to all things, and these "all-lives" are in the whole of Being. For Being is Life; or rather, it is not a single life in all things. For the "One" is not the first for all in that way, or "one" in the sense of being a single unit; rather, it is like one life that is all lives, yet it does not cease to be that one, the first principle there. Does it then come into being after the First? It is, in short, Being. It is also the powers. These are those powers. Because they are in it, all of them are within the whole of its immobility, and those that follow after it. If not all of them. Just as there are "strikes" <note>Perhaps referring to impressions or formative movements.</note> in the earth, so there is life in the All; and these are all things there again. Perhaps they are not "in" it more than the whole is after it. For in this way, the One is also all things; in its being, it does not have things from the outside, but things within itself. How can they be from the outside? Either they themselves are in it to all things; and if they are from the outside, are they outside to those things within it? Or, as many things as are in it, those are the same, and by its own nature again; but as for those outside, how so? Either they are the lives for all, which are all and eternal; such as those in the Living Being. But if there are things in the cosmos, these are from the things there. Or is not every thing in the cosmos a living being? For how could we hold this? Either not every body is ensouled, both that which is in it and that without. But everything is, if it is Being; and if it is Being, it participates in the nature there, even that which is from the outside. If it is in the cosmos, there are also things there that are not "living creatures" <note>Referring to inanimate objects like stones or elements.</note>. But there, everything is life and everything is Intellect and nothing is soulless; it is itself. Not like the things in the cosmos, which are many and of a single form there; and the things of the earth are there, and life is in all of them. There, the "forms" <note>Original: *eide*—the Platonic Ideas or Blueprints.</note> are in all things, or rather, are they those things already mentioned? Or just as the "antennae" <note>Original: *keraiai*—can also mean 'projections' or 'extremities'.</note> are here, they would not be more there; for it is the same thing, and everything is from that source. Or because fire is fire, and not something else. And this also is from there, along with all other things. Why then, is it rather always? Or is it the whole? Or is it simply that all things are perhaps equal, and then again that which is generated is itself and is the whole of what is generated. Which then is also there? Or there, the parts are equal to the whole, but not so in the cosmos. Nature there still "speaks." There are also living creatures, and everything in its full measure. But if Intellect itself is "sensible" <note>In the sense of having a higher form of perception.</note>, then so are the things in the cosmos. All things again, then, and here because they come from some of the things that exist. And he says that the things there are also here. Furthermore, it is so that all those things, or rather all these things here, are there. The things here have a composite nature, and they are in the Living Being. For if it is also in this way again from it and divided. Or because all things there are the "All." And again, the whole of Being is like the things that are one in it for all; like the things for all and for all. And for them to be the things for all, and all being all things for all, just as the things here for all are the things from there. And where the "for all" is instead of "from there"; the things for all and for all are the things for all, and there all things are for all and for all. For this is there; but the "for all and for all" here is not the same for all; but the things there are for all, such as the things for all, where "for all and for all" exists; or rather, not all things are equal.

Furthermore, the soul is here; it is necessary that it be among other things, yet as if proceeding from itself. And in the heavens, these things are immediate, for their nature is quite divided. In all things, having entered into it, it is not only each thing in a way itself, but undivided. It is itself, and that which proceeds from it is also there. And in the universe, it is everywhere, and in the universe, the whole is present. Looking upon it in the way it participates, it says that everything proceeds from that one. <margin>15</margin> And in the world, it is everywhere. Having been received, it is agreed that in the way it participates, it will be in the same "other" just as that one will be. # Ethics 6

life, nor is any of them the cause. For a person rejoices if they see their own good. And it is necessary that this [the good] be oneself, for that is what is good. If, then, it is true that each thing is a certain good, then in the act of living, to perceive is always desirable. This is because life is not a mere "thing," but the act of living is itself a kind of perception. <note>In the Aristotelian tradition, "life" is not a static object we possess, but the active process of sensing and knowing.</note> Consequently, to live and to perceive is always desirable, because it allows one to recognize oneself as a good. If, therefore, living and perceiving are the same thing and are desirable, then it is necessary that one also perceives their friend, for the friend is also something perceivable. 

In this way, one’s own sense of self is well-perceived. For friends differ in this regard, that they perceive both themselves and one another. And again, if the nature of happiness <term>eudaimonia: the state of flourishing or "living well"</term> is to know oneself, then to perceive a friend is to perceive life itself. To see another living is, in a sense, to see one’s own life. But one must truly perceive. What is said by all these thinkers—though they are not always grateful for the source—is that one’s own life is always preferred. It seems reasonable by nature to embrace oneself; if choosing another life is desirable, it is only because existence itself is necessary to that choice. To oneself, then, the self is the choice of the good. 

For if one is known to themselves, they are known as something good. There is a peace in any life that is chosen because of this self-knowledge, which leads to happiness. Since perception is directed toward the good, it might seem infinite, yet it must be limited. That which is naturally constitutive of us is the ability to walk within ourselves. For how could things exist alone? This is why it appears that the unjust man does not truly perceive himself. Friendships <term>philia: a broad term for friendship, ranging from family bonds to business partnerships and deep soul-mates</term>, however, are entirely based on perception. 

This differs from one’s own pleasures; in the case of the friend, there is an advocate. It is the returning of what has happened to its causes. Thus, things are given back to what is kin. Above all, a man rejoices in himself, or because of himself. First, it was intended for the soul to lead a person down, as it were, and to make them perceive. Because of this, the good is chosen when it is loved. Do they see this by nature? Further, just as there are states of indifference and luck, which some say mean one does not need to think, they are likely wrong. Perception belongs to this [the self], not to others. Whether one thinks with ambition or as a cause of something else—how do they make these things perceived? Either as something better than themselves, or as the offspring of the good, which is more desirable. Instead of mere perception, one knows the particulars of each thing by perception, yet maintains other things within themselves. Toward the community, neither life itself nor those things wished for oneself are chosen unless there is a choice to live with the beloved and to be happy alongside them. Since they are in the same state, they find moderation in pleasant things.

<meta>catchword: so that</meta>

<column-break/>

<margin>6</margin>
So that nothing shall be in vain, but friendships exist because of the good, while men [associate] because of pleasure or utility. But perhaps this is how things must be done, for people are accustomed to doing things not because they are "so," but because they are useful. So even if life is caused by nature, you would appear worse if you were led away by it. <note>original: "Ὅμηρόν" (Homer)</note> One might bring in Homer and speak against this. But they turn away from some of these things, while others do not exist. The cause of our choices is found in that which is within us—to receive the causes of life. Life itself, and the work of the hand regarding those specific things there [in the world], whether it be achieving a goal or being happy.

For example, to face danger through courage; without this, there is disorder, and without form, there is the destruction of holiness. But it is not for a fool to do this. Most things seem to gather around this point. For this reason, there will be dispute, and one might reasonably be at a loss. Why is this so, if the goods of none of these things existed only within themselves? It seems that life is chosen so that there might be a "carrying," but an irrational life [is not]. Therefore, the chance to taste something sustains us. For social interaction produces friendship. If choice is not irrational, and if pleasure exists apart from life, then life does not belong to everyone in the same way. But happiness does. The more these things are present, the greater the good. It is perhaps a matter of virtue and exists according to it. For whether life is such a "well-being," or its forms, virtue itself is not just for living, but for the abundance of the form of Reason. 

Things are taken away, but the Good itself is not. From that source, all good things come to be. For good lives are the offspring [of the source]. Or rather, life is life because of the source. While men use many things, they ask: "In exchange for what good is life?" There is also reasoning, through which the good exists. It belongs to Reason. Thus, life is a matter of judgment, based on everything we have, just as offspring and desire achieve the same end. Since what follows the good is influenced by the passions, existence in all these things is the cause of the good. This is where "living well" is most necessary. For it would be strange if someone lived without perception, or if wisdom were taken away and given to others.

How, then, is life the primary good? For if life were in him, and he still lived, it would be so. Rather, it is because life is an activity. Therefore, even the one who contemplates the image <note>Likely referring to the reflection of the higher world in the physical</note> rejoices along with his perception. And he would never taste the joy of himself without it. He chooses existence because of the Good. Life is good, and to live is to perceive. In their existence, in the act of perceiving, it is as if someone says: "Eat of these things." It seems that he possesses his own nature for the sake of this. It is a new thing, as Socrates said, to exist with perception. But when there is nothing of himself for himself, without the self, then living belongs to all things according to nature, together with perception, however it may appear to be, even when it is indistinguishable from the natural state.
