Things that are good exist by nature. For those things that exist by nature are truly natural, and they are not merely "other" but are good and worthy of choice <term>periaireta: things one would deliberately choose for their own sake</term>. Moreover, among all things, or rather among those many things pertaining to the self, one recognizes them because they are good. For through nothing else that comes to be has it become manifest. The Good is like a sensible sign <note>original: "tekmar aisthētikon"</note> in one's native city; it is because of this that it is also called just. For it is not yet clear to me. But it is not just anywhere in this way; it is a necessity that it is itself the Good. Or perhaps happiness <term>eudaimonia: a state of flourishing or well-being</term> consists in its very placement. For the things within that state, being of a divine nature, are good; for to the decent man <term>epieikēs: the equitable or "fair-minded" person who looks beyond the strict letter of the law</term>, that which comes from the higher realm is always his own, while other things come from himself. And goods are thus. For if the majority of things were to become such, then in this way it truly is good, and not that it is not. For long-appearing things seem to the spirit to be so, but the Good is not like that. And this very thing: he loves the Good because of itself. And that which is under it. For this is not to be; it is itself, or if it is not of itself. For they are preserved by being themselves. This is what has been built for me; and whatever is good for oneself, it happens to be of a similar kind. It is manifest that we call it good. He, however, for whom it is "the useful," says it becomes good; for she <note>Refers to the soul (psychē), which is feminine in Greek.</note> possesses the good itself, so that it becomes first to himself, and he who is above will speak well of it, demanding it and referring back to it. On the one hand, for the highest, because the Good itself is that which leads, the attainment of it is good; but it also always obeys more. The remaining things are subordinate, not existing for their own sake even if they exist for him; and he leads this based on what he possesses, which is most properly "the Good" because those things also flourish for him. 

What then is "Being," through which things exist? Being consists of calculations and analogy. But bodies, or the soul? In turn, the things that are. Animals likewise. For the soul, "to be" is to live. Or also those things that are her goods. If it is so, then this is also by nature in potentiality. Because each thing, being contemplated, creates something, and these are the properties of the Good. It exercises each one, while other things and the properties of it. Some things seek to flee. Others, then, seek them as goods. The base man <term>phaulos: the "common" or "morally careless" man</term> is more involved in this; but if in himself it is summed up and that it becomes natural in the grasping of it. He seeks this. So that, his choices can come into being according to himself. Or to be good for himself by becoming so. For it has a function. What then would "to live" be? Perhaps a certain life from oneself, assuming nothing else. If this were so, his good would be to himself, as if coming from himself. For "to be" is to be oneself. For from that which exists. From the remaining statement they exist as happy, or those for whom the good of each exists. When the wicked exists, there is all greed and the greatest injustices. But the good in the soul, or the act of being happy, comes from oneself; so that the remaining things also come to her, except for the living or existing happiness. Thus, for all, "to live" is what comes to be.

<column-break/>

That it is chance <term>tychē</term> is a matter of faith; it is most wondrous or praiseworthy that something better happens to someone by itself; it happens to live among the happy. Therefore, if there should be anything, it is beautiful to love it in another way. And if it should happen among many things, they are good because they exist by nature, and saying they are good if the majority are not according to nature. Because it is by nature, this is not the Good; rather, those things are more of an image, nor is it a matter of grace but the Good itself. Therefore, in the numbering of the audits of war <note>This likely refers to the "accountability" or "reckoning" (euthynai) of generals in a city-state.</note> they are well-regarded. Just as among the ancients, the families were not all together; but because of nature it does not happen in the fatherland when divided because of these things, and because of this itself—thus and especially so. Not every generation <term>genesis: becoming or birth</term> is evil, and the will is wise. How much more; but there is an honorable race and decent men within it. For one is a certain kind of being. If the individual thing should exist. Still nature was necessary; but that which is through the end <term>telos: the ultimate purpose or goal</term>. And such is she. Loving those things into which she entered. And she makes manifest the visible things. And those things through a little. For she is not—and this virtue is not entirely similar. For one must live in virtue. Through misanthropy <note>original: "misanthrōpias" — the hatred of humanity</note> as in hopes of the good it shall be; and that the child of a base man is sweet to all is not so. If indeed it is—because of him what sort of person the decent man is. For it is not power and glory, but if there shall be something it is not—for these works and the better ones are his, but the whole is the decent good. What then are the free things? The Good is more for him. And because of this we are persuaded. But because it is not good for itself, much more from which it is good for him, nor is this of him—but he possesses it. Moreover, all things of her, because the things according to nature are not the majority, from whence there is something good. But to her, it is good itself. And there it is lacking to him, or what he is, for he is a portion of the Good. And the blessed man <term>makarios: one who possesses a divine, unshakeable happiness</term> is both happy and for the rest he experiences it. Which is the Good. For he who seeks would not, if it were good for him, love it more. Let these things be the Good. So that he himself also tries the Good; and his things by nature, loving there the things under them. Therefore one must consider the principles <term>archai: the starting points or first causes</term>. If indeed there is some other principle, through which another is ordered by the senses, it is good for itself. Better than the intellect <note>original: "nou" — the Mind or Intellect</note> is that from which it was born. And the referral back to such a principle, if one might know it. And opinion by nature and through the Good. But by nature, whatever is always; so that it also becomes separate. If it is the end, etc. But they call it the Good because of itself. To have the Good is his own. For what one might call "expedient," of such things—it also comes to be towards him as being good. That it is. Let the Good be, how much or of what kind, not just "to live," which having towards it, is not equal nor does it come to be, etc.

<meta>This page transitions from the metaphysical discussion of the One and the Good (seen on page 241) to a specific ethical analysis of human agency. # Ethics, Book 3

This produces an anomaly. And that which is said from [point] 21, which we do not calculate truly, is worth seeking. We seek this: whether we do other things for its sake, or because of it? Or rather, toward what should one contemplate the Good? Or even if someone in the second <gloss>meaning the second book of the Ethics</gloss> did not mark this correctly. And we assign to each thing what is appropriate, especially that which possesses the Good. But as for things that are not like that, they are directed toward whatever may be willed. For we would not call it "Good" simply because it is willed in truth. For the will is no evil thing, or so it seems. Will <term>boulēsis: a rational wish or desire for an end, distinct from mere impulse</term> is like a movement or a certain disposition of desire. And desire itself. For it seems that the will is referred toward the human good. But if what is chosen is not truly [good], but is the apparent good <term>phainomenon agathon: something that seems good to an individual but may not be objectively good</term>. If this is so, there is also the Good; that which is willed by nature is chosen. But through the deception found in the many, pleasure—being what it is, but not the Good itself—appears to be the Good. Since it is loved, though it was not [truly] lovable. Pleasure creates the deception of the things mentioned. And this order. But the Good shall be everywhere, or rather it is thought to exist, or rather because only the Good—or as he said, fortunately—is pleasure. But that is the cause. In the soul, the Good is contemplated as being. This is without clear [evidence] immediately being established or lost. But virtue is not [one of] these. As for these things, there is something chosen and voluntary. If it pleases certain natures, so that children might appear—or rather these things happen for its sake, just as he says the cause is always the Good as nature, in those things where it will produce another. But before this, there seems to be a necessity toward the Good, and first something happens through pleasure. Because of this, because of necessity. Or according to the difficulties, if indeed pleasure is the Good. But by virtue—and it is well said—the same man is also blessed. But also such a person has a cause of the Good, he who speaks or knows something. For wickedness, when it enters, will desolate the senses, and then again. Or rather from misfortunes immediately. He would not remain, then, he who possessed the first things and was good. But to all those things produced through themselves, every virtue—for the good things are involuntary, while other painful things are dragged along, which he did not even declare as the beginning of his arguments. Then again, not because you are, not from some outside source to have the mother of the Good. Or because from those things toward the Good, this [virtue] results. So that not only itself, or because of others. Virtue, then, takes up each thing for itself. Because of the seeking itself. For it is not in turn in judgment, or this too, or every other virtue; if then it is thus, we correctly place the "being" and all other things. And again this, everything else.

<column-break/>

<margin>Will</margin> Having returned then to this point. Perhaps it is not even worth asking whether <gloss>in the second [book]</gloss> that which one wills is the Good or the apparent good. There are those who say that the "willed" was the Good. But if someone chooses incorrectly, it is not [truly] "willed." For if it is willed, it is also good. But that [wrong choice] was evil. If someone should say again that the apparent good is the "willed," then the "willed" will not be so by nature, but whatever seems [good] to each person. And different things seem [good] to different people. And if it is so, then opposites [would be good]. If these views do not please, one might say that the "willed" in an absolute sense and in truth is the Good, but to each individual it is the "apparent good." To the virtuous man <term>spoudaios: the serious or morally excellent person who serves as a model for others</term>, it is that which truly is [the Good]; to the base man, it is whatever happens to seem so. Just as in the case of bodies: to those in good health, healthy things are those which truly are such; but to the sickly, other things [seem healthy]—even bitter things, sweet things, hot things, and heavy things. It is similar regarding our dispositions. For the virtuous man judges each thing correctly, and in each case, the truth appears to him. For each disposition has its own particular beautiful and pleasant things. And the virtuous man differs most, perhaps, in seeing the truth in each thing, being as it were the "standard and measure" <note>original: "kanōn kai metron"</note>. But to the many, deception seems to occur because of pleasure. For it seems to be the Good, though it is not. They choose pleasure, then, as the Good, and they flee pain as an evil. Now, if virtue is concerned with passions and actions, and actions are among particulars, and particulars are voluntary <term>hekousia: actions performed with knowledge of the circumstances and the internal power to act</term>, then virtue would also be in our power. Likewise, vice as well. For in those things where acting is in our power, not acting is also in our power. And where "no" is, "yes" is also. So that if acting—when it is beautiful—is in our power, then not acting—when it is shameful—will also be in our power. And if not acting—when it is beautiful—is in our power, then acting—when it is shameful—will also be in our power. If, then, doing beautiful things and shameful things is in our power, and this was [the meaning of] being good or evil, then it is in our power to be decent or base. As for the saying that "no one is voluntarily wicked, nor involuntarily blessed," <note>This is a famous Socratic paradox. While Aristotle agrees no one is "unvoluntarily happy," he argues against the idea that wickedness is simply a result of ignorance.</note> the latter part seems false, the former true. For no one is blessed against their will, but wickedness is voluntary. Otherwise, one must dispute what has just been said, and one must not say that man is the principle and the father of his actions just as he is of his children. If these things are apparent, and we cannot trace them back to any other principles besides those within us—of which the principles themselves are in us—then the actions themselves are in our power and are voluntary. To these things, both the private actions of individuals and the actions of the legislators themselves seem to bear witness. For they punish and take vengeance on those who do wicked things—those who do not act by force or through ignorance for which they themselves are not the cause. But they honor those who do beautiful things, as if to encourage the latter and restrain the former. Yet, regarding things that are neither in our power nor voluntary, no one encourages us to do them—as there would be no point in being persuaded not to feel heat, or pain, or hunger, or any other such thing. For we will experience them nonetheless.

<summary>This page explores the Aristotelian concept of the will, arguing that virtue and vice are voluntary because they are within our power. It distinguishes between the true Good sought by the virtuous person and the "apparent good" (often mere pleasure) that deceives the many.</summary>

# Ennead 5.2

...lest they should lead themselves toward what is best for them, but rather, that which is, which is no longer being <note>Plotinus is discussing the paradox of the One: it is the source of all being but is itself "beyond being."</note>. God happens to be there. For if He were in the form of each thing; then all things [would be Him]. All things are under His productions, as I say. Nor again did being flow through the first Mind <term>Nous: The Divine Intellect, the first emanation from the One, containing all the Forms or Ideas</term> that we perceived, but perhaps through some discursive thought or a certain form, a certain life; and if we spoke of Him as such, then Being would already exist; for it possesses everything that is meant to be; which was necessary. Since alongside the discursive soul <term>psyche dianoetike: the part of the soul that reasons through logic and sequence, rather than immediate intuition</term>, which has form, it is the same as before; if indeed it is generated in a certain way and into a multitude. It is ridiculous to think it is like the earth. If it belongs to them, they possess the greater parts. The whole will be divided, created by or within the form as an image or a phantom of a ship, by measure.

Because this form is the Soul. So that here, the agreement will be separate, and that which is not again a plant. And thus the soul of philosophers shall be established without fear, nor is it any other vision, for with such a thing, the whole or another is in harmony. And by this again, it is like a shape to them. All is the same; and whatever is all; or new discursive thought, this "one" or the soul. For the other things follow. It is responsible again for all things. Or if all are one Reason <term>Logos: the formative principle or "blueprint" that organizes the material world</term> again in the soul, it will then remain among its divine kin. It would appear to be the same, and if not a vision, then life again. For if it even makes nature great, it is by and in the same. For if indeed the beauty in the whole is good, let them not suspect anything about it. Because in it and through it, as much as itself is thus; then it follows the wealth of it. In the discursive faculty, the best of beings is considered in nothing else but thought; the best is innate; if indeed it appeared to itself. But when again it permits another, or when it becomes persuaded, then it would be the producer that remains. For it is again and again infinite. Or it is already the whole. It will be concerning sense-perception; from what would happen if it seemed to separate. And to be again either all things or this itself. For not even the whole of life was as it was of old. It stands not as that which was generated. Or even in those who took these things. It will be the same life. For if again there is a generation. God is in all of them; the things that must be beautiful are various; for even the great is so. Again the beautiful itself, not looking with the eyes at these things. Truly beautiful. It would be hidden from these things if it were so. What again does it do; it must be of the parts; or even in this way, a shape. It sees with the discursive mind; or the whole to all again in this way, or even here; but again the thought was of old. Or under what forms;

<note>catchword: is seen</note>

<column-break/>

It is seen from that source. That which is adorned by form, but is now every form, having become a portion before being existed. Whether it is generated; it has been shaped by form and species; nor is it possible to depart, nor again will it be persuaded. Whence there is no fear of things in the realm of generation <term>genesis: the physical world of change, birth, and decay</term>, because it does not exist in the same way; all things indeed, are not thus; all things are, and not falling short of the magnitude itself; and whatever it may be; but it is a necessity, especially for these to exist. For if it is great, being in themselves; then the divine is all one. It is a monad <term>monas: a single, indivisible unit; the ultimate principle of unity</term>. The things before substance are greater, or to that extent. For it holds itself from itself most of all. But nothing of it, those things which are nothing of it, will be pushed back; it is substantiated by nothing, nowhere. By what is that which comes from it, if it is equal to it, nothing? It will be the same. Both shall be; and if all things, which were nothing of it, were not. So that it will be neglected; but the same things could not do others. One must not think of intellection <term>noein: the act of divine or pure intellectual perception</term> in this way. For thus, being without fear, there is neither shape nor form nor the choral dances. It generated and worked from the same things. But you learned that God is such; and if life shall be here again, it is as if being perfected. For it is not into these lives again. This world exists, and there shall be another. And it is beautiful because of that one; whence it is not [merely] beautiful. One must contemplate where that which generates the world is. For this world is not of every season, if it is anything beautiful, it is a great beauty. For it generates from itself and makes it more beautiful. That which is its own is rich in beauty. For it is not [merely] beautiful. What sort and what not. Or even the whole at the beginning, not being beautiful at all. Or the beginning. And much beauty. Every form. But that which is generated is itself formless; but another is something specific in form. Or if these are not said to be the whole, this is not form, by another. Or it claims it was necessary to be formless. But that which participates is beautiful, because form is a power <term>dynamis: potential or active power</term>. If indeed that which is beautiful is greater, it will become more perishable from form. But these are seen by the many; lest by holding to beautiful things, if one neglects the participation, it becomes beautiful. For that which is formless is a species and, or that which is away. Form again is perhaps taken away if it is every form. Such as that in the Reason, or having been destroyed by another to have a share. By the discursive faculty. But if they say they are not of one another. And in that way, just as a blue-eyed sight, or by the discursive mind; and yet all things are bright, such as one saw in this way, and would have, lest it be only form. Because these things are of a certain kind. And these things are such as to generate by necessity under that one.

<summary>This page discusses the emanation of the Soul and the material world from the Divine Intellect and the One, emphasizing how beauty and form are derived from a higher, formless source. Plotinus argues that the "Reason-Principles" (Logoi) organize the world, and that true beauty is found in participating in these divine forms rather than in mere material shapes.</summary>

# Ennead 5.2

...within itself, nor is that anything other than Justice. From where, then, does this arise? For that famous inquiry regarding Alcibiades <note>original: "ἀλκιβιάδου γὰρ ἡ ζήτησις". Plotinus refers to the Platonic dialogue *Alcibiades I*, which questions whether knowledge of justice is innate or learned from others.</note> asks whether he had it from another or from himself. If indeed it is within him, then there are other forms of life; man is desirable to himself. And as many things as might harm him [are avoided] because he pays attention to what is *there* <note>In Neoplatonism, "there" (ekei) always refers to the higher Intelligible realm of perfect Forms, while "here" (enthade) refers to our physical world.</note>. For he truly held the principles of those same things even here; for all things that are with Him have come to be here. Just as there is a certain wise man *there*, and especially the good; this is clear also from the nature of chance. Leaving these matters as they are, and the rest:

What then is it that comes from there? We must understand that it is known by one’s own [intellect]. You saw that nothing is outside of it. For it is not "that," but it is "in there"; from which all other things are derived. That Reason <term>Logos: The formative, rational principle that bridges the higher Intellect and the physical world.</term> shall exist if one looks toward that realm. It is the one of many.

If the things *there* exist (as is reasonable), then the things in the world exist by those same causes. Instead of being newly made, they have been there for a long time. The Soul itself has been doing the same things for a long time, but in different places; or rather, for all things, or for the majority of causes, which is why he speaks of a "cause in the world." For the Soul, there is a hearth <note>original: "ἑστία". A reference to the central, stabilizing fire of the cosmos.</note>, and she acts according to the riddle of Plato <note>Likely referring to Plato's *Timaeus* and the "moving image of eternity."</note> regarding motion and the causes of things in this realm, explaining why each exists. If the things *there* exist by their own nature, and not following a specific desire, then the things arising from it exist together. Let us place them under a shadow; hence not only those things, but even the things of our neighbors exist according to nature. Whenever, therefore, they are in time in this realm, it is because this belongs to their Essence. These things themselves are either the same or very close. But God says that each one is a unity, and something that has been generated, and will be again as they believe.

If, then, that which belongs to generated things has been generated, it has also been generated from *there*. The remainder shall exist in such a way as to follow that, but as it is *there*; it lets all things go except for [the essence]. It is as if we have known someone who drank a complex, varied wine <note>Plotinus uses the metaphor of "varied wine" to describe the Intellect—which is a single "drink" or essence that nevertheless contains a multitude of distinct "flavors" or Ideas.</note>. Each thing within it would be something sweet.

We shall say, then, that the matter of the wine is spoken of in this way. Or rather, it is here; that which exists by its own nature, analogous to the wine, is seen from itself as something participated in by the rest. Because he who watches sees a marvelous and blessed doctrine; the whole shall not be the same, but it shall be sweet, because he is a Painter. Regarding the shining of Beauty, it is clearly seen. It obtained, <insert>as if</insert> by law, not from someone else, but from itself. That which he said was seen in the world is the most true. This will appear as we said. But the nature of the one who contemplates must be considered <insert>indeed</insert>. For it possesses this very thing, which you might think is the heaven, since he looks into it; yet he looks not as if by the senses, but—

<meta>This page continues the metaphysical exploration of the Divine Mind (Nous) and how the human soul perceives the "Intelligible" realm. It follows the previous discussion of justice and innate knowledge, moving now into the specific mechanics of internal vision and the "ladder" of spiritual ascent.</meta>

# Ennead 5

<column-break/>

...was fashioned by a certain projection, and from there he saw, as if an image of gods, those who were running. And in this way, look at the man, or he will appear to himself, not as someone who brings or needs something from elsewhere. If he is given everything, then indeed—but to speak generally—he who is about to see, I tell you now that such a person is greater; not just for men but for others too. The sorrow having been silenced, all things become present again in him. He sees not what sort of thing it is, but he becomes that which he sees. Within himself already, the lover has become the beloved <note>original: "ἐρ' ωτων γενομένο' ἐρ' ώτων" - Plotinus frequently uses the language of Plato's *Symposium* to describe the soul's erotic longing for the Divine.</note>. We are driven by this, whether we perceive it or not. We do not know that it is not the external beauty that is appearing, but the beauty within. For the sea <note>Plotinus often uses the sea as a metaphor for the vastness of the Soul or the turbulence of the material world.</note> obeys, and it is as if one is in islands, receiving everything into oneself, far from the rest of the noise. 

For the sake of this, one belongs neither to himself nor to another, but to all. For he does not think of this or that within himself, but he belongs to the Beloved. Rather, he is no longer just "he," but has been transformed. He shall be written down as being Likened to the Mind <term>Nous: The Divine Mind or Intellect, the second hypostasis in Neoplatonism, which contains the perfect Forms of all things.</term>. Other things belong to him by Reason <term>Logos: The formative principle that translates the perfect Ideas of the Mind into the physical world.</term>. Remaining there, he is not even himself; for the water and the earth are left behind as he circles. There is that which you received under your own power; for this touch is not according to the flesh.

A silent drama of those things is performed; they speak of "studies" <note>original: "μαθήματα" - referring to the mathematical and philosophical disciplines required for the soul's ascent.</note> regarding the self. This self-learning exists through purification <note>original: "καθάρσει" - the process of stripping away material attachments to reveal the soul's true nature.</note> and through worldly order. Upon this are the ladders <note>original: "κλίμακας" - the *scala naturae* or spiritual ladder the soul climbs to return to the One.</note> that one must believe in. The journey is toward that place; they set out upon this through education. In this journey, one does not merely hear of it, but returns to his own part. I became a glory by living according to that change, looking back at what is there. This is simply the self. He gave this to us humans, near to him, so that we would not be diminished. There already is the totality, in my experiences. For they are spoken of as being within us. Nor is that one hidden, if he does not speak to us; being held above in himself, where there is no learning. We are spoken of in hushed tones, not as something inexpressible, nor do I say it to someone who does not see. Let us depart and be speechless, with the tongue, or with all our being.

<column-break/>

...but whenever—but if to know is to know the things outside—knowing is without, lest it be somewhere, this or that, in a light. We shall say it is nowhere; but consider him to be his own leader, if he carries himself. He alone is for himself; or he is not "somewhere," but he is in his own generation. But he is an image of himself; this generation is to be for himself. If this "knowing" were not the case, then he would know himself. Some do not even consider him and his own attributes as worthy of being in himself, or of motion; or they call him irrational. Some see these things; they shall stand there. But there is no need for him to belong to anyone, since we took his "Thinking" to be his own work. For it was not possible for "myself" to exist as his foundation. 

The substance of the Intelligible <note>original: "νοητοῦ" - the realm of pure Thought and Reality that exists before the physical world.</note> and the thinker is not according to itself; rather, Thinking is the Intelligible to the one who thinks. By what means is this thinking received by him? For if his "Being" were this, it would be his alone. Either "Thinking" is his being, or in some way it is his generation, whether he happens to think or not. If "Being" is something else of his, let him think. But if it is so, then it is not surely so. For they might say that knowledge is two things, yet it is of the same cause. Even if they say many things: if "being himself" is for himself, then being is also "the other," and whatever they see. If he exists by thinking, whatever was once generated might ask if Thinking is the thinker. To him, thinking is of thinking. 

What then would he be to himself if he sees himself to be these things? But if he agrees that these things are, and if they are those things which he thinks—if they are those things, they are his thinking. Either his Being is himself, or it is another. But if it is—I carry this in thinking, and knowing the Mind to be "just" is right. If that which has become does not have the same identity as the Intelligible, but comes from it, it will come to the Mind by that same path. Why then is he thinking in what he sees of his own? 

<margin>15.</margin>
For he who does not think is mindless <note>original: "ἀνόητος" - can mean both "unthinking" and "foolish."</note>. Since his nature is analogous, this precedes me: the unknown. To whom it is not necessary to be, because we think of that which comes from this as a lover, and he loosed his own and led himself, because they are not the same. Of those things, again, he knows himself; and if he is a lover of it, it is not "that" himself but "it." How then is he of himself? If it is clear what things are his, even these things would be as if painted upon them, as being what they are. But these things are what he sees there. I say: he is that which he thinks in himself. But if it is not of him, but if it is, yet not another thing for him; without those things which he is. We say these things are not surely of him, if someone says... but you have been ignorant that it belongs to him; but that it is for him. For truly...

# Ennead 6

The Good belongs to those who are deemed worthy, yet it is also something else. For the process of being persuaded comes to an end; those things that are kindled from the Good cease once they are known, so that their Form <term>Idea: The eternal, perfect blueprint or "Form" of a thing in the intelligible realm.</term> might better prevail. For it does not preserve the "is" of a thing if that thing becomes nothing to no one. And for this reason, it is again not easy to describe their nature. What is it to know? Or in what way will it compel us? Along with what is there, it is because of the Good—or is the grasp of it equal for all? Rather, it is through a participation in the Good, or a sacred honor. For the Good is also that which follows from them, such as their existing state, or that which exists in itself. And nothing comes from this except that it is Good; this is entirely Good for its own sake. But if not, it would not be the Good, but merely something useful to it. For the Good exists through itself. If, therefore, it exists by the fact of its becoming, then it is Good. But if Thought <term>Noesis: The activity of the Divine Mind (Nous); a direct, intuitive "seeing" of truth rather than step-by-step reasoning.</term> is its Good, or belongs to it as an attribute, it would set it apart. It is set apart both for itself and because of the Good. But if Thought were added to it, the thinking of the Good would be subordinate to it, yet it would still be directed toward its Good. If it depends on Thought, its Good comes from Thought, whether or not it originates from the Good; such is the nature of the thinking of the Intelligible, or even the Good itself, or the Good as the very earth. If it depends on sensation, it is necessary to accept that sensation is about the Good itself. But how is the kind of thing surrounding it not transformed? We find it within oneself, whether it exists or not. For this reason, one should not take it to be under this category, for the Good is the cause. Therefore, one must again understand every substance <term>Hypostasis: An individual reality or "substance," particularly the three primary levels of Plotinus's universe: The One, the Intellect, and the Soul.</term> to be taking itself back toward Thought. But that state of being comes from the Intelligible, as if it possessed its own shape. All these things have been written without any prior hypothesis, and they all seem consistent. It would come into being through a process of generation. Indeed, in this way, Thought—if it does not think of itself—must think of something else. Because of that which is known and caused, when it does not happen according to itself, it is not yet of itself. But again, Thought belongs to that which is upon it—perhaps then, it is divided toward this. And yet, this does not belong to Thought. If one sees that all of it will act, and participates in it, it makes it so; and they would come to be through Thought. But if all things are generated, and they do not all come toward us, then one would not see everything otherwise, nor would things in generation, or Thought itself, be reckoned by all. But if one holds everything in himself, as if by Thought or such an opinion, or a substance, or those things near it—what then? Because to be means to be brought into being by it; if they were to examine this truthfully, other things are posterior to it. If everything is in it, let it appear that Thought belongs to it. It has its own "but." It has reached a stopping point. And even sensible things say that each thing is something, or it is nothing. Thus, the Essence <term>Ousia: The true being or "substance" of a thing; in Neoplatonism, true Essence belongs only to the eternal realm, not the physical one.</term> of the Intelligible follows next; let it be of it.

<column-break/>

<margin>6</margin>
...to become a sweet and delightful pleasure. And this would be in accordance with what happens, though not for everything. This is naturally produced by the same cause, but looking toward what follows. Just as it is not infinite because of this, so too for the rest. For it is not only the Good of men, but also of the others. To the whole cosmos, everything is visible. For the Good is that which all things desire <note>original: "ὃ πάντες ἐφίενται" - This is a classic philosophical definition of "The Good" dating back to Aristotle's Ethics, which Plotinus here adapts to his mystical system.</note>. But this is not the same for all; in some it is because of the primary cause, in others because of the secondary. Therefore, one should not think that it is a single thing concerning the virtues, or think of Virtue <term>Arete: Excellence or "virtue." For if not—we saw the Good itself, yet the same thing is not always praised. For example, to be produced by nature makes it already easy to lead; then it is through practice. Either virtue is according to nature, or it is acquired. Just as it is, then: look at knowledge gained through practices, or through holy promises, but it is Good because of nature. For from where it was planted, it is already implanted in living beings. But the best of the kinds is implanted as Good. But if the Good is innate to it—if it is the best—it is not because of Matter <term>Hyle: The physical "stuff" of the universe, which Plotinus views as the lowest level of reality, often described as "non-being."</term>, but because of the cause itself. For that which is according to nature is, in the truest sense, the best. But indeed, it is clear that the Good is not to be used as if through great wickedness. If it is natural in this way, the Good becomes a substance. If it exists because of another, it is not Matter itself but that which is before it. If this is so, if it is not infinite, some of them will be the Good. If it touches upon a substance—first because of the Essence or the Activity <term>Energeia: The active expression or "work" of a thing's essence. The sun's light is the "activity" of the sun's essence.</term>. And if it has the greatest activity, or a lesser one. For indeed, the activities of men are either alone, or those directed toward the outside are for their own sake; it is not Essence, but it exists upon the matter of Essence, and this is the wonder of it. For one is not upon these things, but he touches upon the First itself, before his own grasp of it. Because the truth appeared to some to be the final thing. If it is not the cause that comes to be, it is either through Thought, or a Thought that has come to be. But if through Thought all becomes Thought, then Thought would not be from the Good, for it is inferior to it. Thus, it is not the Good. But one might call it the Good, since that which happens is also good. For this is already so. But it is directed toward the same as the Good, because of Thought. But if it is nonetheless Good, it is so by the contact with its very being. And because of having it, it comes from its providence for the Good. If...

...regarding universal **providence**, one considers it to be a kind of **good**. Therefore, it is necessary for the one who fountains forth good things to be good himself. <meta>This page continues the discussion of the Good and Providence, but shifts toward the Pythagorean influence on Plotinus, specifically the symbolic role of the number four (the Tetrad) in organizing virtue, the physical body, and the senses. And regarding the same principles and the same realities according to the ancient reckonings, when we speak of **the four** <note>original: "τοῦ δ'". In Pythagorean thought, the number four or 'Tetrad' represents the physical world, justice, and the foundational elements.</note>, this is also the case for those being educated. For **the four** is nothing other than what we call virtue and the practice toward a right opinion; therefore, the number four is studied by them both in relation to other things and within examples. Because of these things, it is also set apart in the external life for the sake of virtue and for the sake of **assimilation to him** <note>A reference to "likeness to God" (homoiosis theo), a central goal in Neoplatonism.</note>.

I ask this while saying: that they are asking in an orderly fashion. And while this small part is equal, the idea of the four is a remaining part of the one who asks. But in relation to the concept of virtue, the primary and sovereign things are found in the four. And generally, the whole of the universe is set apart by the number four; even if it is nowhere seen as an opinion, the four remains with these same things. You will seek, then, how the whole of the four exists after the numbers. He said regarding this that either we are not known, or every number is the four. And in this living being, he has known it thus: that the living being moves with straight motions through the **four senses** <note>Plotinus often groups the senses or faculties to align with numerical archetypes.</note>, for indeed the hands and the feet exist for nourishment and for walking—these are the four—and for other activities, serving them.

This belongs to the inquiry. Never of another kind. But in the questioning toward those who are withdrawn <margin>Note: Regarding the voice and body</margin> neither the voice nor the body exists. Which also serves the living being, and through which the voices and that which the voice signifies toward the activities, or by the body’s own nature, it distinguishes those things toward the sensible world. And if this is so, it would come from the object of prayer through the four, but he in turn thinks that the soul’s own nature would again become the soul. For how could the concept of this four be "possessed by a spirit" <note>original: "δαιμονίζεσθαι". This likely refers to a state of divine inspiration or being influenced by a lower spirit (daimon).</note> through itself, which is also the study of the four? It has been said that, in a sovereign sense, it is everything. For the whole is directed toward the things that come after the four, ending there. In this, they possess what is theirs. This is of those things that differ, as if in a sovereign sense because of the "one," and through the whole of it, the elements themselves. And again, the soul’s relation to this. An order through all things and a beginning, because one should not speak merely by the number. Because this exists in the underlying subject, every portion might again become something, yet it is painful because there is nothing toward which to speak. It must be heard that even those things toward which they look are nothing. But if virtue is entirely in the portion of **piety** <term>Eusebeia: Reverence or piety. In this context, it refers to the soul's proper orientation toward the Divine.</term> which is seen through the images, then in all such things they would speak.

It is necessary for those who seek. Such a thing from interpretation is not even of the higher senses of the four. Because he showed that the four is toward the **desiring part** <note>original: "ἐπιθυμητικὸν". The lowest part of the Platonic tripartite soul, associated with physical drives.</note>, just as when **spiritedness** <note>original: "θυμὸς". The middle part of the soul, associated with anger, courage, and pride.</note> is born, it holds the convictions. But the one who knows the methods of the body possesses these things. If, then, these things are so, there is a certain good fortune toward them. It is said sovereignly that if he does not receive it, it is contemplated within them. In those things where the soul is the four, if anyone uses the **imagination** <term>Phantasia: The faculty that creates or retains mental images; the bridge between sense-perception and intellect.</term> of the senses. Nor could it ever be. Therefore, **reason** <note>original: "λογισμὸς". The calculating or discursive faculty of the mind.</note> will especially exist, but toward the bad and the evil, it participated in the number four, even if it were not necessary. And the bodies are a living being of it. Everything...

### . Eusebius, Book 6 .

And through the prayers of the saints, just as they are for us as well. For they do not long for any of the earthly things, but rather to be released from their bonds <note>A common Neoplatonic and early Christian metaphor for the soul's liberation from the physical body.</note>. If indeed they still perceive God while living, as he says, like friends of God <unclear>under-knowing</unclear>. There shall be a certain voice for them even while living, just as Paul enigmatically suggests in other matters, and as he prophesies for that person. For so that we might not die the death, God dwelled among us. This is what Jeremiah spoke of, and the hand of the Lord was upon him; this is also what Paul suggests to his own followers. For the God who is present is not only ours, but is also death <note>The author suggests that God is present even in the experience of death, transforming it.</note>.

This is what Paul says, but one must realize this not regarding those on the outside, but regarding those among us who are the chosen and capable—or rather, God was ancient even to those on the outside, but specifically to our people. For among us, everything is fire. Thus, even fire is not out of place, but even God is His own light. And just as fire is not without fruit, His light is fire. The prophet indicated that He is both fire and sea; the fire that exists through Him is God. And in this they erred, for it was not so from of old. But it is their [the saints'] part to be released by Him. Regarding the resurrection, he does not speak toward this, he who is <unclear>not</unclear> <unclear>in these</unclear> His light. For the Holy God is the same one who is both fire and light. And because this fire is a burning heat, he declares this same Good to be a washing <note>A reference to the "laver of regeneration" or baptism, where the "fire" of the Spirit cleanses rather than destroys.</note>. And this is the loving-kindness of God, making a flame like a spirit, which He also says through Moses. For God Himself is a **consuming fire** <note>original: "πῦρ καταναλίσκον". A direct quote from Deuteronomy 4:24 and Hebrews 12:29.</note>, not only to those who are strangers to Him, but also to His own friends, through the Craftsmanship [of the Word], and through this also to the angels. He, in turn, loves through Himself. For He is our God. The Holy God is both fire and light.

through this
is the friendship 
of God.
</margin>

<unclear>Therefore</unclear> if God is light, how is His light not also fire? And how is His fire not also His light, so that He may dwell within the light? And how could God be the one whom the prophet called His throne? And what is the cause of the fire? There is a way in which it is a cleansing for sinners; for it is known in the divine light. And if the light is also fire...

---

So it may be. It is likely that he first saw Potamiaena <note>Potamiaena was a famous 3rd-century martyr in Alexandria known for her purity and courage.</note> by herself. Perhaps this too was seen by him: a sign appearing, something strange and unheard of, even twelve days after her martyrdom. He [the soldier] had long laughed at such things and cross-examined the man. Nevertheless, he was persuaded by the cause that appeared to him after her death, announcing the grace she found in prayers. If he held God Himself in such a way, he was capable of every counsel. He spoke, therefore, to the man. Even in the face of unbelief, so that those things and God might draw near. When she appeared to him, he said: "O man! If only you had some faith, O man." If one shares in God, they possess even more than these things. She said, at any rate, that she would come to him after the third day and place a crown upon him <note>Referring to the crown of martyrdom.</note>. This was indeed fulfilled. For it was known to all how the Soldier <note>This refers to Basilides, the Roman soldier who protected Potamiaena from the mob and was later converted by a vision of her.</note> acted, and how he <unclear>made</unclear> the unbelievers and the sinners believe after this life. When and how he would be accused by friends, because of this. And if he was to pass through a temptation, he learned the answers bit by bit. Even after this life. When, having hastened his arrival before the formal ceremony. He suggests that he bears Potamiaena with piety.

He was driven toward those who practiced idolatry, as we said, and again he went out among them. Now the rhythm has become full by her announcement, and he hastened the release. Explaining that which had passed. Or because he says he is persuaded by him, that he is called for a certain cause of God. This is the truth. Since he speaks again, as if regarding grace. Since, therefore, there is not such a hope after it, or if anyone should consider the habit and life. But again, in this way, it comes into experience. But also the hope of what follows, having been taught at some time. This is necessary, having received it when the Savior also came to us. Or even the names. Or even that it might happen. This was a friend even to the passions, and he held courage for the soldiers, and acted kindly toward him who does these things, essentially leading the passions from a lower state to the Good. But he did not suffer the present things, having dared to hasten through force. And as for death, which I lead most clearly, he is enlightened by fire, thus to all. He was about to receive the same as <unclear>Potamiaena</unclear>, or to receive the soul at the very end. Since even through the answers after these things he was seized, saying: "Never," not wishing to happen. Confessing. Being truthful in his thought. Which he himself will necessarily confirm.

<note>The header likely refers to Book 5 of Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics, which discusses justice, despite the manuscript's attribution to Plotinus.</note>

That which does not follow things in motion, such as the bodies of things being produced, we would set aside if we were to find such a thing. That which falls under perception, in the way that each thing is most related to itself; let us consider this for ourselves. One might be at a loss based on what has been said, whether the deficiency is according to the straight line in the primary sense, or if it is considered according to the opposite. For he says he did not make the straight line itself by the straight line, but by the tension outside of the straight line. And because of this, regarding **This** <note>referring to a specific philosophical premise</note>, when he thinks of the straight line as existing only by points, whether it is the combination of these two, or how it might seem to be the same. He says it seems to **This** by the identity of these things: since they appear to be their successes, it is clearly not hidden that through them there is another likeness of having been judged. These things seem to delight history because of it. And this is the opinion concerning character, just as it is for the rest. For the same manner belongs to those things under us. It delights the souls. The same manner of delight and of judgment exists, just as we were acting on our own behalf. Similarly also regarding the passions, of the things happening through them, because the softness belongs to the whole of it: but also those things that are not bodies having suffered, if they happen to them. And the **Good** exists, and the praise of the virtues of each. This, therefore, is the best. And for that which we wish, first **will** is shown to be **judgment**. For there is the **will**, through which we act. But the **will** has need of the good. And that which leads toward the virtues exists in the good. So that this man is not the **will** that is in need. For the same things happen to us alone. There are **wills** of the good, one not through attraction, and the other in the opinion of judging what kind of intellect to set toward what it wishes for us. The **will**, then, is a matter of dispute, but the **wish** is determined: and the matter is that souls are produced for everyone according to each, a pain of mine, but concerning the good, there are the agreements of all. For that which produces is the **Good**: and pain is related to perception. But the nature of the good is contemplative of them. And this is the cause of what is "up to us" <note>original: "ἐφ' ἡμῖν" (eph' hēmin) – a technical term for moral responsibility and free agency</note>. When we do not happen upon what we wish, we feel pain. Because of what exists. Many of them are not equally powerful concerning the same thing: more so. And habit is not first, but before the other demonstration, the opinion is what is "up to us." Just as the matter first held, so that for the rest, by judging the other things, it might at some time have the will in a state of fulfillment. For in this way it holds only with difficulty. Nevertheless, equal things were being wronged: but no one let us dare: their **Reason** <note>original: "Logos"</note> is clear. For they themselves by opinion as to how the equal things hold. It is—

<column-break/>

The judge is equal toward both sides, that is, he is the "equalizer." The judge wishes to be, as it were, **living justice** <note>original: "dikaion empsychon" – a famous Aristotelian definition of a judge as justice personified</note>. And people seek a judge as a "middle man," and some call them "mediators," believing that if they happen upon the middle, they will happen upon justice. Justice, therefore, is a certain middle point, if indeed the judge is as well. The judge restores equality. It is just as if a line were cut into unequal segments; that by which the greater segment exceeds the half, the judge takes away and adds to the smaller segment. When the whole is divided in two, then they say they have their own, when they receive the **equal**. The **equal** is the middle between the greater and the smaller according to **arithmetic proportion**. For this reason, it is also called "just" (*dikaion*), because it is "in two" (*dicha*), as if one were to say "split-justice" (*dichaion*), and the judge a "splitter" (*dichastēs*). <note>This is a Greek linguistic pun: the word for "just" sounds like the word for "in two halves."</note> For when from two equal things one part is taken from one and added to the other, the latter exceeds the former by these two parts; for if it were taken away but not added, it would exceed by only one. It exceeds the middle, therefore, by one, and the middle exceeds that from which it was taken by one. By this, therefore, we shall recognize what we must take away from the one who has more, and what to add to the one who has less: for that by which the half exceeds, this must be added to the one who has less, and that by which the half is exceeded by the greatest, this must be taken away from the greatest. Let lines AA, BB, and ΓΓ be equal to one another: <margin>judgment</margin> from AA let segment AE be taken away, and let segment ΓΔ be added to ΓΓ: so that the whole ΔΓΓ exceeds EA by ΔΓ and ΓΖ: and thus it exceeds BB by ΔΓ. <note>This describes a geometric proof used to illustrate corrective justice.</note> This also applies to the other arts: for they would be destroyed if the producer did not produce a certain quantity and quality, and the receiver did not receive this same quantity and quality. And this name, "justice," has also come to apply to the needs of exchange. <margin>judgment</margin>

It seems to some that **reciprocity** <note><term>reciprocity: original "antipeponthos"</term> – the idea of "suffering in return," or an eye for an eye.</note> is simply justice, just as the **Pythagoreans** said; for they defined justice simply as "suffering in return from another." But reciprocity fits neither distributive justice nor corrective justice. And yet they wish this to be what is called the **Justice of Rhadamanthus**: <note>Rhadamanthus was a mythical judge of the underworld known for his inflexible and stern "eye for an eye" justice.</note> "If a man should suffer what he did, right justice would be done." For in many cases it is in disagreement. For example, if an official struck someone, he ought not be struck back; and if someone struck an official, he ought not only be struck, but also be punished. Furthermore, there is a great difference between the voluntary and the involuntary. But in associations involving exchange, such justice—reciprocity—holds things together, but according to **proportion** and not according to equality. For by proportional reciprocity, the city remains together. For people seek either to return evil—and if they cannot, it seems to be slavery—or to return good. And if they do not, no exchange occurs. And it is by exchange that they stay together. Therefore, they place the **Temple of the Graces** <note>original: "Charites" – the goddesses of charm, beauty, and reciprocity</note> in a prominent place, so that there may be a return of favor: for this is the special characteristic of grace. For one must serve in return the one who was gracious, and in turn, that person must begin again by being gracious.

It also critiques the Pythagorean idea of simple reciprocity, arguing instead for a proportional exchange that maintains social bonds within a city.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's late-period explorations into the nature of the Absolute (The One), transitioning from Ennead VI.8—concerning the Will of the One—into Ennead VI.9, which discusses the Good or the One. ### Ennead VI, Tractate 8

By transferring terms from lesser things, it becomes impossible to apply proper names to those things found there <note>original: "εκείνοις" - a common Neoplatonic way to refer to the higher, divine realm</note>. For this reason, it is said to be the traditional way; and if hope appears greatest, it is called so by the tongue, but not by its own lot. For all things are under it, toward which they tend and into which they are unified; it is the principle of dissimilar things. And its nature is that in which all things reside, yet it is a principle without being shared, belonging only to itself. If it should come to be by its own power, through what words could you think of it? If someone were to force it into namelessness, it still remains for us a possession of our own, as if one were to speak of it toward itself. It is as if its being belongs to itself, saying that "it is somehow thus." But if someone should think otherwise, it has no need of itself; even if it were not chosen, or if it were not yet said of it. These things do not belong to it, for it is not even "above" itself. If one wished to speak of its nature, it would be these things. 

Nor would necessity be found in it, for to be "One" comes from itself. But unity in a plurality might be spoken of when it obeys, or when one says "it is somehow thus." It is as if its being belongs to itself. One should not think of it as being in the same state. For how could that which stops things from coming together <note>The translator interprets "παύων συνάρη" as the principle that prevents the collapse of distinctions while maintaining unity.</note> be the same? Even if it were more, so that it might come to be, how could it not be so already? As for faith and its departure, if faith itself is not through some chance—but if it is by chance, we would find it standing still. But so that it might receive itself, it is not for all to signify; for how could it be with understanding? What would one think? That its nature is entirely thus; it holds the summit, and this is the principle, because it is here. It possesses an activity in its nature; to its own identity belongs that which was not possible to be otherwise: to be the principle of all things. It must be so, and nothing more, a bedfellow of the good, and perhaps thus. Not in these things, but in those prior to what I call "him" in no place; as the theorems show. I say this not only because he does not "exist" in a limited way, but because he acts; for he is not other, but is. Within the One itself and in the principle is Necessity. He is the same, and **He is his own father** <note>original: "αυτός εαυτού πατέρα" - a radical claim by Plotinus that the One is the cause of its own existence and will.</note>. For this is equal to all; this, therefore, came to be. But it was not the first. For he was not for himself, but simply was. This "nothingness" is not even what must be; therefore, this is to be as the "well-being" <note>term: <term>εὖ εἶναι</term> (well-being) - the idea that the One is not just existence, but the highest form of Goodness.</term> is, because there could be no other. That which is "other" is only because he is the principle. But those things after him, being the same for themselves, appear as his own. For thus he is, and by this he is bound to himself, having such a connection; and in this way, he is Kingly.

<column-break/>

### Ennead VI, Tractate 9

When these things are so: if they should depart, destruction follows. For in this way, they have their being from the One; as if such a power were present, all these things are the One. It is as if this were the underlying substance; even if the One has not yet come to be, nor been brought about by that other—for it is not such, nor does it enjoy each thing. If it is thus, then the One exists in this way, and is constituted by itself. That which is constituted for each thing, the One is the constitution of each. Not indeed that it is the "one" of nature, but how could one say it? Even in a specific "one," if one applies the name. For where the One is constituted, the nature is different; but if one considers the nature of each thing in which it exists, that would not be the One. For it is not the case that if there is an essence <term>ουσία</term>, there is also the One. Even if someone is in a specific thing, this is not it, nor is it nature. Then, if one possesses the "each-ness" of each; but if not of all, it is the One itself. It is for all; for to all things, being is to be "one." And wherever it might be among us, it is the cause for those things there. So that one could not say it possesses the whole; for that which came together was that which is "there." So that the whole, or the One, just as in the many arguments where they come together, is not the same as the One, nor is the One those things. But the One, however it might be brought, is only thus: it is necessary to be entirely. But it is not a sign; for one might speak of the earth. Still, it exists: **all animals and plants** <note>Plotinus uses biological examples to show that when a living thing loses its internal unity, it ceases to be a living thing and becomes mere matter.</note>, which have their unity from a bond; and when the One departs, they are no longer the same, but the One is thus. So also is the body; just as with animals and plants, which have the One from a bond. And when the One departs, they are no longer the same, but the One is thus. So also is the body, even as the many. It is of a nature to be; even if it is not yet the One. These are the powers; of all of it, it does not enjoy it, for it holds it. One would not even say; so that it came together. For of the whole, to have it in no way came together so that it might be the One, in order that it might be itself, if indeed it is to be from the One. And by this, nature is; and the one in each thing. Thus it is constituted; and the many in the many. The One came together with the many and in it. If indeed it is itself that which came together; if indeed nature, the thing by nature, will preserve the connection of what came together. For it would not be taken away from the One without it, nor if it once came together, but the One is that thing, wherever it might not have been joined. If one should say it is taken away, it would be that which gives it "being"; for they are given to me to be. It is, therefore, in those things where it exists, and it comes to be in the whole—and indeed it—

<margin>308</margin>
—for it would be from the One. To that which is contained in each form <term>εἴδει</term>, how could it come to be even before the form? For it is not from a part; where is the whole, or in what does the whole come to be? Where the One is for all, it is not in the many. And by this, it will come to be for him. If indeed it should come to be for no one, unless it is to suffer.

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the nature of the One and Being, moving into the technical distinctions of how things participate in "Essence" and "Life." It follows the previous discussion on the namelessness of the first principle by examining the "Generas" or categories of reality.</meta>

# Ennead VI.11

The cause of its own stability would not exist if it did not stand there. As for its progression <note>original: "προκοπῆς"</note> at any time, every place is available to it. Since it exists outside of <term>Being</term> <note>original: "ὄντος" — In Neoplatonism, "Being" refers to the realm of eternal, unchanging reality, distinct from the physical world of change.</note>, and is not the self-same thing, there is nowhere it remains; nor is it standing still. But its parts do not remain, as they are not among the things that endure; they are carried through places where their being resides, due to their own lack of existence. Nothing among these things is produced within the same state, nor would it become the same as the <term>Essence</term> <note>original: "οὐσίας" — often translated as "Substance," it refers to the inner core or "what-ness" of a thing.</note> of each. Now, while that which is moved follows each path, it does so only as far as it can run along with that which is perishable. In its genus, however, it remains itself; thus, the same forms might come to be in it. 

Since it is from above—and even if it has gone astray—each thing, because it is from above, is nothing other than what it happens to be. From where are these things carried to this point? Because everything would be snatched away again by that which is joined to it. For it does not destroy so much as it has already composed. Since it is different, it has already been brought together where being truly exists. He says: every essence, and of these essences, that which belongs to that being, exists by being a part of it; it truly stands together. But when it is here, derived from that source, it is completed. We must, therefore, leave these things aside, as they are like <term>Matter</term> <note>original: "ὗλαι"</note> in relation to what truly exists. Either they already possess forms through themselves, or they are not the things of the souls. 

Furthermore, they exist as participants in those higher realms—either as things that do not live, or as things that are indeed living. The differences between them are the genera concerning life. For either these exist because none of the beings are life itself, or the life of living things is mortal. It is not "sovereign" <note>original: "κυρίαν"</note> in this way; for it is this very thing of theirs, or because this life consists in the difference between them. Some beings possess their essence in themselves and in life, as if having it in a certain genus through both reason and sensation. This does not persuade; for not even here does the power belong to it. Rather, as the opinion of it stands, it is not even "well," but this is the greater thing. Let it be so, then: either in this way, or the nature is the same. 

Either the "goods" are not within it, or the essence is the essence of essence. As for the rest, as most forms of life are, they are all naturally inclined to look toward it, or they all live by it. Some no longer do so, or they are utterly destroyed by the greater. Others exist so that they may have more mortal lives, being of another genus. This is because that <term>Activity</term> <note>original: "ἐνέργεια" — the active, manifesting power of a thing's nature.</note> extends to those things that come from it. All things are living. If, again, one looks toward heaven, its generation is more abundant from the point where the exit <note>original: "ἔκβασις" — the "procession" or flowing forth of reality from its source.</note> occurs. Therefore, while it stands within its own nature, it is entirely within the images of life. It does not possess the same <term>Hypostasis</term> <note>original: "ὑπόστασιν" — a technical term for a substantive, underlying reality or "level" of existence.</note> by participating in it, nor do we as humans. Because such a life is one, it is completed as self-evident, burning and sovereign.

<summary>Plotinus examines how the "procession" of life and essence from the higher realm into the physical world creates different grades of being, noting that earthly things are mere images of the stable, sovereign Activity found in the divine.</summary>
<keywords>Being, Essence, Life, Procession, Hypostasis, Form, Activity, Neoplatonism, Plotinus</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the investigation of the First Principle (the One or the Good). Having previously discussed how the One is beyond traditional "Being," Plotinus now addresses whether the Good exists by "chance" or "accident," arguing instead that its existence is identical to its own Will and Activity.</meta>

# Ennead VI

...with this, there is no imitation <note>original: "μίμημα"</note> as if it were moving toward the Good itself. This very thing was its purpose: to strive toward it and to reach it. But since the nature of the <term>Good</term> <note>For Plotinus, "The Good" is the ultimate source of everything, existing above even the level of Intellect or Being.</note> is without a prior foundation <note>original: "ἀνυπόστατος" — meaning it is not caused by or dependent on anything beneath it.</note>, and because that nature is what it is, it would be false to say that the Good "happened" to be without being what it is; for there was nothing else there for it to be. Moreover, it is not merely some specific thing, nor is it the case that the same attributes belong to it as to each individual thing. We must consider the <term>Reason-Principle</term> <note>original: "λόγον" (Logos) — the ordering principle of the universe.</note> both in life and in the Good itself—and this was according to its own desire. But in the <term>Hypostasis</term> <note>original: "ὑποστάσει" — here referring to the actualized reality or "standing under" of the Good's existence.</note> of the Good, it stands apart within its own permanence, extending through all that exists. For if its existence were dependent on something else, then its <term>Activity</term> <note>original: "ἐνέργεια" (energeia) — the active state of being.</note> would be in another and not in itself. Nor is its being a mere coincidence <note>original: "σύμπτωσις"</note>; rather, being an activity itself, it was its own work. It has been shown that to be the "Self" is itself an activity, and that it illuminates itself as far as it is touched. Therefore, the Good exists. And within it is its own "laying-hold" <note>original: "ἐπιβολή" — a direct, intuitive grasp or focus.</note> of what it truly is, not in the reality of another. Because this did not happen to it by some chance encounter, it is <term>Beyond-Essence</term> <note>original: "ὑπερούσιος" — a core Neoplatonic concept meaning the One is "above" or "beyond" the level of defined being or substance.</note> and is the very Hearth of reality. That which was discovered, that which shone forth from him, is more than himself; he was and is that very thing. Just as he shaped himself and ordered himself, so was he ordered. And if his <term>Choice</term> <note>original: "προαίρεσις" — the power of deliberate choice or will.</note> exists, it was his own, and it is the same as his actual reality. He was exactly as he ordered himself to be; therefore, he is not what he "happened" to be, but exactly what he himself willed.

<margin>16</margin> 16. How then could anyone say that his existence is not according to chance, if he is not his own reality and within himself, or if he is something else? For instance, let it be that he is "this." But if being itself is something else—for that which is "other" participates in it—then being is "above." Yet the <term>Soul</term> <note>original: "ψυχή"</note>, in the state where it was soul, was its own soul, and was never the soul of another. And it was the same with itself. But if the Good did not come into being from something else, then it was no longer the same as itself. To be what it was means it came into being not by chance. This means it is its own cause. If it were its own cause and its own reality, then these things, coming into being from a beginning, are because of it and through it; in this <term>Essence</term> <note>original: "οὐσίᾳ" — the true nature or substance of a thing.</note> these things exist, and it is what it is not by chance. It is the friend of the principle of being itself. In the whole of its being, the things around it exist because of it, and it exists as <insert>self-chosen</insert> <note>original: "αὐτοπροαίρετον" — a term emphasizing that the Good's existence is a result of its own sovereign will.</note>. It is the cause because of itself, and thus it is impossible for chance to appear. Since that principle is the Good, the will of that Good is within it, as it possesses the same Good as its own existence. The investigation is drawn toward what is "dear" <note>original: "φίλου" — implying a natural affinity or love for the Good.</note>. If, then, that which is desirable is of such a kind, it is the same as itself in the highest degree. I say "of such a kind" because its being is within its own reality; I say it is of such a kind because its being is through itself. And in the reality...

<summary>In this passage, Plotinus argues that the Good (the One) is not a product of chance or "luck," but is its own cause whose existence is identical to its own supreme Will and Activity. He concludes that the Good is "self-chosen," meaning its nature is exactly as it wills it to be, making it the sovereign source of all order.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's dense metaphysical argument from Ennead VI.8, specifically focusing on the self-directed nature of the First Principle (the One). It transitions from the idea that the Good is not a "coincidence" to the radical claim that the One is its own cause and its own "wakefulness."</meta>

### - To Be - 5 - H.

In this case, the maker is not something else; rather, the First Principle is solely itself. Furthermore, since it is the **Cause** solely by and through itself, its "Being" <note>original: "εἶναι" — the state of existence</note> cannot belong to another. This state of being "through itself" means not only that its **Substantial Existence** <note>original: "ὑπόστασις" (Hypostasis) — the foundational reality of a thing.</note> is not dependent on another, but that it is exactly as it is by its own nature. For it must be itself. It possesses nothing that is derived from the things for which it provides existence. Instead, it fulfills its own being as a self-contained source.

The **Reason-Principle** <note>original: "λόγος" (Logos) — the governing order or rational explanation.</note> clearly shows this, unless it perhaps misleads us. And yet, why does it say this? When we exclude the physical body from our considerations, we find the Cause and that which produces all things. Just as light acts according to a living reason, we certainly do not attribute the First Principle to mere chance. For we cannot say of "Light" that it does not possess its own being. Since it is Light, and no "father" <note>i.e., a prior generating cause</note> exists for it, its existence follows from what is within it. Again, that which is within its substantial existence is not something else; it is the core of its own design.

It is beneficial to remove any idea of external necessity. If the Cause is God himself, or the ancient principle that contains all things, then it proceeds from him in such a way that he is not "made," but is himself the very essence of it. He is the cause of the **Good**. If one subordinates him to a prior cause, one is mistaken; rather, through these arguments, we see he possesses his own **Substantial Existence** from himself. It is not an accident that happened to him; he is the source of all other things. Rather, his being "through himself" is seen in how he regards himself. How could he "carry" himself away from himself? For he does not carry himself like a burden; he is his own master in total tranquility. This is the Truth: he is his own substantial existence.

For his **Activity** <note>original: "ἐνέργεια" (Energeia) — the active, dynamic expression of a being's nature.</note> is permanent. If "God" is what he loves, and he is his own activity, then his activity is not for another, but is his own. His power and his cause coincide as one. If, therefore, he exists most especially around himself as he wills, and was not "made" by another, then he looks toward himself as if he had "created" himself <note>Plotinus uses "created himself" metaphorically here to describe the One's absolute self-determination.</note>. Thus, it is not **Chance** <note>original: "τύχη" (Tyche) — luck or random occurrence.</note> that rules him; he exists for himself. As you might say, nothing "happened" to him by accident.

The power of the Cause is this: they know it twice over. By his own goodness toward himself, he remained in himself, marveling at what he is—never falling into a mere "hypothesis" of existence. Whatever he does is not for another, but he is the single **Activity** centered upon himself. This is what it means "to be." He therefore "brought himself into existence," not by enduring his own activity as something that "became" <note>Plotinus distinguishes between "becoming" (changing) and "being" (eternal activity).</note>, but as his own activity—a state of **Wakefulness** <note>original: "ἐγρήγορσις" — a metaphor for the pure, conscious clarity of the One's existence.</note>. This is an eternal waking, a supreme state, and indeed, it is the essence of...
