It should not be permitted at all to think otherwise. Everything is a matter of **Providence** <note>original: "ἐπιμελές" — care or divine oversight</note>, both in a natural sense and prior to the individual parts of existence. These parts belong to themselves. Yet, the Principle gives to itself through the highest **Cause** <note>original: "αἰτία" — the reason or source of a thing's existence</note> found within us. For those things, it is the whole. For all things, there is a **Reason-Principle** <note>original: "λόγος" (Logos) — the governing rational order</note>, but for those, it is their own. They say that **Anger** <note>original: "θυμὸν" — spiritedness or wrath</note> properly comes into being. But the Whole is not entirely subject to it. Among those things that are fitting in the presence of God, the opposite occurs. But the opposite, as was said, exists before the unfolding of actual events. For it is not "as if," but rather as if **Theology** <note>original: "θεολογίαν" — the study or discourse of the divine</note> and the work of mourning proceeded from there; yet it is no such work. It is not in that manner. Perhaps it is because it is fitting, prior to the unfolding of events. For while some things belong to those who are well-pleased, so that there were certain trials for all, the Principle remains unaffected. Since they said, according to their own views, that it belongs to her. As for the things of the **Senses** <note>original: "αἰσθήσεων" — perceptions or sensory inputs</note>, which he names in these terms, we understand from this that we do not find the Cause within the nature of God alone. Within is that which is. The things of God also cause a stir. But it is not so; it happened as if **Chance** <note>original: "τύχη" (Tyche) — fortune or random coincidence</note> were acting. But it stands together with him. It is possible to speak of its "Being," just as one might support it with praises. This person seemed to have an **Inspiration** <note>original: "ἐπίπνοιαν" — a divine breathing-into or influence</note> from God in everything, as if certain things were preserved there; but this is contrary to the nature of belief. Since, therefore, speaking of it at all led to irrationality, he said this so that whatever might be. It is not even correct to speak of the things of **Memory**, nor that which is beside the end, according to the **Law**. These are obstacles. In the process of becoming, he forgave them. Just as he himself is of each of these. And every Reason-Principle, and with certainty. Among the more noble things, it exists. Indeed, it is upon these, for them. And the same things, which is his own, which is his whole, so that even before this it was either worthy, or in relation to other things, but also the things before. In the case of, let there be nothing, and the things within them. But all the ancient things are his. His own, which. Or again, even he himself in the prayers to whom he mixed. Or she did not act. But he spoke of him, as if by **Abstraction** <note>original: "ἀφαίρεσιν" (Aphaeresis) — the philosophical method of defining something by what it is NOT</note> of him who is already even less than the whole. The Reason-Principle is especially that of the Law over all things. To vote for them. Regarding the Cause. For in this way nothing is worthy, which he knew so as not to draw another in, which also through the whole, to agree or through the Cause before that in which it is. Thus we have both what has been born to God, and the whole being in its own, or he brought forth the Cause for them; **He begat himself and makes himself, and creates his own being as God** <note>This is a pivotal Neoplatonic claim: the First Principle is not "created" by another but is the self-actualizing source of its own existence.</note>, and as if establishing himself toward the kind of knowledge he held, to participate in this way, or the life and the things written or all of theirs. ### Ennead VI.

It is necessary for the same light to shine upon it as upon the righteous. This is the greatest power: when a thing does not depart from the **One** <note>original: "τοῦ ἑνός" (tou Henos) — the ultimate, simple source of all reality in Neoplatonism</note>. But the more steps it takes away, the less it remains among the things that truly are. Therefore, it is necessary that this life itself belongs to that which is being given life; and here too, it is according to something. But if, as he says, you take it away, you will divide it; and then it is no longer a living thing in the same way, though it might still live for a time. 

What then of the **Will**? It becomes a circle again within its subject. For it is most truly itself and comes from that which it becomes; or rather, it would become near to the One. But the nature of the circle will be split, and part of it was like a **triangle** or a **parallelogram**. If it is measured through the diameter, it is destroyed; for the union between the parts ceases. Yet those parts existed before; by receiving a union, which is the **Monad** <note>original: "ἡ ἐνάς" — the unit or state of being one</note>, and which is most characteristic of the **Soul** <note>original: "ψυχῆς" — the third hypostasis in Plotinus's system, which gives order to the physical world</note>, it brings them forward. If someone were to take this principle and apply it even to bodies: 

This is what we must consider—that which holds bodies together. I seek the greater principle, because he dreads their preservation. For it is not the body itself, as such, but the **participation** <note>original: "μετέχειν" — the Platonic concept where material things share in the qualities of higher Forms</note> in the One itself. 
For the soul ceases at this point; or rather, it ceases when it holds it together, or when it no longer receives this, but lets it go. But it was long ago necessary to say that all things come from it, from that which is thus the appearing one. For those things which arrive from the One, leaving it behind, do not even remain themselves. Do they live? They must differ greatly from those things they flee from. If their nature has departed from itself, and the "one" within it is in another, how can it exist? Because it was not undeniably the same, it would become their destruction; for it is not even possible for anything to exist if each thing were not this very thing according to its own **kind** <note>original: "γένος" — the class or category of a being</note>, itself by itself.

---

->On the Good, or the One.<-

<margin>⊕</margin>
All beings are beings by the **One**—both those that are primarily beings, and those that are in any way said to be among beings. For what would anything be, if it were not "one"? For if the "one" is taken away, those things no longer exist. An **army** <note>original: "στρατός"</note> is not an army unless it is one; nor is a **choir** <note>original: "χορός"</note> or a **herd** <note>original: "ἀγέλη"</note> unless they are one. Neither is a **house** or a **ship** a house or a ship unless they possess the "one"—for the house is a single entity, and so is the ship. If they lose this, they would no longer be a house or a ship. Therefore, even continuous magnitudes would not exist if the "one" were not in them. When they are cut, as much as they lose their unity, they lose their very being. And so it is with plants and animals, which are each a "one." If they should lose this through being <unclear>divided</unclear> into a multitude, they lose their nature and become other things. 

If indeed anything exists, it is because of unity. Even **health** <note>original: "ὑγεία" — the harmonious balance of the body</note> exists when the body comes together into one; and **beauty** <note>original: "κάλλος"</note> exists when the form of the One takes hold of the nature of the parts. And the **Soul** itself exists when it is unified into one and into a single agreement. Indeed, the Soul leads all things to the "one," crafting, molding, and shaping them into a <unclear>form</unclear>—

<summary>Plotinus argues that "The One" is the indispensable foundation of existence; without unity, complex entities like armies, houses, and living organisms lose their identity and cease to be. He concludes that the Soul's primary function is to impose this necessary unity upon the world.</summary>
<keywords>The One, unity, being, existence, Soul, health, beauty, Enneads, Neoplatonism, metaphysics</keywords>

And the <unclear>of the</unclear> these things, from the intellect from there so that of the reasonings. Or in his own things it provides. And to the reasonings a whole <unclear>certain</unclear> from the thought by reflection. But since it has been said, to say the thing, the things of the causes <unclear>for</unclear> of God and the generation; so that the things of the need of the intellect [are] the judgments. For the. But some <unclear>of the</unclear> those [who have] the sensible and numerical opinion, or they prepare it. For it is that <unclear>indeed</unclear> to move intellection, and the cause. Since the [love] of friends, according to which also the "well" to him. <unclear>In</unclear> all the analogy of nature. There is also the mathematical [disposition]. For either the mathematical <unclear>but</unclear> as the many [do]. For the one not being understood, because it fulfills the things in itself. But by the command <unclear>of the</unclear> somehow it proceeds. For example, the removal of the passions in the assumptions of them, which is <unclear>indeed</unclear> according to their law. In many, or at once the Father, the world is similar, and the one <unclear>in</unclear> all in the whole. The voice itself is similarly mixed; but not thus in the <unclear>certain</unclear> [other], in the lord the soul. And faith. Because some things [are] also the sensible things. <summary>This page discusses the hierarchy of being, contrasting the transient nature of sensory pleasure and "becoming" with the eternal stability of the Intellect and mathematical forms. It explores how the soul uses reason (Logos) and mathematical disciplines like geometry to ascend from physical sensations toward divine truths.</summary>

# • On the 5th Book •

<column-break/>

<page-num>259</page-num>
<header>· Euseb[ius] · 5 ·</header>

...so that there might be no need to punish even here, things for which the prophet of old lamented the turning away <note>original: "ἐκτροπὴν" — a turning away or deviation from the right path.</note>; naming them through many ways, even though nothing of it belongs to him. Regarding that which is his own, [it is] because he is not in anger, and the event is to be blamed; being known rather to the one who clearly demands it. The act of doing; and this man shall be near. That man is not among his own friends, as is the case with the jealousies among us; for with him the things of God are so; and especially there; for we have understood. And that which immediately and appropriately falls under [the scope] was urging. And upon this, to confess in the church <note>original: "ἐκκλησίᾳ" — referring here to the assembly of believers or the Christian Church.</note>; so that they might signal to one another their names; if any of them should be spoken of. Furthermore, nothing is received into it. It was necessary, both reasonably and safely, and properly to receive [instruction] from us. For the things we seek, having set them before us; let the one who seeks us not persuade us that he seeks before... saying that he is, or rather being persuaded. But rather the same things and they themselves in the same word, in the voice, and in faith; to both; for more so to all; and the religion <note>original: "θρησκεία" — religious practice or worship.</note> of the one who seeks. For he would not have said, or, that being and being signified in the search; lest more than some should be drawn away among those who are equal, and these things into the whole together; to be pious toward him; but not by seeking something before believing; it was necessary in another. Therefore, when it is not, if indeed he should seek; for before a man, the one who seeks goes to rest. It belongs to greater things to seek them; but as for myself; again that of me and of the second. For both are especially correct in their expressions. And the darkness received it <note>original: "ἔκλαβε δὲ τὸ σκότος" — an allusion to the Prologue of John's Gospel regarding light and darkness.</note>; but it remains hidden to each of them; for to which he gives the cause is not repentance, nor did anyone say "of me" and concerning the thing sought... for whenever having perceived his own things, they do not persuade with the voice; if when having known his things he tries them, or thus it is more. Not even contrary to these were they to impose anything; but as it might happen to the thing sought; so that you yourself may receive it, for it was necessary for him. In the earth. For speaking by hypotheses from those things lying within herself, all that is from me is pious. And all from the race; let his knowledge be spoken of. May it be well; it would be for all. And to the one who knows; there is one to whom it is, but to another it is not, he does not say; let us forget if not even the others there, but he saw from us under him, he has in the whole, through him no one will take advantage; nor will he receive greater things, as many as are from him; such a word, as neither toward itself, nor perhaps ever toward another to be placed. And if it is this or that, so that it may be, or to seek, and well; because of this he will also be chosen. For the others there is no cause, and therefore he will give of those things; for that which, or before...

<column-break/>

...having prevailed in power. Generally, the things chosen by them will first be chosen by them; for to choose them, even before the argument, was not at all easy; because they utter nothing, they give no handle immediately and before the argument. But when they also receive an answer, there will be faith <note>original: "πίστις" — faith or trust, often contrasted in philosophy with "episteme" or certain knowledge.</note>; and especially these people; for faith might come about through this, not by falling under any of the refutations, but by standing apart. In this way we also seek this, so that we may drive toward it, not so that we might stand apart; but since we hold back when we drive toward it; for where we drive, we depart. But that is not the "driving" which we seek. Nevertheless, let me be the one seeking. If there were someone even from me of the thing sought. And indeed, the one who seeks has both the voice and the voice of the thing sought; yet surely not that of the thing found; for he will not give faith to the thing sought, but to that of the search. And it shall be, even if someone gives before seeking, if indeed he has provided even before searching. But the seeker, lest he have nothing, then because of not having, and because of seeking, he took hold of it. For what do these people say to persuade us to be ignorant of what we know? Or where should we use stones, so that the departure might happen? But we seek so that, being knowing, we might be able to find; for just as our ignorance is not due to this person, so it is not toward knowing, which we ourselves have by receiving it. Therefore not even if they come to our search. Because they do not seek, this faith is the faith of all faith. For it is not because of coming to faith that they seek; but the clever ones themselves, by seeking, having piety, it might happen yet in another way; but I by faith and by knowledge; and especially by that of seeking. And let there be a forged voice of the seeker. For not knowing, he sets him at naught, so that their case might be sought, and he gives the seeking. For not even before the proclamation was the fabrication. But it must be sought, it will lead to the very beginning. For if none of these things exist, the search has been demonstrated. For thus also the same things; and for there is more. And light, and to be outside of the dialogue. Is not this also a word being given to him? To make the voices themselves toward the same end. For everyone who seeks finds <note>original: "πᾶς γὰρ ὁ ζητῶν εὑρίσκει" — a famous quotation from Matthew 7:8, used here to bridge Christian teaching with philosophical inquiry.</note>. Not faith; but also that of the others. For something might come to be called by another thought, but not by the necessity of being persuaded by that thought. So that even the seeking might happen upon the pious one himself. As it was likely, saying to the thing sought, he said that not even this man knew the faith hidden before their search. And having obtained the things of the pious by promise, we know; and otherwise we do not even know how to view the other hopes. Or perhaps because of this he may be persuaded, if indeed he has believed him, so that he may know also by faith; or perhaps seeking from there; for it is not for the sake of finding; for all seeking is for him by his faith.

<summary>This page explores the relationship between faith (pistis) and philosophical inquiry (zetesis), arguing that the act of seeking does not contradict piety but can lead to a deeper understanding of religious truth. It features early Christian terminology and scriptural allusions, likely excerpted from Eusebius or a similar Patristic source.</summary>

# • On the 6th Book •

<column-break/>

<page-num>259</page-num>
<header>· Eusebius · 6 ·</header>

What then? If these things are so, and everything is outside of our choice <note>original: "αἵρεσιν" — here meaning the power of personal choice or free will, rather than 'heresy.'</note>, one might say that we are moved by that [higher power] and suffer through it. Is it not then better to be among the things outside? But the passions are being removed; for it follows that they are bound. When and how does choice occur, if those things are removed, and placed in order toward that which is graceful? For even that which is desirable, if it is ever a cause, follows the patterns of our inner thoughts. For instance, perhaps it is for the protection of that [higher] part; it is our own, for we all hold ourselves to what is above. Having been accomplished, it belongs to another; it is a necessity of being; but the things of God are clear.

Should one wish to deviate from the law; or if in political matters, a necessity defined by nature would allow nothing outside of it. When even the same thing happens instead of one, a deed would occur; but as he says, it is from the outside, and yet (and that it seems to be). For you will say to them, they are filled with another, yet outside of him. But when there is no force, there is no excuse. These are independent substances <note>original: "ὑποστάσεις" — foundational realities or 'hypostases,' a key term in both Neoplatonism and Early Christian theology.</note>, and yet... This too might seem to be outside, enjoying good fortune as if through God. But he thought that nothing had come to each. It belongs to the soul when she looks upon the other, or if there is any dwelling given to her; but when we add to it, it is not within the power of all of us, such as a graceful nature, and outside, not even if it persuades.

For this reason, even the weakest man has faith in him, from whom he exists. Then we must observe. First, he himself is persuaded. Concerning what do we say of ourselves? Some things are carried along; but concerning what we say, and the things with them, let me work together in secret. For it is enough to be content with much. The habit is similar, or even greater. Such a soul would not be, but that which is through itself; or if one should think so. But if all things are like our own substance <note>original: "ὑποστᾶσα" — our individual existence or reality.</note>; there is the irrationality of children, which is equal to these. Or the earth, which is both the soul and the statue; but because it is in her power, or by the force of nature; it is from that very place; or something is in vain; it is to be handled. For if not in all these things, and to all such a man, as one might say to all, if it is by force; for the things are in that place. Or that which does not reign over those who are in such a state.

To us, this would especially belong; to the one called the Father of all <note>original: "πάντων πατέρα" — a common philosophical and theological title for the Creator.</note>; calling us toward the Father; and perhaps to define where the path of exit and enjoyment lies. And whether the soul remains, or no longer; the things concerning God are kept in silence. For with him, there is his own life; they are something more than his own. To think. Nothing at all was then necessary; or the disappearance of the law concerning that which was beautifully distributed. To exist, at least, for those for whom it is to experience well-being; and all things would not even be thought to perish; for the things in the... which might not happen to bodies, but a fear of abundance. As if, at least, not toward the things according to essence.</note>

<column-break/>

<page-num>260</page-num>

And according to causes; but these same things are not as they have been written; one should therefore record an opinion that is discordant with this because of its deficiency; namely, that he did not ordain the wicked causes. But the external things are divine; since we do not hope in God, and that all of us are given over through his anger; and that it is necessary to maintain an impulse, so that the whole might exist; not wickedly; but the things leading us toward God; for indeed, he is not the cause <note>A reference to the famous Platonic principle: "God is blameless" (theos anaitios).</note>; but the same thing might become better. God is indeed blameless. The world possesses all things; having been made by him; but when he shall establish it, but also insofar as it has the cause, from which the father might not lead it forth.

One might have an opinion, as a foundational solution; an opinion that is light; such as is likely, like the eternal things and the things concerning us, where there is the greatest order. But if these things being so should not perish; they are not chosen for the sake of need; but when living ceases, may he have no pains; a life that is truly pure <note>original: "ζωὴν καθαρὰν ὄντως" — a central goal in Plotinian ethics: the purification of the soul from material attachment.</note>; such as to be a doer of good for the soul; for because of her, all things exist. But toward the things according to essence; for that which is not from God, what is from herself and from what is written; and because of the cause. He does not say it is her, nor indeed does he say: it is upon him; but of a like nature to her; and that also; the things here after; and one must look upon them; for if anything is with difficulty; or the results; through a separate vision.

He says it is unchangeable; by nature, both herself and others; making him. For we were saying that he himself is the cause of each; furthermore, even if the particular causes relate to the universal concerning him; nor are they the last things; but if they are the last things; let none of these be in death; to the soul. Since therefore; for it is not seasonable that they should know the one <margin>and</margin> who fashions <note>original: "πλαστικὸν" — the plastic or formative power of the soul/nature.</note>; it is upon this; for the things of the cause are not otherwise; or even. It is then; for it has hope and honor; nor indeed; nor the whole; it is again; for it does not seem to me that anything exists after him; let it happen even according to what is most just; or for someone to come into being.

For the soul places all hope in herself, before God; for either, because he is; even if, because there is death; and if a cause should arise, how then is it a cause? The things established are from the gods, or not... only by observations; but because, because of him; not; for piously some; as many as there are entirely; both the being of the soul and what has been written in part; but in his excellence, one might say both are according to him. And if there are also two living beings again; if indeed they exist, and they are everything to all; I would not let go; toward the eternal things; and the choice of generation; and of that...

<summary>This page addresses the theological and philosophical tension between divine providence and human choice, arguing that God is blameless (anaitios) for evil and that the soul retains a degree of self-causation. It emphasizes that the soul's true nature is found in "pure life" and "good order," looking toward the eternal rather than the material.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the previous discussion in Eusebius to a section titled "Ethics 5." # • Ethics 5 •

...happening in between. Since it is by nature to be, for the sake of death, and the things of the multitude and concerning love; when therefore if death should occur, like a unit <note>original: "μονάδα" — a monad or single entity, central to Neoplatonic thought.</note> to the good, except by necessity; the love of the mortal, likewise also the last things. Indeed, the works within them are not again, but all these things at once; for from there they become again, as if from the unseen into this which is seen. Thus we were first beholding these things, if you wish, as in the soul. So that they are not, because these and the words, being before and again will be entangled because it is held thus; but they come from the same; and that is what we seek. Since it was thought true. Because it is as if a change of itself. Insofar as it is; being known to be correct. Not even from where, nothing else than towards falsehood; wherefore also it is truth. And to those for whom there is choice <note>original: "προαίρεσις" — deliberate choice or moral purpose, a key term in Aristotelian and Stoic ethics.</note> it commands them. So as to learn these things, that it seeks to be analogous to its own desire. For it is not the same thing peculiar to humans themselves. And the love of that which proceeded. And those as a measure, such as opinion being the causes, for whom they are voluntary. Both the arts and the sciences we are able to fulfill, so that the purpose for which we are able is for all. Since a part of them, by which we also subsist there. From where in the things before it was established as just, as to lesser things; and not even, the reason <note>original: "λόγος" — the guiding principle or rational structure of the universe.</note>. Some portion of light is a mind <note>original: "νοῦς" — the divine intellect or higher consciousness.</note>. Especially everything automatic. Correctly. First then let it be, especially to those by necessity in the same just, as in learning. Every human being the same; that not even when they find it nevertheless. So that, because death found it so that the living might have justice; it made a fellowship. <unclear>It is</unclear> and <unclear>and</unclear> as if <unclear>it is</unclear>...

<column-break/>

<margin>C:</margin>
These are will, action, and choice. First then, we seek what choice is. Wherefore let us go through it briefly. We say concerning choice that it is not anything other than what is peculiar to man, because no other animal has it, but the rational being alone. This is clear through the things we charged as necessary to choose. For opinion belongs to those who choose, as it is likely to happen, lest it escape the notice of any of the others, that it is not all their own; for it does not have it. The will is peculiar to choice, just as the very name "choice" <note>original: "προαιρέσεως" — the Greek word literally suggests "choosing one thing before another."</note> implies; and it is not in irrational beings, but in those who became such when they learned from a wise man, but not in the form and nature of each of them. But will appeared to differ from the voluntary and involuntary. For while every choice is voluntary, the voluntary <margin>10</margin> is not all choice. It is peculiar to reason, but the voluntary exists; and the voluntary exists even in animals. So that choice is in those things where it appears. Just as happiness is manifest; following its own nature. It is from what is one's own; wherefore there is a privation of it towards himself. So that also that which is "up to us" <note>original: "ἐφ' ἡμῖν" — the standard philosophical phrase for free will or agency.</note> is in the first discourses. Wherefore also the things from us in which we are placed by the laws; so that even then in the things after these; as if the things from them are not even up to us to come, those who have become masters of the things that are disordered in their power, or those owing penalties, except as many as towards these, let us speak with that one. Since then he spoke of those who are in harmony concerning choice, but also he himself (for it is clear) also chooses these things. Behold, perhaps again and through his own cause he has authority. For of those in whom the willing is moved. Just as then concerning opinion. For the voluntary things are those concerning which choice exists. For opinion is of false things. Since then how they choose, he gave a cause from God as they live with visions. It is clear that—to fail often, except also because of thinking by the hands of those who make the experienced try it, for this very thing himself. For I do not think it is a search, if these things are, or not... but as that it is a contract. Upon this everyone, when they choose something among animals. For choice cannot be, but also it makes a serious form <note>original: "ἰδέαν" — idea or essential form.</unclear> of him. It is lost, and all under others. Because every one again. And he said near that the soul is not thus by nature. But also towards faith, as also everything else. Sometimes as if not even if we praise it. So that nothing would be left, except to be the things towards him as a human. So also in the others, in which he is voluntary, he is the cause to himself. Nor in it nor to come of the things that, in that one happens the things happening towards himself. It harmonizes...

The text explores how choice relates to the soul's movement from the unseen realm to the visible world and its connection to divine justice and personal responsibility.</summary>
